## `Tensile/LoopModel/` — the θ schedule decoder, in full

This report documents every module, class, function and private helper in
`Tensile/LoopModel/`. It is written to be read with no other document open. Every concept the
source's comments allude to is defined here in full; every algorithm is given as pseudocode or as
a precise statement of what it computes; every design choice is accompanied by the alternatives
that were considered, the cost model, and concrete advice for extending it.

### 0. Orientation

#### 0.1 What this package is

`LoopModel` is a **schedule decoder**. It takes a description of a GEMM main loop — the tiling,
the staging path of each tensor, the loop order, the prefetch depths, the buffer counts — and
produces a **rolled loop-nest intermediate representation** (LoopIR) with:

* one instruction node per *op-class* (defined below), placed at the loop level where it belongs;
* symbolic rotation-buffer indices instead of physical register names;
* explicit software-pipeline structure (prologue peel, steady loop, drain peel, short-loop arm);
* a **named dependency** (`Await`) attached to each instruction that must wait for something;
* a machine-checked certificate that every hazard the schedule creates has been discharged.

It emits no assembly. Downstream, `Tensile/Lowering/loopir_to_gir.py` converts LoopIR into GIR (an
SSA/CFG form), GIR passes assign physical registers, memory tokens, fences and pointer swaps, and
`gir_to_rocisa` finally emits gfx1250 instructions. `LoopModel` is the *front half* of that
pipeline: it decides **what happens when**, and deliberately knows nothing about addresses.

#### 0.2 The three-layer split, and why it matters for reading the code

| Layer | Modules | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Core** | `ir.py`, `theta.py`, `geometry.py`, `latalg.py`, `sizing.py`, `placement.py`, `sigma_c.py`, `ledger.py`, `emit.py`, `validate.py`, `decoder.py` | No TensileLite `Solution` **key** is read, and no target instruction is named in a **decision**. A generic async-copy + compute + completion-counter machine. The exceptions that do exist are catalogued in 0.2.1 and are all inert. |
| **Renderer** | `render.py` | The **printing** exemption: it prints `tdm` / `ds_read` / `vmem_ld` / `vgpr` / `wmma` because the dump is read next to real gfx1250 assembly. Its module docstring says so explicitly. |
| **Addon** | `translate.py`, `bridge.py` | The **only** place TensileLite `Solution` keys are *read*. `translate.py` maps a parameter dict onto the core's vocabulary; `bridge.py` maps a real `Solution` dict onto that parameter dict. Nothing in the core imports either. |

##### 0.2.1 The rule stated exactly, and the four places the core does not meet the naive version

An earlier revision of this report — and of `translate.py`'s own docstring — stated the rule as
"a grep for `MIWaveTile`, `DepthU`, `PrefetchLocalRead` in the core returns nothing", and offered
that grep as the whole enforcement mechanism. **That claim is false and is retracted here.** Run
today over `LoopModel/*.py` it returns `bridge.py geometry.py placement.py translate.py`, and
widening it to `DepthU` adds `theta.py` and `emit.py`. Nothing about the design changed; the claim
was simply never re-checked after the measurement comments were written. What is actually true
splits into four cases, and only the first two are the layering rule:

1. **No core module reads a `Solution` key.** This is the real invariant and it holds: no
   subscript, `.get`, or `getattr` anywhere in the eleven core modules names a TensileLite
   parameter. The core's whole input is a `Theta` and a `DepthMap`. Verify it with
   `grep -nE '\["(MIWaveTile|DepthU|PrefetchLocalRead|PrefetchGlobalRead|TDMSplit[AB]?|MXBlock[AB]?|ScheduleIterAlg|LoopOrder|VgprPartition)"\]' LoopModel/*.py`, which returns only
   `bridge.py` and `translate.py`.
2. **No core decision branches on a target instruction name.** Also true. The core's dispatch
   vocabulary is `Space`, `Counter`, `HOP_ROLE` and the obligation kinds — all closed enumerations
   defined in `ir.py` and `theta.py` (sections 3.2, 3.9, 4.3.1).
3. **Parameter names appear in core *comments*, 28 times, most of them inside `MEASURED`
   provenance notes.** `placement.py` has twelve (`MIWaveTile`, `MIWaveGroup`, `TDMSplitA/B`,
   `PrefetchLocalRead`, `VW`, `PGR1/PLR1`, `MXBlock`, `MatrixInstK`, `DepthU`), `theta.py` seven,
   `emit.py` six, `geometry.py` two, `ledger.py` one. Three of those are not provenance notes and
   should be named: `geometry.py` carries no `MEASURED` marker at all — its two mentions sit in
   `quantum_axes`'s docstring as a worked illustration of the innermost-first rule — and
   `ledger.py:184`'s `PGR2` is an inline explanation of the `S_shared = δ` case. The remainder each
   record *which real kernel
   configuration a defect was measured on* — for example `placement.py:readahead_reach`'s "MEASURED
   2026-08-21 — bf16 NT KMN MI[16,16,32] MIWaveTile[2,2] DU64 (n_s=2) PGR2 SIA4". These are
   deliberate and should **not** be purged: a measurement with no configuration attached is not
   reproducible, and the alternative — restating the configuration in the core's own vocabulary —
   would make the note unmatchable against the YAML that produced it. They are inert: no code
   reads them.
4. **Four target-flavoured *strings and identifiers* survive in core code.** These are real, small,
   and worth knowing about:
   * `geometry.py:wmma_grid` — the function name says `wmma`. It computes the compute-atom grid
     `(m_tiles, n_tiles, k_tiles)` for one reduction chunk and contains no instruction knowledge;
     the neutral name would be `atom_grid`. `sizing.py:mma_shape` is its only caller.
   * `theta.py:Hop.__post_init__` writes the literal `"tdm"` as the inferred `kind` for a
     global→shared hop, and `Hop.is_bulk` tests `kind == "tdm"`. This one **is** load-bearing —
     `is_bulk` gates presence (section 4.4.3) — so the string is a decision input. The neutral
     spelling is `"bulk"`; the rename is mechanical (two writes, one comparison, plus
     `render.py`'s verb table, which is exempt anyway).
   * `ledger.py` and `emit.py` write `"wmma"` as the *role* half of an `Endpoint` and of a
     `_site_awaits` key. It is compared only against itself, so it is a private tag whose spelling
     leaked; `"compute"` would do.
   * `validate.py:_unbound_placement_refs`'s error text falls back to `"wmma"` when an op carries
     no token list, and two of its nine property messages say `wmma`. Diagnostics only.

   None of the four changes a scheduling result, and all four are cheap to rename. **This paragraph
   is the whole record of them** — they are stated here rather than fixed silently because the
   `"tdm"` one is not purely cosmetic: `Hop.kind` crosses into the GIR lowering, which pattern-matches
   the same literal, so a rename is a two-package change and wants to be done deliberately. Ranked
   for a future cleanup: `wmma_grid` → `atom_grid` (pure rename, one caller); the `"wmma"` role tags
   in `ledger.py` and `emit.py` → `"compute"` (compared only against themselves); `validate.py`'s
   diagnostic strings (text only); and `"tdm"` → `"bulk"` last, with the downstream match updated in
   the same commit.

**The enforcement mechanism, corrected.** The grep that means something is the one in case 1 —
`Solution` **subscripts**, not bare identifiers — plus a review rule that any new occurrence of a
parameter name in a core module must sit inside a `MEASURED`/`#NNN` provenance comment. A bare
identifier grep cannot distinguish a provenance note from a violation, which is exactly why the
old claim drifted false without anyone noticing.

#### 0.3 Reading the source comments

The source docstrings are unusually long and carry three kinds of shorthand that are *not* explained
in the tree:

1. **Section markers** written with a section sign followed by a dotted number — the ones that
   occur are `2.1`, `2.2`, `2.4`, `2.5`, `2.6`, `2.7`, `2.8`, `2.9`, `3.3`, `3.6`, `4.1`, `4.3`,
   `4.4`, `4.6`, `5.1`, `5.2`, `5.3`, `5.3.1`, `5.3.2`, `5.4`, `5.5`, `5.6`, `6.1`, `6.2`, `7` and
   `7.1` — and **lemma numbers**
   (Lemma 1, Lemma 3b, Lemma 3d, Proposition 7, Theorem 6, Definition 1). These point into a design
   note that lives outside `Tensile/` and is not shipped with it.
2. **Task numbers** written `#NNN` (e.g. `#212`, `#245`, `#274`). These are the project's own issue
   tracker; section 20's known-gaps subsections reproduce the ones that are still open, with what
   each one blocks.
3. **Author questions** written `Qnn` — `placement.py:PeelDepths`'s `deferrals` field says "Author
   question Q29",
   `emit.py:_check_peel_is_emittable` says "QUESTIONS_FOR_AUTHOR Q29, ANSWERED", and
   `translate.py:_canonical_ord` refers to "Q34". These are numbered entries in a running list of
   questions put to the author of the design note; the list is not in the tree either. **You do not
   need it.** The three that appear in the shipped source are decoded in full here, once:
   * **Q29 — may a level carry a retime offset at a level *outer* to the op-class's own home
     level?** Answered yes, and it is an ordinary non-negative entry of the retime matrix, not a
     special case; but it *relocates* instances across a loop back edge rather than deepening a
     peel, and this decoder refuses to emit it. Section 9.6 gives the concept, the record, the
     three conditions and what lifting the refusal requires.
   * **Q33 — when a free-axis sibling of the reduction chunk sits *outer* to it, does a register
     group still get a read-ahead?** Answered no: the group leaves the reload traversal, so its
     derived depth `dr_g` is 0. Section 7.10 gives the veto in full, with the measurement.
   * **Q34 — a six-letter loop-order word that reorders only part of the traversal.** The open
     half is whether "reorders the whole tree" and "reorders 12 of 96 instances" are the same
     move or two; section 16.5 documents the canonicalisation that sidesteps the question today.

**Nothing in this report depends on that external note or on that question list.** The table below
is a decoder ring so that a reader of the source can translate its shorthand into the concepts
defined in this report — every claim is inlined, so no lookup is required.

**A collision worth naming before the table.** The source's markers and this report's own sections

* A source marker is always written **without** the section sign and introduced as such — the left

| Definition 1 | The depth map is indexed by the *placement*, not by the operand — a region-split tile is two placements of one operand. | §4.10, §4.10.1 |

#### 0.6 Citation convention

Source locations in this report are written `file.py:symbol` — never `file.py:line`. This package
churns hundreds of lines per working session (four modules were touched on the same day this report
was written), so line anchors rot within a day while symbol names are stable and greppable.

Cross-references *inside* this report are written `§N`, `§N.M` or, in running prose, "section N.M".
As 0.3 sets out, a `§`-number in this report's own text always names a section of this report; the
source's markers, which are spelled the same way in the source, are written here without the sign
and introduced as source markers.

---

### 1. The vocabulary

Everything below is defined here; none of it requires outside reading. The names match the
identifiers used in the source so the two can be read together.

#### 1.1 The schedule point

A **schedule point** (the source calls it *theta*, spelled `θ` in comments and `Theta` in code) is
a seven-part description of one main-loop schedule:

```
theta = (tile, path, ord, off, S, rho, Phi)
```

* **`tile`** — the set of traversal axes and how they were split. Splitting `DepthU` into an outer
  chunk axis and an inner substep axis is a `tile` choice; so is cutting a macro-tile into
  storage-disjoint *regions*; so is partitioning a register fragment into reuse *groups*.
* **`path`** — for each tensor, the list of hops its data takes (`global → shared → register`, or
  the one-hop `global → register` direct-to-register form).
* **`ord`** — the outer-to-inner permutation of the traversal axes. This is `Theta.ord`, a list of
  `Mode` objects.
* **`off`** — the *retime matrix*: how many iterations of a given level an op-class runs **ahead**
  of the consumer it feeds. Stored as `Theta.off_map`, keyed `(operand, role, level)`.
* **`S`** — the *depth map*: how many rotating buffers each placement has. Derived, not authored
  (see §4.4 and §4.5).
* **`rho`** — the agent assignment: `ρ.resort`, a set of `(mode, agent-level, extent)` saying
  which looped mode each agent level traverses instead of the coordinate (§2.8 move 2). Since #303
  it is the SINGLE agent authority: `Hop.rho_span`, `Hop.region_agent_relative` and
  `agent_served_modes()` are projections of it. It was previously typed as an opaque per-op-class
  selector, which is why it sat empty and unread for the whole implementation.
* **`Phi`** — the fusion partition: which op-classes' movements merge into one cooperative
  instruction. Stored as `Theta.fuse_groups`.

There is deliberately **no address field**. Addresses, swizzles and per-lane fragment layouts are a
separable enrichment layer that provably changes no scheduling decision, so the core treats an
address as opaque. `ir.py`'s module docstring carries a step-by-step recipe for re-adding address
support as an additive layer if a future kernel needs it (§3.1.1).

#### 1.2 Op-class

An **op-class** is *one operand's movement along one hop*. `A`'s `global → shared` copy and `A`'s
`shared → register` read are two different op-classes of the same operand. This is the unit
everything is keyed on:

* `off` is indexed by op-class × level (hence the `role` component of the key);
* the ledger's endpoints name op-classes;
* the emitted tree contains exactly one node per op-class per level.

The **role** of a hop is `copy` (`global→shared`), `read` (`shared→register` or the one-hop
`global→register`), or `store` (any register/shared → coarser space). The mapping is the table
`theta.HOP_ROLE`, and `Hop.role` looks itself up in it.

The **trajectory sense** of an op-class is `forward` (running toward compute) or `reverse` (running
away from it, i.e. an epilogue store). It is *not* the same as the role: in a store round trip
`register → shared → register → global`, the middle leg's role is `read` while its trajectory is
reverse. The distinction matters because the peel construction hoists a forward op-class *backward*
(prefetch) and a reverse one *forward* (defer).

#### 1.3 Presence and broadcast

The **presence set** of an op-class is the set of inner (statically unrolled) loop axes whose value
changes what that op-class does. The complement is its **broadcast set** — the axes it is constant
over.

For a *data* operand this is inherent to the contraction: `A[m,k]` is constant over `n`, so `n` is
in `A`'s broadcast set; `B[n,k]` is constant over `m`. This one fact drives:

* **where** the op-class is emitted — at the innermost mode of its presence set;
* **how often** it reloads — the product of extents of the axes its register group is *not*
  constant over;
* **how long** a value is live.

Presence is a **per-hop** fact, not a per-operand one, and this is one of the sharpest edges in the
package. A bulk cooperative copy that moves an entire tile in a single instruction does not vary
over the inner axes *at all* — they are all in its broadcast set — so it sits at the outer chunk
level. Cut the tile into `n` storage-disjoint regions and exactly one axis comes back into that
hop's presence: the region axis, because now there is one instruction per region. That is
`geometry.hop_broadcast`, §2.2.3.

Three kinds of inner axis exist, and the third was added late:

* **free** axes — in the accumulator's presence (the output's `m`/`n` tiles);
* **reduction** axes — inner axes *absent* from the accumulator's presence (the contraction `k`);
* **agent-served** axes — traversed by the *agents* rather than by the coordinate. When
  `MIWaveGroup` places wave `w` entirely inside storage region `w`, nothing in the read/compute nest
  varies over the region axis (each wave sees one region), yet the bulk copy still walks all of
  them. Deriving "reduction" by subtraction misclassifies such an axis, so
  `Theta.agent_served_modes` names the class explicitly and `Theta.reduction_modes` subtracts it.

#### 1.4 Levels, `ord`, and inner-vs-outer

`Theta.ord` is the full outer-to-inner permutation of loop modes, including the outer reduction
chunk level. A `Mode` carries a name and an extent, and the **extent alone** tells outer from inner:

* `extent > 0` — an **inner** level. Its trip is a compile-time constant, so the loop is fully
  unrolled; the register ring rotates inside it.
* `extent == 0` — an **outer** level. Its trip is a runtime problem dimension, so it is a real loop
  with a back edge, needing a software-pipeline peel; the shared-memory ring rotates across it.

This is a single field, not a boolean plus an enumerated level kind, and that is deliberate: adding
a coarser outer level (a persistent / grid-stride tile loop) is a new `Mode` with `extent=0`, not a
new decoder branch.

The **reduction chunk** is the *innermost* outer level (`Theta.reduction_chunk_mode`). Five things
key on it and must never disagree: the shared ring depth, the read's shared-source rotation, the
emitted steady `Loop`, the `Bind` its peel steps pin, and the peel depth at that level. Before this
was centralized, three call sites used `outer_modes()[0]` and two used `[-1]` — identical while
there is exactly one outer level, silently divergent the moment a second exists.

Because `ord` is a permutation, the traversal over any subset of modes is a **monotone mixed-radix
counter**: each mode has a stride equal to the product of the extents of the modes inner to it.
`placement._ord_strides` computes exactly that.

#### 1.5 Steps, generations, and flat positions

Within one chunk, the inner nest visits a sequence of **steps** — one per point of the inner
traversal. A step's **flat position** `P` is `sum over modes of stride(mode) * index(mode)`,
restricted to the modes in question.

A **generation** is one filling of a rotating buffer: `(chunk, value)` for a shared buffer,
`(iteration, value)` for a register group. The word is overloaded in the source and the two senses
are worth keeping apart: a *shared generation* is which of the `S_shared` ring buffers, i.e. which
chunk's data; a *storage region* is a spatial split of one tile within one buffer. Two region
coordinates of one operand live in the **same** shared generation at different offsets.
`placement._generation_map`'s docstring names this conflation explicitly because an earlier round of
work made it.

#### 1.6 Retime (`off`)

`off(op-class, level) = d` means: this op-class's instance for iteration `i` of `level` is issued
during iteration `i − d`. It is **non-negative by type**. Deferral — issuing *later* — is not a
negative offset; it is a positive offset on a *reverse-trajectory* op-class, which gets the mirrored
peel. `emit._check_peel_is_emittable` rejects a negative entry as ill-typed with that explanation.

Two offsets exist on the shipping parameter path:

* `off(copy, chunk)` = the global prefetch depth (how many chunks ahead the bulk copy runs);
* `off(read, substep)` = the local prefetch depth (how many reduction substeps ahead the register
  read runs).

`off` being keyed by op-class rather than by operand is what makes `off(read, chunk)` — a read
carrying an *outer*-level offset — expressible at all; under an operand-only key it would be the
same key as `off(copy, chunk)`.

#### 1.7 Hazards, obligations, and completion classes

A **completion class** is a nameable set of operations a synchronization primitive can wait on.
`ir.Counter` defines three: `C_copy` (global→shared), `C_read` (shared→register), `C_load`
(global→register). Which hardware counter realizes each is the backend's business; the class is a
model object.

An **obligation** is a hazard the schedule creates and must discharge. Four kinds exist and they are
a **closed set** (`ir.RAW_KINDS`, `ir.WAR_KINDS`):

| Kind | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `RAW-residency` | A true dependency: the consumer needs the value the producer moved. |
| `crossing-RAW` | A true dependency created when this trip's read-ahead reaches into a chunk this trip's own copy fills. |
| `rotation-WAR` | An anti-dependency where the refill writes a *different* slot than the one being read — safe to hoist. |
| `inplace-WAR` | An anti-dependency where the refill writes the **same** slot the current consumer reads — the refill must be issued *after* that consumer. |

`readahead-residency` is a fifth kind carried in the ledger but deliberately *not* in
`OBLIGATION_KINDS`: it is a structural requirement on the prologue, not a wait, and it is checked
directly rather than turned into an `Await` (§8.3, §8.6.4).

The `is_war` / `is_raw` predicates over that closed set replaced eight sites that did
`kind.endswith("WAR")`. A suffix test standing in for a vocabulary fails in both directions the
moment the vocabulary grows, and it *did* fail: matching the suffix forced copy-last on
`crossing-RAW` obligations that needed copy-**first**.

#### 1.8 The two rings

Two independent rotating buffer sets exist:

* the **shared ring**, depth `S_shared`, rotating on the outer reduction chunk. Its slot index is
  `chunk mod S_shared`.
* the **register ring**, one per *reuse group* of a fragment, width `W`, rotating on the group's
  rate modes inside the unrolled body. Its slot index is the mixed-radix rate index mod `W`.

The register width `W` lives in a derived band `[L, R]`:

* `R` — the **reload rate**: how many distinct values one group holds per chunk = the product of
  extents of the modes the group is *not* constant over.
* `L` — the **live-peak floor**: the peak number of simultaneously live generations, computed as a
  cyclic interval-overlap over three unrolled iterations, sampling the middle one.

`W < L` is a race (two live values in one name); `W > R` is waste. `W` is the searched coordinate;
`L` and `R` are derived. §4.4 gives the algorithms.

#### 1.9 The movement quantum

A single hardware instruction may move **several tile coordinates**: a wide `ds_load` covering two
adjacent tiles, or a sub-agent broadcast where two half-waves receive the same register. The
**movement quantum** describes that merge, and it is modelled as **two expressions over the tile
index**:

```
carrier(t)  →  which instruction carries tile t   (tiles sharing a carrier are ONE movement)
slot(t)     →  which position inside that instruction's destination holds t
```

Load-versus-broadcast is then *derived*, not declared: a wide 2-tile load gives each tile its own
slot (two tiles → two registers); a sub-agent broadcast maps partners onto the *same* slot (two
tiles → one register). `registers written = |{slot(t)}| over the carrier group`. A schema of
`(axis, factor, kind)` tuples would have to be *interpreted* differently per kind at every consumer;
two expressions are only ever *evaluated*.

The structural consequence is the important one: **the coordinates inside one quantum are one
presence point**, hence one step and one generation. So an axis absorbed into a quantum is subtracted
from that hop's presence set, and the merged load cannot straddle a generation *by construction* —
`ord` orders modes, and no reordering can get inside a single presence point.

**A quantum FOLDS an axis; it does not simply delete it.** A `q`-wide quantum on an axis of extent
`N` cuts it into `N/q` **carrier groups**: the intra-group coordinate leaves the hop's presence, and
the **group index stays**. Full absence is only the degenerate case `q = N`. So the unit is a
*factor of an axis*, never the axis, and `1 < q < N` is the ordinary partial fold — an extent-8 axis
under a 2-tile load leaves 4 group indices present, not 0 and not 8.

`geometry.quantum_factors` is that derivation, returning `{axis: factor}`; `geometry.quantum_axes` is
its `factor == extent` view, kept so every caller that only wants "fully absorbed" is unchanged and
cannot drift from it. The factor is read off the **carrier map**, not computed as `gcd(q, extent)` —
only divisors are tried and each must have every block of `f` consecutive coordinates riding one
carrier, so a ragged fold is never produced. On a contiguous map the largest admissible divisor *is*
`gcd(q, extent)`, which is the regularity clamp, obtained rather than imposed; on a distributed
(sub-agent) map `gcd` is not even the relevant quantity, which is why the map and not the width is
the authority. This is why the shipping `MIWaveTile [8,7]` keeps single-tile loads on its odd axis:
no divisor of 7 above 1 divides a power-of-two load.

**The quantum is DERIVED IN THE CORE, from `ρ` and `Φ`.** §2.2 of the model is explicit that "the
quantum is *not a new field*: a carrier group is exactly a `Φ` fuse group over the tiles that `ρ` has
placed on the agents that one instruction spans … `θ` names the members". `Hop.phi_width` is Φ (how
many movement instances merge into one cooperative instruction) and `Hop.rho_span` is ρ (**how many
sub-agents** the group is distributed across), and `geometry.derive_quantum` composes them into the
`carrier`/`slot` pair. `Hop.quantum` survives only as an explicit override for a fold not expressible
as `(Φ, ρ)`; using it is a declared deviation, not the default path.

Earlier the target built a `QuantumMap` and the core only evaluated it. That was a *third*
representation alongside ρ and Φ: nothing cross-checked it against them, and a supplied map cannot be
searched, whereas ρ is a searched distribution. `placement.py` still records four attempts to have
the core derive the merge from *addresses* — scan the free modes for a "contiguous-looking" axis;
test whether the pair shares a generation and narrow if not; refuse when the pair straddles a storage
region; split an axis to *create* the pair — and each of those was an address assumption in disguise.
Deriving from ρ/Φ is a different thing entirely: those are θ fields, not addresses.

**ρ is an AGENT COUNT, and getting that wrong is a silent miscompile.** ρ was once passed
`span["vectorWidth"]` — a vector width where the model wants a number of sub-agents. TileSpan's
partition is the **half-wave**, so ρ = 2. With ρ = 1 the guard `ρ % Φ` read `1 % 2 ≠ 0`,
`derive_quantum` returned `None`, and θ modelled *no fold at all* while the leaf folded and the WMMA
read both blocks through the `matrix_{a,b}_scale` selector. The carrier is identical with and without
ρ — ρ moves only the **slot** — so the load count was always right and only the register naming was
wrong. MEASURED 2026-08-24: mxf8 `MIWaveTile [2,8]` + TileSpan, `LONKM`/`LONMK` at `TDMSplit=0`,
49152 of 65536 values wrong; correct after ρ became the sub-agent count, 38/38 on hardware.

#### 1.10 Regions and fusion

A **storage region** is a piece of a macro-tile that is cut into storage-disjoint parts so that the
bulk mover can issue one instruction per part. `Operand.region_modes` names the axes that enumerate
them and `Operand.split` counts them.

**Fusion** (`Phi`) merges op-classes into one cooperative instruction. On a wave-separated bulk
mover, one descriptor is aliased across two operands and a single instruction serves both, with wave
parity selecting which. Fused members are paired **by region index** — region `j` of `A` moves with
region `j` of `B` — and the two operands may be cut on *different* axes; the pairing is by index,
not by a shared mode. A fused group with *mixed* region counts has no region-`j` instance for its
unsplit member, so it moves whole (and `translate.params_to_theta` emits a note saying the requested
split was not applied to that copy hop).

`Theta.movement_units` is the single authority for "which cooperative movements exist and how many
region instances each has"; both the emitter and the downstream lowering read it, because deriving
it twice invites the two to disagree.

#### 1.11 Rolled emission and named dependencies

The emitted IR is **rolled**: one `Inst` per op-class per level, with rotation slots kept as
symbolic `Expr` objects. Node count is `O(#op-classes × #levels)`, *independent of trip count*. The
renderer performs a partial unroll as a **view**; the stored IR stays rolled.

Waits are emitted as **named** dependencies (`Await(dep=<producer endpoint>, counter=<class>)`) with
the numeric count left unset (`count = -1`). Two sound backends exist: one that materializes a
numeric count, and one that discards the markers and re-derives synchronization from the emitted
dataflow. This decoder targets the second, so a count computed here would only be overwritten. The
named form is guaranteed to cover whatever issue order the backend commits to.

---

### 2. `latalg.py` and `geometry.py` — the arithmetic floor

#### 2.1 `latalg.py` — integer layout arithmetic (66 lines)

**Concept.** The scheduling core needs exactly three "layout" facts: integer tile counts, a
stride-zero (broadcast) test, and a per-lane register-packing count. It used to get these by calling
into a spatial-layout library (`logical_divide`, a null-space computation, `recast`/`coshape`).
`latalg` replaces those three calls with plain integer arithmetic so a mergeable build carries no
layout-library dependency. Every function documents the library operation it stands in for.

**Scope, stated honestly in the module docstring.** Every use in `geometry.py` is over *contiguous
1-D* layouts (one extent, unit stride) or a product of independent extents. Nothing here composes
strides, reads an address, or handles a general nested layout.

| Function | Computes | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `latalg.tile_split(n, t)` | `(per_tile, n_tiles)`. For the divisible case, `(t, n // t)`. | Non-divisible falls back to `(min(t,n), ceil(n/t))`, but callers guard divisibility so only the exact case is load-bearing. |
| `latalg.n_tiles(n, t)` | The tile **count** = `tile_split(n,t)[1]`. | Clamped to `≥ 1`. |
| `latalg.per_tile(n, t)` | The per-tile **extent** = `tile_split(n,t)[0]`. | Clamped to `≥ 1`. |
| `latalg.product(extents)` | The product of a list of extents, each clamped to `≥ 1`. | Stands in for building a layout over a mode set and reading its size. |
| `latalg.recast_count(elems, scale)` | `ceil(elems / scale)` — packing sub-units into groups of `scale`. | Matches the library's round-up behaviour: `recast((4,),4)=1`, `recast((1,),4)=1`, `recast((16,),2)=8`. |

##### 2.1.1 The five functions in prose, and what each one is standing in for

The table is the reference; this is the part a reader needs in order to change one of them safely.

**`tile_split(n, t) -> (per_tile, n_tiles)`** is the primitive; the next two are projections of it.
It answers "if I cut an axis of `n` elements into tiles of `t`, what is the tile extent and how many
tiles are there?" In the divisible case the answer is the trivial `(t, n // t)`, and the divisible
case is the *only* one the decoder produces — every caller has already checked divisibility, either
in `translate.py` when the mode extents are built or in a `Solution.py` rejection. The
non-divisible fallback `(min(t, n), ceil(n / t))` exists so the function is total rather than
raising, and it is the shape the layout library it replaced returns; it is not exercised. If you
find yourself relying on it, that is a signal that a divisibility guard is missing upstream, not
that this function needs work.

**`n_tiles(n, t)`** is `tile_split(n, t)[1]`, clamped to at least 1 — the *count*. It is what a
`Mode`'s extent is: how many compute-atom tiles fit along one axis. `geometry.axis_tiles` is the
one function written to call it (see 19.6.1 on why that call site is currently dead).

**`per_tile(n, t)`** is `tile_split(n, t)[0]`, clamped to at least 1 — the *extent*. It has **no call site on the
shipping path** (19.5) — it is retained as the peer of `n_tiles`, for the region arithmetic its
docstring names: given a free axis of `n` elements cut into `groups` storage-disjoint regions, the
per-region extent is `per_tile(n, n // groups)`. The two projections exist separately, rather than
callers unpacking the tuple, because a caller that wants only one of them and unpacks both is one
typo away from using the wrong element — and the two are numerically equal whenever `n == t²`, which
is a shape that occurs (a 16-element axis in 4-element tiles), so such a typo survives a spot check.

**`product(extents)`** multiplies a list of extents, clamping each to at least 1. It stands in for
"build a layout over this set of modes and read its size", and it is the single implementation
behind every "how many tiles over these axes" question in `geometry.py`: `free_tiles`, `k_tiles`,
`reduction_tiles` and `presence_tiles` are each a mode filter followed by one `product` call. The
per-element clamp, rather than a clamp on the result, is what makes an accidental extent-0 mode
behave as a scalar axis instead of collapsing the whole product to zero.

**`recast_count(elems, scale)`** is `ceil(elems / scale)`: how many groups of `scale` sub-units it
takes to hold `elems` of them. Its one caller is `geometry.frag_regs`, packing a fragment's per-lane
elements into registers, and the round-*up* is the load-bearing half — a fragment of 1 element in a
4-element register occupies one register, not a quarter of one. The docstring pins three values
(`(4, 4) -> 1`, `(1, 4) -> 1`, `(16, 2) -> 8`) precisely because the rounding direction is the thing
a reimplementation gets wrong.

##### 2.1.2 Derivation, alternatives and trade-offs

**Why integer arithmetic at all, rather than a layout library.** The five operations above are the
*entire* layout surface the scheduling core needs, and each one is one or two lines of integer
arithmetic. The prototype obtained them from a spatial-layout library, which brought a general
nested-layout algebra — composition, strides, coalescing, complement — of which the decoder used
four entry points on contiguous one-dimensional layouts only. Three arguments decided the
replacement, in order of weight:

1. **Mergeability.** TensileLite ships as part of a library build with a fixed dependency set. A
   vendored spatial-layout package would have to be reviewed, licensed and maintained inside that
   build for the sake of about twenty lines of arithmetic. This is the reason the change was made
   and it is not a technical one.
2. **The surface was a lie about the code's generality.** Calling `logical_divide` on a
   `Layout((n,), (1,))` looks like the decoder handles general layouts. It does not, and never did:
   the address algebra is deliberately outside this model (3.1.1). Writing the arithmetic out makes
   the actual scope — contiguous one-dimensional, or a product of independent extents — visible in
   the module docstring rather than hidden behind a general API.
3. **Cost, which is the weakest argument and is included for completeness.** All five are `O(1)`
   with constants in the tens of nanoseconds; the library calls allocated layout objects and were
   perhaps an order of magnitude slower. Section 19.5 measures the whole module at well under 0.1%
   of a decode either way. Nobody should reintroduce or remove a dependency here for speed.

**The alternative that was rejected, and the one that remains open.** Rejected: keeping the library
and vendoring only the four entry points. That is the worst of both — the general API's surface with
none of its testing, and a vendored copy to keep in sync. Still open: pushing these five up into
`geometry.py` and deleting the module. `latalg.py` exists as a separate file mainly to mark the
boundary the dependency used to sit on, and with the dependency gone that marker has less value each
year. Against deleting it: the module docstring is the only place the *scope* statement lives, and
a scope statement inside a 221-line `geometry.py` is easier to lose.

**The honest weakness: there is no oracle.** Removing the dependency also removed a differential
self-test that had compared each operation against the library on random inputs. The oracle is not
shipped with this tree, so the test was dropped rather than faked. The consequence is concrete: a
sixth operation added here has nothing to check it against, and the rounding-direction class of bug
(`recast_count`) is exactly the kind a differential test catches and a hand-written test does not,
because the author who gets the rounding wrong writes the expectation wrong too. **Mitigation, if
you add one:** state the expected values from the *specification* of the operation, not from running
it, and include at least one input where round-up and round-down differ and one where an extent is 1.

**The clamping is defensive and it hides things.** Every function clamps its inputs and its result
to at least 1. That makes the module total — no `ZeroDivisionError`, no negative tile count — which
is what a derivation layer called from inside a loop nest wants. It also means "extent 0" and
"extent 1" are indistinguishable at this layer, so a mode that should have dropped out of `ord`
entirely, and one that is genuinely a single tile, produce identical arithmetic. Nothing currently
depends on telling them apart (`translate.py:_canonical_ord` drops most extent-1 modes before they
ever become `Mode`s — though it deliberately KEEPS a degenerate extent-1 inner mode whose paired
split mode is live, so such a mode does reach this layer; `theta.py` itself has no extent-1 filter,
only the `extent == 0` outer/inner test), but if a future caller does, it must make that distinction *above* this module.

#### 2.2 `geometry.py` — the one owner of presence arithmetic (357 lines)

**Concept.** Everything numeric the decoder used to fit by hand — the compute grid, the per-region
block size, a fragment's register width, and which axes an operand is broadcast over — is derived
here from *structural* inputs: mode extents, which axes an operand indexes, a fragment's element
footprint, and the region partition count. The rest of the core imports only plain ints and plain
sets from this module and never sees a layout object.

##### 2.2.1 `axis_tiles(macro_elems, atom_elems)`

Number of compute-atom tiles along one axis, in **element space**: `n_tiles(macro, atom)`. This is
how a `Mode`'s extent *should* be obtained (tile extent ÷ atom extent) rather than typed by hand —
e.g. wave M of 64 elements over a 16-element instruction M gives 4 M-tiles.

##### 2.2.2 `_inner_axes(theta)`

One line: `[(name, extent) for m in theta.inner_modes()]`, in `ord` order. Called by
`broadcast_axes` and `hop_broadcast`. The quantum family does **not** route through it: it needs the
axis list already filtered of broadcast and reduction modes, which is `_quantum_candidate_axes` —
extracted for exactly that reason, so `quantum_factors`, `quantum_axes` and `hop_fold` share one
candidate derivation instead of three copies of the filter.

##### 2.2.3 The presence family

**`broadcast_axes(theta, op)`** — the intra-iteration axes this operand's *data* is constant over.
It is the union of two sets:

```
broadcast_axes(op) =  (op.fragment.broadcast_axes  ∩ inner axes)
                    ∪ (theta.agent_served_modes()  ∩ inner axes)
```

The second term is the agent-served subtraction from §1.3: a wave reads, computes and accumulates
inside its own region, so a region axis served by the agents is broadcast for every *data* consumer.
There is exactly **one** subtraction point, so the read coordinate, the free-mode list, register
naming, the compute-grid projection and the register footprint cannot disagree. The bulk copy is
untouched — `hop_broadcast`'s bulk branch never calls here.

**`derive_quantum(hop)`** — §2.2's carrier group as `Φ` applied to `ρ`: the `QuantumMap` **derived,
not supplied**. `Φ = hop.phi_width` tiles ride one instruction and `ρ = hop.rho_span` counts the
sub-agents they are spread over.

```
phi <= 1 and not rho          ->  None          (identity merge: SILENCE, not a map)
carrier(t) = t // phi                            (either shape: phi tiles per instruction)
rho > 1 and phi % rho         ->  None          (the group cannot divide over the agents)
rho > 1: slot(t) = (t mod phi) // rho            (DISTRIBUTED: rho tiles share one register)
else:    slot(t) =  t mod phi                    (CONTIGUOUS: each tile its own register)
```

ρ moves the **slot**, never the carrier — the instruction count is the same either way, and what
changes is how many registers one instruction writes (`|{slot}| = Φ/ρ`). At TileSpan (Φ=2, ρ=2) every
tile gets slot 0: one register holds block `2g` and `2g+1`, the lower and upper half-wave, and the
WMMA's scale selector picks. That *is* the broadcast, expressed rather than flagged. Returning `None`
is deliberate silence — a supplied `carrier(t) = t` would mean "θ decided: merge nothing" and would
stop the leaf folding tiles that really do share an instruction.

`hop_quantum(hop)` returns the explicit `hop.quantum` override if present, else this derivation.

**`quantum_factors(theta, op, quantum)`** — `{axis: factor}`, how many **consecutive coordinates** of
each axis one instruction carries. This is the full derivation; `quantum_axes` below is its
fully-spanned view.

```
if quantum is None: return {}
candidates = inner modes not in broadcast_axes(op) and not reduction modes
             (each with extent > 1; a degenerate axis is spanned by everything, so say nothing)
flatten the candidates into a tile index, ord order, innermost fastest
for each candidate axis a with stride s and extent e:
    best = max f dividing e such that every coordinate rides its own group's leader:
             for all t:  carrier(t - ((t//s) mod f)*s) == carrier(t)
    record a -> best  when best > 1
```

Only **divisors** of the extent are tried, so a ragged fold is never returned — §2.2's regularity
condition, obtained rather than imposed. On a contiguous map the largest admissible divisor is
`gcd(Φ, extent)`, which is exactly the paper's clamp; on the distributed map `gcd` is not the
relevant quantity at all, which is why the **carrier map** and not the width is the authority.

**`quantum_axes(theta, op, quantum)`** — the `factor == extent` view of `quantum_factors`: the axes
one instruction spans **whole**, which therefore leave the hop's presence entirely. A *partially*
folded axis is deliberately absent from this set — it keeps `extent // factor` group indices in
presence, so subtracting it here would drop coordinates that still vary. Keeping it a derived view
rather than a second implementation is what stops the two drifting; a differential over 1080
(op, config) points recorded **0** disagreements with the older standalone version.

**`hop_fold(theta, op, hop)`** — the *partial* folds only (`1 < factor < extent`), i.e. the
complement of `quantum_axes` within `quantum_factors`. Bulk hops fold nothing. This is the single
place the partial fold is decided; `emit._first_touch_modes` turns it into the read's `mode % q == 0`
guard and `loopir_to_gir._absorbed` carries it into GIR.

<details><summary>The constancy test, in full</summary>

```
candidates = inner modes not in broadcast_axes(op) and not reduction modes
flatten the candidates into a tile index, ord order, innermost fastest
for each candidate axis a with stride s and extent e:
    spanned if, for every base tile t with digit(a) == 0 and every v in 1..e-1:
        carrier(t + v*s) == carrier(t)
```

</details>

That is: an axis is spanned exactly when varying it alone never changes the carrier. The
**innermost-first rule falls out rather than being imposed**: at a wave-tile of 2 with a region split
the in-region fan axis is degenerate, so a 2-tile load fills the region axis and *that* is what gets
absorbed; at a wave-tile of 4 the same load fills the in-region axis and the region axis stays
present, because tiles 0 and 2 then have different carriers. Both answers come out of the same
constancy test.

The candidate set comes from `broadcast_axes` (a data fact) and the reduction set, **never** from the
presence family — `hop_broadcast` is what presence is built from, so consulting presence here would
close a loop.

Cost: `O(A · E · T)` where `A` is the candidate count, `E` the max extent and `T` the flat tile
count — with `T = product of extents`, this is `O(T · sum of extents)`. On shipping shapes `T ≤ 16`,
so it is negligible; on a hypothetical wave tile of 8×8 with four live axes it would still be under a
thousand carrier evaluations. If it ever matters, memoize `carrier_of` (it is a pure `Expr.eval`).

**`hop_broadcast(theta, op, hop)`** — presence **per hop**. This is the function that makes bulk-ness
and presence the same fact rather than two:

```
if not hop.is_bulk:
    return broadcast_axes(op) ∪ quantum_axes(op, hop.quantum)
else:
    present = op.region_modes ∩ inner   if op.split > 1 else {}
    return inner_axes \ present
```

Both halves are the same rule at two widths: a bulk cooperative load spans *every* inner axis, a wide
per-lane read spans the ones its quantum covers. That is why the quantum belongs here and not in a
fold rule at the leaf — absorbing it is what makes the merged coordinates one presence point.

The `op.split > 1` test in the bulk branch is load-bearing: a tile with a region *mode* but only one
region (the scale operands are like this) still moves in one instruction, so the hop varies over
nothing. Having an axis is not the same as having more than one value along it. Dropping this test
made the per-region completion note fire for a single-region operand — a real behaviour change, and
the reason both of the hand-rolled expressions this function replaced are cross-checked against it in
`test_loopmodel.test_per_hop_presence_REPRODUCES_the_two_hand_rolled_expressions_it_replaced`.

##### 2.2.4 The tile-count family

| Function | Computes | Why it exists separately |
|---|---|---|
| `geometry.free_tiles(theta, op)` | Product of extents of the operand's **own free presence modes** (presence minus reduction). | Presence-derived, so it works for inputs, scales and the accumulator with no name or role test. Reads each `Mode`'s own extent — no name→Mode re-lookup. |
| `geometry.k_tiles(theta)` | Product of extents of the **reduction** modes. | A schedule-level quantity: how many reduction substeps a chunk has. Explicitly **not** per-operand. |
| `geometry.reduction_tiles(theta, op)` | Product of extents of *this operand's* presence modes that are reduction modes. | The peer of `free_tiles`. `1` for an operand broadcast over the reduction (the accumulator). |
| `geometry.presence_tiles(theta, op)` | Product of extents of the operand's **whole** presence set. | Equals `free_tiles × reduction_tiles` by construction. This is the presence-derived replacement for `free_tiles × k_tiles`. |

The `presence_tiles` correction is a measured bug fix worth recording: multiplying an operand's
footprint by the schedule-level `k_tiles` silently over-counts any op-class broadcast over the
reduction, by exactly that factor. The accumulator came out at `4 × 2 × 16 = 128` registers for a
tile that holds `4 × 16 = 64`.

##### 2.2.5 `wmma_grid(theta)`

`(free_tiles(input0), free_tiles(input1), k_tiles)` — the matmul grid for one chunk. The two inputs
are identified as `role == 'input'` operands that have a register-destination hop, taken in schedule
order. There is **no `'A'`/`'B'` literal**. A kernel with a different input count is out of the
matmul-primitive scope and simply gets `1` for the missing factor.

##### 2.2.6 `frag_regs(theta, op)`

Registers one fragment occupies per lane:

```
if reg_bytes % elem_bytes == 0:
    scale = reg_bytes // elem_bytes            # elements per register
    return recast_count(frag_elems, scale)     # ceil(frag_elems / scale)
else:
    return ceil(frag_elems * elem_bytes / reg_bytes)   # sub-register elements
```

E.g. 64 one-byte elements into 4-byte registers → scale 4 → 16 registers; 16 two-byte elements →
scale 2 → 8 registers. The second branch is the fallback for element sizes that do not divide the
register size.

##### 2.2.7 Trade-offs for `geometry.py`

* **Complexity.** Every function except `quantum_axes` is `O(#inner modes)`, with `#inner modes ≤ 8`
  on the shipping vocabulary. `quantum_axes` is as analysed above. None of this is a build-time cost
  concern.
* **The single-source discipline is the whole value.** The measured failures in this area were all
  *two derivations of one rule*: `emit.copy_insts` reproducing the bulk-presence answer by testing
  `op.split` and reaching for `op.region_modes` itself; two separate linear scanners existing to
  re-look-up a `Mode` from a name. Both were deleted by making the presence family return `Mode`
  objects and by routing bulk-ness through `hop_broadcast`.
* **Where to extend.** If a hop kind appears that is neither "bulk, spans everything" nor "per-lane,
  spans its quantum" — say a partial cooperative mover that spans two of four axes — the right change
  is to make `hop_broadcast`'s bulk branch consult a per-hop spanned-axis set derived the same way
  `quantum_axes` derives one, rather than adding a third branch. The two branches are already the
  same rule; a third would break that.
* **Sharp edge.** `broadcast_axes` folds the agent-served set into a *data* fact. This is correct for
  every consumer that asks "what does the data depend on" and wrong for anything that wants "what
  does the coordinate index". No current consumer wants the latter, but if one appears, split the two
  rather than adding a keyword argument — the whole point of the single subtraction point is that
  callers cannot choose.


---

### 3. `ir.py` — the IR vocabulary

`ir.py` is 736 lines and defines 47 names, of which only 15 are classes. It has no imports beyond
`dataclasses` and the stdlib `operator` module, and it imports nothing from the rest of the package —
it is the bottom of the core, and every other core module builds on it. Nothing in it knows what a
GEMM is, what a wave is, or what gfx1250 is. What it knows is: values live in *spaces*, moving a
value between two spaces takes an instruction whose completion can be waited on, a compute op
consumes registers, and loops/peels/guards arrange those ops in time.

This section covers each declaration in the order the file declares it, because that order is also
the dependency order: spaces and counters, then the movement quantum, then the two payload
op-classes, then the symbolic-expression layer (`Expr`, `Pred`), then `Placement`, then the hazard
vocabulary and `Await`, then the tree nodes (`Inst`, `Loop`, `Branch`, `Bind`, `Peel`, `Cond`).

#### 3.1 What kind of IR this is

##### 3.1.1 Address-free by construction, and the recipe for undoing that

The single most consequential property of this IR is stated in the module docstring: **it carries no
physical address, thread, lane, or instruction-width information**. A `Load` node says "operand `A`
moves from shared to register, filling the fragment at this presence coordinate, this many registers
wide". It does not say which lane reads which byte.

Two consequences follow, and both are load-bearing everywhere downstream.

**The IR is *rolled*, and therefore already collapsed.** Each op-class appears exactly *once*, at the
loop level where it is present (section 1.3), with its rotation slot left as a symbolic `Expr` such
as `(iter)%2`. The node count is `O(#op-classes × #levels)` and is *independent of the trip count*.
There is no `--collapse` renderer and no per-instance `Inst`, and the docstring explains why in
historical terms: an earlier version of this IR *did* enumerate one `Inst` per thread/address
instance — a `ds_read` fanned out into many concrete loads carrying distinct addresses — and a
`--collapse` renderer folded runs of identical-`semantic` ops back into `(inst) ×N` for display.
Removing the layout algebra removed the enumeration, so the stored IR *is* the collapsed form and
there is nothing left to fold. The `Dim` / `Slot` / `Pad` address-slot classes and the collapse
machinery were deleted with it. If a stale document mentions any of those four names, it predates
this revision.

**Re-adding addresses is an additive layer, and the docstring specifies it.** The recipe, reproduced
here so a future maintainer does not have to re-derive it:

1. Add a `layout` / `addr` field on `Placement` (or a parallel `AddrPlacement` class) carrying the
   per-lane element→(register, byte) map plus any swizzle. **Leave `Placement.space`, `.slots` and
   the group labels exactly as they are** — the logical slot and the physical layout are different
   facts, and the whole point is that scheduling only ever consults the logical one.
2. Add an *optional* renderer/backend pass that expands one rolled `Inst` into per-lane /
   per-transfer instances by walking that layout. This revives the old per-instance stream as a
   downstream **view**, never as the stored IR. `Load.semantic` and `Mma.semantic` (section 3.4.3,
   section 3.5.2) are retained precisely as the fold key such a view would re-collapse on — that is
   their only remaining purpose.
3. Instruction width in elements-per-transfer is a *lowering* of the hop's `vector_elems` (a field
   of `theta.Hop`, not of this module) multiplied through the layout. Compute it in that pass, not
   in the schedule model.

The invariant to keep: the schedule point and this IR stay address-free; addresses live in the
enrichment pass and in the TensileLite decoder. The reason this is safe is the separability property
recorded in section 1.1 — the layout algebra provably changes no scheduling decision, so it can be
bolted on without re-deriving anything here.

##### 3.1.2 Everything is a plain dataclass

Every node is a `@dataclass`. The payload/expression types (`QuantumMap`, `Load`, `Mma`, `Expr`,
`Pred`, `Placement`, `Await`) are `frozen=True`; the *tree* types (`Inst`, `Loop`, `Branch`, `Bind`,
`Peel`, `Cond`) are **mutable**. That split is deliberate and is exercised: the issue-order
refinement in `sigma_c.py` reorders instruction lists in place, and several unit tests mutate a
correct tree into a defective one to prove a gate catches it (for example
`test_loopmodel.test_gate_catches_misplaced_drain_refill` splices a refill into the middle of a read
stream by assigning into `drain.body[0]`). If you freeze `Loop` or `Bind`, both of those stop
working and the gates lose their negative tests.

The frozen half is what makes the stream trivially serializable and hashable, and it is why `Load`
and `Mma` can be used as dictionary keys and set members without defensive copying.

##### 3.1.3 Where this module sits in the pipeline

Producers: `emit.py` constructs every node type except `Branch`. `translate.py` and
`KernelWriter.py` construct `Expr` and `QuantumMap` (the latter builds a `QuantumMap` for the MX
scale read in `KernelWriter._loopModelTarget`, which is the only place in the tree that supplies a
non-identity quantum today).

Consumers: `render.py` (three text views), `validate.py` (nine structural properties),
`ledger.py` (the discharge gate), `sigma_c.py` (issue-order refinement), and
`Lowering/loopir_to_gir.py` (the real codegen consumer, which turns each `Inst` into GIR `Move` /
`Mma` operations). `Lowering/gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py` imports exactly one symbol from this
module — `is_war` — and `Lowering/gir/render.py` imports exactly one — `OBLIGATION_KINDS`. Those two
imports are the entire surface this module exposes *below* the LoopModel package, and both exist for
the same reason: the hazard-kind vocabulary must have one owner (section 3.9).

#### 3.2 Spaces and completion counters

##### 3.2.1 `ir.Space`

A bare namespace class with three string constants:

```python
class Space:
    GLOBAL = "global"; SHARED = "shared"; REGISTER = "register"
```

It is not an `Enum`. The values are the strings that appear in dumps and in `Placement.space`, and
the ordering that matters (which space is "coarser") is not defined here but in `theta.py`, as
`_SPACE_RANK = {GLOBAL: 0, SHARED: 1, REGISTER: 2}`. Keeping `Space` a plain string namespace means a
node can be constructed from a literal in a test without importing the class, and comparisons in
`loopir_to_gir` (`if src_space == Space.SHARED`) are ordinary string equality.

The cost of not using an `Enum` is the usual one: a typo like `"registers"` produces a `KeyError`
from `HOP_COUNTER` rather than an immediate `AttributeError`, and nothing forbids a fourth space
string from being invented at a call site. In practice the `HOP_COUNTER` lookup catches it at node
construction, which is early enough.

Three spaces is enough for the currently modelled paths: `global→shared→register` (the staged path),
and `global→register` (direct-to-register, one hop). `theta.HOP_ROLE` additionally names the three
*reverse* hops (`register→shared`, `shared→global`, `register→global`) as role `store`, so the space
vocabulary is already wide enough for an epilogue; what is missing is the modelling, not the names
(section 19).

##### 3.2.2 `ir.Counter` — completion classes, and why they stopped being mnemonics

A **completion class** is a nameable set of operations that a synchronization primitive can wait on
(section 1.7). `Counter` enumerates three:

| Constant | Value | Hop it tracks |
|---|---|---|
| `Counter.COPY` | `"C_copy"` | `global → shared`, the bulk staging movement |
| `Counter.READ` | `"C_read"` | `shared → register`, the fragment read |
| `Counter.LOAD` | `"C_load"` | `global → register`, the one-hop direct transfer |

The values are *model* names. They were once the gfx1250 wait mnemonics (`"s_wait_dscnt"` and its
siblings), and the docstring records both the defect and the measurement that motivated the change:
carrying hardware instruction names in the backend-agnostic core, where **the mnemonic was matched by
nothing** — the only consumer was the renderer, which stripped the `s_wait_` prefix and the `cnt`
suffix back off in order to display the class. So the mnemonic was pure liability: it constrained
nothing, was read by nobody, and made a module that claims to be target-independent grep-positive for
a gfx1250 instruction (work item #162). A backend targeting a counter machine maps `C_copy` /
`C_read` / `C_load` onto its own instructions; that mapping is the backend's table, not this one's.

The renderer still shortens them for display — `render._counter_tag` — but now that is a display
choice over a model name rather than a round trip through a hardware name.

##### 3.2.3 `HOP_COUNTER` — the single extension point

```python
HOP_COUNTER = {
    (Space.GLOBAL, Space.SHARED):   Counter.COPY,
    (Space.SHARED, Space.REGISTER): Counter.READ,
    (Space.GLOBAL, Space.REGISTER): Counter.LOAD,
}
```

A module-level dict from `(src, dst)` to completion class. Two things read it: `ir.Load.counter`
(section 3.4.2) and `theta.Hop.counter`. Neither stores the answer, so adding a row is genuinely the
whole change needed to support a new source/destination pair — every `Load` picks it up, and the
ledger, which keys obligations on `Hop.counter`, picks it up too.

**Why deriving the completion class from the hop is legitimate rather than a shortcut.** In the
general schedule-space formulation, the assignment of op-classes to completion classes is its own
free coordinate (the source calls it `π`): a machine could expose several counters per hop kind, or
one counter shared across hop kinds, and choosing among them is a real scheduling decision. Deriving
the class from the hop *fixes* that coordinate to one profile — the only legal profile when the
hardware exposes exactly one counter per hop kind, which is the case for the target this decoder
serves. The docstring is explicit that this is a **specialization, not a missing axis**: an
implementer targeting one counter profile is choosing the specialization; they are not deleting the
degree of freedom. If a future target exposes two independent shared-memory counters, `HOP_COUNTER`
stops being a function of the hop and has to become a function of `(hop, policy)` — at which point
the right change is to make it a method on `theta.Hop` that consults a policy field on `Theta`, not
to add a second dict here.

**Complexity and cost.** A three-entry dict lookup, `O(1)`, evaluated once per node render and once
per ledger row. Nothing here is a compile-time concern.

**Sharp edge.** `HOP_COUNTER` has *no* entry for the three store hops that `theta.HOP_ROLE` does
name. `theta.Hop.counter` therefore raises `KeyError` on a `register→shared` hop. This is not a bug
today — no store hop is ever constructed, because the epilogue is unmodelled — but it is the first
thing that will break when someone models it, and the failure will be a bare `KeyError` from a dict
literal rather than a message. If you are the person adding store support, add the three rows *and*
a fourth counter constant in the same commit, and give the lookup a `.get` with a message naming the
unsupported hop.

#### 3.3 `QuantumMap` — the movement quantum as two expressions

##### 3.3.1 The abstraction

Section 1.9 defines the movement quantum: one hardware instruction may move several tile
coordinates, and the coordinates inside one quantum are *one* presence point — one step, one
generation, one completion. `QuantumMap` is how that fact is written down. It is a frozen dataclass
with exactly two fields, both `Expr`-shaped objects over the **operand's tile coordinate**:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class QuantumMap:
    carrier: object   # Expr over the tile coordinate -> instruction index
    slot:    object   # Expr over the tile coordinate -> position within that instruction
```

`carrier(t)` answers *which instruction carries tile `t`*; tiles that share a carrier are one
movement. `slot(t)` answers *which position inside that instruction's destination holds `t`*.

The design claim — and it is the reason this is two expressions and not a schema — is that
**load-versus-broadcast is derived, not declared**. The two mechanisms differ only in the *range* of
`slot` over a carrier group:

| Mechanism | `carrier(t)` | `slot(t)` | Registers written |
|---|---|---|---|
| wide load, 2 tiles | `t // 2` | `t % 2` | 2 (two distinct slots) |
| sub-agent broadcast | `t − stride·((t % 2·stride) // stride)` | `t % stride` | 1 (partners share a slot) |
| the two composed | compose | compose | counted, not cased |

So `registers written = |{slot(t) : t in the carrier group}|`, and `coordinates served = the carrier
preimage`. Nothing is tagged "this one is a broadcast". The alternative that was rejected was a
schema of `(axis, factor, kind)` tuples; the objection is concrete rather than aesthetic — a schema
has to be *interpreted* differently per `kind`, and every consumer then re-implements the
interpretation, which is exactly the "two derivations of one rule" failure shape that section 2.2.7
records as the dominant bug class in this package. Here every consumer only ever *evaluates*.

##### 3.3.2 It is supplied from outside, never derived here

The merge is a consequence of the address layout and of how the emitter folds transfers, and the
schedule core is address-opaque. So the expressions are computed **outside** the core — in
`KernelWriter._loopModelTarget`, from target facts, handed through `bridge._read_quantum` into the
parameter dict, and attached to a hop by `translate` — and the core only evaluates them. The
docstring puts the quantum in the same standing as the depth map input: a value from outside that
the model reasons over but does not choose. `placement.py` records four separate attempts to have
the core *derive* the quantum and why each was an address assumption in disguise; that discussion
belongs to section 6 of this report, but the conclusion is enforced here by the field simply being
`object` and never being constructed by any core module.

`None` means the identity merge — one tile per instruction. It is always admissible and it is the
default on `Load.quantum` and the value in every shipping kernel configuration except the MX scale
read.

##### 3.3.3 `_QUANTUM_VAR`, `quantum_var()`, `identity_quantum()`

```python
_QUANTUM_VAR = "tile"

def quantum_var() -> str:
    return _QUANTUM_VAR

def identity_quantum() -> QuantumMap:
    return QuantumMap(carrier=Expr(var=_QUANTUM_VAR), slot=cst(0))
```

`_QUANTUM_VAR` is the module-private name of the free variable a quantum's expressions are written
over. `quantum_var()` is the public accessor, and it exists for exactly one reason: a builder
*outside* the package (`KernelWriter`) must write its `Expr` over the same symbol the evaluator will
bind, and hard-coding the string `"tile"` in two repositories' worth of code is how those two drift.
`KernelWriter._loopModelTarget` calls it and binds the result to a local `t` before building its
`digits` expressions, so the symbol appears once per producer.

`identity_quantum()` returns the safe form: `carrier(t) = t` (every tile its own instruction),
`slot(t) = 0`. Note that it is *not* what `Load.quantum=None` is replaced by anywhere in the emit
path — `None` is handled by the consumers directly as "no merge" — so `identity_quantum` is used only
where a caller wants a non-`None` object with identity behaviour. It is the value you want in a test
fixture that needs to prove a quantum-aware code path is a no-op under the identity merge.

##### 3.3.4 The four methods

All four take an optional `env` (a dict of loop-mode name → int) which is merged with the tile
binding before evaluation, so a quantum expression may in principle also reference loop modes; no
current producer does, but the plumbing costs nothing.

```
carrier_of(t, env)  ->  int
    e = dict(env); e["tile"] = t
    return carrier.eval(e)        if carrier has .eval, else int(carrier)

slot_of(t, env)     ->  int       # the same, over `slot`

group(t, extent, env) -> tuple    # the carrier PREIMAGE
    c = carrier_of(t, env)
    return tuple(u for u in range(max(1, extent)) if carrier_of(u, env) == c)

regs(t, extent, env)  -> int
    return len({slot_of(u, env) for u in group(t, extent, env)})
```

`carrier_of` and `slot_of` both accept a *plain int* in the field instead of an `Expr` — the
`hasattr(..., "eval")` test — which is a small convenience for hand-written fixtures and for a
constant carrier. It also means a typo that puts a string in the field fails with a `ValueError`
from `int()` rather than an `AttributeError`, which is marginally better.

`group` is the one with a real design decision in it. It computes the preimage **by enumeration over
`range(extent)`**, not by multiplying out the extents of the axes the carrier is constant over. The
docstring gives the reason: the preimage is *total* over any carrier expression, including ones whose
group is not a contiguous run — the sub-agent broadcast partner sits `stride` away, not adjacent, so
a "spanned axes product" formulation would either miss it or need a second case. Enumeration has one
case.

`regs` counts the distinct `slot` values over the group. This is the operational definition of the
wide-load/broadcast distinction from section 3.3.1, and the docstring flags it: *counted, not
declared*.

**Complexity.** `group` is `O(extent)` carrier evaluations, and `regs` is `O(extent)` on top of that.
`extent` here is the operand's tile count along the merged axes — on shipping shapes it is 2 or 4,
and the flat tile count `T` used by `geometry.quantum_axes` (which drives most quantum evaluation) is
at most 16. An `Expr.eval` is a handful of integer operations. The whole quantum machinery is
therefore free at build time. If it ever is not — say a hypothetical 8×8 wave tile with four live
axes — the fix is memoization on `carrier_of`, which is a pure function of `(id(self), t,
frozenset(env))`; there is no algorithmic problem to solve, only a caching one.

**Sharp edge.** `group(t, extent)` clamps `extent` to at least 1 via `max(1, extent)`, so
`group(t, 0)` returns the group computed over the single coordinate `0`, not the empty tuple. A
caller that passes a genuinely zero extent gets a silent wrong answer rather than an error. No
current caller can pass zero (extents are clamped positive throughout `geometry`), but the clamp is
the same defensive habit section 2.1 flags in `latalg`.

#### 3.4 `Load` — the transfer op-class

##### 3.4.1 Concept and the full field list

`Load` is one of the two payload types an `Inst` can carry. It names a transfer: move `tokens` from
space `src` to space `dst`. It is frozen. Every field, with what sets it and what reads it:

| Field | Type / default | Meaning | Set by | Read by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tokens` | `tuple` (required) | The op-class names moved together. `len > 1` is a **fused** load: one hardware instruction carrying several operands, still one completion. | `emit._copy_inst` (all members of a fusion group), `emit.read_inst` (`(op.name,)`) | `ledger.discharge_once.produces`, `ledger.check_ledger_discharged`, `loopir_to_gir._convert_load`, `render._load_line`, `validate` P5 |
| `src` | `str` (required) | A `Space.*` value. | the hop | `Load.counter`, `loopir_to_gir` |
| `dst` | `str` (required) | A `Space.*` value. | the hop | `Load.counter`, `sigma_c` |
| `kiter` | `int` (required) | The reduction-chunk iteration this op feeds — the issue coordinate. | always `0` today | nothing |
| `part` | `int = 0` | Which transfer of a multi-instruction load this is. | always `0` today | nothing |
| `n_parts` | `int = 1` | How many transfers this tile splits into; `1` means not split. | always `1` today | `render._load_line` (prints `/N` when `> 1`) |
| `coord` | `tuple = ()` | The semantic position this transfer fills, as `((axis, value), …)`. | `emit.read_inst`, `emit._copy_inst` | everything that locates an instance |
| `size_regs` | `int = 0` | Registers **one instruction** moves. | `emit.read_inst` via `sizing.frag_regs` | `loopir_to_gir`, `render` |
| `size_bytes` | `int = 0` | Bytes one instruction moves, for a shared destination. | `emit._copy_inst` | `loopir_to_gir`, `render` |
| `advance` | `int = 0` | The read-ahead this transfer carries, in flat presence positions. | `emit.read_inst` | `sigma_c.order_sigma_c`, `render._load_line` |
| `quantum` | `object = None` | A `QuantumMap`, or `None` for the identity merge. | `emit.read_inst` via `_read_quantum` | `loopir_to_gir`, `Lowering/gir/quantum.py` |

Three of these — `kiter`, `part`, `n_parts` — are **structurally dead in the shipping emitter**, and
that deserves saying plainly rather than leaving a reader to grep for it.

* `kiter` is documented as "the K-loop iteration this op feeds — the issue coordinate", and it is a
  genuine concept, but the rolled IR does not enumerate iterations: the enclosing `Loop` supplies the
  chunk index, so every constructed `Load` passes `0` positionally and nothing reads the field. Under
  an unrolled per-instance IR it would be the instance's chunk. It is a vestige of the enumerated
  form described in section 3.1.1.
* `part` / `n_parts` are the **intra-tile transfer fan-out** of one movement, and `emit._copy_inst`
  carries a long comment specifically to stop a reader confusing them with the region count: a
  region-split copy emits *separate* `Inst`s per region (region 0 and region 1 of `A` are distinct
  movements of one op-class, not sub-transfers of one movement), so the region is a *coordinate*,
  carried in `coord`, while `part`/`n_parts` would describe splitting one movement across several
  hardware transfers — which the model does not do. They are wired only into `render._load_line`,
  which prints `/N` when `n_parts > 1`, a branch no shipping dump reaches.

Deleting the three would be a defensible cleanup; keeping them is also defensible because they are
the fields a per-instance expansion layer (section 3.1.1) would immediately need. What is *not*
defensible is leaving a future reader to discover by experiment that `kiter` is always zero, which is
why it is recorded here.

##### 3.4.2 `Load.counter` — a derived property, never a stored field

```python
@property
def counter(self) -> str:
    return HOP_COUNTER[(self.src, self.dst)]
```

The completion class is derived from the hop on every access rather than stored at construction. The
rationale in section 3.2.3 applies: one table, one extension point, and no possibility of a node
whose stored counter disagrees with its own `src`/`dst`. The only consumer is `render._load_line`
(via `render._counter_tag`); the ledger reads `theta.Hop.counter`, which is the same lookup on the
schedule-point side. Cost is a dict hit per render.

##### 3.4.3 `Load.semantic` — the fold key, currently unread

```python
@property
def semantic(self):
    return ("load", self.tokens, self.src, self.dst, self.size_regs, self.size_bytes)
```

The identity for folding a run of equal-`semantic` ops: two `Load`s equal here differ *only* by index
or offset. The docstring notes that `counter` is omitted because it is derived from `src`/`dst` and
would be redundant.

**This property has no consumer anywhere in the tree.** A grep for `semantic` across
`Tensile/` finds only unrelated uses of the English word. It is retained deliberately, as step 2 of
the address re-add recipe states: an expansion pass that fans one rolled `Inst` into per-lane
instances needs a key to re-collapse them on for display, and this is that key. A future maintainer
should either use it for that purpose or delete it together with `Mma.semantic` and `Inst.semantic`;
what they should not do is assume some pass depends on it.

Note the field selection: `coord` and `advance` are **excluded**, which is what makes the key a
*run-fold* key (adjacent instances differing only in position collapse) rather than an identity. If
you extend `Load` with a field that changes what the instruction *is* rather than where it points,
add it here too.

##### 3.4.4 `coord` — the semantic position

`coord` is a tuple of `(axis_name, value)` pairs, where `value` may be `None`. `None` means *the
enclosing `Loop` for that axis supplies the digit* — this is what makes the IR rolled. A concrete int
means the position is pinned (a peel step, or a read-ahead-shifted coordinate).

The two producers fill it differently and the difference matters:

* `emit.read_inst` builds `coord` over the operand's **presence modes only** (section 1.3). A
  broadcast axis carries no coordinate at all — not `(axis, None)`, but absent. When the read carries
  a read-ahead shift, the shift is re-decomposed per presence mode by `placement._shifted_coord`, so
  the advance *carries out of the reduction axis into the free modes* rather than wrapping inside
  the tile.
* `emit._copy_inst` builds `coord` as `((axis, None), …)` over **every axis the movement is
  enumerated by** — and there is a measured defect behind that wording. A copy split into
  `M_split × K_split` regions is correctly wrapped in both loops and emits the right *number* of
  instances, but an earlier version named only the representative axis in the coordinate, so every
  instance carried `{'K_split': v}` alone. The downstream region walk reads the coord; with the
  `M_split` digit missing it computed no flat region index, dropped the movement, and emitted **no
  region increment at all** — the descriptor never walked `A`'s regions. A 90-configuration sweep
  passed for weeks over a walk that did not exist, because the checker skipped instances whose flat
  index was undefined. The lesson generalizes past this field: *a coordinate must name every axis
  whose enclosing loop supplies one of its digits*, or the value that loop supplies is never
  recorded anywhere.

##### 3.4.5 `advance` — the prefetch/in-place shape

`advance` is the read-ahead this transfer carries, measured in **flat presence positions** (the
group's read-ahead depth multiplied by the reduction mode's traversal stride). Two values matter, and
they are a shape, not a magnitude:

* `advance == 0` is **INPLACE**: the read is *not* hoisted. It issues in place, one line before the
  compute op that consumes it.
* `advance != 0` is **PREFETCH**: the read is hoisted ahead of the consumer it feeds.

The field is on the node even though it is derivable from `coord` (at zero advance every coordinate
value is `None`), and the docstring justifies the redundancy: the shape is a first-class fact of the
schedule, not a side effect of how the coordinate happened to be rendered.

What actually consumes it is `sigma_c.order_sigma_c`, and the reason is subtle enough to restate.
The issue-order refinement defers a refill past the consumers whose registers it overwrites. An
INPLACE read has **nothing to defer**: it is already positioned after the consumer it vacates — that
consumer belongs to the *previous* generation, across the loop back edge — and moving it past *this*
generation's consumer would strand that consumer with a register nothing filled. So `sigma_c` tests
`getattr(m.op, "advance", 0)` and only defers hoisted refills. Getting this wrong does not produce an
error; it produces a schedule that reads a register before anything wrote it.

`render._load_line` prints `advance=N` when non-zero. That printing was added late (work item #289):
before it, the per-instruction prefetch/in-place answer was only inferable from where the line
happened to sit in the dump, while the per-group depth was visible in a different view entirely.

##### 3.4.6 `quantum` on the node, and why it is not redundant with `coord`

`Load.quantum` holds the `QuantumMap` (section 3.3) for this transfer, or `None`. The docstring
argues at length that it is not redundant with `coord`, and the argument is the presence rule from
section 1.9: an axis absorbed into the quantum is **absent from that hop's presence set**, so it does
not appear in `coord` *at all*. Without the quantum on the node, the node says "one transfer, one
coordinate" while the hardware instruction fills the whole product of the absorbed extents — and
every consumer sitting at a non-leader coordinate looks unfed.

`theta.Hop.quantum` carries the same `QuantumMap`; the node copy is what survives into the IR.
`Lowering/loopir_to_gir` expands it into one register `Ref` per covered coordinate, so **one
instruction produces several definitions**. That is the SSA-honest reading of a multi-tile load, and
it is what lets reaching-definition analysis match the second tile's compute op to the load that
actually filled its register.

The concrete failure this prevents was measured: with an MX scale read whose quantum absorbs the
operand's entire presence set, the scale read was emitted **zero times** — the presence set emptied,
so there was no level at which to place it. Both halves of that (the emission and the coverage) had
to be fixed together.

Today `quantum` is `None` in every shipping kernel except the MX scale read path, which is why
`test_loopmodel.test_a_load_line_shows_its_quantum_and_advance_and_a_wmma_names_its_real_operands`
constructs a `QuantumMap` by hand rather than going through a kernel: an unexercised branch that
prints the wrong thing is still wrong.

#### 3.5 `Mma` — the compute op-class

##### 3.5.1 Fields

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Mma:
    a: str; b: str; acc: str
    kiter: int
    coord: tuple = ()
    scales: tuple = ()
    block: str = ""
```

One matrix-multiply-accumulate: `acc += a * b`, optionally scaled. `a` / `b` / `acc` are **display
strings** naming the operands (`emit.wmma_inst` passes `"A[m,k]"`, `"B[n,k]"`, `"C[m,n]"`). `coord`
