locates the op in the compute grid as `((axis, value), …)`, with `None` values supplied by the
enclosing loops, exactly as on `Load`. `scales` is a tuple of display strings for the scale operands
(`("MXSA[m,k]", "MXSB[n,k]")` when the configuration is MX-scaled, else empty). `block` names the
hardware group this lane-level op belongs to — the set of ops issued together — and
`emit.wmma_inst` sets it to `"A(k)*B(k)"`.

`kiter` is `0` on every constructed `Mma` and is read by nothing, for the same reason as on `Load`.

The sharp edge here is that `a` / `b` / `acc` / `scales` are **strings for humans**, and real operand
identity comes from elsewhere. `loopir_to_gir._convert_mma` says so in a comment and derives the
operands from the enclosing read list instead. This is a genuine weakness — the binary `A`/`B`
literals in `emit.wmma_inst` are exactly the kind of two-input assumption the MX work exists to
remove — and it produced a real invisibility defect: the renderer's `_mma_line` hard-coded
`C[...] += A*B` and never read these fields at all, so a decoder naming the wrong operand rendered
identically to one naming the right one. That was fixed on the renderer side (the line now reads the
fields); the underlying string-typing is still there.

##### 3.5.2 `Mma.semantic`

```python
@property
def semantic(self):
    return ("mma", self.block or tuple(ax for ax, _ in self.coord), bool(self.scales))
```

Two compute ops fold together iff they belong to the same hardware `block` — falling back to the
*axis names* of the coordinate when `block` is empty — and agree on whether they are scaled. Like
`Load.semantic`, it has **no consumer today** and exists as the re-collapse key for a hypothetical
expansion view. The fallback to axis names (not axis *values*) is what makes it a run-fold key: two
ops at different points of the same grid have the same semantic.

#### 3.6 `Expr` — the symbolic index language

##### 3.6.1 What problem it solves

The IR is rolled, so a rotation slot cannot be an integer: the slot of the read in the steady body is
`iter % 2`, and which of `0` or `1` it is depends on a loop index that does not exist until the
backend materializes the loop. `Expr` is the smallest language that can write down every index the
decoder needs, and it is deliberately *tiny* — no general arithmetic tree, no operators, no parser.
It is a **flat record with four independent contributions**, summed, then optionally reduced mod a
modulus. Every consumer either evaluates it (`eval`), asks what it depends on (`free_vars`), or
prints it (`render`); nobody pattern-matches on its structure except `loopir_to_gir._expr_raw`, which
evaluates it without the modulus.

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Expr:
    var:    str = ""     # a single loop-mode name, or "" for a constant
    mod:    int = 0      # modulus; 0 means no reduction
    add:    int = 0      # constant offset
    terms:  tuple = ()   # ((mode, coef), …) mixed radix; SUPERSEDES `var` when non-empty
    digits: tuple = ()   # (terms, add, ((coef, div, ext), …))
    carry:  tuple = ()   # (terms, add, div)
```

##### 3.6.2 The four contributions, and what each is for

**(a) The single-variable form `(var + add) % mod`.** A shifted coordinate, or a rotation slot over
one loop mode. `Expr(var="iter", mod=2)` is "which half of a double-buffered shared ring this chunk
uses". `Expr(var="", add=3)` is the constant 3, which is what `cst` builds.

**(b) `terms` — the mixed-radix linear form `(Σ coef·var + add) % mod`.** A rotation slot whose
register group cycles over *several* rate modes: the rotation width ranges over the product of the
group's rate modes, not over one mode, so the slot index is a weighted sum of several loop indices.
`placement` builds this at one site (`Expr(mod=d, terms=tuple(reversed(terms)))`). When `terms` is
non-empty it **supersedes** `var` — `var` is not added on top. That is a silent precedence rule, and
it is the one structural trap in the type: an `Expr` with both `var` and `terms` set silently drops
`var`. Nothing constructs one, and nothing checks.

**(c) `carry` — a floor-divided rollover.** The tuple is `(carry_terms, add, div)` and contributes

```
+ (add + Σ coef·env[mode]) // div       over carry_terms = ((mode, coef), …)
```

This models the read-ahead **rolling over into the next reduction chunk**. A read at flat traversal
position `P = Σ stride(m)·index(m)` that fetches `P + shift` targets chunk
`iter + (P + shift) // N_inner`, where `N_inner` is the number of positions in a chunk. With the
reduction axis outermost-of-the-inner-nest this collapses to the familiar single-mode
`iter + (K + dr) // S_sub`; under any other traversal order it is the general carry, and it is what
keeps the shared-buffer sequence **monotone** — one swap per back edge, which a pointer toggle can
express. `add` is the shift; `div` is `N_inner`. Two sites build it: `placement._readahead_carry`
(returning `Expr(carry=(cterms, shift, stride), mod=ext)`) and `placement._read_placement` for the
shared source slot (`Expr(var=outer_var, mod=sd, carry=(cterms, shift, n_pres))` — note this one uses
`var` *and* `carry` together, which is legal and additive; only `terms` supersedes `var`).

**(d) `digits` — several mixed-radix digits of one shifted position.** The tuple is
`(terms, add, ((coef, div, ext), …))` and contributes

```
+ Σ coef · (((add + Σ c·env[m]) // div) mod ext)
```

Where `carry` extracts *one* floor-divided quantity, `digits` extracts *several digits of the same
shifted position* `P + add` and recombines them in mixed radix. This is what a rotation slot needs
when the group cycles over more than one reduction rate mode: the shifted rate index is
`Σ radix_m · digit_m(P + shift)`, and each `digit_m` is its own `(// stride_m) mod ext_m`. With a
single rate mode it degenerates to one digit and coincides with `carry` whenever the outer `mod`
equals that mode's extent — which is every group under the default width policy, and is why the
field could be added late without disturbing existing configurations (work item #254).

`digits` is also the field `KernelWriter._loopModelTarget` uses to express a movement quantum
without needing a division operator in the language: `carrier = Expr(digits=(((t,1),), 0, ((1, tpr,
BIG),)))` is `t // tpr` (one digit, divisor `tpr`, extent chosen large enough not to wrap), and
`slot = Expr(digits=(((t,1),), 0, ((1, 1, tpr),)))` is `t % tpr`. So the quantum's two expressions
are ordinary `Expr`s, which is what lets `QuantumMap` reuse the whole vocabulary instead of
inventing one.

##### 3.6.3 `free_vars()`

```python
def free_vars(self) -> set:
    names = set()
    if self.var: names.add(self.var)
    names.update(m for m, _c in self.terms)
    if self.carry:  names.update(m for m, _c in self.carry[0])
    if self.digits: names.update(m for m, _c in self.digits[0])
    return names
```

The set of mode names this expression references. Its docstring states the invariant that makes it
necessary: **`eval` substitutes 0 for an unknown name rather than failing**, so "is this expression
resolvable in this environment?" is a question `eval` cannot answer and `free_vars` must. There is
exactly one implementation, and three places need it — `Bind.bound_env` (section 3.14),
`Placement.at`'s `_fix` (section 3.7.3), and `validate._unbound_placement_refs`.

Note that `free_vars` collects `var` even when `terms` is non-empty and therefore supersedes it. That
over-approximates (it reports a dependency `eval` will ignore), which is the safe direction for every
current caller — an over-approximation means "treat it as unresolved", which loses precision, never
soundness.

##### 3.6.4 `eval(env)`

```
eval(env):
    if terms:  v = add + Σ coef·env.get(mode, 0)
    else:      v = (env.get(var, 0) if var else 0) + add
    if digits: (dterms, a, fields) = digits
               pos = a + Σ c·env.get(m, 0)
               v += Σ coef · ((pos // max(1,div)) % max(1,ext))
    if carry:  (cterms, a, d) = carry
               v += (a + Σ c·env.get(m, 0)) // max(1, d)
    return v % mod if mod else v
```

`env` is a plain dict of `name → int`. The `max(1, …)` guards make a zero divisor or a zero extent
behave as 1 instead of raising `ZeroDivisionError`; that is defensive rather than meaningful, and it
converts a construction bug into a wrong number.

The behaviour that matters most is `env.get(name, 0)`: **an unbound name evaluates to zero, silently
and by design.** This makes the renderer able to print a partially-bound tree without crashing, and
it is precisely the property that caused a real defect in that renderer (section 3.7.3). Every caller
that cannot tolerate a fabricated zero must gate on `free_vars` first.

##### 3.6.5 `render()`

Produces the human string. The shape is: build a `body` from `terms` (or `var`, or the bare
constant), append the `carry` term as `+(inner)//div`, append each `digits` field as
`(inner)//div%ext` (with a `coef*` prefix when the coefficient is not 1), and finally wrap in
`(body)%mod` **only if** there is at least one symbolic contribution — a pure constant with a modulus
renders as the constant, not as `(3)%2`.

One detail is worth keeping if you rewrite this: the single-var branch formats the offset with
`f"{self.add:+d}"`, producing `iter-1` rather than `iter+-1` for a negative offset. That is the kind
of thing that is invisible until a dump is diffed against a previous one.

`render` is display-only. Nothing parses it back, and nothing should — the entire reason `Pred`
exists in structured form (section 3.8) is that a previous revision *did* have a consumer parse a
predicate string.

##### 3.6.6 `cst(n)`

```python
def cst(n: int) -> Expr:
    return Expr(var="", add=int(n))
```

The constant expression. Note `mod=0`, i.e. **no modulus**. That is the right default for a constant
coordinate but it is the wrong thing for a *pinned rotation slot*, and `Placement.at` exists partly
because of it — see section 3.7.3, where using `cst(value)` would drop the ring width.

##### 3.6.7 Derivation, cost, and advice

**Why a flat record and not an expression tree.** Four independent, summed contributions cover every
index the decoder has needed in two years of work: a shifted coordinate, a one-mode ring, a
multi-mode ring, a chunk rollover, and a multi-digit rollover. A general tree (`Add`, `Mul`, `Mod`,
`FloorDiv` nodes) would express all of these and more, but it would force every consumer to
implement a visitor, and the two consumers that matter — `eval` and `free_vars` — are currently four
and seven lines. The flat form also makes the type trivially hashable and comparable, which several
call sites rely on implicitly (`Expr` instances land in tuples that get compared).

**What it costs.** `eval` is `O(#terms + #digit-fields)` integer operations, and the largest observed
term count is 3 (a two-axis register rotation plus a chunk term). It is called once per rendered
line, once per GIR node constructed, and inside `geometry.quantum_axes`'s constancy scan — the last
of which is the only place the count can grow, and section 2.2.3 bounds that at well under a
thousand evaluations. There is no compile-time cost here worth optimizing.

**What breaks if you change it.** Three things:

1. **Adding a fifth contribution** means touching `eval`, `free_vars`, `render`, `Pred._runtime`
   (which re-implements the free-variable scan — see the defect noted in section 3.8.3), and
   `loopir_to_gir._expr_raw`. That is five sites, and `Pred._runtime` is the one that will be
   forgotten, because it is a duplicate rather than a caller.
2. **Changing the `terms`-supersedes-`var` precedence** silently changes every slot expression that
   sets both. None does today, so the safe move is to *forbid* it: a `__post_init__` raising when
   both are set costs nothing and removes the trap.
3. **Making `eval` raise on an unbound name** would be the principled fix for the fabricated-zero
   problem, and it is tempting. Do not do it without auditing the renderer: `render_unrolled`
   deliberately evaluates partially-bound expressions, and section 3.7.3 records that a related
   change to make symbolic retention unconditional broke 409 tests.

**Concrete advice for a future extender.** If you need a new index shape, first check whether it is
`digits` with a different field list — `digits` is general enough to express `//`, `%`, and their
composition over an affine position, which is most of what a mixed-radix traversal needs. If you
genuinely need a new shape, add it as a fifth *field* (not a nested tree), and add a
`test_loopmodel` case that pins `eval` and `render` on a hand-computed value, because there is no
oracle in this tree to check an index formula against.

#### 3.7 `Placement` — logical storage, and the symbolic-retention decision

##### 3.7.1 The abstraction

`Placement` names the **logical** storage an instance reads or writes. It is explicitly *not* the
physical register colour — colouring is a downstream lowering. Fields:

| Field | Type / default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `space` | `str` | `global` / `shared` / `register`, taken from the hop. |
| `slots` | `tuple = (("", Expr()),)` | **Per register group**, the rotation slot as a symbolic `Expr`: a tuple of `(group-label, Expr)` pairs. |
| `reg_off` | `int = 0` | Offset of this fragment within its buffer, in registers. |
| `byte_off` | `int = 0` | The same, in bytes. |
| `src_slot` | `object = None` | For a shared→register read: the **source** shared-buffer generation, as an `Expr`. |

`slots` being a *list of labelled slots* rather than one slot is what supports a fragment split into
several reuse groups with different rotation policies. The docstring's example is a two-half register
fragment where the low half rotates a 2-ring and the high half stays in place:
`(("lo", Expr(var="min", mod=2)), ("hi", Expr()))`. A shared or global placement carries the single
unlabelled slot `(("", Expr(...)),)`, and `render` special-cases exactly that shape.

`src_slot` is the read's **consume** side, and it is distinct from `slots` (the register
*destination*). Its modulus is the shared ring depth: `mod > 1` means the shared buffer
double-buffers and swaps at the reduction-chunk boundary; `mod <= 1` means a single in-place shared
buffer with no swap. It is `None` when the read has no shared source — a direct global→register
transfer. Carrying it on the read is what lets a consumer select the right shared half without
re-deriving the generation; before it existed, only the copy knew which buffer it had filled.

##### 3.7.2 `Placement.render()`

Formats as `space[buf<slot>]` for the single-unlabelled-slot case and
`space[g0=buf<e0>,g1=buf<e1>]` when the slots are labelled, then appends `<-lds[buf<src_slot>]` if
there is a source slot, then `@r<reg_off>` or (failing that) `@b<byte_off>`. The `elif` on the
offsets means a placement carrying *both* offsets prints only the register one; no producer sets
both.

The `<-lds[` marker is the string several unit tests key on to find the shared source of a read in a
dump — `test_loopmodel`'s drain-slot test splits lines on it — so it is effectively part of the
contract even though it is a display string.

##### 3.7.3 `Placement.at(env, keep_unresolved=False)` and its nested `_fix`

This is the most consequential eight lines in the module, so it is worth reading in full:

```python
def at(self, env, keep_unresolved=False):
    def _fix(e):
        if keep_unresolved and (e.free_vars() - set(env or {})):
            return e
        return Expr(var="", add=e.eval(env), mod=e.mod)   # concrete value, keep the modulus
    return Placement(self.space,
                     tuple((g, _fix(e)) for g, e in self.slots),
                     self.reg_off, self.byte_off,
                     src_slot=(_fix(self.src_slot) if self.src_slot is not None else None))
```

**What it computes.** A new `Placement` with each slot expression evaluated in `env` to its concrete
buffer *value*, **while preserving the ring modulus**. That second half is not cosmetic. A pinned
prologue or drain read must show a concrete buffer index *and* still carry the rotation width, which
a downstream consumer (the GIR register-band computation) reads off `slot.mod`. Emitting `cst(value)`
would give `mod=0` and silently drop the width — every group would look like a 1-deep ring. Hence
`Expr(var="", add=e.eval(env), mod=e.mod)` rather than `cst(e.eval(env))`.

`at` is pure: it returns a new `Placement` and never mutates. It is called from
`emit.fill_reads` (concrete slots for a prologue coordinate), from `render._reg_slots`'s caller when
an environment is available, and from `render.render_unrolled` with `keep_unresolved=True`.

**The `keep_unresolved` option, and the lesson attached to it.** The default is `False`, which
resolves *everything* — including expressions whose free variables the environment does not bind, in
which case `Expr.eval` substitutes 0 (section 3.6.4) and the placement shows buffer 0.

That default is wrong for exactly one consumer and right for every other. The renderer's unrolled
view walks the drain body with `iter` deliberately unbound — the drain's chunk index depends on the
runtime trip count, so there is no honest value to bind — and so every drain read was rendered in the
*first steady trip's* frame: a buffer index the schedule never chose, printed indistinguishably from
one it did. That is a fabricated fact in a debug dump, which is worse than a missing one, because the
dump is what a developer diffs against real assembly.

The fix was to make retention **opt-in**, and the reason it is opt-in rather than the new default is
measured, not theoretical: *making retention unconditional broke 409 tests and both codegen paths.*
That number is the honest measure of how much downstream code assumes a concrete `Placement`. The
codegen consumer (`loopir_to_gir`) calls `pl.src_slot.eval(env)` and `_expr_raw(...)` and needs an
integer; the register namer needs a concrete slot to build a name from; `validate` P5 asserts that a
read at a pinned coordinate resolves to a concrete slot. Handing any of them a symbolic `Expr` does
not fail loudly — it fails as a `TypeError` deep in a formatting call or, worse, as a name that does
not match its own definition. So: **`at` is on the codegen path, and the codegen path must always
receive a concrete `Placement`.** If you are tempted to flip the default, the 409 is the number you
are volunteering to work through.

**Resolution is per-`Expr`, not per-`Placement`, and that is also load-bearing.** A drain read's
*register* slot is genuinely resolvable in the renderer's environment while its *LDS source* slot is
not. Blanking both would hide a number that is real — the same defect pointing the other way. So the
test is inside `_fix`, applied to each slot and to `src_slot` independently.

**The unit-test contract.** `test_loopmodel.test_the_unrolled_drain_does_not_invent_a_buffer_index_for_unbound_iter`
(the test whose body is quoted in section 3.7.4 below) pins all three halves:

```python
free = Expr(var="iter", mod=2)
pl   = Placement("register", (("g0", Expr(var="", add=1, mod=2)),), 0, 0, src_slot=free)
kept = pl.at({}, keep_unresolved=True)
assert kept.src_slot is free                      # unresolvable slot handed back UNTOUCHED (identity)
assert kept.slots[0][1].free_vars() == set()      # resolvable slot still pinned
assert pl.at({}).src_slot is not free             # the DEFAULT is unchanged
```

The `is` comparisons are deliberate: `_fix` returns the *same object* on the retention path, so a
future refactor that rebuilds an equal-but-distinct `Expr` will trip the test. The same test also
asserts non-vacuity at the dump level — some *steady* read must render a concrete LDS slot — so the
drain assertion cannot be satisfied by a renderer that simply stops pinning anything.

##### 3.7.4 Cost, and advice

`at` is `O(#slots)` expression evaluations plus, on the retention path, `O(#slots)` `free_vars`
computations; `#slots` is 1 or 2. It allocates a fresh `Placement` and fresh `Expr`s per call, which
happens once per rendered line and once per prologue fill instance — a few thousand small objects for
a large kernel, which is nothing next to the rest of kernel generation.

Advice, in decreasing order of value:

* **Do not add a third mode.** The right shape for "how much do I resolve" is the boolean it already
  is, applied per-`Expr`. A three-valued policy would immediately need a policy object, and the two
  callers want opposite ends.
* If you need `at` to be *faster* (it is not currently hot), the cheap win is skipping the rebuild
  when `free_vars()` is empty and `mod` already matches — a placement whose slots are already
  concrete is returned unchanged. That is a two-line change with no semantic effect.
* If you add a field to `Placement`, remember `at` reconstructs positionally: `Placement(self.space,
  <slots>, self.reg_off, self.byte_off, src_slot=...)`. A new field added anywhere but the end will
  be silently dropped by `at` while every other code path keeps it — a divergence that shows up only
  after the placement round-trips.

#### 3.8 `Pred` and `_PRED_OPS` — structured predicates

##### 3.8.1 Concept, and what it replaced

A guard in the emitted tree is a comparison: "the trip count is at least the peel depth", "this
substep index is below the read-ahead bound", "this is the first touch of the enclosing mode". `Pred`
is that comparison as a structured object:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Pred:
    lhs: Expr
    op:  str
    rhs: object = 0        # int OR Expr
```

The left side **reuses `Expr`** — the same mixed-radix/carry index language — so there is no second
formula language in the IR. The right side is either an `int` (the common guard or residue pin, e.g.
`T >= 2`) or another `Expr` (a symbolic bound such as the steady back edge `iter < T − M`, where the
bound depends on the runtime trip). Both are read **by field**.

What it replaced was a free-form string on `Cond.pred`, which forced the lowering to parse it; the
commit message for the change describes the parser as "lots of special rules". The failure mode of a
parsed predicate is not that it crashes — it is that a new guard shape produces a string the parser
almost handles.

Three canonical instances, from the docstring:

| Guard | `Pred` |
|---|---|
| peel validity `T ≥ M` | `Pred(Expr(var="T"), ">=", M)` |
| drain-step residue pin `iter%2 == 1` | `Pred(Expr(var="iter", mod=2), "==", 1)` |
| first touch `M_inner == 0` | `Pred(Expr(var="M_inner"), "==", 0)` |

##### 3.8.2 `_PRED_OPS` and `__post_init__`

```python
import operator as _operator
_PRED_OPS = {">=": ge, ">": gt, "==": eq, "<": lt, "<=": le, "!=": ne}
```

A module-level dispatch table from operator string to the `operator` module's function. One table,
evaluated the same way everywhere, so there are no per-call `if` chains and adding an operator is one
row. `Pred.__post_init__` raises `ValueError` when `op` is not a key:

```python
def __post_init__(self):
    if self.op not in _PRED_OPS:
        raise ValueError(f"Pred.op {self.op!r} not in {sorted(_PRED_OPS)}")
```

This is the same closed-vocabulary discipline as the obligation kinds (section 3.9): the check
happens once, at construction, rather than at each of the places that would otherwise dispatch.
`test_loopmodel.test_pred_structured_eval_and_render` pins it by constructing `Pred(Expr(var="x"),
"≈", 0)` inside `pytest.raises(ValueError)` — note the non-ASCII operator, chosen so the test cannot
accidentally pass because of a near-miss with a real operator.

The frozen dataclass plus a validating `__post_init__` is a slightly unusual combination worth
noting: `__post_init__` on a frozen dataclass may *read* fields but may not assign them, so this
pattern only works for validation, never for normalization. If you ever want `Pred` to canonicalize
(say, rewrite `a > b` as `b < a`), you must do it in a factory function, not here.

##### 3.8.3 `Pred._runtime(e, env)` — the static/runtime split

```python
@staticmethod
def _runtime(e, env):
    if not hasattr(e, "eval"):
        return False                                    # a plain int is always known
    syms = ([e.var] if e.var else []) + [m for m, _ in e.terms] + \
           ([m for m, _ in e.carry[0]] if e.carry else [])
    return any(s and s not in env for s in syms)
```

True iff the expression references a symbol absent from `env` — i.e. a runtime problem dimension such
as the trip count `T`, which no compile-time environment can bind. A plain `int` right-hand side is
never runtime.

**This is a duplicate of `Expr.free_vars`, and it is out of date.** It scans `var`, `terms` and
`carry` but **not `digits`**, which was added later. So a `Pred` whose left side uses the `digits`
field and references a mode absent from `env` is classified as *statically known*, and `eval` will
happily evaluate it with that mode substituted as 0 — returning a concrete `True`/`False` where it
should return `None`. No current producer builds such a `Pred` (the only `digits` expressions are
quantum carriers/slots and rotation slots, none of which becomes a predicate left side), so the
defect is latent rather than live. It is exactly the "two derivations of one rule" shape section
2.2.7 describes, and the fix is a one-liner: replace the body with
`return bool(e.free_vars() - set(env or {}))` and delete the local scan. That is the single highest-
value cleanup in this file.

##### 3.8.4 `Pred.eval(env)` and `Pred.render()`

```python
def eval(self, env):
    if self._runtime(self.lhs, env) or self._runtime(self.rhs, env):
        return None
    rv = self.rhs.eval(env) if hasattr(self.rhs, "eval") else self.rhs
    return _PRED_OPS[self.op](self.lhs.eval(env), rv)
```

**Three-valued**: `True`, `False`, or `None` meaning *not statically decidable — this is a runtime
branch*. Consumers depend on the distinction. `render.render_unrolled` honours a resolved guard by
unrolling only the taken arm and emits both arms when the answer is `None`; the same convention
appears in the test-suite walkers (`test_loopmodel`'s `_walk` honours a resolved suppression guard on
a pinned drain substep). A backend lowers a `None` predicate to a real compare-and-branch.

The asymmetry to be aware of: `eval` returns `None` for *runtime*, and Python treats `None` as falsy.
Any consumer that writes `if pred.eval(env):` silently takes the false arm for a runtime predicate.
Every current consumer tests `is None` explicitly first; a new one must too.

`render()` formats as `"<lhs> <op> <rhs>"`, using `rhs.render()` when the right side is an `Expr` and
`str(rhs)` when it is an int. `test_pred_structured_eval_and_render` pins the exact output
`"(iter)%2 == 1"`, which also pins `Expr.render`'s parenthesization rule for a modulus.

##### 3.8.5 Cost and advice

`eval` is two `free_vars`-scale scans plus two `Expr.eval`s — a few dozen integer operations, called
once per guard per rendered view and once per guard during GIR lowering. Nothing to optimize.

If you add a predicate that is not a binary comparison — a conjunction, say — resist adding an `and`
operator to `_PRED_OPS` (the table maps to *binary integer* comparisons, and a conjunction's operands
are predicates, not `Expr`s). The clean extension is a separate node type or a tuple-of-`Pred` field
on `Cond`, so that the three-valued `eval` composes explicitly (`None and False` must be `False`, not
`None`, and no operator table will get that right for you).

#### 3.9 The closed obligation-kind vocabulary

##### 3.9.1 The declaration

```python
RAW_KINDS        = frozenset({"RAW-residency", "crossing-RAW"})
WAR_KINDS        = frozenset({"rotation-WAR", "inplace-WAR"})
OBLIGATION_KINDS = RAW_KINDS | WAR_KINDS
```

These four strings are the ledger's hazard classes (section 1.7 defines what each one means), and
**this is the only place in the tree where the set is enumerated** (work item #276, step 1). Anything
that needs to know whether a kind is a true dependency or an anti-dependency asks here.

Note what is *not* in the set: `readahead-residency`. The ledger constructs obligations of that kind,
but they are a structural requirement on the prologue rather than a wait — they are checked directly
against the prologue body instead of being turned into an `Await` — so they are deliberately excluded
and never reach `is_war`. `emit`'s await-index builder skips them explicitly. If you add
`readahead-residency` to `RAW_KINDS` "for completeness", you will make `is_war` accept it and every
downstream branch will start treating a structural check as a schedulable dependency.

##### 3.9.2 `is_war(kind)` and `is_raw(kind)`

```python
def is_war(kind: str) -> bool:
    if kind not in OBLIGATION_KINDS:
        raise ValueError("unknown obligation kind %r — the ledger hazard classes are a CLOSED "
                         "set %s.  Add the new kind to RAW_KINDS or WAR_KINDS in LoopModel/ir.py; "
                         "do not let it default, because every issue-order and await decision "
                         "downstream branches on this answer." % (kind, sorted(OBLIGATION_KINDS)))
    return kind in WAR_KINDS

def is_raw(kind: str) -> bool:
    return not is_war(kind)
```

`is_war` answers "is this an **anti**-dependency — must the writer wait for prior readers?"
`is_raw` is its complement over the closed set, and it inherits the raise: an unknown kind raises
from `is_raw` too, which is the right behaviour and easy to get wrong if you implement `is_raw`
independently.

Callers: `emit.py` at four sites (the await-index filter, the note text, the fused-copy prologue
filter that drops WAR obligations when filling empty buffers, and the prologue fill's await filter),
`sigma_c.is_war_copy`, and — across the package boundary —
`Lowering/gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py`, which partitions an instruction's dependency list into WAR and
RAW buckets with `(war if is_war(kind) else raw).append(...)`. `render.py` and
`Lowering/gir/render.py` use the *set* rather than the predicate, to mark an unrecognised kind in a
dump rather than raising inside a debug view — the right call for a renderer, and a good example of
when to use the set directly.

##### 3.9.3 Why a checked set beats a suffix test — the concrete history

The previous form of this dispatch was `kind.endswith("WAR")`, at **eight** call sites. The docstring
names the problem exactly: that is *a suffix test standing in for a vocabulary*, and it fails in both
directions the moment the vocabulary grows.

* A new anti-dependency whose name does not end in the letters `WAR` silently joins the RAW arm.
* A new true dependency whose name happens to end in those letters — the docstring's hypothetical
  `read-after-WAR` — silently joins the anti-dependency arm.

Neither shows up as an error. **Both show up as a schedule**, which is to say as either a slower
kernel or a wrong answer, discovered on hardware. And it is not hypothetical: `ledger.py` records one
measurement of exactly this failure — matching the suffix forced *copy-last* ordering on
`crossing-RAW` obligations that required *copy-first*, and the fix there was to narrow the test to an
explicit kind. That is one bug already paid for by the suffix form.

The membership test is not merely a tidier spelling. `is_war` is **total over a checked set**, so an
unknown kind raises *here*, once, instead of being silently classified as RAW at eight call sites.
"Not in my list" and "is a true dependency" are different facts, and only one of them is safe to
schedule on. A vocabulary that cannot be extended by accident is the point.

##### 3.9.4 The near-collision with the LDS hazard labels

The source comment flags a second vocabulary that nearly collided with this one:
`Lowering/gir/analyses/lds_hazards.py` defines bare `"RAW"` / `"WAR"` / `"WAW"` labels for *edges in
the LDS hazard graph*. Those are not ledger obligations. But `"WAR"` matches the old suffix test
exactly, so the two vocabularies were one typo away from being cross-dispatched: an LDS hazard-edge
label flowing into `is_war` would have answered `True` and looked entirely normal.

Under the closed set it answers by raising. `test_loopmodel.test_obligation_kind_vocabulary_is_closed`
asserts the disjointness directly, importing `lds_hazards` and checking that neither
`lds_hazards.RAW` nor `lds_hazards.WAR` is a member of `OBLIGATION_KINDS`.

##### 3.9.5 The unit-test contract

`test_loopmodel.test_obligation_kind_vocabulary_is_closed` is the whole contract, and it is worth
enumerating because it pins properties that are easy to break:

1. `RAW_KINDS.isdisjoint(WAR_KINDS)` — the two halves do not overlap.
2. `OBLIGATION_KINDS == RAW_KINDS | WAR_KINDS` — the union is exactly the set.
3. `Await.__dataclass_fields__["kind"].default in OBLIGATION_KINDS` — the *default* value of
   `Await.kind` is itself a member. This catches the specific mistake of renaming a kind and leaving
   the default string behind.
4. For every kind in each half, `is_war` and `is_raw` are exact complements.
5. For each of `"anti-dependence"`, `"read-after-WAR"` and `""`, `is_war` **raises** with a message
   containing `"CLOSED set"`, and the test's failure message spells out what the old suffix test
   answered for each: `False` for the first (a new anti-dependency scheduled as a true dependency)
   and `True` for the second (a true dependency scheduled as an anti-dependency).

A separate test, `test_loopmodel`'s await-rendering check, asserts that every rendered await line
carries `<kind>` for some kind in `OBLIGATION_KINDS` — so the vocabulary is also pinned at the
display layer, where a mis-labelled await would otherwise make a correctly-ordered and a
wrongly-ordered body dump identically.

##### 3.9.6 Advice

Adding a kind is: one line here (choose the correct half — that choice *is* the semantics), and then
grep for `OBLIGATION_KINDS` to find the two renderers. Nothing else needs to change, because every
dispatch goes through `is_war`. Do **not** add a kind that is neither a true nor an anti-dependency
(the `readahead-residency` case); those belong outside the set, checked directly, and the ledger
already demonstrates how.

#### 3.10 `Await` — a named discharge point

##### 3.10.1 The abstraction

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Await:
    dep:     str
    counter: str
    scope:   str = "wave"
    count:   int = -1
    note:    str = ""
    kind:    str = "RAW-residency"
```

An `Await` attached to an `Inst` says: *the value named `dep`, on completion class `counter`, must be
complete within processor scope `scope`, before this instance issues.*

`dep` **names a producer op-class-generation, not a count**. That is the whole design (section 1.11):
a named dependency covers every legal issue order, so a decoder that emits names does not have to
commit to one order. `emit._site_awaits` builds `dep` from the ledger obligation's producer endpoint,
optionally qualified with the generation being consumed.

| Field | Set by | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| `dep` | `emit._site_awaits` from `Obligation.producer` | `ledger.discharge_once`, `ledger.check_ledger_discharged`, `loopir_to_gir._deps_of`, `render._await_line`, `emit`'s dedup key |
| `counter` | the obligation's `Hop.counter` | `ledger.check_ledger_discharged` (coverage), `loopir_to_gir`, `render` |
| `scope` | `emit._scope_of` | `render._await_line`, `emit`'s dedup key |
| `count` | **nothing** | nothing |
| `note` | `emit._site_awaits` | `render._await_line` |
| `kind` | mirrors `Obligation.kind` | `sigma_c`, `emit`, `dep_defuse`, `render` |

##### 3.10.2 `count = -1` — a slot deliberately left empty

`count` is the lowering of a named dependency into a *selector residual* — the numeric "wait until at
most N of these are outstanding" a counter-based backend needs. It is **left unset (`-1`) by this
decoder, and nothing writes it.**

The justification is that two sound backends exist. One materializes a numeric count. The other
discards the markers and re-derives synchronization from the emitted dataflow — its own
counter-insertion pass recomputes the number from what was actually emitted. This decoder targets the
second, so a count computed here would only be overwritten, and the named form is guaranteed to cover
whatever issue order the backend ultimately commits to. The slot exists so a raw counter-based
backend can fill it; that lowering is deferred work.

The design note worth carrying: *the number is a cached derivation, never authored*. If you implement
the count-materializing backend, compute it in a pass over the finished tree and write it into these
slots; do not compute it at `Await` construction time, where the issue order is not yet frozen
(`sigma_c` runs after the awaits are attached).

`render._await_line` prints the count only when it is non-negative, so today it never appears.

##### 3.10.3 `scope` — modelled, printed, and not yet load-bearing

`scope` is the processor scope the discharge must reach: `"wave"` (the default) or `"block"`.
`emit._scope_of` widens a cross-agent dependency to block scope — when the reader and the refiller
are different waves inside one workgroup, program order relates nothing across them, so a wave-scoped
selector does not cover the hazard.

`emit._scope_of`'s own docstring is explicit about the limits of the current implementation, and it
is repeated here because a reader of `ir.py` alone would over-read the field: `scope` today reaches
the differential fence-harness report and the renderer, and the actual barrier emitter never receives
it. So the field is *correct and inert*. Making it load-bearing is tracked work, and it has to be
measured against a known over-synchronization regression — an earlier revision emitted several times
as many barriers as the hand-written path.

Two `Await`s are considered the same for deduplication when `(str(dep), counter, kind, scope)` match
(`emit._copy_inst`'s fused-group union). `note` is deliberately excluded from that key: it is display
text, and two awaits differing only in prose are one await.

##### 3.10.4 `kind` — the field that decides issue order

`kind` is the ledger hazard class of the obligation this `Await` discharges, drawn from the closed
set of section 3.9 and mirroring `Obligation.kind` so there is one source of truth.

It is not decoration. **A `*-WAR` await means its owning instance must be *issued after* those
readers** — an anti-dependency is discharged by position, not only by waiting — and that is precisely
what the issue-order refinement in `sigma_c` uses to place refill copies last. A `RAW-residency`
await means the consumer needs the producer's value and must wait for it.

There is a historical defect attached: an earlier `emit` helper that stamped counts onto awaits
**dropped `kind`** while rebuilding them, which made both the issue-order gate and the downstream WAR
edges vacuous — every await looked like a true dependency, so nothing was ever ordered last and the
gate had nothing to check. The rebuild path was removed. The renderer likewise did not print `kind`
for a long time, with the consequence that a correctly-ordered body and a wrongly-ordered body
produced *identical dumps*; `render._await_line` now prints `<kind>` and appends
`[issue AFTER those readers]` for a WAR.

##### 3.10.5 `note`

Free-form display text, set by `emit._site_awaits` to one of two strings — "refill WAR: slot vacated
by prior read" for an anti-dependency, or the corresponding residency phrasing for a true dependency.
Read only by the renderer. It carries no semantics and must not acquire any; if you find yourself
wanting to branch on `note`, the fact you want belongs in a field.

#### 3.11 `Inst` — one op-class instance

```python
@dataclass
class Inst:
    op:        object          # a Load or an Mma payload
    placement: object = None   # a Placement with symbolic slots — or a dict, see below
    agent:     str = "w0"
    awaits:    tuple = ()

    @property
    def semantic(self):
        return self.op.semantic
```

`Inst` is the tree node that carries a payload. There is **one `Inst` per op-class per level** — the
loop nest around it supplies the iterations, and nothing is enumerated (section 1.11). It is
*mutable* (see section 3.1.2): `sigma_c` reorders instruction lists in place, and several negative
tests mutate an `Inst` list to construct a defective tree.

`Inst.semantic` simply forwards to the payload's `semantic`, and inherits its status: no consumer
(section 3.4.3).

**`agent`.** The issuing agent's role label. `emit` sets it to the module constant
`_SINGLE_ROLE = "w0"` at all four construction sites, and nothing reads it. It is the node-level
half of the agent-assignment component of a schedule point (section 1.1), which is present in the
data model and currently unpopulated; the residual gap there is *exactness*, not expressibility,
because the per-hop agent-relativity flag already carries the fact that actually matters today. The
renderer does not print it either. If you begin populating agents, `render` and `validate` both need
to learn about it in the same change, or you will get a multi-agent tree that dumps as single-agent.

**`awaits`.** A tuple of `Await`. Empty is normal — most instances have no obligation to discharge at
their site. `ledger.all_awaits` walks the tree collecting these, and `ledger.check_ledger_discharged`
checks both *coverage* (every obligation's completion class is awaited somewhere) and *position*
(the discharge sits at a legal point relative to the readers). `ledger._replace_awaits` rebuilds an
`Inst` with a new tuple — one of the few places the mutability is not used, because the payload and
placement are shared by reference.

**`placement` holds two different shapes, and this is the sharpest edge in the node vocabulary.** For
a `Load`, it is a single `Placement`. For an `Mma`, `emit.wmma_inst` sets it to a **dict keyed by
operand name**, `{op.name: Placement}` — the register placement the compute op *consumes*, per read
operand, so that GIR can lower coordinate→register-name for the compute source identically to the way
it does for the read destination. Both are derived from the same `placement._read_placement` helper
(the read carries the read-ahead-shifted slot, the compute op the un-shifted consume slot), which is
what keeps definition and use naming the same register under any loop order.

Every walker therefore has to handle both shapes, and they do it with an `isinstance(pls, dict)`
test — `validate._placement_exprs` is the clearest example:

```python
pls = inst.placement
for pl in (pls.values() if isinstance(pls, dict) else [pls]):
    ...
```

This is a hack, and naming it is the point. The type-honest alternatives are (a) a `placements:
dict` field distinct from `placement`, or (b) a small `PlacementSet` wrapper with a uniform
iteration protocol. Either would be an improvement; both require touching every walker, which is why
neither has happened. If you are adding a *third* consumer of `Inst.placement`, add the wrapper first
— the two-shape rule is currently re-derived in `validate`, `render` and `loopir_to_gir` — the first
two with an `isinstance(pls, dict)` test, the third by dispatching on the node type (`pl =
inst.placement` in the Load path, `pls = inst.placement or {}` in the Mma path) — which is already
three derivations of one rule.

#### 3.12 `Loop` — a real loop level of the rolled nest

##### 3.12.1 Fields

```python
@dataclass
class Loop:
    mode:        str            # the loop index name, e.g. "iter", "substep", "min"
    trip:        object = ""    # the CONTROL EDGE: a Pred (outer) or an int (inner)
    role:        str = "w0"
    bodies:      list = None    # list of body-sequences
    body_ranges: tuple = ()     # per-body half-open (lo, hi); () = each spans the whole trip
    outer:       bool = False   # structural: pipelined runtime level vs statically unrolled level
```

**`trip` is the continuation control edge, not a display extent.** For an `outer` (pipelined,
runtime) loop it is the continuation *predicate* the backend lowers into a back edge — a `Pred` such
as `iter < T − M`. For an inner unrolled level it is the static repeat *count*, a plain `int`. This
is the literal reading of the principle that every control edge in the schedule must be carried in
the IR rather than reconstructed: the steady loop's back edge is a fact of the schedule, so it is a
field.

**`outer` is an explicit structural flag and is never inferred.** `emit` derives it from whether the
mode is one of the schedule point's outer modes. The alternative — inferring it from `trip` being
symbolic rather than an int — was rejected because it conflates two different questions: *which ring
and which peel apply to this level* (a structural fact) versus *what is this level's trip value* (a
quantity). A statically-known outer level would break the inference immediately.

**`role`** is the agent role for this level, defaulting to the single-role `"w0"`. `emit` propagates
it when rebuilding a `Loop` (`_peel_first_touch` and the unrolling helper both copy `n.role`
through), and nothing else reads it. Like `Inst.agent`, it is present-but-inert plumbing for agent
specialization.

##### 3.12.2 Multi-body loops: `bodies`, `body_ranges`, `__post_init__`

An ordinary loop has one body. But a loop level whose body *differs before and after a boundary* can
be emitted as several sub-bodies over disjoint sub-ranges instead of one body carrying a
per-iteration predicate. `bodies` is a list of body-sequences taken in program order, and
`body_ranges[i]` is the half-open `(lo, hi)` range of the trip over which `bodies[i]` runs.

The range is what makes the multi-body form mean anything at all: *without* it, N bodies run
back-to-back every iteration and are indistinguishable from one concatenated body. *With* it, the
emitter can peel a first-touch guard into the loop structure —

```
for m in range(trip):        becomes      for m in [0, 1):   R; Y
    if m == 0: R                          for m in [1, trip): Y
    Y
```

— so the predicate is not evaluated per iteration. `emit._peel_first_touch` performs exactly this
transformation.

`__post_init__` does two things:

```python
if self.bodies is None:
    self.bodies = [[]]
if self.body_ranges and len(self.body_ranges) != len(self.bodies):
    raise ValueError(f"Loop({self.mode}): {len(self.body_ranges)} body_ranges for "
                     f"{len(self.bodies)} bodies — one range per sub-body")
```

The first is the standard mutable-default dance: a dataclass cannot default a field to `[]`, so the
default is `None` and `__post_init__` substitutes a single empty body. The second is the pairing
invariant — either there are no ranges (every body spans the whole trip) or there is exactly one
range per body. A mismatch is a construction error, caught at construction.

##### 3.12.3 `Loop.ranged_bodies()`

```python
def ranged_bodies(self):
    end = self.trip if isinstance(self.trip, int) else None
    if not self.body_ranges:
        return [(0, end, b) for b in self.bodies]
    return [(lo, hi, b) for (lo, hi), b in zip(self.body_ranges, self.bodies)]
```

Returns `[(lo, hi, nodes)]` — each sub-body paired with the half-open iteration range it runs over.
`hi` is `None` when the trip is symbolic (an outer runtime loop), meaning "to the end".

This method is **the authority for the pairing**, and the docstring says so in those words. The rule
it encodes: a consumer that *unrolls* — the renderer, the GIR lowering — must walk each body over its
own range, while a consumer that only wants the instructions can iterate `bodies` directly. What no
consumer may do is zip `bodies` against `body_ranges` at a call site, because the no-ranges case
(where `body_ranges` is empty and every body spans the trip) would zip to nothing and silently drop
every body.

`test_loopmodel`'s multi-body test asserts the agreement directly:

```python
assert [(lo, hi) for lo, hi, _b in lp.ranged_bodies()] == list(lp.body_ranges)
```

which pins that the method does not reorder or synthesize ranges when they are present, and the
surrounding test exercises the empty-ranges path through the renderer.

The `isinstance(self.trip, int)` test deserves a note: `trip` is `""` by default and a `Pred` for an
outer loop, so anything non-int yields `hi = None`. A `Loop` left with the default `trip=""` and no
ranges therefore reports `(0, None, body)` — "spans everything" — which is the harmless answer, but
it does mean a forgotten trip does not announce itself here.

##### 3.12.4 `Loop.body` — a property that raises on purpose

```python
@property
def body(self):
    if len(self.bodies) != 1:
        raise ValueError(f"Loop({self.mode}) has {len(self.bodies)} sub-bodies — use `bodies` or "
                         f"`ranged_bodies()`; `.body` is the single-body convenience only")
    return self.bodies[0]
```

The single-body convenience. It **raises** on a multi-body loop rather than returning `bodies[0]`,
and the docstring gives the reason bluntly: silently returning the first and dropping the rest is how
a `bodies[0]` convenience turns a multi-body schedule into a wrong one — the dropped body is real
work, and nothing downstream would notice its absence.

This is a deliberate, load-bearing exception in a data class, and the test suite depends on it:
`test_loopmodel._walk_bodies`, the helper that yields every mutable instruction list for fixtures
that reorder instructions, carries a comment explaining that it yields the *lists themselves* rather
than their owners precisely because `.body` raises. Note `body` is a *read-only* property with no
setter, so `loop.body = [...]` raises `AttributeError` while `loop.body[:] = [...]` (in-place slice
assignment through the returned list) works — and the latter is the idiom the negative tests use.

##### 3.12.5 Cost and advice for `Loop`

`ranged_bodies` allocates a list per call, `O(#bodies)` with `#bodies` at most 2 or 3. It is called
inside the renderer's and the lowering's recursive descent, so it runs once per loop node per walk —
tens of calls for a large kernel. Irrelevant.

The extension advice is about *what not to do*: if you need a loop whose sub-bodies overlap, or whose
ranges are symbolic, do not widen `body_ranges` to hold `Expr`s. `ranged_bodies` returns ints and
`None`, and both the renderer's unroller and the GIR lowering iterate `range(lo, hi)` over the
result. A symbolic range means the body cannot be unrolled at all, which is a different node — the
right shape is a nested `Loop` with its own `Pred` trip.

#### 3.13 `Branch` — the explicit rotation selector

```python
@dataclass
class Branch:
    mode:    str            # the loop mode the residue is taken over
    modulus: int            # S — the number of residues, hence of arms
    arms:    dict = None    # {residue-int: body-sequence}
    outer:   bool = False   # True iff this pins an OUTER-level residue

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.arms is None:
            self.arms = {}
```

A switch on `selector = mode % modulus`, one arm per residue: arm 0 is the ops that run when the
residue is 0 (using buffer 0), arm 1 the ops for residue 1, and so on. It makes register rotation a
first-class control structure rather than only an index expression. `__post_init__` is the standard
mutable-default substitution.

**No emitter builds a `Branch`.** The rolled IR expresses rotation with the symbolic slot `Expr`
instead — the two are interchangeable views of the same fact, and the code chose the symbolic slot
because it keeps the tree rolled (a `Branch` with `modulus` arms is an unrolling by `modulus`). What
`emit` does build for first-touch guards and peel residue pinning is `Cond` and `Bind`, not `Branch`.

The node is nonetheless kept alive and handled by every walker: `validate._unbound_placement_refs`
treats it as a *binder* (its residue selector introduces `mode` into scope, so a placement under an
arm may legitimately reference it), `render` has three separate `isinstance(node, Branch)` branches
across its three views, and `__init__.py` exports it. `render.render_ir`'s docstring was corrected at
one point specifically because it advertised `Branch` arms that no dump emits.

So: dead as a producer, live as a vocabulary item, and cheap to keep. The one thing to know is that
the `Branch` code paths in the walkers are **untested by any shipping configuration** — if you start
emitting `Branch`, expect the first few walks to be wrong, and add fixtures before you rely on them.
`outer` is the structural marker consistent with `Loop.outer` / `Peel.outer` / `Cond.outer`: it is
`True` when the residue being pinned belongs to an outer level.

#### 3.14 `Bind` — pinning an outer induction over a straight-line body

##### 3.14.1 Concept

```python
@dataclass
class Bind:
    mode:  str            # the outer induction being pinned, e.g. "iter"
    value: object         # an Expr giving the bound value
    body:  list = None

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.body is None:
            self.body = []
```

A prologue or drain step is *one reduction chunk of the peeled outer loop, pinned to its issue
index*. `Bind` is that pin: over the straight-line sub-body, the outer induction `mode` takes the
value `value`.

The concrete assignments the emitter makes:

* prologue step `j` → `iter = j − M` (a concrete `Expr`, since `j` and the peel depth `M` are both
  compile-time),
* drain step `t` → `iter = T − M + t` (symbolic: `T` is the runtime trip count).

Because the value is an `Expr`, **every slot and coordinate under the step sees a defined `iter`**.
That is the improvement over what it replaced: the previous form pinned a peel step with
`Cond(iter % d == residue)`, a predicate over an `iter` that *no enclosing scope defined*. A guard
that constrains a free variable is not a binding — the placement expressions underneath still had
nothing to evaluate against, and `Expr.eval` supplied its silent zero. `validate` property P4 now
rejects that shape explicitly ("drain steps must each be a `Bind`, not a `Cond`/`Branch` pin"), and
`test_loopmodel.test_gate_catches_...` reverts a correct tree to the old free-`iter` `Cond` form to
prove the gate fires.

A walker descending into a `Bind` pushes `env[mode] = value` — or carries it symbolically, which is
the whole subtlety of the next method.

##### 3.14.2 `Bind.bound_env(env)`

```python
def bound_env(self, env):
    v = self.value
    if all(f in env for f in v.free_vars()):
        return {**env, self.mode: v.eval(env)}
    return env
```

Returns `env` extended with `mode → value`, **if and only if `value` is statically resolvable in
`env`**. A prologue step's `j − M` is a constant, so it binds a concrete int. A drain step's
`T − M + t` references the runtime trip symbol `T`, which no compile-time environment contains, so
`bound_env` **leaves `mode` unbound** and returns `env` unchanged.

That asymmetry is deliberate and is the reason `Expr.free_vars` exists as a separate authority
(section 3.6.3): asking `eval` would have produced a number (with `T` silently zero) and there would
have been no way to tell the two cases apart. Leaving the mode unbound keeps the drain body symbolic,
and the GIR lowering then resolves the drain's buffer generation *relative to the steady loop* rather
than pinning a concrete generation that would be wrong for every trip count but one.

Note the method returns the *same* `env` object on the unresolvable path and a *new* dict on the
resolvable one. Callers must use the return value rather than assuming mutation; every current caller
does (`walker(n.body, n.bound_env(env))`).

##### 3.14.3 `Bind.render()`

`f"bind {self.mode} = {self.value.render()}"`. Display only.

##### 3.14.4 Cost and advice

`bound_env` is one `free_vars` set-build plus a dict copy — trivial, called once per `Bind` per walk.
The dict copy is `O(|env|)` with `|env|` bounded by the loop-nest depth (at most 7).

The advice: `Bind` binds *one* mode. If you need a step that pins two (a two-level peel — the tail
loop work will need exactly this), nest two `Bind`s rather than widening `mode`/`value` into
parallel tuples; every walker already recurses through `Bind.body` and will handle nesting for free,
whereas a tuple form needs each walker taught.

#### 3.15 `Peel` — the prologue/drain node

```python
@dataclass
class Peel:
    kind:  str            # 'prologue' | 'drain'
    mode:  str = ""
    k:     object = 0
    body:  list = None
    outer: bool = True

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.body is None:
            self.body = []
```

The hoisted first-`k` (`kind='prologue'`) or last-`k` (`kind='drain'`) iterations of loop `mode`, as
a **straight-line body with no back edge**. Its contents are fixed by the retime matrix: how far ahead
each op-class runs determines what has to be issued before the steady loop can be entered and what
remains to be issued after it exits. It may also hold instances hoisted out of an *enclosed* level —
the cross-level boundary term.

`Peel.__post_init__` is the same mutable-default substitution as everywhere else in this file: a
dataclass cannot default a field to `[]`, so `body` defaults to `None` and is replaced with a fresh
empty list per instance. Without it, every `Peel` in the process would share one list.

`kind` is read structurally: `validate._is_prologue` and `validate._is_drain` test it, `ledger`'s
prologue-coverage check locates the prologue body by it, and `render` labels the stage from it. It is
a two-valued string with no validation; a typo produces a `Peel` that every `_is_prologue` test
silently rejects. Given that `Cond.kind` has a documented four-value vocabulary and `Pred.op` is
validated in `__post_init__`, adding the same two-line check here would be consistent and cheap.

`k` is typed `object` and defaults to `0` because it may be either an int (the concrete peel depth
`M`) or symbolic; `emit` passes the int `M` at both construction sites.

`outer=True` by **construction**, not by inference: a peel is always over an outer level, because the
peel transform applies to the pipelined loop. The field exists so walkers can test `outer` uniformly
across `Loop`, `Branch`, `Peel` and `Cond` rather than special-casing the node type — the same
structural-marker discipline described for `Loop.outer` (section 3.12.1).

`validate._unbound_placement_refs` treats `Peel` as a **non-binder**: it recurses into the body
*without* adding `mode` to the bound set. That is correct and important — a `Peel` states that
iterations were hoisted, it does not say which one this instance is. The `Bind` inside each step is
what supplies that, which is precisely the P3/P4 property the pair enforces together.

#### 3.16 `Cond` — a first-class conditional

##### 3.16.1 Concept

```python
@dataclass
class Cond:
    pred:  object          # a Pred (structured)
    then:  list = None
    els:   list = None
    kind:  str = ""        # the generic, backend-agnostic meaning of this guard
    label: str = ""        # an advisory scaffold hint, set DOWNSTREAM, never by the core
    outer: bool = False    # True iff this pins an OUTER-level step

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.then is None: self.then = []
        if self.els  is None: self.els  = []
```

The primary use is the **peel-validity guard**: a software pipeline's steady region is only reachable
when the loop is long enough to fill and drain the pipe. A too-short loop must take a degenerate path
— skip the steady body entirely and run a chain of pinned steps instead. Making that a *node* rather
than an implicit assumption is what lets a backend lower the boundary correctly from the IR alone;
before it existed, the short-loop path was reconstructed downstream from a comparison the IR did not
contain.

`then` and `els` are body-sequences and either may be empty; `Cond.__post_init__` performs the
mutable-default substitution for **both** of them (`None` → a fresh `[]`), so a consumer may always
iterate either arm without a `None` check. The whole-tree shape `emit` returns when
the peel depth is non-zero is:

```
Cond(kind="peel_validity", pred = T > M,
     then = [ Peel(prologue), Loop(<chunk>, outer=True, trip=Pred(iter < T-M)), Peel(drain) ],
     els  = [ Bind(chunk=0){…}, Cond(T>1){ Bind(chunk=1){…} }, … ])
```

At zero peel depth the guard and both peels vanish and the bare steady `Loop` is returned.

##### 3.16.2 `kind` — the generic vocabulary, and the layering rule it enforces

`kind` carries the **backend-agnostic** meaning of the guard. Four values are produced by `emit`:

| `kind` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `peel_validity` | The pipeline-length guard: the steady region runs only when the trip exceeds the peel depth. |
| `readahead_suppress` | The read-ahead substep would cross the reduction bound, so this read is suppressed at this position. |
| `first_touch` | A read that is invariant over an enclosing mode and should be issued once, on that mode's first iteration. |
| `short_step_validity` | Inside the degenerate arm: this pinned step runs only if the trip reaches it. |

The rule the field encodes is a **layering rule**: the core emits `kind` and *only* `kind` — no
TensileLite scaffold names. The mapping from a generic `kind` to which of the code generator's
labelled branch regions an arm routes to lives entirely in a downstream GIR pass. That pass reads
`kind` and writes `label`.

##### 3.16.3 `label` — advisory, downstream-populated, and gate-enforced empty in the core

`label` is a scaffold-branch hint such as `"toPGR1"`. It is populated by the GIR scaffold pass, never
by the core. A consumer whose own loop-count scaffold already emits the comparison uses the label to
route each arm to its matching region instead of re-emitting the branch; a from-scratch backend
ignores the label entirely and lowers `pred`.

`validate` property P8 enforces that the core leaves it empty. This is a genuinely useful gate: the
temptation to write `label="toPGR1"` at the emit site is strong (it is one line, and the information
is right there), and doing so would put a code-generator-specific string into the layer that is
supposed to have none — the exact violation the whole three-layer split exists to prevent (section
0.2). A gate that fails the build is a better defence than a comment.

##### 3.16.4 `pred` and `outer`

`pred` is a `Pred` (section 3.8) — read by field, never parsed. The docstring's examples are the
validity guard `Pred(Expr(var="T"), ">=", M)` and a step pin
`Pred(Expr(var="iter", mod=2), "==", 1)`; the latter shape is now handled by `Bind` instead
(section 3.14.1), and the docstring's mention of it is a leftover from before that change.

`outer` marks a `Cond` that pins an outer-level *step*, consistent with the `outer` flag on `Loop`,
`Branch` and `Peel`. It is `False` for the peel-validity guard, which is an ordinary conditional and
not a step split — and the distinction matters to walkers that count steps.

##### 3.16.5 How consumers treat `Cond`

* `render.render_unrolled` calls `pred.eval(env)`; on `True` it descends only `then`, on `False` only
  `els`, and on `None` (runtime) it shows both.
* `validate._unbound_placement_refs` recurses into both arms **without** binding anything — a `Cond`
  is not a binder, which is why a `Cond`-based residue pin left `iter` free and P4 now forbids it.
* `Lowering/loopir_to_gir` lowers both arms into real basic blocks and a conditional branch; a later
  GIR pass may then *fold* the degenerate arm into the drain chain when the two are shown to be
  dataflow-equivalent.

#### 3.17 Cross-cutting notes on `ir.py`

##### 3.17.1 Complexity, and where compile-time cost sits

Nothing in this module is a compile-time concern. Every operation is `O(1)` or linear in a quantity
bounded by the loop-nest depth (≤ 7 modes), the slot count (≤ 2), the fusion-group size (≤ 2), or the
tile extent inside a quantum (≤ 4 today, ≤ 16 in the widest plausible shape). The whole IR for a
large kernel is a few hundred nodes, because it is rolled: node count is `O(#op-classes × #levels)`,
independent of trip count and of tile size.

The one place where a caller can make this module hot is `geometry.quantum_axes`, which evaluates a
carrier expression `O(#candidate axes × extent × flat tile count)` times. That cost belongs to
`geometry`, not here, and section 2.2.3 bounds it; the mitigation if it ever matters is memoizing
`QuantumMap.carrier_of`, which is pure.

##### 3.17.2 Summary of weaknesses, hacks and dead code

Collected in one place so a maintainer can triage them:

| Item | Status | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `Load.kiter`, `Load.part`, `Load.n_parts` | Constructed with fixed values; `n_parts` reaches only an unreachable render branch. Vestiges of the per-instance IR. | section 3.4.1 |
| `Mma.kiter` | Always `0`, read by nothing. | section 3.5.1 |
| `Load.semantic`, `Mma.semantic`, `Inst.semantic` | No consumer. Retained as the documented fold key for a future expansion view. | sections 3.4.3, 3.5.2 |
| `Inst.agent`, `Loop.role` | Always the single-role default; read by nothing. Plumbing for agent specialization. | sections 3.11, 3.12.1 |
| `Await.count` | Never written; the count-materializing backend is deferred work. | section 3.10.2 |
| `Await.scope` | Correct and computed, but the barrier emitter never receives it. | section 3.10.3 |
| `Pred._runtime` duplicates `Expr.free_vars` **and omits `digits`** | Latent defect; no current producer triggers it. One-line fix. | section 3.8.3 |
| `Expr`: `terms` silently supersedes `var` | Unenforced precedence trap; a `__post_init__` check would remove it. | section 3.6.2 |
| `Inst.placement` is a `Placement` for a load and a `dict` for a compute op | Real type hack; `isinstance(dict)` duplicated at three consumers. | section 3.11 |
| `Branch` | Complete vocabulary item with no producer; its walker paths are untested. | section 3.13 |
| `Mma.a`/`b`/`acc`/`scales` are display strings | Real operand identity comes from elsewhere; the binary-input literals are the assumption the scaled-format work exists to remove. | section 3.5.1 |
| `HOP_COUNTER` has no store-hop rows | Raises a bare `KeyError` the day the epilogue is modelled. | section 3.2.3 |
| `Peel.kind` unvalidated | Inconsistent with `Pred.op`; a typo silently disables every `_is_prologue` test. | section 3.15 |

##### 3.17.3 The three properties to preserve

If you change this module, preserve these, in this order of importance:

1. **Address-freeness.** No field here may name a lane, a byte address, a swizzle or a physical
   register. The re-add recipe in section 3.1.1 is the sanctioned way to want one.
2. **No backend vocabulary.** The `Counter` values were once hardware mnemonics; they are not now,
   and the reason (nothing matched them, the renderer stripped them back off) is a warning about the
   general shape. `Cond.label`'s emptiness in the core is the same rule with a gate behind it.
3. **Closed vocabularies raise.** `Pred.op` and the obligation kinds both validate against an
   enumerated set at the single place the set is written down. When you add a fifth kind of anything
   in this file, give it the same treatment — the alternative is a silent misclassification that
   surfaces as a schedule.


---

### 4. `theta.py` — the schedule point and the depth map

`theta.py` (1070 lines, core layer) is the package's data model. It defines the six dataclasses the
rest of the decoder reads — `Mode`, `Fragment`, `Hop`, `Operand`, `Theta`, `DepthMap` — the two
small vocabularies that classify a hop (`HOP_ROLE`, `FORWARD`/`REVERSE`), and the derivations that
turn a schedule point into the depth map `S`. It imports only `ir` (for `Space`, `Counter`,
`HOP_COUNTER`) at module scope and `geometry` lazily inside one method; nothing in it knows what a
GEMM kernel generator is.

The file splits cleanly in two, and this report splits with it:

* **This section (§4)** covers the *structure*: what a schedule point is made of, how a level is
  told from an inner axis, how an op-class is named, how the retime matrix is read, how presence is
  computed, how the three-way axis classification works, and the `DepthMap` container.
* **§5 continues** with the *rate/quantum machinery* that fills that container: `_inner_steps`,
  `_rate_broadcast`, `_group_value_seq`, `group_rate`, `group_live_peak`, `_reg_read_off`,
  `group_width`, `_free_tile_index_seq`, `resident_free_tiles`, `derive_S`, `_shared_depth` and
  `build_S`. §4.10 defines the container those functions write into; it does not derive a single
  depth.

Everything below uses the vocabulary of §1 without redefining it: op-class (§1.2), presence and
broadcast (§1.3), levels and `ord` (§1.4), step and generation (§1.5), retime (§1.6), completion
class (§1.7), the two rings (§1.8), the movement quantum (§1.9), region and fusion (§1.10).

#### 4.0 What a schedule point has to be able to say

Before the field list, the shape of the problem. A main-loop schedule has to answer five questions,
and the whole of `theta.py`'s structure is the smallest set of records that can answer all five
without a name test anywhere:

1. **Where does each instruction sit in the loop nest?** Answered by presence: an op-class is
   emitted at the innermost level it varies over. Needs an ordered level list (`Theta.ord`) and a
   per-op-class broadcast set.
2. **How far ahead of its consumer does it run?** Answered by the retime matrix `Theta.off_map`,
   keyed by op-class × level.
3. **How many buffers does it rotate through?** Answered by the depth map `S` — one number per
   *placement*, where a placement is (op-class, storage region, rotating coordinate).
4. **Who else touches the same storage?** Answered by `Theta.agents` plus the per-hop
   `region_agent_relative` flag; the derived predicate is `Theta.agent_distributed`.
5. **Which instructions are physically the same instruction?** Answered at two granularities: the
   fusion partition `Theta.fuse_groups` (several op-classes riding one cooperative instruction) and
   the movement quantum `Hop.quantum` (several tile coordinates riding one instruction).

Nothing in that list mentions an address, a register number, a wait count or a hardware mnemonic,
and nothing in `theta.py` contains one. That is the invariant the module exists to hold.

The **construction discipline** is equally load-bearing and is stated here once rather than repeated
at each field: with three exceptions, every field of every dataclass in this file is *authored* by
the addon layer (`translate.params_to_theta`, §16) and merely *read* by the core. The three
exceptions are `Theta.notes` (appended to by `emit` as a diagnostic channel), `DepthMap.depths`
(written by `build_S`, §5) and `Fragment.parts` (normalized in place by `Fragment.__post_init__`).
A core module that writes any other field is doing something the layering forbids.

#### 4.1 `Mode` — a level, and the one bit that says which kind

##### 4.1.1 The record

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Mode:
    name:   str
    extent: int = 0
```

Two fields. `name` is an opaque string; the core never parses it, never compares it against a
literal like `"k"` or `"m"`, and never derives a role from it. `extent` is the mode's **static trip
count**, and `0` is a sentinel meaning "trip not statically known".

`Mode` is the only frozen dataclass in the file. Freezing is deliberate and cheap: the presence
family returns `Mode` objects by value all over the decoder (`inner_modes`, `presence_modes`,
`reduction_modes`, `free_modes`), and a frozen record can be shared without a defensive copy and
hashed into a set. Before the presence family returned `Mode`s it returned bare strings, and callers
that needed an extent had to look the `Mode` back up by name — two separate linear scanners existed
in the tree for exactly that lookup (the surviving one is `Theta.free_extent`, §4.1.6).

##### 4.1.2 `Mode.is_outer` — the whole inner/outer distinction

```python
@property
def is_outer(self) -> bool:
    return self.extent == 0
```

This one-line property carries more weight than anything else in the file, so it is worth stating
the equivalence in full. `extent == 0` means all of the following at once, and they are the same
fact seen from five places:

| `extent > 0` (**inner**) | `extent == 0` (**outer**) |
|---|---|
| trip is a compile-time constant | trip is a runtime problem dimension |
| loop is fully unrolled; no back edge | real loop with a back edge |
| the **register** ring rotates over it (§1.8) | the **shared** ring rotates across it (§1.8) |
| no software-pipeline peel needed | needs a prologue/drain peel and a short-loop guard |
| enters rate and live-peak products | must never enter a rate product (its trip is symbolic) |

Why a single integer rather than a boolean plus an enumerated level kind: the decoder must be able
to grow a *coarser* outer level — a persistent / grid-stride tile loop above the reduction chunk —
and under an enumerated kind that is a new enum member plus a branch at every consumer. Under
`extent == 0` it is a new `Mode` in `ord` and nothing else. The one place that still cannot absorb a
second outer level is the emitter, which can only build a `Loop` region for the reduction chunk; it
*refuses* a coarser peel rather than silently dropping it (`emit._check_peel_is_emittable`, §9.7).

The sharp edge: `extent == 0` is also what a genuinely empty axis would look like. Nothing in the
tree constructs an inner mode with extent 0 — `translate._canonical_ord._keep` drops extent-1 modes
and never emits extent-0 ones — but if a future translator did, that mode would silently become an
outer level and the decoder would try to peel it.

##### 4.1.3 `Theta.levels()` — the full permutation

```python
def levels(self):
    return list(self.ord)
```

A defensive copy of `Theta.ord`, outer→inner, *including* the outer levels. `levels()[0]` is the
outermost level. The emit nest and the peel skeleton walk this list; `placement._peel_depths` keys
its per-level depth vector on it. The copy is not incidental — `emit` iterates while building, and
handing out the live list would let a caller reorder the schedule point by accident.

##### 4.1.4 `Theta.outer_modes()` and `Theta.inner_modes()` — the two projections

```python
def outer_modes(self):  return [m for m in self.ord if m.is_outer]
def inner_modes(self):  return [m for m in self.ord if not m.is_outer]
```

Both preserve `ord` order, so `outer_modes()` is outermost-first (a persistent level, then the
reduction chunk) and `inner_modes()` is the intra-chunk traversal in the order the unrolled nest
visits it. `inner_modes()` is the single list that `geometry._inner_axes`, the presence family, the
rate machinery of §5, the read nest and `sizing` all iterate; excluding the outer levels from it is
what keeps a symbolic runtime trip out of every rate and register-pressure product.

For a schedule point with no outer level at all — a legacy shape where the reduction chunk loop was
implicit rather than a real `ord` mode — `outer_modes()` is empty and `inner_modes()` is the whole
of `ord`. Every consumer is written to survive that (`reduction_chunk_mode` returns `None`,
`reduction_chunk_name` returns its `default`), but `translate` always emits the outer `iter` mode, so
the empty case is only exercised by hand-built test fixtures.

##### 4.1.5 `Theta.reduction_chunk_mode()` and `reduction_chunk_name(default=None)`

```python
def reduction_chunk_mode(self):
    outer = self.outer_modes()
    return outer[-1] if outer else None

def reduction_chunk_name(self, default=None):
    m = self.reduction_chunk_mode()
    return m.name if m is not None else default
```

The **reduction chunk** is the innermost outer level. `ord` is outer→inner and any coarser outer
level (a persistent tile loop) sits *above* the chunk, so the chunk is `outer_modes()[-1]`.

This accessor exists because five distinct things key on that one axis and must never disagree:

1. the shared ring depth `S_shared` (`_shared_depth`, §5);
2. the shared-source rotation of a read (`placement._read_placement`);
3. the steady `Loop` node `emit.build_ir` emits;
4. the `Bind` its peel steps pin;
5. the peel depth *at* that level (`placement.PeelDepths.M` and `copy_off()`).

Before it existed, three call sites wrote `outer_modes()[0]` and two wrote `outer_modes()[-1]`. With
exactly one outer level those are the same object, so the split was invisible; the day a second,
coarser outer level appears they become two different axes and the decoder emits a loop over one and
a ring over the other. The fix was not to pick a winner but to remove the index from the call sites
entirely (provenance: #113/#156). Nine call sites across `placement.py`, `validate.py`,
`loopir_to_gir.py` and the tests now route through `reduction_chunk_name`.

`reduction_chunk_name`'s `default` argument is the "legacy θ" escape hatch: consumers that need a
string for a message or a dictionary key pass `"iter"` (this is what `validate.validate_loopir` and
`loopir_to_gir` do) so a fixture without an outer level does not crash on `None.name`.

Note what this accessor is *no longer* on the list for: the **peel is per level**, not per chunk.
`placement._peel_depths` returns a vector `M_ℓ` indexed by level name, because the peel construction
peels *every* level carrying a non-zero retime, and keying peel depth only on the innermost outer
level silently drops every coarser-level `off`. What the peel still uses this accessor for is "the
depth *at* the chunk" (`PeelDepths.M`, `PeelDepths.copy_off()`), which is the one level the emitter
can currently build a region for.

##### 4.1.6 `Theta.free_extent(mode_name)`

```python
def free_extent(self, mode_name):
    for m in self.ord:
        if m.name == mode_name:
            return m.extent
    return 1
```

A linear name→extent lookup over `ord`, returning `1` for an unknown name. Three callers:
`placement.readahead_prologue` (through `_group_value_range`) and `sizing.operand_footprint_regs`
both need the extent of a fragment's
`grouping_mode` (a *name*, because `Fragment` stores it as a string), and one test. It is `O(|ord|)`
with `|ord| ≤ 8`, so the scan is free.

Two sharp edges. First, the `return 1` fallback conflates "no such mode" with "an axis of extent 1";
a typo'd `grouping_mode` therefore reads as a degenerate axis rather than raising. Second, it does
*not* filter to inner modes, so `free_extent(reduction_chunk_name())` returns `0`, not `1` — the
name says "free" but the function will happily answer for an outer level. Both callers only ever
pass a `grouping_mode`, which is always an inner mode, so neither edge is live today. If you add a
caller, pass an inner mode name or add the filter.

This function is the last survivor of the two hand-rolled name→`Mode` scanners that existed before
the presence family started returning `Mode` objects. It survives because `Fragment.grouping_mode`
is genuinely a string (a `Fragment` is authored before `ord` is finalized), not because a `Mode` was
unavailable. If `Fragment` ever gains a `Mode`-valued grouping field, delete this.

#### 4.2 `Fragment` — the register-buffer structure of one operand

##### 4.2.1 Concept

An operand's tile fan is delivered out of rotating VGPR buffers. `Fragment` describes *how that fan
is partitioned into independently-rotating pieces*, and nothing else — it holds no register numbers,
no widths, and no addresses.

The abstraction is the **reuse group**. A fragment's fan is cut into groups; each group cycles
through its own number of buffers, that count being the group's rotation **width** `W`. The
motivating shape is a two-width, same-rate point: the lower-M-half of `A` and the higher-M-half,
