  so the data model is ready. The blocker is the equal-partition assumption in `sizing` and in the
  grouping-mode divisibility, both documented as accepted exceptions.
* **Per-region completion.** `Theta.per_region_completion=True` is fully modelled here and in the
  downstream IR; the missing piece is a per-region completion token on the backend. When it exists,
  nothing in this file changes.

#### 4.14 What this section does not cover

The rate and quantum machinery that *fills* the `DepthMap` — `_inner_steps`, `_rate_broadcast`,
`_group_value_seq`, `group_rate`, `group_live_peak`, `_reg_read_off`, `group_width`,
`_free_tile_index_seq`, `resident_free_tiles`, `derive_S`, `_shared_depth` and `build_S` — is
deliberately left to **§5**. Those functions consume everything defined above: `group_rate` reads
`Fragment.group_broadcast` and the reduction set to compute the reload rate `R`; `group_live_peak`
walks `_inner_steps` to compute the live-peak floor `L`; `group_width` resolves
`Fragment.policy_of` into a number inside `[L, R]`; `_shared_depth` reads `Operand.lds_buffers` and
the retime at `reduction_chunk_name()`; and `build_S` writes one `DepthMap` row per placement using
`SHARED_GROUP` and the fragment's `groups()`.


---

### 5. `theta.py` (continued) — rates, quanta, broadcast and fusion

#### 5.0 What this section covers

Section 4 described the schedule point as a *data object*: the `Mode` / `Fragment` / `Hop` /
`Operand` / `Theta` dataclasses, the retime map `off`, and the `DepthMap` container that holds the
derived depths. This section covers the *derivations* that live in the same file — the machinery
that turns a schedule point into numbers:

* **the movement quantum** (`theta.Hop.quantum`) — how several tile coordinates collapse into one
  hardware instruction, and why load-versus-broadcast is a *consequence* of that description rather
  than a flag on it;
* **the broadcast family** — `Theta.presence_modes`, `Theta.agent_served_modes`,
  `Theta.reduction_modes`, `Theta.free_modes` and their string helpers, plus
  `Fragment.group_broadcast`;
* **`theta._rate_broadcast`** — a *second, separate* nullspace computation, deliberately not the
  same function as the presence-side one, and the single most misunderstood twenty lines in the
  package;
* **the rate machinery** — `_inner_steps`, `_group_value_seq`, `group_rate`, `group_live_peak`,
  `_reg_read_off`, `group_width`, `_free_tile_index_seq`, `resident_free_tiles`, and the
  `derive_S` / `_shared_depth` / `build_S` drivers that call them;
* **Φ, the fusion partition** — `Theta.fuse_groups`, `Theta.movement_units`,
  `Theta.tensor_instrs_per_kiter`, `Theta.agent_distributed`, `Theta.per_region_completion`, and
  what "one fused movement" means for hazard accounting.

Section 5.7 sweeps up the remaining names in `theta.py` whose *primary* home is section 4, giving
each a short but real statement of what it computes, so that this file's definition list is fully
covered between the two sections and a reader who arrives at section 5 first is not stranded.

---

#### 5.1 The movement quantum: `carrier` and `slot`

##### 5.1.1 The problem it solves

The decoder's whole vocabulary is built on *tile coordinates*. An operand's register fan is a grid
of tiles; a read op-class visits one tile per inner-traversal step; the register ring rotates once
per distinct value. Every count in the package — the reload rate, the live peak, the read-ahead
prologue size, the number of emitted `Load` instances — is ultimately a count over that grid.

Real hardware does not honour that one-tile-per-instruction assumption. Two mechanisms break it:

* **A wide load.** One `ds_load_b64` fetches the bytes of two adjacent tiles into two consecutive
  registers. Two coordinates, one instruction, two destination registers.
* **A sub-agent broadcast.** Two half-waves of one wave receive the *same* value into the *same*
  architectural register; each half-wave then treats it as its own tile. Two coordinates, one
  instruction, **one** destination register.

If the model does not know about the merge, three things go wrong at once. The instruction count is
double the truth. The generation bookkeeping is wrong, because the model believes the two
coordinates can be scheduled independently and land in different rotation slots when in fact one
instruction cannot write two slots. And the presence set is wrong, because the model believes the
op-class varies over an axis it does not actually step along.

##### 5.1.2 The abstraction: two expressions, never a schema

`Hop.quantum` holds an `ir.QuantumMap` (the dataclass itself is section 3's; what follows is what
`theta` requires of it). It is exactly **two integer-valued expressions over the operand's flat
tile index `t`**, written in the same `ir.Expr` mini-language the rotation slots use:

```
carrier(t)  ->  which instruction carries tile t
slot(t)     ->  which position inside that instruction's destination holds tile t
```

Two derived quantities follow by evaluation alone, with no interpretation:

```
coordinates served by one instruction = carrier-preimage of t
                                      = { u in [0, extent) : carrier(u) == carrier(t) }
registers written by one instruction  = |{ slot(u) : u in that preimage }|
```

`ir.QuantumMap.group` computes the first and `ir.QuantumMap.regs` the second;
`ir.QuantumMap.carrier_of` and `ir.QuantumMap.slot_of` are the evaluators that bind `t` to the
free variable named by `ir.quantum_var()` (the literal string `"tile"`). `ir.identity_quantum()`
is `carrier(t) = t, slot(t) = 0` — one tile per instruction — and `Hop.quantum = None` means
exactly that, which is why `None` is the default on every hop and why nothing in the core needs a
"has a quantum" branch.

##### 5.1.3 Load versus broadcast is **derived**, not declared

This is the design point the abstraction exists for, and it is worth stating flatly because it is
the thing a maintainer is most likely to undo.

| mechanism | `carrier(t)` | `slot(t)` | slots per carrier group | registers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| wide 2-tile load | `t // 2` | `t % 2` | 2 | 2 |
| sub-agent broadcast, stride `s` | `t - s*((t % 2s) // s)` | `t % s` | 1 | 1 |
| the two composed | composition | composition | product | product |

A **sub-agent broadcast is simply partners sharing a slot.** Nothing anywhere is tagged
`kind="broadcast"`. The model asks `|{slot(u)}|` over the carrier group and gets 1 for a broadcast
and 2 for a wide load, from the same three lines of code.

The rejected alternative was a schema: a list of `(axis, factor, kind)` tuples, with `kind` in
`{"wide", "broadcast"}`. Its fatal property is that **every consumer must interpret it**. The
presence computation would need one branch per kind; the register count another; the generation
check another; the renderer another. Each of those branches is a place where the two kinds can
drift apart, and a third mechanism (say, a strided gather that serves four coordinates into three
registers) means editing every consumer. With two expressions there is nothing to branch on: a new
mechanism is a new pair of `Expr`s written by whoever knows the address layout, and every existing
consumer keeps working because all it ever did was evaluate.

##### 5.1.4 Supplied, never derived — and the four attempts to derive it

`Hop.quantum` is an **input** to the schedule point, on exactly the same footing as `S`
(the depth map) and `Hop.vector_elems`. It is built outside the core, in `bridge.py`, from target
facts, and handed in. The core only evaluates it.

The reason is the address-opacity rule (section 1.1): which tiles one instruction covers is a
consequence of the address layout and of the emitter's byte-level folding, and the core has no
addresses. `theta.Hop`'s docstring records **four** attempts to have the core work it out anyway,
and states that each one turned out to be an address assumption wearing a different hat:

1. *Scan the free modes for a "contiguous-looking" axis and assume the fold happens there.*
   "Contiguous" is a statement about addresses.
2. *Test whether the candidate pair shares a buffer generation, and narrow the quantum if it does
   not.* This is the model telling the hardware what it may do; the hardware has already folded.
3. *Refuse the fold when the pair straddles a storage region.* Same problem, plus it makes a legal
   kernel undecodable.
4. *Split an axis so that the pair the emitter wants is created by the tiling.* This invents a
   `tile` move to explain an addressing coincidence.

Concretely, the shipping producer is `KernelWriter._loopModelTarget`, which passes a
`ReadQuantum` entry per operand through `bridge.kernel_to_params`'s `target` argument. The
unit-test fixture `test_loopmodel._two_tile_fold` builds the same map by hand
(`carrier(t) = t // 2`, `slot(t) = t % 2`) and its docstring is explicit that it is written out
rather than imported from the producer, "because the point of the test is that the CHECK works on
a supplied map, and a test that imported the producer would pass on a producer that had drifted."
That is a good habit to keep when extending this area.

##### 5.1.5 What θ *does* with the quantum: one presence point

`theta.py` itself contains no quantum arithmetic. What the quantum buys is entirely structural, and
it is one sentence:

> **The coordinates inside one quantum are ONE presence point.**

An op-class is *present* on the inner axes it varies over. If one instruction covers tiles `t` and
`t+1`, then stepping the axis that separates them does **not** produce a second instruction — so
that axis is not one the op-class varies over, and it leaves the hop's presence set. The
subtraction happens in `geometry.quantum_axes`, which is called from `geometry.hop_broadcast`,
which is called from `theta.Theta.presence_modes` when a `hop` argument is supplied (section 2.2.3
gives the algorithm; the test for whether an axis is spanned is "varying this axis alone never
changes `carrier`").

Three consequences follow, and all three are load-bearing:

* **One presence point ⇒ one step.** The traversal visits the merged coordinates once, not twice,
  so the emitted instruction count matches the hardware instruction count.
* **One step ⇒ one generation.** `ord` is a permutation of *modes*; a presence point is a leaf of
  that traversal. No reordering of `ord` can insert anything between two coordinates that are the
  same presence point. So a merged movement **cannot straddle two buffer generations by
  construction** — there is no representable schedule in which it does.
* **One presence point ⇒ one rate step.** Because `group_rate` (section 5.3.3) multiplies the
  extents of the modes the group varies over, an absorbed axis drops straight out of `R`, and
  therefore out of the band `[L, R]` and out of the register footprint. A 2-tile fold on a
  4-extent axis halves the group's reload rate, with no code anywhere that knows why.

The third point is the one that has behavioural teeth. There is a recorded defect (#275) in which
the MX scale read's quantum absorbed *the whole* of its presence set, leaving the read with an
empty presence — and the emitter, which places a node at the innermost mode of the presence set,
placed it nowhere and emitted the scale read **zero times**.

##### 5.1.6 What the tests pin

Four tests in `Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py` fence this area, and between them they encode the
history:

* `test_absorbing_the_spanned_axis_removes_the_straddle_on_the_shipping_path` is the positive
  contract: with the real `ReadQuantum` supplied through the bridge,
  `geometry.quantum_axes(th, mxsa, hop.quantum) == {"M_inner"}` and `"M_split"` is *absent* from
  `th.presence_modes(mxsa, hop=hop)`. It then rebuilds GIR and asserts the scale operand emits
  exactly half as many read acts as its parent — the b64 fold made visible as a count. Its own
  comment records that this axis answer was **re-pointed**: it used to be `{"M_split"}`, from a
  conflation in which a wave's second tile (physically inside region 0) was labelled region 1 and
  carried region 1's memory token. Once the split axis became agent-served (section 5.2.3), the
  wave sits inside one region and its two tiles live on `M_inner`, which is what the 2-tile load
  actually spans.
* `test_a_merged_load_carries_the_UNION_of_the_generations_it_covers` pins the *repair* on the
  shared-memory side: if a merge does cover two source generations, the one emitted instruction is
  named by **both**, not by a leader's. The fixture is deliberately synthetic, and its docstring
  explains why at length: the behaviour was first seen on a real cell (`KMKNMN` × unsplit, where
  the read-ahead advance carried across a region sibling and put a `ds_load_b64`'s two halves on
  LDS tokens 9 and 8), that cause was fixed, and a test keyed to a real kernel would then have
  stopped testing anything. A test that needs a live defect for its fixture is not a test.
* `test_the_quantum_check_still_reports_a_REGISTER_straddle` is the non-vacuity control and the
  statement of the asymmetry: the shared-memory half of a straddle is repairable by a union (one
  instruction, several source buffers, name them all), and the **register** half is not — one
  instruction cannot write two rotation bases — so it must remain a reported violation.
* `test_the_quantum_check_is_CLEAN_on_every_cell_now_that_the_carry_is_gone` sweeps four loop
  orders × two split settings and asserts zero violations, with the pre-fix measurements written
  into the docstring (three cells fired, and they were exactly the three that miscompared on
  hardware). It is a regression guard in the reverse direction: if the read-ahead sibling carry
  returns, the straddle returns and this fires.

##### 5.1.7 Extending the quantum: concrete advice

* **Do not add a `kind` tag.** If you need a mechanism the two expressions cannot express, the
  first thing to check is whether it is really a *third* expression (for example, a per-lane
  predicate) rather than a variant of the existing two. Adding a third `Expr` field with a
  documented default is additive; adding an enum is not.
* **The evaluator is pure and uncached.** `ir.QuantumMap.group` evaluates `carrier` once per tile
  in `[0, extent)`, so `geometry.quantum_axes` is `O(#candidate axes × max extent × tile count)`
  per hop. With shipping tile counts of 4 to 16 this is a few hundred `Expr.eval` calls per kernel
  and does not register. If a future shape pushes the tile count into the hundreds, memoize
  `carrier_of` on `(id(expr), t)` — it is a pure function of `t` once the environment is fixed.
* **Only the LoopIR dump prints it.** `LoopModel/render.py:_shape_str` appends
  `quantum(carrier=…, slot=…)` whenever `Load.quantum` is set, and *both* branches of `_load_line`
  (the shared-destination copy line and the register-destination read line) call it, so a merged
  movement is visible there. The **GIR** dump does not print the quantum itself — it shows only the
  absorbed axes, as `<spans …>` on a `Ref` (`Lowering/gir/render.py:_covers_str`). When you are
  debugging a count mismatch against a GIR dump, check the quantum before believing it.
* **`Hop.vector_elems` and `Hop.quantum` are different facts.** `vector_elems` is elements per lane
  per instruction (a width); `quantum` is which *tile coordinates* one instruction serves (a
  merge). A change to one does not imply a change to the other, and the bridge computes them from
  different target keys.

---

#### 5.2 Broadcast: three derivations of related facts, kept apart on purpose

Everything in this subsection answers some version of "which axes is this thing constant over?".
There are **three** answers in the tree, they are computed by three different functions, and the
package's most expensive class of bug has been assuming that any two of them are one.

| question | answer computed by | lives in |
|---|---|---|
| which inner axes is this operand's **data** constant over? | `geometry.broadcast_axes` | `geometry.py` (section 2.2.3) |
| which inner axes does **one instruction of this hop** span? | `geometry.hop_broadcast` (which folds in `geometry.quantum_axes`) | `geometry.py` |
| which inner axes does **one register rate-group** not reload on? | **`theta._rate_broadcast`** | `theta.py`, section 5.2.5 |

The first two are the *presence* family and share a derivation. The third is a **separate
nullspace computation** and shares nothing with them but its shape.

##### 5.2.1 `Theta.presence_modes(op, hop=None)`

The entry point to the presence family, and the only one the rest of the core calls.

```
presence_modes(op, hop) :=
    ns = geometry.broadcast_axes(theta, op)          if hop is None
         geometry.hop_broadcast(theta, op, hop)      otherwise
    return [m for m in theta.inner_modes() if m.name not in ns]
```

It returns `Mode` objects (not names) in `ord` order, and the return type is the point of a
completed refactor: the family used to be string-only, which forced any caller that needed an
extent to look the `Mode` back up by name, and two separate linear scanners existed in the tree to
do exactly that. `Mode` is a frozen dataclass, so returning it is free.

`hop=None` is the **operand data** question, and it is the default because the derived families
below (`reduction_modes`, `free_modes`) are defined off the data presence, and because nine call
sites all mean that hop. Passing a `hop` gives the *per-hop* answer: a bulk cooperative copy spans
every inner axis in one instruction, so its presence is just its region axes (empty if the tile is
not actually cut), while a per-lane read varies over everything the data does minus whatever its
quantum absorbs.

The `geometry` import is function-local. `geometry` never imports `theta` — it takes a `theta`
*object* as its first argument — so this is not a cycle, only a deferral that keeps the module
import order clean.

##### 5.2.2 `Theta.output_operands()`

`[o for o in self.operands if o.is_output]` — the accumulator op-class or classes. Trivial, but it
is the anchor of the reduction definition below, and it is the reason there is no `theta.op("C")`
anywhere in the core.

##### 5.2.3 `Theta.agent_served_modes()` — the third kind of inner axis

**Concept.** The model classified inner axes two ways: *free* (in the accumulator's presence) and
*reduction* (everything else, **by subtraction**). Subtraction is the flaw: it assigns "reduction"
to any axis that leaves the accumulator's presence, whatever the reason.

There is a reason that has nothing to do with contraction. When a region-split tile is handed out
one region per wave, each wave reads, computes and accumulates entirely inside *its own* region.
Nothing in the read/compute nest varies over the region axis — each agent sees exactly one value of
it — yet the axis must stay in `ord`, because the bulk cooperative copy still walks all the
regions. The axis is **traversed by the agents rather than by the coordinate**. It is neither free
nor reduction.

**Algorithm.**

```
agent_served_modes():
    out = {}
    for op in operands:
        rms = op.region_modes                          # the axes enumerating its regions
        if not rms or max(1, op.split) <= 1: continue  # a region AXIS with one region is nothing
        if any(hop.region_agent_relative for hop in op.hops if not hop.is_bulk):
            out |= set(rms)
    return out
```

Two guards, both load-bearing. `op.split <= 1` skips an operand that has a region *mode* but only
one region (the MX scale operands are exactly this shape): having an axis is not the same as having
more than one value along it. And the `region_agent_relative` flag is read from the **non-bulk**
hops only — which is the whole asymmetry the class exists to express. `translate.py` sets
`Hop.region_agent_relative` on the **read** hop and never on the copy hop, from
`wave_region_span < split`. The copy's region really is a coordinate (the cooperative mover walks
every region by index); the read's region is a property of *which wave is executing it*.

**Why it is named explicitly rather than patched at consumers.** The docstring records the measured
failure. `theta._rate_broadcast` (section 5.2.5) excludes a **free** region mode from the register
ring but keeps a **reduction** one. Before the third class existed, an agent-served region axis was
misclassified as a reduction, so it stayed in the rotation, and the rotation-slot `Expr` referenced
a mode that no emitted `Loop` binds — the LoopIR structural checker reported `P3/P5 ... UNBOUND
M_split`. Every consumer of `reduction_names()` inherited the misclassification. Naming the class
turns the two-way split into a three-way split at **one** definition point instead of at each
consumer.

The test that guards it, `test_the_wmma_is_placed_by_presence_not_by_the_nests_depth` (its assertions
are quoted around `agent_served_modes` in `test_loopmodel.py`), is worth reading as a model of how
to write a guard for this shape. It asserts, for three configurations, that

```
{inner modes} \ ({output presence} ∪ {reduction modes})  ==  agent_served_modes() ∩ inner modes
```

i.e. that the modes falling outside the two-way classification are **exactly** the agent-served
ones — "any OTHER mode leaving the wmma's presence is a new fact, not this one". That guard was
written to fail the day the classification became three-way, and it did fail, on purpose. It then
pins the equivalence that made the change emit-neutral: the deepest mode in the wmma's presence
equals the deepest mode that is *not* agent-served, so the compute node lands in the same place it
always did. Byte-identical output across both codegen suites was the evidence.

##### 5.2.4 `reduction_modes`, `free_modes`, and the string helpers

**`Theta.reduction_modes()`** is the contraction axes:

```
reduction_modes() = inner_modes  \  (∪ presence(output op-class))  \  agent_served_modes()
```

returned as `Mode` objects in `ord` order. Defining it off the *accumulator's* presence rather than
by an operand-name test or a "present on all inputs" heuristic is what makes it general for batched
and einsum-shaped contractions: a batch axis is present on the output and a reduction axis is not,
even though both index every input. It is empty if the schedule point carries no output op-class,
which is a malformed main loop — `translate.params_to_theta` always constructs the accumulator.

Note there is deliberately **no** stored `reduction_modes` field on `Theta`. One existed, was never
written and never read, and its docstring claimed "set by translate" — a second authority that could
disagree with the derivation. It was deleted (#158).

**`Theta.free_modes(op)`** = `presence_modes(op)` minus the reduction modes: this operand's own
output subscripts. The free-tile index sequence and the resident-tile live peak iterate exactly
these, with no operand-name or role test anywhere.

**`Theta.presence(op)`**, **`Theta.reduction_names()`**, **`Theta.free_names(op)`** are thin string
projections of the three above — `presence` and `free_names` return lists in `ord` order,
`reduction_names` returns a **set** because every caller does a membership test or sorts it. The
direction of the dependency is fixed and stated in a comment: the `Mode`-returning form is
canonical and the string form is derived from it, never the other way round. The string forms exist
for two genuine consumers — set algebra inside this file, and the name lists that cross into the
GIR layer through `Program.meta`.

**`Theta.free_extent(mode_name)`** is a linear scan of `ord` returning that mode's extent, or `1`
if the name is not a mode. It is used where a caller holds a *name* (a fragment's `grouping_mode`,
which is stored as a string) and needs the extent. The `1` default is defensive and silent: a typo
in a `grouping_mode` string produces an extent of 1 rather than an error, and the resulting
footprint is quietly too small. If you are adding a new string-keyed mode reference, prefer
resolving it to a `Mode` once at construction.

##### 5.2.5 `_rate_broadcast(theta, op, group)` — the second nullspace, and why

**State it plainly: this is not `geometry.broadcast_axes`, it must not be replaced by a call to it,
and assuming the two share one derivation is a specific historical error.**

They answer related questions about the same operand and they agree on the common terms, which is
precisely what makes the confusion durable. The difference is what the axis is being asked *about*:

* `geometry.broadcast_axes` asks a **data / grid** question: does the value this operand delivers
  depend on this axis? `A[m,k]` does not depend on `n`. The answer decides where the op-class is
  emitted and which coordinates index it.
* `_rate_broadcast` asks a **storage / reload** question: does *this one rotating register group*
  have to be refilled when this axis steps? A group is a *partition of the grouping mode's values*
  — sibling values of that mode select a **different group**, i.e. a different physical fragment,
  not a refill of this one.

The two therefore disagree on at least two axis classes, and the disagreement is the entire content
of the function:

```
_rate_broadcast(op, group) =
      op.fragment.group_broadcast(group)         # the data broadcast — the shared term
    ∪ { m in op.region_modes : m not a reduction mode }    # FREE region axes: spatial, not reload
    ∪ { op.fragment.grouping_mode }              # if set: partitions storage, not reload
```

`grouping_mode` is in the rate-broadcast set and *not* in the data-broadcast set: the operand's data
absolutely does vary over its M fan, which is why the fan is still indexed for the grid; but group
`lo` is not reloaded when you step from an `lo` value to an `hi` value, because that is a different
group. A fragment with `grouping_mode = None` keeps its fan **in** the rate, and there the fan *is*
the rotation — the same axis, opposite classification, decided by whether the partition exists.

##### 5.2.6 The `free`-only qualifier on region modes, and the measurement behind it

The region-mode term carries a qualifier — `not a reduction mode` — and the docstring says the
qualifier is the whole of it. The reasoning:

* A **free**-axis region split is a storage partition. Sibling values name a *different fragment*.
  So the split multiplies the **number** of groups (which is what `resident_free_tiles` and the
  footprint's `region` factor count) and leaves each group's band `[L, R]` alone. Excluding it is
  correct.
* A **reduction**-axis region split is not a partition of anything. The two "regions" are
  successive substeps of one tile, held in the same group, simultaneously live because they feed
  different matmul instances of one iteration. It must stay in the rate.

The measurement is recorded in the source verbatim and is the clearest single illustration of what
this function controls. On a TN layout with the reduction-axis half of the region split enabled, the
`K` axis was re-factored from one mode of extent 2 into `K_split` (extent 2) × `K_inner` (collapsed
to 1). Without the `free` qualifier, `K_split` was excluded from the rate, so:

```
R (group_rate)      2  ->  1
W (group_width)     2  ->  1
every read's slot        0
```

The emitted assembly loaded region 0 and region 1 into the *same* register pair, and both matmul
instances read whichever landed last: 1152 of 1152 numeric comparisons failed, with a correct
descriptor and correct addresses. The invariant the qualifier preserves is stated exactly:
re-factoring one axis as a product of two must not change the product, and an unsplit kernel of the
same shape gets `R = 2` from `K_inner` alone.

##### 5.2.7 `Fragment.group_broadcast(group=None)`

Returns `set(self.broadcast_axes)` — the fragment's data-broadcast set — and **accepts and ignores**
the `group` argument. The docstring is honest about why: the broadcast set is uniform across a
fragment's slots, so there is one set, and the parameter exists only for call-site symmetry with
the rest of the per-group API.

This is the extension hook for anything that wants per-group broadcast. If a future partition is
uneven, or if a group is deliberately confined to a sub-range of an axis the rest of the fragment
spans, this is the one function to change, and every caller already passes the group.

##### 5.2.8 Advice for a future maintainer of the broadcast family

* **Never collapse `_rate_broadcast` into `geometry.broadcast_axes`.** They agree on the data term
  and diverge on the grouping mode and on free region axes. A refactor that "removes duplication"
  here reintroduces the 1152-failure shape above and the `UNBOUND M_split` shape from section 5.2.3.
  If you want the duplication gone, the correct move is the opposite one: give the *rate* question
  its own named concept ("reload axes") in a docstring and keep the function, rather than making
  one of them call the other.
* **The three-way axis classification has exactly one subtraction point** (`reduction_modes`
  subtracting `agent_served_modes`). If a fourth reason for an axis to leave the accumulator's
  presence appears, name the class there; do not special-case it at a consumer.
* **`agent_served_modes` is `O(#operands × #hops)` and is called from `reduction_modes`, which is
  called from `free_modes`/`free_names` — once per `_free_tile_index_seq`, hoisted above its
  `for c in steps` loop — and, per rate group, from `_rate_broadcast` via `reduction_names`.**
  It is recomputed a great many times per `build_S`. Every input is immutable for the lifetime of a
  decode, so this is the single cheapest memoization in the file: a `functools.lru_cache`-style
  cache keyed on `id(theta)`, or an explicit `Theta._derived` dict populated once. Measure before
  bothering — the sets are tiny — but it is the first thing to try if decode time ever shows up.

---

#### 5.3 The rate machinery: `R`, `L`, `W`

The register ring is described by three numbers per rate group. Section 1.8 introduced them; this
subsection is the algorithm.

* **`R`, the reload rate** — how many *distinct values* one group holds over one reduction chunk.
  The ceiling of the width band: holding more names than there are distinct values is pure waste.
* **`L`, the live peak** — the largest number of *simultaneously live* generations of the group.
  The floor of the band: cycling fewer names than are simultaneously live means one name holds two
  live values, which is a race.
* **`W`, the rotation width** — the number actually chosen, and the value the depth map stores.
  `W` is a *searched* coordinate; `L` and `R` are *derived* bounds on it.

The invariant is `L ≤ W ≤ R`, and out-of-band requests are **repaired**, not refused (section
5.3.6).

##### 5.3.1 `_inner_steps(theta)`

```
_inner_steps(theta) -> list of {mode_name: value}
    modes  = theta.inner_modes()                      # ord order, outer to inner
    ranges = [[(m.name, v) for v in range(m.extent)] for m in modes]
    return [dict(c) for c in itertools.product(*ranges)]   or [{}] if there are no inner modes
```

The complete intra-chunk traversal, one dictionary per step, in `ord` order (rightmost mode
varying fastest, which is what `itertools.product` gives and what `ord`'s outer-to-inner convention
requires). Everything else in this subsection is a function of this list.

Shape and size: the list has `T = product of inner extents` entries, each a dict of up to
`#inner modes` integer entries. On shipping configurations `T` is between 2 and 64 — a bf16 NT
kernel with `KMN` order has `T = 2 (substep) × 2 (M) × 2 (N) = 8`; the six-axis MX-scaled fp8
shapes reach `T = 64` when every one of `K_split, K_inner, M_split, M_inner, N_split, N_inner` has
extent 2. It is materialized rather than generated because it is walked several times per group.

It is also **recomputed**: `derive_S` builds it once and threads it through `group_width`, but
`resident_free_tiles` calls `_inner_steps` again for itself. That is the first thing to fix if you
ever want this file faster (section 5.3.9).

##### 5.3.2 `_group_value_seq(theta, op, group, steps)`

The **value identity** the group holds at each step:

```
_group_value_seq(op, group, steps):
    ns = _rate_broadcast(theta, op, group)
    return [ tuple((m, v) for m, v in sorted(coord.items()) if m not in ns)
             for coord in steps ]
```

Each element is a canonical, hashable projection of the step coordinate onto the modes the group
*does* reload over. Two steps carry the same value exactly when their projections are equal. The
`sorted` is what makes the tuple canonical (dict iteration order is insertion order, and `steps`
dicts are built consistently, but sorting removes the dependence). The projected-away axes are
precisely `_rate_broadcast`'s set — which is why the choice of nullspace in section 5.2.5 flows
directly into every number below.

Output shape: a list of `T` tuples, each of length `#reload modes`. For a group that reloads on
nothing (fully broadcast), every element is the empty tuple `()`, and the group holds one value all
chunk.

##### 5.3.3 `group_rate(theta, op, group)` — the ceiling `R`

```
group_rate(op, group):
    ns = _rate_broadcast(theta, op, group)
    R  = 1
    for m in theta.inner_modes():
        if m.name not in ns: R *= m.extent
    return R
```

`R` is the number of distinct values one group of one fragment holds per reduction chunk — the
product of the extents of the modes the group actually reloads over. It is `O(#inner modes)` plus
the cost of `_rate_broadcast`, so effectively free.

The subtlety worth internalizing is the one the docstring insists on: **a fragment split `r` ways
has the same per-fragment band `[L, R]` as an unsplit one.** The split multiplies the *number of
groups* (which `resident_free_tiles` and the footprint's region factor account for), not any single
group's rate. A concrete example from the reference configuration: a fragment whose whole fan
would give `R = 8` splits into `lo` and `hi`, and each of those has `R = 4`, not 8. Computing 8
per group is the over-count this function is written to avoid, and it would inflate the register
footprint by the split factor.

`group_rate` is exported from the package (`LoopModel/__init__.py` lists it), because a tuner or a
diagnostic wants to ask for `R` without reconstructing the depth map.

##### 5.3.4 `group_live_peak(theta, op, group, steps, post_war=True)` — the floor `L`

**Concept.** A *generation* of a register group is one filling of it: the pair `(iteration, value)`.
A generation is *live* from the first step that reads it to the last. `L` is the peak number of
generations live at one moment. If the rotation cycles fewer names than that, two live values share
a name, and one of them is destroyed before its consumer runs.

**Algorithm** — a cyclic interval-overlap, made non-cyclic by unrolling:

```
group_live_peak(op, group, steps, post_war):
    T   = len(steps)                            # steps per chunk
    off = 0 if post_war else _reg_read_off(theta, op)
    seq = _group_value_seq(op, group, steps)    # value identity per step

    gens = {}                                   # (iteration, value) -> [first_step, last_step]
    for s in 0,1,2:                             # THREE unrolled iterations
        for i, v in enumerate(seq):
            step = s*T + i
            gens[(s, v)] = [min(existing, step), step]

    intervals = [(first - off, last) for (first, last) in gens.values()]

    peak = 0
    for p in range(T, 2*T):                     # sample the MIDDLE (steady) iteration only
        peak = max(peak, count of intervals containing p)
    return max(1, peak)
```

Three iterations are unrolled and only the middle one is sampled. That is the standard trick for
turning a cyclic overlap into a linear one: the middle iteration sees both its predecessor's
tail-live generations and its successor's read-ahead, so it is a genuine steady-state sample,
whereas iteration 0 has no predecessor and iteration 2 no successor.

**Two peaks, and they are different numbers.** The `post_war` flag selects the interval:

| `post_war` | interval | what it measures |
|---|---|---|
| `False` — *prefetch-overlap peak* | `[first_read − off, last_read]` | the read is issued `off` substeps early, so a generation overlaps the *next* generation's read-ahead. This is what free double-buffering needs, and it can exceed `R`. |
| `True` — *post-WAR peak* (the default, and the band's real floor) | `[first_read, last_read]` | **no** `−off` extension. An in-place refill is serialized behind the last read of the slot it overwrites, so it cannot overlap across the boundary; what remains is only the within-chunk overlap of *distinct* values. |

The post-WAR distinction is what makes a single-buffer group legal at all, and the two cases are:

* **Sequential values** — value `t` is fully read before value `t+1` is first read (two substeps
  read one after the other). The intervals do not overlap, `L = 1`, and one buffer refilled in
  place is enough.
* **Interleaved values** — the traversal returns to an earlier value after visiting a later one
  (`k0, k1, k0, k1`, which is what a deep operand held across an inner fan looks like). The
  intervals do overlap, `L = 2`, and `W = 1` would be a simultaneous-input race.

The consumer that needs the post-WAR floor is the order-aware register strategy in `translate.py`:
it wants to drop a group to `W = 1` exactly where the group is sequentially refillable, and to be
clamped up to the real floor where it is not. So `off` — the prefetch depth — is deliberately **not
part of the floor**; it is what the `unroll` policy *buys* above the floor.

**Cost.** `intervals` has at most `3T` entries (three iterations × up to `T` distinct values), and
the sampling loop is `T` positions each scanning every interval: `O(T²)` with a constant of 3. At
`T = 64` that is roughly 12 000 containment tests per call, and `group_width` calls it **twice**
(both peaks) for every group of every operand. This is the single hottest thing in `theta.py`, and
section 5.3.9 says what to do about it.

**Sharp edge — the `niter = 3` constant is only sound while `off ≤ T`.** The sampling window
`[T, 2T)` sees intervals from iterations 0, 1 and 2. A generation from a hypothetical iteration 3
would start at `3T + first − off`, which enters the window only if `off > 2T + first`; a generation
from iteration 2 already is modelled. So the construction is safe for `off ≤ T`, which holds
comfortably on shipping shapes (`off` is the local prefetch depth, 0 to 3; `T ≥ 2`). It is not
checked anywhere. If a future configuration pushes the read-ahead past the inner trip count, raise
`niter` to `2 + ceil(off / T) + 1` and widen the sampling window correspondingly — do not simply
assume the number 3 is a safety margin.

##### 5.3.5 `_reg_read_off(theta, op)`

The register read-ahead depth for one operand:

```
_reg_read_off(op):
    if not op.hops: return 0                          # the accumulator: no input trajectory
    substep = the INNERMOST inner mode that is a reduction mode      (None if there is none)
    return max(0, theta.off_at(op, READ, substep))    if substep else 0
```

It reads the first-class retime map rather than any field on the hop, because the retime lives in
`Theta.off_map` keyed by `(operand, role, level)`. The level it keys on is the innermost reduction
inner mode — the substep the read prefetches along — found by scanning `inner_modes()` in reverse
for membership in `reduction_names()`. Returns 0 for an op-class with no input trajectory or with
no reduction ring at all.

Note the *role* in the key: `READ`. This is the case the op-class keying exists for. Under an
operand-only key, an operand's read-ahead at the substep level and its copy prefetch would be
indistinguishable keys the moment both levels coincided.

##### 5.3.6 `group_width(theta, op, group, steps)` — the searched value `W`

This is where `S` actually gets its register-side numbers.

```
group_width(op, group, steps):
    R           = group_rate(op, group)
    L_floor     = group_live_peak(op, group, steps)                    # post-WAR
    L_prefetch  = group_live_peak(op, group, steps, post_war=False)    # prefetch-overlap
    choice      = op.fragment.policy_of(group)

    if choice == 'inplace':      return max(1, L_floor)
    if choice is an int:         return max(L_floor, min(choice, R))   # CLAMP, never reject
    W = R if choice == 'unroll' else L_prefetch                        # 'floor' -> L_prefetch
    return max(L_floor, min(W, R))                                     # clamp into [L_floor, R]
```

Four policies, one knob (`Fragment.group_policy`, resolved by `Fragment.policy_of`):

| policy | intent | value |
|---|---|---|
| `'unroll'` | maximum scheduling freedom, one buffer per distinct value | `W = R` |
| `'floor'` | double-buffer just enough to hide read latency | `W = L_prefetch`, clamped |
| `'inplace'` | minimum registers; a single slot refilled in place where that is legal | `W = L_floor`, i.e. **1 where sequentially refillable, clamped up where interleaved** |
| an `int` | an explicit interior point an autotuner searched | clamped into `[L_floor, R]` |

Note that `'inplace'` is *not* unconditionally 1. It asks for the post-WAR floor, and the post-WAR
floor is 1 exactly when the group's values are sequential. On an interleaved group it comes back as
2, which is the rescue: a policy that means "as few as legal" cannot be allowed to produce an
illegal width.

**The clamp-versus-reject decision.** The integer branch used to `raise ValueError` on an
out-of-band request. That was fixed after a review of the decoder's totality, and the rationale is
worth stating because
it is a design principle for the whole decoder: **the decoder must be total.** A schedule point
whose width is below the floor and one exactly at the floor emit the *same* kernel, because the
model clamps; so refusing the first while accepting the second buys nothing and turns a repairable
request into a build failure. In practice the raise aborted the entire library build from inside a
parallel worker when a tuner passed `W = 1` for a group whose post-WAR floor was 2.

The **band itself is unchanged and still authoritative**: `W ≥ L` because a rotation cannot cycle
fewer names than are simultaneously live (that is a race, not a slowdown), and `W ≤ R` because
holding more names than there are distinct values is storage spent on nothing. What changed is only
the response to a request outside it.

`test_an_explicit_W_outside_the_band_is_CLAMPED_not_rejected` pins both directions — `W = 1`
clamped up and `W = 99` clamped down — and adds a third assertion that the clamp is a clamp and not
a pass-through (`S.get(...) != 99`). Its docstring records that no test covered the old raise, which
is why the raise survived as long as it did.

**Two derivations of "floor", and they are different.** The `'floor'` policy uses `L_prefetch`
while the band's lower bound and `'inplace'` use `L_floor`. This is deliberate and is the kind of
detail that reads like a bug: the policy named "floor" means "the width that double-buffers to hide
read latency", which is the prefetch-overlap peak; the band's floor means "the width below which
the rotation races", which is the post-WAR peak. `L_prefetch ≥ L_floor` always, and the final
`max(L_floor, min(W, R))` makes the band authoritative whichever the policy asked for. If you
rename anything here, rename the policy, not the variables.

**Two related regressions the tests pin.** `test_plr0_register_depth_is_two` asserts that with no
read-ahead at all the register depth is 2, not 1: the two `K` substeps of one chunk are
simultaneously-live matmul inputs, so `R = 2`, and the single-group default policy is `'unroll'`.
The docstring records the failure mode: a `'floor'` policy picked `L_prefetch = 1` (no read-ahead
means no prefetch overlap), collapsing both substeps into one register name, and the matmul read a
clobbered register. And `test_mxfp8_two_rate_derivation` is the derivation anchor for the whole
band mechanism: a two-part fragment with `strategy=1` derives `(lo, hi) = (2, 1)` — same rate,
different widths — and the resulting operand footprints come out at 192 and 256 registers, matching
a hand-built reference point. `test_mxfp8_max_sched_both_unroll` is the control: `strategy=0` makes
both parts `'unroll'` and the answer becomes `(2, 2)`.

##### 5.3.7 `_free_tile_index_seq(theta, op, steps)`

The operand's own free-axis tile index at each step, as a mixed-radix combine:

```
_free_tile_index_seq(op, steps):
    free_modes = inner modes whose name is in theta.free_names(op)     # ord order
    for each step coord c:
        idx = Σ_j  c[free_modes[j]] * (product of extents of free_modes[j+1:])
        emit idx
```

That is a flat position over the operand's *own* free presence modes — presence minus reduction —
with the innermost mode varying fastest, consistent with `ord`'s outer-to-inner convention. It is
presence-derived, so there is no operand-name or role test: the accumulator, the inputs and the
scale operands all go through the same three lines.

Output: a list of `T` non-negative integers, ranging over `[0, product of free extents)`.

##### 5.3.8 `resident_free_tiles(theta, op)`

**Concept.** How many of the operand's free-axis tiles are *simultaneously resident* under the
current `ord`. This is the residency half of the loop-order story, and it is the reason changing
`ord` changes the register footprint:

* free axis **innermost** — the traversal turns over cleanly, only a window of tiles is live at a
  time, minimum footprint, more read traffic;
* free axis **outer** with the partner operand's axis sweeping inside — every free tile is
  revisited on each inner pass, so all of them are resident: the full fan.

**Algorithm.** Exactly `group_live_peak`'s interval-overlap, run on the free-tile index sequence
instead of a rate group's value sequence:

```
resident_free_tiles(op):
    steps = _inner_steps(theta);  T = len(steps)
    off   = _reg_read_off(theta, op)
    seq   = _free_tile_index_seq(op, steps)
    if not any(seq): return 1                      # no own free mode -> one tile
    ... identical 3-iteration unroll, [first-off, last] intervals, peak over [T, 2T) ...
```

Note it uses the **prefetch-extended** interval (`off` is always subtracted), unlike
`group_live_peak`'s default. That is consistent: a tile the read-ahead has already fetched is
resident, whatever the WAR ordering does to the refill.

There is **no separate residency knob.** The docstring is explicit: block reuse — holding fewer
tiles resident and reloading more often — is expressed as a smaller rotation width `W`, via the
register partition plus its width policy. The derived live peak is the reuse the loop order allows,
and nothing overrides it. `sizing.resident_free_tiles` is a one-line forwarder to this function, so
the sizing layer cannot grow a second answer.

##### 5.3.9 Cost, weaknesses and how to make the rate machinery faster

**Where the time goes.** For one decode, with `P` operands, `G` groups per operand and `T` inner
steps:

| function | cost | shipping magnitude |
|---|---|---|
| `_inner_steps` | `O(T · #inner modes)` | `T ≤ 64`, modes ≤ 6 |
| `_group_value_seq` | `O(T · #modes · log #modes)` (the per-step `sorted`) | trivial |
| `group_rate` | `O(#inner modes)` | trivial |
| `group_live_peak` | **`O(T²)`** | ≈ 12 000 comparisons at `T = 64` |
| `group_width` | `2 × group_live_peak` | the dominant term |
| `resident_free_tiles` | `O(T²)` + a second `_inner_steps` | once per operand |
| `derive_S` | `P · G ×` the above | `P ≤ 5`, `G ≤ 4` |

So a decode is order `P · G · 2 · T²` interval tests — on the largest shipping shape, a few hundred
thousand cheap operations, tens of milliseconds of Python. `KernelWriter` caches `(theta, S)` per
kernel name precisely because two consumers (register sizing at kernel init, and GIR construction
at emit time) would otherwise each pay it. That cache is what keeps this off the profile; if it is
ever removed, this subsection becomes the hot spot.

**Five concrete improvements, in the order a maintainer should attempt them.**

1. **Compute `L_prefetch` lazily.** `group_width` computes *both* peaks unconditionally, and the
   `'unroll'` and `'inplace'` policies never look at `L_prefetch`. On the shipping strategies
   (`strategy=0` makes every group `'unroll'`; `strategy=1` makes the first `'unroll'` and the rest
   `'inplace'`) `L_prefetch` is computed and discarded for **every group of every kernel**. Moving
   it inside the `'floor'` branch halves the dominant cost for free and changes no result.
2. **Replace the `O(T²)` sweep with a difference array.** The peak of a set of integer intervals
   over a bounded range is a linear scan: `+1` at each start, `−1` after each end, prefix-sum, take
   the maximum over `[T, 2T)`. That turns `O(T²)` into `O(T + #intervals)`. The intervals here are
   already integer-bounded (`[−off, 3T)`), so this is a mechanical rewrite of about ten lines.
3. **Extract the shared live-peak helper.** `group_live_peak` and `resident_free_tiles` contain the
   *same* fifteen lines — three-iteration unroll, `gens` dict, `[first−off, last]` intervals, peak
   over the middle window — differing only in which sequence they consume and whether `off` is
   applied. That is a `_live_peak(seq, T, off)` waiting to be written, and it is also the right
   place to fix the `niter = 3` soundness condition (section 5.3.4) once instead of twice.
4. **Thread `steps` into `resident_free_tiles`.** It is the only function in the group that calls
   `_inner_steps` itself; every other consumer receives the list from `derive_S`. Passing it in (or
   memoizing `_inner_steps` on `id(theta)`) removes a full re-materialization per operand.
5. **Memoize `_rate_broadcast` per `(op, group)`.** It is called by `_group_value_seq` and by
   `group_rate`, and it recomputes `reduction_names()` — which recomputes `presence_modes` for
   every output operand, which recomputes `geometry.broadcast_axes` — every single time. This is
   the deepest recomputation chain in the file.

**Honest weaknesses.**

* **`if not any(seq)` in `resident_free_tiles` is a truthiness test on integers.** It means "every
  free-tile index is zero", which is the intended condition (the operand has no free axis of extent
  greater than one), but it reaches that conclusion by treating `0` as falsy rather than by asking
  `theta.free_names(op)`. It happens to be correct for every sequence `_free_tile_index_seq` can
  produce; it would be clearer, and robust to a change in the index encoding, to test the mode list
  directly.
* **The `max(1, ...)` clamps are everywhere and they hide degenerate inputs.** `group_rate` can
  return the product of a zero extent only if an *inner* mode had extent 0, which the outer/inner
  classification forbids by definition; but `group_live_peak`, `resident_free_tiles` and
  `_shared_depth` all end in `max(1, ...)`. A genuinely broken schedule point therefore produces
  `1` rather than an exception. That is the totality principle again, and it is a deliberate
  trade — but when a width comes out as 1 and you did not expect it, check whether it is a real
  floor or a clamped nothing.
* **`Fragment` is a mutable dataclass and the tests mutate it in place.**
  `test_an_explicit_W_outside_the_band_is_CLAMPED_not_rejected` assigns
  `A.fragment.group_policy = {"*": 99}` on a live schedule point. That works, and the depth map is
  rebuilt afterwards, but it means `Fragment` cannot be made frozen or shared between operands
  without breaking tests, and it means nothing memoized on a `Fragment` is safe unless the
  memoization is invalidated on mutation. `Fragment.__post_init__` also rewrites `self.parts` in
  place (expanding an integer `N` into the tuple `(1,) * N`), which is another reason it is not
  frozen.

##### 5.3.10 The drivers: `derive_S`, `_shared_depth`, `build_S`

These three assemble the `DepthMap` (the container itself is section 4's). They are listed here
because they are the only callers of everything above.

**`derive_S(theta) -> DepthMap`** builds the **register** half:

```
derive_S(theta):
    steps = _inner_steps(theta)
    S = DepthMap()
    for op in theta.operands:
        if op.is_output: continue          # the accumulator has no mainloop rotating ring
        for group in op.fragment.groups():
            S.set(op.name, group, group_width(theta, op, group, steps))
    return S
```

No authored literals: every register depth in the map is `group_width`'s answer, keyed by the
group's **label** (`Fragment.groups()`). The accumulator is skipped because it holds one value per
output tile across the whole reduction — there is no ring to have a depth, and its footprint is a
separate additive term in `sizing.operand_footprint_regs`, not a multibuffer entry.

**`_shared_depth(theta, op) -> int`** is the **shared-memory ring** depth for one operand, and its
one-line summary is: **it reads the target's buffer count, it does not derive it.**

```
_shared_depth(op):
    if no hop of op has dst == SHARED:  raise            # a direct-to-register operand has no ring
    if op.lds_buffers:                  return max(1, op.lds_buffers)
    return max(1, off(op, COPY, reduction_chunk))        # unstated -> fall back to delta
```

Three things in that are load-bearing. First, the **raise** on an operand with no shared placement:
every caller already guards on the operand touching shared memory, so reaching this is a caller
bug, and any number returned instead would be a fiction. `test_dtv_operand_has_no_shared_ring_depth`
pins it. Second, **the depth is `op.lds_buffers`, not the prefetch depth `δ`.** Deriving it from
`δ` is a real, quiet bug: the two *coincide* at the common double-buffered prefetch setting, so
every test agreed, and they diverge at prefetch depth 1 against a double-buffered allocation, where
the model said 1 and the kernel had 2. A depth-1 ring has no rotation, so the decoder emitted no
buffer swap at all while the kernel's addressing, its second buffer offset block and its memory
token all still alternated, and every copy overwrote the buffer being read.
`test_shared_depth_is_the_buffer_count_not_the_prefetch_depth` is the regression, and
`test_per_operand_lds_buffers_and_off_are_independent` pins that the two are separately settable
per operand (one operand at depth 1 beside another at depth 2). Third, there is **deliberately no
`S ≥ δ` assertion here**: on this target the copy's prefetch depth is a *global-read* depth, the
staged write into shared memory is a separate serialized step, and a real shipping configuration
has a single shared buffer with a prefetch depth of 2. Asserting the inequality against the wrong
`δ` would reject it. A genuine check belongs against the local-write offset once the write side is
modelled at all (#116).

**`build_S(theta) -> (S, floor)`** is the public entry point: it runs `derive_S`, copies the result,
and adds one `SHARED_GROUP`-keyed row per operand that touches shared memory. It returns the
combined map **and** the pure register floor, the latter for reporting only — the renderer prints
both so that a reader can see where a width came from. `SHARED_GROUP` is the reserved label
`"shared"` under which the shared ring lives in the same map as the register groups; every caller
that means "a register group" must filter it out, and `sizing.operand_generations`,
`ledger.build_ledger` and `KernelWriter` all do.

---

#### 5.4 Φ — the fusion partition

##### 5.4.1 Concept: what fusion is, and what it is not

**Fusion** merges several op-classes' *movements* into one cooperative instruction. The concrete
hardware situation on the target is a wave-separated bulk mover: one descriptor is aliased across
two operands, a single instruction is issued, and wave parity selects which operand's bytes that
wave actually moves. Two op-classes, one instruction, one completion event.

The schedule point stores this as `Theta.fuse_groups`: a list of lists of op-class name tokens. A
group of length 1 is meaningless and `translate` filters those out, so every stored group has at
least two members. `Theta.fuse` is a separate integer recording *which preset* the translation
layer used to build the groups; **nothing in the core or in the lowering reads it** — it is
informational residue, and a maintainer should not add a consumer for it without first deciding
whether `fuse_groups` alone is enough (it has been so far).

Two things fusion is explicitly **not**:

* It is **not** the cross-agent test. An earlier version of `Theta.agent_distributed` made fusion
  the entire predicate ("the members of a fused group disagree about their carrier"). That is
  wrong in a way that produced a race: a **lone** operand cooperatively loaded by four waves is
  cross-agent with no fusion anywhere, and the fusion-based predicate returned `False` for it, so
  no fence was emitted. It only stayed unreachable because the parameter bridge happened to weld
  the fusion flag to multi-wave operation. Section 5.4.5 covers the corrected predicate.
* It is **not** a region-split mechanism. Fusion and region splitting are orthogonal moves that
  interact (section 5.4.3), but a fused group of unsplit operands is one whole movement and a split
  unfused operand is several movements.

##### 5.4.2 `Theta.movement_units()` — the single authority

```
movement_units() -> [ (unit_key, members, n_regions) ]

    copy_ops = [o for o in operands if o.hops and o.hops[0].dst == SHARED]
    by_name  = {o.name: o for o in copy_ops}
    for op in copy_ops (in schedule order):
        key = the first fuse_group containing op.name, filtered to copy ops   (as a tuple)
              or (op.name,) if op is in no group
        skip if this key was already emitted
        members = [by_name[n] for n in key]
        splits  = { max(1, m.split) for m in members }
        n_regions = the single split if all members agree, else 1
        emit (key, members, n_regions)
```

* **`unit_key`** — a tuple of op-class names, the identity of the movement. A lone movement's key
  is a one-tuple, which is what makes an unfused kernel's obligations, `Await` dependencies and IR
  dumps byte-identical to the pre-fusion behaviour.
* **`members`** — the `Operand` objects, in the order the fuse group lists them.
* **`n_regions`** — how many region-indexed *instances* this movement emits.

The docstring's justification is the important part: both the emitter (which builds the movement
nodes) and the downstream lowering (which must know a movement's completion granularity to key its
memory token) need this fact, and **deriving it twice invites the two to disagree.**
`emit.build_ir` reads it into a `_units` dict; `ledger.movement_name` walks it to map an op-class
name to its movement; the GIR lowering copies it into `Program.meta["unit_regions"]`; and the
token-assignment pass reads it from there rather than re-deriving. Four consumers, one derivation.

##### 5.4.3 Members pair **by index**, and what a mixed group means

The region-pairing rule is the piece most likely to be got wrong by someone extending this.

A region-split tile is cut into storage-disjoint parts, and the bulk mover emits **one instruction
per part**. When two split operands are fused, region `j` of `A` moves together with region `j` of
`B` — giving movements `AB0` and `AB1` for a two-way split. **The pairing is by index, not by a
shared mode.** The two operands may be cut on entirely different axes (one on its `M` fan, the
other on its `N` fan); nothing requires them to name the same mode, and the emitter's
`_region_mode_of` labels a heterogeneous group by one representative member's axis.

`n_regions` is therefore the *shared* split count, and only when every member agrees. A **mixed**
group — say a two-way-split operand fused with an unsplit scale operand — has **no region-1
instance of the unsplit member to pair with**, so the pairing is undefined and the group moves
**whole**: `n_regions = 1`. That is a perfectly legal schedule (a coarse copy feeding split reads
is allowed), but it silently discards the split the caller asked for on that copy hop, so
`translate.params_to_theta` appends an explicit note:

> `NOTE: fused group [...] has mixed region splits {...} — region-index pairing is undefined, so
> the group moves WHOLE and the requested split is not applied to its copy hop (the reads stay
> split)`

Saying so in the notes rather than letting the split vanish is the pattern to follow for any future
degradation in this area.

##### 5.4.4 What a fused movement means for completion — and for the ledger

This is the reason fusion is in the model at all rather than being a lowering detail.

**A Φ group is ONE cooperative instruction, so it completes ONCE.** Every member's data becomes
resident at the same instant. There is no per-member completion event, and therefore:

* there is **one** hazard obligation for the movement, not one per member;
* both endpoints of that obligation name the **movement**, not a member;
* a consumer of *any* member awaits that single event.

`ledger.movement_name(theta, opname)` implements the naming: it walks `theta.movement_units()`,
finds the unit containing `opname`, and returns the bare op-class name for a lone movement or the
whole member tuple for a fused one. Because both endpoints of the obligation are built from that
name, the per-member entries **collapse in the ledger's dedup set** and a single `Obligation`
object is what every member's consumer matches. The same rule is applied on both ends of the
chunk-crossing dependency as well: one cooperative copy, one crossing obligation, matched by every
member's crossing read — "two per-member obligations would be two accounts against one
instruction."

The recorded defect (#195) is exactly the failure to do this: duplicate `Await` markers, one per
member, against a single instruction.

There is a **guard** in `emit.build_ir` that belongs to this rule: the members of a fused group
must share the same prefetch retime. One instruction cannot move operand `X`'s chunk `iter+off_X`
and operand `Y`'s chunk `iter+off_Y` at the same time, so heterogeneous `off` within one group is
ill-posed and is rejected with a message naming each member's offset, rather than silently forcing
everyone onto a representative's value.

There is also a **known open sharp edge** here (#213): a Φ group whose members disagree about
whether their copy must be issued *before* or *after* the reads in the body is resolved by an
`any()` over the members rather than being rejected. That is the same class of defect as the
mixed-`off` case, but it has not yet been given the same treatment.

##### 5.4.5 `Theta.agent_distributed(opname)` — are this op-class's shared hazards cross-agent?

```
agent_distributed(opname):
    if no hop of op has dst == SHARED:  return False     # never staged: no shared buffer at all
    return self.agents > 1
```

**Concept.** The refill-after-read ordering that discharges a rotation hazard is
`complete(read)` then `issue(refill)`, composed through **program order on one agent**. The moment
a byte's writer and its reader are different agents, that composition does not exist: an agent's
own completion counter retires only its own transfers, so it gives it no edge at all to a transfer
another agent issued. The remedy is a synchronization primitive with a scope wider than one agent.

The predicate is deliberately coarse. In a GEMM **every** agent reads the whole staged tile, so as
soon as two agents cooperate on one shared buffer the hazard is cross-agent — there is no need to
ask *which* agent wrote *which* byte. `Theta.agents` is a plain count, and it is the only place the
model knows an agent exists at all; the model never learns what a wave is.

**Consumers.** `emit.py` uses it to pick an `Await`'s scope (`"block"` when distributed, `"wave"`
otherwise); the GIR lowering copies the per-operand answers into `Program.meta`, where the
shared-memory hazard analysis and the GIR dump both read them.

`test_a_cross_agent_RAW_residency_is_BLOCK_scoped_not_wave` is the fixture, and it is a good model
of a non-vacuous test: it builds both a four-agent and a single-agent schedule point from the same
kernel dict, asserts the multi-agent case widens the true-dependency waits to block scope, asserts
the single-agent case leaves them at wave scope (so a rule that returned `"block"` unconditionally
would fail), and additionally asserts that the rotation-anti-dependency was **not** widened — the
alternative remedy there is a spare buffer slot, not a wider fence.

**`Theta.rho`** is the field where a *narrower* claim would live — "this movement is confined to one
agent after all". It exists, it is a dict from op-class token to an opaque agent selector compared
only for equality, and it is **always empty**: nothing populates it and nothing reads it. Do not
describe ρ as implemented. The genuinely agent-aware fact the model does carry is
`Hop.region_agent_relative` (section 5.2.3), which is why the residual gap tracked as #165 is about
*exactness*, not expressibility.

##### 5.4.6 `Theta.per_region_completion` — π, the completion-granularity choice

A region-split movement emits one instruction per region. Whether those instances share one
completion class or carry distinct ones is a *policy*, and it is stored as a boolean on the
schedule point:

* **`False` (the default)** — all region instances of an op-class share one completion class, so a
  read must await **every** region and no region may remain in flight. This is what the consuming
  backend implements today.
* **`True`** — each region instance is its own completion class, so a read of region `j` awaits
  only region `j` and the other regions stay in flight; the overlap then falls out of the counting
  rule rather than being scheduled.

The model handles both, and the GIR layer models both. `theta.py`'s comment on this field still says
the assembly-emitting adapter rejects `True`; it no longer does. That refusal lived in
`gir_to_rocisa._token_ids`, which used to push a single int through mutable writer state, and it was
deleted when the ids became a tuple (`_token_ids`: "Passing the tuple removes the channel and the
refusals with it"). `True` therefore lowers to assembly today, silently. `translate` also emits a note when `True` is requested on a schedule
point where no operand is actually region-split, since the setting is then vacuous.

##### 5.4.7 `Theta.tensor_instrs_per_kiter()` — and a real inconsistency

```
tensor_instrs_per_kiter():
    byname = {o.name: o for o in operands if o.hops and o.hops[0].dst == SHARED}
    fused  = every token appearing in any fuse group
    n = 0
    for g in fuse_groups:                 # each fused group: one instruction PER REGION
        n += max(max(1, o.split) for o in g's members present in byname)
    for name, o in byname.items():        # unfused copies
        if name not in fused: n += max(1, o.split)
    return max(1, n)
```

The intent is the count of *distinct* global-to-shared instructions per chunk — the quantity a
backend would need if it were tracking one shared completion counter for all of them. Fusion
reduces the count, and a region split multiplies it.

**This is a second derivation of a fact `movement_units` already owns, and the two disagree on a
mixed-split fused group.** For a group `{A(split 2), MXSA(split 1)}`:

* `movement_units` reports `n_regions = 1` — the pairing is undefined so the group moves whole
  (section 5.4.3), and `translate` has already emitted a note saying so;
* `tensor_instrs_per_kiter` takes `max` over the members' splits and reports **2**.

The over-count is harmless *today* only because the value is dead: `emit.emit_mainloop` places it
in its result dictionary under the key `"tensor_per_kiter"` and **nothing in the tree reads that
key** — not the renderer, not the lowering, not `KernelWriter`. It is a reporting field with no
reporter.

This is the "two derivations of one rule" shape that section 5.2 warns about, caught before it
could do damage. The correct repair is three lines: make `tensor_instrs_per_kiter` sum
`n_regions` over `movement_units()` and delete its own loop. Do that if you ever wire the value to
a consumer; do not extend the current implementation.

A related, milder inconsistency in the same neighbourhood: `movement_units` and
`tensor_instrs_per_kiter` both identify a copy operand by `o.hops[0].dst == SHARED` (the *first*
hop), whereas `_shared_depth`, `build_S`, `ledger` and the GIR lowering all use
`any(h.dst == SHARED for h in o.hops)`. The two predicates agree on every trajectory shape the tree
constructs — a staged operand's first hop is its copy, and a direct-to-register operand has no
shared hop at all — but they are three spellings of one question, and a trajectory with a
register-to-shared leg later in the path (the epilogue store, #116) would split them apart. When
the store side is modelled, unify them first.

##### 5.4.8 Extending Φ: advice

* **Add consumers to `movement_units`, never a parallel derivation.** The whole value of the
  function is that it is the only place a movement's identity and region count are decided. If you
  need a new per-movement fact (say, which agent subset carries it), add a fourth element to the
  tuple or return a small dataclass — do not compute it beside the call.
* **The `n_regions` degradation is silent unless someone reads the notes.** If mixed-split groups
  become common, promote the `translate` note to a first-class field on the movement tuple
  (`requested_split` alongside `n_regions`) so a consumer can see that a split was dropped rather
  than never requested.
* **Cost is negligible and does not need optimizing.** `movement_units` is
  `O(#copy operands × #fuse groups × group size)` — five operands, at most two groups, two members
  each. It is called once per `build_ir` and a handful of times from the ledger. Leave it alone.
* **If a fused group ever needs members with different retimes**, that is not a relaxation of the
  guard in `emit.build_ir`; it is a statement that they are not one instruction, and the right
  model change is to split the group.

---

#### 5.5 `Fragment` — the object the rate machinery reads

Every input to sections 5.2 and 5.3 arrives on one dataclass. `Fragment` describes the register-side
structure of one operand's placement: how its tile fan is partitioned into rotating groups, what
each group is constant over, and how each group's width is to be chosen. It is worth reading as the
*input surface* of the rate machinery rather than as a container.

| field | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `broadcast_axes` | `set[str]` | the loop axes this operand's **data** is constant over. `A[m,k]` gives `{"n"}`. The model's structural primitive: it drives presence, the reload rate and the live range. It used to be a per-register-name nullspace, but it was always uniform across a fragment's slots, so it is one set. |
| `parts` | `int` or `tuple` | the register partition. The **normal form is an integer `N`** meaning "split into `N` equal groups"; a tuple stays available for explicit or uneven slot counts. `len(parts)` is the group count; each entry is that group's share of the fragment's registers. |
| `labels` | `tuple` or `None` | optional pretty names per group (`("lo","hi")`); purely cosmetic, defaulting to `g0, g1, …`. |
| `grouping_mode` | `str` or `None` | the tile **mode whose values the register groups partition**. A group *is* a subset of this mode's values, not a slice of the register file. `None` on a non-split fragment, where the fan stays in the rate. |
| `group_policy` | `dict` or `None` | `label -> 'unroll' \| 'floor' \| 'inplace' \| int`, plus an optional `"*"` default. The one knob that sets `W`. |

**`Fragment.__post_init__`** performs the single normalization: if `parts` is an integer `N`, it is
rewritten in place to `(1,) * N`, with a `ValueError` for `N < 1`. Everything downstream can then
assume a tuple. This mutation is why `Fragment` is not a frozen dataclass.

**`Fragment.group_labels()`** returns the labels: `tuple(self.labels)` when given, otherwise
`("g0", "g1", …)` of the right length. **`Fragment.groups()`** is an alias that exists to make
call sites read as "the reuse groups" rather than "the pretty names"; both return the same tuple,
and the group is *identified by its label* — the depth map, the width policy and the ledger all key
on it.

**`Fragment.size_of(label)`** is that group's register-slot count: `parts[labels.index(label)]`.
It returns `1` for a label it does not recognize rather than raising, which is a silent failure
mode — a stale label in a `group_policy` dict will not be reported here.

**`Fragment.total_slots()`** is `sum(parts)` — the denominator in
`sizing.group_regs`, which apportions a fragment's registers across its groups as
`frag_regs * size_of(group) // total_slots`.

**`Fragment.policy_of(group)`** resolves the width choice with a three-level lookup: the per-label
entry, then the fragment's `"*"` default, then `'unroll'`. It is the single source of `W`'s intent
and it is what lets one fragment carry two different widths over the same rate — the two-part
reference point is `lo = 'unroll'`, `hi = 'inplace'`, giving widths 2 and 1 with `R = 2` for both.
`translate._register_policy` is the only in-tree producer: strategy 0 makes every part `'unroll'`,
strategies 1 and 2 make the first part `'unroll'` and the rest `'inplace'`, and the docstring is
explicit that this layer picks *intent* only — the order-aware clamp to the realizable floor happens
in the core, in `group_width`.

**`Fragment.group_broadcast(group=None)`** is covered in section 5.2.7: it returns the fragment's
data-broadcast set and ignores its argument.

**The equal-partition assumption.** `grouping_mode`'s docstring states it and
`sizing.operand_footprint_regs` enforces it: `len(parts)` must divide the grouping mode's extent,
and an indivisible case raises rather than computing a wrong footprint. This is an *accepted scope
exception*, not an oversight — the per-part footprint formula is already shaped for uneven
partitions (`sum over parts of W_part × |part|`), so lifting it means carrying each group's own
value-subset size on the `Fragment` and deleting both the scalar `part_vals` and the guard. That is
the concrete extension recipe if an uneven partition is ever wanted.

#### 5.6 Invariants this half maintains, and what breaks if you change them

A checklist for a reviewer:

1. **`L ≤ W ≤ R` for every register group**, enforced by clamping in `group_width` and by nothing
   else. Break the lower bound and two live values share a register name; break the upper bound and
   registers are allocated for values that do not exist.
2. **`R` is per-group and per-fragment, never per-operand.** A region split multiplies the number
   of groups, not any group's rate. Violating this over-counts the footprint by the split factor.
3. **A free region axis is out of the rate; a reduction region axis is in it.** Section 5.2.6; the
   measured cost of getting it backwards was every numeric comparison failing.
4. **The rate nullspace and the data nullspace are two functions.** Section 5.2.5.
5. **The coordinates inside one movement quantum are one presence point**, hence one step and one
   generation. Section 5.1.5.
6. **A Φ group is one instruction, one completion, one obligation** — with both endpoints named by
   the movement. Section 5.4.4.
7. **The shared ring depth is read from the target, not derived from the prefetch depth.**
   Section 5.3.10.
8. **Every out-of-band request is repaired, not refused.** The decoder is total. Section 5.3.6.
9. **`movement_units` is the only derivation of what the movements are.** Section 5.4.2, with the
   one live violation named in section 5.4.7.

#### 5.7 The remaining names in `theta.py`

These are the definitions whose primary treatment is the schedule-point half of this file
(section 4). They are listed here with a short, real statement of what each computes, so that the
file's definition list is complete from either entry point and so that a reader who arrives at the
rate machinery first is never blocked on an undefined term.

**Traversal axes.**

* **`Mode(name, extent)`** — one tiled traversal axis, a frozen dataclass. `extent` is the *static*
  trip count and `0` is the sentinel for "not statically known".
* **`Mode.is_outer`** — `extent == 0`. The single intrinsic outer/inner test: an outer level is a
  real runtime loop with a back edge (the reduction chunk, or a future persistent level); an inner
  level is fully unrolled and is where the register ring rotates. Everything else in the file is
  this predicate filtered.
* **`Theta.levels()`** — `list(self.ord)`, the full outer-to-inner permutation. The emission nest
  and the peel skeleton walk these; `levels()[0]` is the outermost.
* **`Theta.outer_modes()`** / **`Theta.inner_modes()`** — the two filters of `is_outer`.
  `inner_modes()` is what the whole of section 5.3 iterates; outer levels are excluded so that a
  symbolic runtime trip can never enter a rate or footprint product.
* **`Theta.reduction_chunk_mode()`** — the **innermost** outer level, i.e. the level one whole
  staged tile of data is copied for; `None` if there is no outer level. Five things key on it (the
  shared ring depth, the read's shared-source rotation, the emitted steady loop, the binding its
  peel steps pin, and the peel depth at that level) and they must never disagree; three call sites
  once indexed `outer_modes()[0]` and two `[-1]`, which are the same answer while there is exactly
  one outer level and silently different the moment there are two. Route every such lookup through
  this accessor.
* **`Theta.reduction_chunk_name(default=None)`** — its `.name`, or `default`. `_shared_depth` and
  the ledger use this form because they need a level *name* to index `off_map`.

**Hops and op-class roles.**

* **`COPY` / `READ` / `STORE`** — the op-class role vocabulary: the second half of `off`'s row
  index. An op-class is (operand, hop), and the role is what distinguishes an operand's read at a
  level from its copy at the same level.
* **`HOP_ROLE`** — the table mapping `(src space, dst space)` to a role. Global-to-shared is
  `COPY`; shared-to-register **and** global-to-register are both `READ` (a one-hop
  direct-to-register trajectory *is* the read); anything moving to a coarser space is `STORE`.
* **`Hop(src, dst, vector_elems, kind, split, quantum, region_agent_relative)`** — one leg of a
  trajectory. `vector_elems` is elements moved per instruction per lane; `split` is the region
  count for a bulk leg; `quantum` is section 5.1; `region_agent_relative` is section 5.2.3.
* **`Hop.__post_init__`** — infers `kind` when unset: a global-to-shared leg defaults to `'tdm'`
  (the bulk whole-tile cooperative mover), everything else to `'load'` (per-lane). A non-bulk
  global-to-shared leg is expressed by setting `kind='load'` explicitly.
* **`Hop.is_bulk`** — `kind == 'tdm'`. This is what `geometry.hop_broadcast` branches on, so it is
  the switch between "spans every inner axis" and "spans what its quantum covers".
* **`Hop.role`** — `HOP_ROLE[(src, dst)]`, raising a message that names the table when a new space
  pair appears.
* **`Hop.counter`** — the completion class this leg's transfers retire on, from `ir.HOP_COUNTER`.

**Trajectory sense.**

* **`FORWARD` / `REVERSE`**, **`_SPACE_RANK`**, **`trajectory_sense(op)`** — the *whole
  trajectory's* direction, which is **not** the same fact as a hop's role. `_SPACE_RANK` ranks the
