  spaces by distance from compute (global 0, shared 1, register 2), so a hop that increases rank
  runs toward compute. `trajectory_sense` takes the sense from `op.is_output` (an accumulator's
  trajectory is the reflection of an input's) and **cross-checks** it against the summed hop
  direction, raising when the two disagree rather than picking one. The distinction matters because
  the software-pipeline peel is reflected for a reverse op-class — a forward one is hoisted
  backward (prefetch: prologue fills, drain drains) and a reverse one forward (defer: prologue and
  drain swap). In a store round trip `register → shared → register → global`, the middle leg's role
  is `READ` while the trajectory is `REVERSE`, which is exactly the confusion the function ends.
  Three tests pin it: the sense agrees with `is_output` on every operand of a reference point; a
  synthetically reversed accumulator is **refused** by the peel construction rather than peeled the
  forward way (the reflected peel is not implemented, so building it forward would look right); and
  a sense contradicting its own path raises.

**Operands.**

* **`Operand(name, free_mode, hops, fragment, frag_elems, elem_bytes, lds_buffers, region_modes,
  free_split, role)`** — one tensor trajectory. `frag_elems` is elements one lane holds per
  (free-tile, substep) fragment and `elem_bytes` its element size — together the input to
  `geometry.frag_regs`. `lds_buffers` is this operand's shared ring depth (`0` = unstated;
  section 5.3.10). `region_modes` names the axes enumerating storage-disjoint siblings.
* **`Operand.is_output`** / **`Operand.is_input`** — `role == 'output'` / `'input'`. The output
  role is the accumulator op-class: present on the free modes only, register-resident, no input
  trajectory in the main loop (`hops == []`), and the anchor from which `reduction_modes` is
  defined.
* **`Operand.split`** — the region count of this operand's bulk hop, else 1. A per-operand
  convenience over the per-hop truth.
* **`Operand.has_bulk()`** — whether any hop is bulk.
* **`Operand.free_split`** — the **free-axis** region count carried as a plain number rather than
  inferred from `region_modes`. The reason is durability: a region axis whose extent collapses to 1
  is dropped from `ord` during canonicalization, which empties `region_modes` and silently releases
  a veto that depends on it — measured, the read-ahead carry returned and a fold pair was cut
  across blocks. The split is a fact about storage, not about which mode happens to carry the
  coordinate. It is free-axis only, deliberately: a reduction-axis split is not a sibling
  enumeration (section 5.2.6).

**The schedule point's own lookups.**

* **`Theta`** — the dataclass holding `operands`, `ord`, `reg_bytes`, `lanes`, `fuse_groups`,
  `fuse`, `lds`, `rho`, `agents`, `off_map`, `per_region_completion` and `notes`.
* **`Theta.op(name)`** — linear lookup by operand name, raising `KeyError`. `O(#operands)` with
  `#operands ≤ 5`; not worth a dict.
* **`Theta.off_at(opname, role, level_name)`** — the retime offset for one op-class at one level,
  `0` when absent. Accepts either a name or an `Operand`. This is the only sanctioned way to read
  `off_map`; never index the dict directly.
* **`Theta.off_of(op, hop, level_name)`** — the same, with the role read off the hop, for callers
  that already hold it.

**The depth map container.**

* **`SHARED_GROUP`** — the reserved group label `"shared"` under which an operand's shared ring
  depth is stored alongside its register groups in the one map.
* **`DepthMap`** — depth per *placement*, keyed `(op, region, group)`. The `region` component is
  what lets a region-split tile carry two different depths for what is nominally one operand.
* **`DepthMap.set(op, group, d, region=None)`** — store one row.
* **`DepthMap.get(op, group, default=1, region=None)`** — exact row first; a named region with no
  row of its own falls back to the whole-tile row; a region-less query over per-region rows returns
  the value when they agree and **raises** when they disagree, because collapsing a per-placement
  fact to per-operand is the bug the three-part key exists to prevent.
* **`DepthMap.regions_of(op, group)`** — the region indices that have rows, `[None]` for a single
  whole-tile placement. This is the enumeration a per-placement consumer should iterate instead of
  assuming one placement per operand.
* **`DepthMap.groups_of(op, region=None)`** — `{group: depth}` for one placement, routed through
  `get` so the disagreement rule applies.
* **`DepthMap.__repr__`** — a compact one-line dump, `A=[lo:2, hi:1, shared:2]`, with per-region
  rows spelled `group@rN:depth`. Debug output only.


---

### 6. `sizing.py` — counts, bytes and the register footprint

#### 6.1 What this module is for

`sizing.py` is 190 lines and answers exactly two families of question about a schedule point:

1. **How much storage does an operand need?** — in physical registers per lane
   (`operand_footprint_regs`), and in shared-memory bytes for a whole staged tile
   (`operand_tile_bytes`).
2. **How many instructions does a movement cost?** — per hop, per reduction chunk
   (`plan_transfers`), together with the two quantities that division needs
   (`operand_buffer_regs`, `load_regs`).

Plus one shape type, `MmaShape`, which packages the compute grid for one chunk.

Everything here is a **pure function of `(theta, S)`**. Nothing in the module mutates state, caches,
or reads a global; every entry point can be called in any order, any number of times, and two calls
with the same arguments return the same integer. That property is load-bearing downstream: the
kernel generator builds `(theta, S)` once and hands the same pair to a register-sizing consumer that
runs early and to an emission consumer that runs late (section 6.9), and the two must not be able to
disagree.

The module owns **no arithmetic of its own** for tile counts. `free_tiles`, `k_tiles` and
`frag_regs` here are one-line forwards to `geometry` (section 2.2). What `sizing.py` genuinely owns
is the **combination**: which of those primitives multiply together, in what order, and which of
them must *not* appear in a given product. Most of the historical defects in this file were of the
second kind — a factor that was multiplied in when it should have been absent (section 6.8.1) — so
the module is best read as a set of assertions about *orthogonality*, not as arithmetic.

#### 6.2 Position in the package, and who calls what

`sizing` sits directly above `geometry` and `theta` in the layering and below everything that
emits. Its imports are exactly two modules (`geometry`, and `theta` for the reserved label
`SHARED_GROUP`), plus `math.ceil`. It imports nothing from `emit`, `placement`, `ledger` or `ir`,
and nothing in the package imports `sizing` in order to make a *decision* — every consumer uses it
to attach a number to something already decided.

The complete consumer map, verified by grep over the tree:

| Symbol | Called from | Purpose at the call site |
|---|---|---|
| `sizing.frag_regs` | `emit.read_inst`, `emit.fill_reads`, `Lowering/loopir_to_gir._convert_mma`, `render.render_geometry` | stamps `size_regs` on a `Load` node and on a GIR register `Ref`, so a def and a use agree on width |
| `sizing.operand_tile_bytes` | `emit._copy_inst`, `render.render_geometry` | the `size` field of one cooperative movement, summed over the fused members and divided by each member's own region split |
| `sizing.operand_footprint_regs` | `render.render_geometry`; `Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.test_mxfp8_two_rate_derivation` | the `vgpr` column of the derived-geometry dump |
| `sizing.plan_transfers` | `render.render_geometry` | the `ds_reads` column |
| `sizing.mma_shape` | `render.render_geometry` | the `mma grid` line |
| `sizing.free_tiles`, `sizing.k_tiles` | `render.render_geometry` | the `free` and `k_tiles` columns |
| `sizing.operand_buffer_regs` | `sizing.plan_transfers`; `Tests/unit/test_loopmodel` | the numerator of the per-lane instruction count |
| `sizing.load_regs` | `sizing.plan_transfers` | the denominator of the same |
| `sizing.operand_generations` | **nobody** (exported from `__init__.py`, never called) | — |
| `sizing.group_regs` | `sizing.operand_footprint_regs` only | the non-grouping arm's per-group width |
| `sizing.resident_free_tiles` | `sizing.operand_footprint_regs` only | the non-grouping arm's residency factor |
| `sizing._region_count` | `sizing.operand_footprint_regs` only | the grouping arm's region factor |

Two facts jump out of that table and should be stated up front rather than buried:

* **`operand_footprint_regs` is not on the codegen path.** Its only production consumer is the
  human-readable geometry dump. The number that actually sizes the register file is derived
  *separately*, straight off `S`, in the kernel generator (section 6.9). So an arithmetic error in
  the footprint formula produces a wrong column in a debug table, not a wrong kernel — which is
  reassuring for risk and unfortunate for detection, because it means the formula has no
  independent oracle checking it every build. Section 6.5.2 records a concrete inconsistency that
  survived exactly because of this.
* **`operand_generations` is dead code with a public export.** It is listed in `__init__.py`'s
  import block and in `__all__`, so it is API by declaration, but no call site exists anywhere in
  the tree, including the tests. It is documented in section 6.6.1 because a maintainer will find
  it and needs to know both what it computes and that deleting it costs nothing inside this
  repository.

#### 6.3 The compute grid: `MmaShape` and `mma_shape`

##### 6.3.1 `sizing.MmaShape`

A frozen three-field dataclass — `m_tiles`, `n_tiles`, `k_tiles`, all `int` — describing the matmul
grid executed for **one reduction chunk** (one trip of the outer loop, i.e. one `DepthU`-worth of
reduction). It is a *type*, deliberately, rather than a bare tuple: the module docstring's phrase
"returns clean TYPES" is about this. A `(4, 8, 2)` tuple leaves the reader of a call site guessing
which position is which; `shape.k_tiles` does not.

##### 6.3.2 `sizing.MmaShape.count`

A `@property` returning `m_tiles * n_tiles * k_tiles` — the number of matmul instructions issued per
chunk. Trivial, but it is the one number that makes the grid line in the dump checkable by hand
(`render.render_geometry` prints `=> {shape.count} mma/kiter` immediately after the three factors).

##### 6.3.3 `sizing.mma_shape(theta) -> MmaShape`

Wraps `geometry.wmma_grid(theta)`, which returns the triple
`(free_tiles(input0), free_tiles(input1), k_tiles(theta))`. The two inputs are located structurally
— operands with `role == 'input'` that have a hop whose destination is the register space, taken in
schedule order — with **no `'A'`/`'B'` name test anywhere. A schedule with fewer than two such
operands gets `1` for the missing factor rather than an exception, on the grounds that a kernel
without two register-resident matrix inputs is outside the matmul primitive's scope and should not
be blocked by a sizing helper.

Invariant: `m_tiles`, `n_tiles` and `k_tiles` are each `≥ 1` (every underlying `geometry` count
clamps up), so `count ≥ 1` always. Cost is `O(#operands + #inner modes)`.

#### 6.4 The three primitive forwards

Three functions in this module are one-line calls into `geometry` with a longer docstring than
body. They exist so that a consumer that is asking a *sizing* question imports `sizing` and only
`sizing`, rather than reaching past it into the arithmetic floor. That is not cosmetic: `geometry`
also exposes `hop_broadcast`, `quantum_axes` and `broadcast_axes`, which are *presence* facts that
a sizing consumer has no business touching, and the narrower import surface is what has kept the
presence family single-sourced (section 2.2).

##### 6.4.1 `sizing.free_tiles(theta, op) -> int`

Forwards to `geometry.free_tiles`. The number of tiles the operand fans over on its **own free
axes** — the product of extents of `theta.free_modes(op)`, which is the operand's presence set
minus the reduction modes. For a bf16 A operand at a wave tile of 4 along M with no region split
this is 4; for the mxfp8 A of section 6.5.3 (`M_split` extent 2, `M_inner` extent 4) it is 8. It is
`1` when the operand has no free presence mode at all.

Note the asymmetry with the accumulator: the accumulator's presence *is* the free axes of both
inputs, so its `free_tiles` is the whole output tile count (64 in the trace below), not a per-input
fan.

##### 6.4.2 `sizing.k_tiles(theta) -> int`

Forwards to `geometry.k_tiles`. The number of reduction substeps in one chunk — the product of
extents of `theta.reduction_modes()`. **It takes no operand argument, and that is the point.** It is
a property of the schedule, not of a tensor. The docstring's warning is the residue of a measured
defect described in section 6.8.1: multiplying an operand's per-tile footprint by this
schedule-level constant silently assumes every operand is present on the reduction, and the
accumulator is not.

`render.render_geometry` nevertheless prints `k_tiles` on **every** row of its per-operand table,
including the accumulator's, and the dump now carries an explicit note saying so. That is a
rendering compromise, not a claim; do not read the column as per-operand.

##### 6.4.3 `sizing.frag_regs(theta, op) -> int`

Forwards to `geometry.frag_regs`. The number of physical registers **one fragment of this operand
occupies in one lane**. The computation, from `geometry.frag_regs`:

```
elems = max(1, op.frag_elems)                       # elements one lane holds for one tile
if theta.reg_bytes % op.elem_bytes == 0:
    scale = theta.reg_bytes // op.elem_bytes        # elements packed per register
    return max(1, ceil(elems / scale))
else:
    return max(1, ceil(elems * op.elem_bytes / theta.reg_bytes))
```

Worked values from the shipping shapes: 64 one-byte elements into 4-byte registers gives
`scale = 4` and 16 registers; 16 two-byte elements gives `scale = 2` and 8 registers; a 4-element
MX scale fragment of one byte gives 1 register. The second branch is a byte ceiling for element
widths that do not divide the register width; nothing on the current parameter path reaches it.

`frag_regs` is the **per-fragment width the depth map does not contain**, and understanding that
sentence is the whole of section 6.5. `S` counts *generations* — how many copies of a value are in
flight — and says nothing about how wide one copy is. The footprint is the product of the two, and
the historical error the module docstring warns against ("the VGPR footprint is a PRODUCT, never a
merge") was an attempt to fold width into depth.

`frag_regs` is the one function in this module that reaches production codegen. `emit.read_inst`
and `emit.fill_reads` stamp it on every `Load` node as `size_regs`, and
`Lowering/loopir_to_gir._convert_mma` stamps the same value on the register `Ref` each matmul
source names. Def and use therefore quote one number computed once, which is what lets the GIR
def-use verifier compare them at all.

#### 6.5 The register footprint

##### 6.5.1 The formula and what each term means

For an operand whose fragment declares a **grouping mode**, `operand_footprint_regs` computes

```
footprint  =  region_count  ×  Σ over parts ( W_part × |part| )  ×  frag_regs
```

Four factors, deliberately orthogonal. Taken one at a time:

* **`frag_regs`** — the width of *one* fragment in registers, per lane (section 6.4). This is the
  only factor that knows anything about data types.

* **`W_part`** — the **rotation width** of one register reuse group: how many buffers that group
  cycles through. This is the value stored in the depth map, read as `S.get(op.name, group)`. It is
  a count of *generations in flight*, derived in `theta.group_width` by clamping the fragment's
  authored width policy into the band `[L, R]` where `R` is the number of distinct values the group
  holds per chunk and `L` is the peak number simultaneously live (section 1.8). A group with
  `W = 1` is single-buffered and refills in place; a group with `W = R` has a buffer per value.

* **`|part|`** — the number of **grouping-mode values** the part holds. A register group is not a
  slice of the register file; it is a subset of the *values* of one tile mode. If the in-region M
  fan has extent 4 and the fragment is partitioned into two groups, each group owns two M values,
  so `|part| = 2`. The formula writes this per part, so an uneven partition (`lo = {0}`,
  `hi = {1,2,3}`) would be expressible without changing the formula — only the way `|part|` is
  obtained would change (section 6.7).

* **`region_count`** — the number of storage-disjoint sibling regions the tile is cut into. Two
  regions of one operand are two *different* fragments living at two different places, so each
  needs its own registers.

##### 6.5.2 Why the fan appears exactly once — the no-double-count invariant

The single most important property of this formula is negative: **the operand's free fan must
appear in exactly one factor, and it appears in `|part| × region_count`.**

The fan is the set of free-axis tiles the operand supplies to the matmul grid — for A, the M tiles.
There are two places it could plausibly land. It could be in the *rate*, i.e. in `W`: a group that
is not constant over the fan axis reloads once per fan value, so `R` (and hence potentially `W`)
would carry the fan. Or it could be in the *tile count*, i.e. in `|part| × region_count`: the fan is
a set of distinct fragments, each needing its own storage.

Only the second is correct once a grouping mode exists, and `theta._rate_broadcast` enforces it by
adding the fragment's `grouping_mode` — and the operand's **free** region modes — to the set of axes
a group is treated as constant over *for rate purposes*. So `R` is computed over the *held* modes
only (the reduction substeps), the fan is excluded from `W` by construction, and the footprint
multiplies it back in exactly once as `|part| × region_count`.

Get this wrong in either direction and the number is off by the fan, which on a wave tile of 8 is a
factor of eight. The module docstring's "the fan lives in exactly ONE factor ... this is what
prevents the double-count" is naming that hazard.

##### 6.5.3 `sizing.operand_footprint_regs(theta, op, S) -> int` — the algorithm

Three arms, dispatched in this order:

```
operand_footprint_regs(theta, op, S):

    # --- arm 1: the accumulator -------------------------------------------------
    if op.is_output:
        return max(1, free_tiles(theta, op) * frag_regs(theta, op))

    # --- arm 2: a fragment with a grouping mode ---------------------------------
    if op.fragment.grouping_mode is not None:
        region    = _region_count(theta, op)
        gm_extent = theta.free_extent(op.fragment.grouping_mode)
        groups    = op.fragment.groups()                 # tuple of group LABELS
        n_parts   = len(groups)

        if gm_extent % n_parts != 0:
            raise ValueError(... uneven register partitions are OUT OF SCOPE ...)

        part_vals = gm_extent // n_parts                 # |part|, equal partition
        total     = Σ over g in groups of ( S.get(op.name, g) * part_vals )
        return max(1, total) * frag_regs(theta, op) * region

    # --- arm 3: no grouping mode ------------------------------------------------
    total = Σ over g in op.fragment.groups() of ( S.get(op.name, g)
                                                  * group_regs(theta, op, g) )
    return max(1, total) * resident_free_tiles(theta, op)
```

**Inputs.** `theta` (for extents, `free_extent`, and everything `frag_regs` and `_region_count`
need); `op`, an `Operand`; and `S`, the `DepthMap` produced by `theta.build_S`. Only `S`'s register
rows are read — `S.get(op.name, group)` for group labels that come from
`op.fragment.groups()`, which never yields the reserved `SHARED_GROUP` label, so the shared ring
depth cannot leak into a register count through this path.

**Output.** A positive integer: physical VGPRs per lane for this operand's whole register
residence, across every group, every part and every region.

**Invariants.** The result is `≥ 1` for every operand (each arm clamps). It is monotone
non-decreasing in every `W`, in `region_count`, and in `frag_regs`. It is *independent of the loop
order* in arms 1 and 2, and *dependent* on it in arm 3 (through `resident_free_tiles`) — a real and
under-appreciated asymmetry, discussed in section 6.6.3.

**Arm 1, the accumulator.** One live value per output tile, held across the entire reduction. There
is no rotating ring — the accumulator is written once at the top and read-modify-written by every
matmul — so no depth factor appears at all, and `S` is not consulted. There is also no residency
window: every output tile is live for the whole loop by definition, so routing this through
`resident_free_tiles` (which is loop-order sensitive) would introduce an order dependence into a
quantity that has none. The comment in the source says exactly this, and the check `op.is_output`
comes **first** so an accumulator that happened to carry a grouping mode could never fall into arm
2.

**Arm 2, the grouping-mode fragment.** The four-factor formula of section 6.5.1. Note the shape of
the sum: `Σ_g (W_g × part_vals)`, with `part_vals` a scalar hoisted out of the loop only because the
partition is equal. Writing it inside the sum is deliberate — it keeps the expression in the
per-part form the general case needs, so lifting the equal-partition restriction is a change to how
`part_vals` is obtained, not a change to the formula (section 6.7).

**Arm 3, no grouping mode.** `Σ_g (W_g × group_regs(g)) × resident_free_tiles(op)`. Here the
fragment has *not* declared that its groups partition a mode's values, so `theta._rate_broadcast`
leaves the fan in the rate and `W` may already carry part of it; the fan-as-tile-count factor is
supplied instead by `resident_free_tiles`, the loop-order-derived count of how many free tiles are
simultaneously live. `group_regs` splits `frag_regs` between the groups by slot share, so a
one-group fragment gets the whole `frag_regs` and the arm degenerates to
`W × frag_regs × resident_free_tiles`.

##### 6.5.4 A worked trace, with the numbers

The test fixture `Tests/unit/loopmodel_scenarios.py::SCENARIOS["mxfp8_derive"]` is the derivation
anchor: an MXFP8 16×16×128 shape with a two-way region split on both operands, `VgprPartitionA = 2`
and reuse strategy 1 (the min-VGPR strategy: the first group unrolls, the second refills in place).
Evaluating θ for it gives

```
ord  =  iter(outer) · K_inner×2 · M_split×2 · M_inner×4 · N_split×2 · N_inner×4
```

and the following per-operand facts:

| | A | B | C (accumulator) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `frag_elems` / `elem_bytes` | 64 / 1 | 64 / 1 | 64 / 4 |
| `frag_regs` | 16 | 16 | 64 |
| groups and their `W` | `lo:2`, `hi:1` | `g0:2` | `g0:1` (unused) |
| `grouping_mode` | `M_inner` (extent 4) | `N_inner` (extent 4) | `None` |
| `region_modes` / `_region_count` | `('M_split',)` / 2 | `('N_split',)` / 2 | `()` / 1 |
| `free_tiles` | 8 | 8 | 64 |
| arm taken | 2 | 2 | 1 |

A goes through arm 2 with `n_parts = 2`, so `part_vals = 4 // 2 = 2`:

```
Σ_part (W × |part|)  =  (2 × 2)  +  (1 × 2)  =  6
footprint            =  6 × frag_regs(16) × region(2)  =  192
```

B has a single group, so `n_parts = 1` and `part_vals = 4`:

```
Σ_part (W × |part|)  =  2 × 4  =  8
footprint            =  8 × 16 × 2  =  256
```

These are precisely the values asserted by
`Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py::test_mxfp8_two_rate_derivation`, which is the only test in the tree
that exercises `operand_footprint_regs` at all. It asserts the derived widths first
(`S.get("A","lo") == 2`, `S.get("A","hi") == 1`) and then the two footprints, so a regression in the
width derivation and a regression in the footprint combination are distinguishable from the failure
message.

Read the two rows against each other and the no-double-count invariant becomes concrete: A and B
have the *same* fan (8 free tiles) and the *same* fragment width (16), and their footprints differ
only because A's fan is split across two groups of unequal width while B's sits in one group of
width 2. The fan itself contributes `|part| × region = 8` on both rows.

##### 6.5.5 Which arm actually runs — a reachability measurement

The source docstring labels arm 3 the "NON-grouping operand (flagship explicit-W, blocked)" case,
which reads as though it were a rarely-taken legacy path. It is not. A fragment gets a
`grouping_mode` only when the translator finds an in-region fan of extent greater than 1; when the
in-region fan collapses to 1 (a wave tile of 2 with a two-way region split, or a wave tile of 1),
`translate.reg_fragment` sets `grouping_mode = None` and arm 3 runs.

Evaluated over the 22 named fixtures in `Tests/unit/loopmodel_scenarios.py`, counting one
observation per non-output operand:

* **arm 2 (grouping mode): 11 observations**
* **arm 3 (no grouping mode): 43 observations**

So arm 3 is the *majority* path on the fixture set, including the `baseline` scenario. A maintainer
reading the docstring and concluding that arm 3 is dead would be wrong by a factor of four. The two
arms should therefore be maintained as equal peers; in particular, any change to how the fan is
handled must be applied to both, and a test that only exercises the mxfp8 anchor exercises only the
minority arm.

Worked arm-3 examples from the same sweep (single group `g0`, so `group_regs = frag_regs`):

| fixture | operand | `W` | `frag_regs` | `resident_free_tiles` | footprint |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `baseline` | A | 2 | 16 | 1 | 32 |
| `our_split` | A | 2 | 16 | 2 | 64 |
| `order_mnk` | B | 2 | 16 | 2 | 64 |

##### 6.5.6 `sizing._region_count(theta, op) -> int`

```
_region_count(theta, op):
    n = 1
    for m in theta.inner_modes():
        if m.name in op.region_modes:
            n *= m.extent
    return max(1, n)
```

The product of extents of the operand's region modes, restricted to modes that are actually present
in `ord` as inner levels. The `getattr(op, "region_modes", ())` guard makes it tolerant of an
operand-like object without the field; every real `Operand` has it.

It iterates `theta.inner_modes()` rather than `op.region_modes` so that a region mode which was
dropped from `ord` (because its extent collapsed to 1) contributes nothing, and so that the extent
is read off the live `Mode` rather than looked up separately. Cost is `O(#inner modes)`.

**A concrete inconsistency, unnamed until now.** `_region_count` multiplies in *every* region mode.
`theta._rate_broadcast` — the function that decides which axes a register group is treated as
constant over for rate purposes — excludes only the operand's **free** region modes, deliberately
keeping a **reduction**-axis region mode *in* the rate. Its reasoning is sound and is backed by a
measured failure: two regions of a reduction-axis split are successive substeps of one tile, held in
the same group and live simultaneously, so removing that axis from the rate collapses `R` to 1,
collapses `W` to 1, gives every read `slot = 0`, and two regions land in the same register.

But that means a reduction-axis region split is counted **twice** by
`operand_footprint_regs`: once inside `W` (because the axis stayed in the rate, so `R` and hence `W`
grew) and once again as `region_count`. Measured, by taking the `mxfp8_derive` fixture and switching
the split to the reduction axis (`TDMSplit = [1,1,2,2]`, giving `K_split` extent 2 and
`region_modes = ('K_split',)`):

| operand | groups and `W` | `frag_regs` | free fan | `region_count` | reported footprint |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | `lo:2`, `hi:1` | 16 | 8 (`M_inner`) | 2 | **384** |
| B | `g0:2` | 16 | 8 (`N_inner`) | 2 | **512** |

B's fragment is 8 tiles × 16 registers = 128 registers wide, rotating `W = 2` deep over `K_split`,
which is 256 registers. The reported 512 is that doubled again. The corresponding free-axis split
(the `mxfp8_derive` fixture proper) reports 256 for the same B, and there `region_count` is *not* a
double count because the two M regions genuinely are two different fragments.

The fix, if it is a fix, is a one-line narrowing that mirrors `_rate_broadcast` exactly:

```
red = set(theta.reduction_names())
for m in theta.inner_modes():
    if m.name in op.region_modes and m.name not in red:
        n *= m.extent
```

Two cautions before anyone applies it. First, **nothing downstream consumes this number**
(section 6.2), so the only observable change is the `vgpr` column of the geometry dump; do not
expect a codegen difference. Second, a previous audit of the dump saw exactly this divergence —
16 of 60 mxf8 operand rows printing a `vgpr` value that the printed legend could not reproduce —
and resolved it by **correcting the legend to match the code**, adding the note that
`region_count` "is NOT folded into free_tiles when the region mode is a reduction mode"
(provenance: the renderer audit filed as #289). That is a defensible reading if one believes the
reduction regions occupy distinct registers *in addition to* the rotation; it is not the reading
`_rate_broadcast` takes. The two functions cannot both be right, and whichever way it is resolved,
they should be made to share one predicate rather than each spelling their own.

#### 6.6 The three footprint helpers

##### 6.6.1 `sizing.operand_generations(op, S) -> int`

```
operand_generations(op, S):
    groups = { g: d for g, d in S.groups_of(op.name).items() if g != SHARED_GROUP }
    return sum(groups.values()) if groups else 1
```

The sum of the depths of an operand's **register** rate-groups — i.e. how many generations of this
operand are in flight across all its groups at once. For the mxfp8 A of section 6.5.4 it is
`2 + 1 = 3`; for B it is `2`; for the accumulator it is `1`.

Two things matter here even though the function has no callers.

* **The `SHARED_GROUP` exclusion is the entire content of the function.** `DepthMap` stores two
  structurally different kinds of row under one key space: register rate-group depths, keyed by the
  group's label, and the shared-memory ring depth, keyed by the reserved label
  `theta.SHARED_GROUP == "shared"` (section 1.8, section 4.5). They are *different placements* of
  the same operand and summing across them is a category error — a shared ring depth of 2 has
  nothing to do with how many register generations exist. Any new consumer that iterates an
  operand's depth rows must make the same exclusion; `loopModelRegBuffers` in the kernel generator
  independently does so (section 6.9), which is the second instance of one rule written twice.
* **`S.groups_of(op.name)` can raise.** With no `region` argument it folds every region's rows
  together via `DepthMap.get`, which raises `ValueError` when a split operand's per-region rows
  *disagree* rather than silently picking one. That behaviour is asserted directly by
  `Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py` (the test that pops the whole-tile row, sets region 0 to depth 4
  and region 1 to depth 3, then expects `pytest.raises(ValueError, match="placements disagree")`
  from both `get` and `groups_of`). So a future caller of `operand_generations` on a split operand
  with unequal per-region depths gets an exception, not a wrong number. That is intended.

**Status: dead.** It is imported and re-exported by `__init__.py` and called nowhere, in the
package, in the lowering, in the kernel generator or in the tests. It is a plausible building block
for a future footprint variant, and it is three lines, so the cost of keeping it is the cost of
maintaining one more public name. If you delete it, delete both `__init__.py` mentions with it.

##### 6.6.2 `sizing.group_regs(theta, op, group) -> int`

```
group_regs(theta, op, group):
    nslots = op.fragment.total_slots() or 1
    return max(1, frag_regs(theta, op) * op.fragment.size_of(group) // nslots)
```

The register width of **one** reuse group: the group's share of the fragment's registers, prorated
by slot count. `Fragment.parts` is a tuple giving each group's slot count; `total_slots()` sums it;
`size_of(label)` returns this group's entry (and `1` for an unknown label). So a fragment of 16
registers split as `parts = (1, 1)` gives each group 8; `parts = (2,)` is a single group holding the
whole 16; `parts = (1, 3)` would give 4 and 12.

Used only by arm 3 of `operand_footprint_regs`. In arm 3 the fan is *not* factored out into a value
partition, so the fragment's registers are divided among the groups here and multiplied by the
residency factor outside. On every shipping arm-3 configuration `parts == (1,)`, so `group_regs`
returns `frag_regs` unchanged and the split logic is exercised only by arm-2 fragments that never
reach it. That is a real coverage hole: the proration arithmetic (in particular the truncating
integer division, which loses registers whenever `frag_regs × size_of` is not a multiple of
`total_slots`) has no test. If you extend uneven partitions (section 6.7), this division is one of
the two places that will be wrong.

##### 6.6.3 `sizing.resident_free_tiles(theta, op) -> int`

A forward to `theta.resident_free_tiles`, imported lazily inside the function body (a defensive
deferral, not a cycle break — `theta` is already imported at module scope for `SHARED_GROUP`).

It answers: **how many of this operand's free-axis tiles are simultaneously live under this loop
order?** The implementation in `theta` unrolls the inner traversal three times, builds a live
interval per free-tile generation `(unrolled_iteration, tile_value)` from first touch to last touch,
shifts each interval left by the operand's register read offset, and takes the maximum overlap over
the *middle* (steady) unrolled iteration. Same machinery as the register live-peak, applied to the
free-tile index instead of a rate group's value.

The consequence is that the footprint of an arm-3 operand **depends on the loop order**:

* free axis innermost — the fan turns over cleanly, only a small window is live, footprint small,
  local-read traffic high;
* free axis outer with the partner's axis sweeping inside — every free tile is revisited on each
  inner pass, so all are resident, footprint large, traffic low.

That is a genuine modelling result, not an artifact, and it is why there is deliberately **no
separate residency knob**: holding fewer tiles and reloading more often is already expressible, as a
smaller rotation width via the register partition and its width policy. Adding a residency cap would
be a second control over one quantity.

**The asymmetry to be aware of.** Arm 2 does not call `resident_free_tiles` at all — it uses
`|part| × region_count`, which is the *full* fan. So a grouping-mode operand is charged for its
whole fan regardless of loop order, while a non-grouping operand of identical shape is charged only
for the resident window. For arm 2 that is arguably correct (a value partition names disjoint
fragments that all exist), but it does mean the two arms are not two ways of computing one quantity
— they are two different quantities, and a change of `VgprPartition` from 1 to 2 will change the
reported footprint by more than the partition alone explains. Nothing currently depends on the two
agreeing.

#### 6.7 The equal-partition assumption

##### 6.7.1 What the assumption is

Arm 2 computes `|part|`, the number of grouping-mode values one register group owns, as

```
part_vals = gm_extent // n_parts
```

— a single scalar, identical for every part. That is only correct when the grouping mode's values
are divided **equally** among the groups. An uneven partition such as `lo = {0}`, `hi = {1,2,3}`
over an extent-4 mode has `|lo| = 1` and `|hi| = 3`, and the scalar `4 // 2 = 2` describes neither.

The guard is loud and immediate:

```
if gm_extent % n_parts != 0:
    raise ValueError(f"{op.name}: grouping mode '{...}' extent {gm_extent} is not divisible "
                     f"by {n_parts} parts — uneven register partitions are OUT OF SCOPE ...")
```

##### 6.7.2 Why raising is the right behaviour here

Elsewhere the decoder is built to be **total**: an out-of-band request is repaired to the nearest
legal point rather than refused. `theta.group_width` clamps an explicit width into `[L, R]` instead
of rejecting it, precisely because rejecting made the decoder partial and left an autotuner unable
to explore. So a raise in this module is against the grain and needs justification.

The justification is that the two situations are different in kind. A width outside `[L, R]` has a
well-defined nearest legal value and clamping to it produces a schedule that is still correct, only
not the one asked for. An uneven partition has **no** nearest equal partition: silently pretending
the parts are equal would emit a *number* — a footprint — that is simply false, with nothing
downstream able to detect it. Given the choice between a wrong integer and an exception, an
exception is the conservative option, and the docstring records that this was a decision ("an
ACCEPTED SCOPE EXCEPTION ... decided, not an oversight") rather than an unexamined omission.
The work item that settled it is #166.

##### 6.7.3 The second guard, upstream

The divisibility condition is checked **twice**, in two layers, and a maintainer should know that
before trying to reach the raise in `sizing`.

`translate.reg_fragment` — which builds the `Fragment` from the parameter dict — refuses the same
condition earlier:

* if the requested partition count is greater than 1 but the in-region fan has extent ≤ 1, it
  **clamps the count to 1** and appends a note ("no fan to partition"), rather than raising;
* if the count is greater than 1 and does not divide the fan extent, it raises its own
  `ValueError` ("equal partition required").

So on the parameter path the `sizing` raise is unreachable: the translator has already rejected the
input. The `sizing` guard is the backstop for a hand-built θ (the unit tests construct `Theta`
objects directly, and so does anyone debugging), and for a future path that constructs `Fragment`s
some other way. Two guards for one rule is the shape of defect this package has repeatedly hit
(two derivations agreeing on the common case and diverging on the degenerate one), but here they are
not two derivations — they are the same predicate at two layers, and the inner one is a genuine
precondition of the arithmetic immediately below it. Keep both.

##### 6.7.4 What lifting it actually requires

The formula does not change. `Σ_part (W_part × |part|)` is already written per part; only the source
of `|part|` changes. Concretely:

1. **Carry each group's value subset on the `Fragment`.** `Fragment` already knows a per-group
   quantity — `parts`, the slot count, read through `size_of(label)`. The natural extension is a
   parallel per-group grouping-mode value count (or, better, the explicit value set, since
   `placement` also wants to know *which* values a group owns when it builds the read-ahead
   prologue). A tuple aligned with `parts`/`labels` keeps the existing constructor shape.
2. **Replace the scalar** in arm 2 with a lookup: `sum(S.get(op.name, g) * fragment.values_of(g)
   for g in groups)`.
3. **Delete the divisibility guard** in `sizing.operand_footprint_regs` and the matching one in
   `translate.reg_fragment`.
4. **Fix the second truncating division.** `group_regs` prorates `frag_regs` by slot share with
   integer division; with uneven parts this can lose registers (e.g. `frag_regs = 16`,
   `parts = (1, 2)` gives 5 and 10, summing to 15). Either round the last part up, or compute the
   parts as a partition of the integer `frag_regs` rather than independently.
5. **Check the consumers of the partition, not just the sizing.** `translate._register_policy`
   assigns a width policy per label; `placement.readahead_prologue` restricts the prologue's fill to
   the deep group's grouping-mode values — the test
   `test_readahead_prologue_per_group_dr` computes the expected value set as
   `range(gm_extent // len(groups))`, i.e. it hard-codes the equal-partition split too. That test
   would need the same treatment. Lifting the assumption in `sizing` alone would leave the read-ahead
   filling the wrong values, which is a *correctness* change, not a sizing one.

Point 5 is the reason this is more than a one-field extension in practice even though the docstring
correctly describes it as one for this file.

#### 6.8 Instruction counts and byte sizes

##### 6.8.1 `sizing.operand_buffer_regs(theta, op) -> int`

```
operand_buffer_regs(theta, op) = geometry.presence_tiles(theta, op) * frag_regs(theta, op)
```

The number of registers this operand **loads per reduction chunk**: one fragment's worth of
registers for each distinct tile the operand touches in that chunk.

`geometry.presence_tiles` is the product of extents of the operand's *whole* presence set — every
inner mode the operand varies over, free and reduction alike. By construction it equals
`free_tiles(op) × reduction_tiles(op)`, where `reduction_tiles(op)` counts only the reduction modes
**this operand is actually present on**.

**The historical defect (provenance: #212).** The previous form was
`free_tiles(theta, op) × k_tiles(theta) × frag_regs(theta, op)`. That multiplies in `k_tiles`, the
*schedule-level* count of reduction substeps, unconditionally — which silently asserts that every
operand is present on the reduction. The accumulator is not: it is broadcast over the reduction by
definition (the reduction modes are precisely the inner modes absent from the accumulator's
presence). So the accumulator's buffer size came out `4 × 2 × 16 = 128` registers for a tile that
holds `4 × 16 = 64`, a clean factor of `k_tiles` too large.

The fix has no role test, no name test and no operand-kind branch: `presence_tiles` is the same
product for an operand present on the reduction (A and B are unchanged, since for them
`reduction_tiles == k_tiles`) and drops the factor for one that is not. That is the module's
recurring shape — a bug fixed by replacing a global constant with the per-operand quantity it was
standing in for.

The regression test is
`Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py::test_an_operand_BROADCAST_over_the_reduction_does_not_pay_for_it`,
and it is worth reading as the contract:

* it first asserts `k_tiles > 1` on the fixture, with the message *"this fixture must have >1
  reduction substep or the bug is invisible"* — a **non-vacuity guard**, so the test cannot pass by
  accident on a degenerate shape;
* it asserts the partition identity `presence_tiles == free_tiles × reduction_tiles` for every
  operand;
* it asserts `operand_buffer_regs == presence_tiles × frag_regs` for every operand;
* it then splits: for the output operand it asserts `reduction_tiles == 1` and that the **old**
  formula would have been exactly `k_tiles` too big; for the inputs it asserts `reduction_tiles ==
  k_tiles` and that the old and new formulas agree.

That last pair is the part to preserve if the test is ever rewritten: asserting the new value alone
would not distinguish "correct" from "correct for a different reason", and asserting the size of the
old error is what makes the test a record of the defect.

##### 6.8.2 `sizing.load_regs(theta, op, hop) -> int`

```
load_regs(theta, op, hop):
    vw = hop.vector_elems or op.frag_elems
    return max(1, ceil(vw * op.elem_bytes / theta.reg_bytes))
```

The number of registers **one per-lane instruction** of this hop moves: its vector width in
elements, converted to registers by bytes. `Hop.vector_elems == 0` means "whole fragment", so it
falls back to `op.frag_elems`, and the `or` idiom therefore treats `0` and `None` identically —
which is what the field's documented sentinel requires.

Note that this uses a byte ceiling directly, whereas `geometry.frag_regs` prefers an
elements-per-register recast when the element size divides the register size. The two agree for
every divisible case (`ceil(v·e/r)` and `ceil(v/(r/e))` are the same integer when `e | r`), so the
divergence is only in the sub-register-element fallback, and nothing on the shipping path reaches
it. Still, if you ever change the packing rule, change it in both places or route this through
`geometry`.

##### 6.8.3 `sizing.plan_transfers(theta, op, hop) -> int`

```
plan_transfers(theta, op, hop):
    if hop.is_bulk:
        return max(1, hop.split)
    return max(1, ceil(operand_buffer_regs(theta, op) / load_regs(theta, op, hop)))
```

The number of instructions this hop issues per reduction chunk. Two cases, matching the two mover
kinds `Hop` distinguishes:

* **Bulk (`kind == 'tdm'`)** — one cooperative instruction moves a whole tile, so the count is the
  region split: one instruction per storage-disjoint region part, `1` for an uncut tile. Nothing
  about registers or vector widths enters, because a bulk mover does not go through lanes.
* **Per-lane (`kind == 'load'`)** — total registers to move, divided by registers per instruction.
  Both operands of the division come from this module, so the units cannot drift.

The result is a *count*, not a schedule: it says how many instructions exist, not where they go.
Placement is `placement`'s and `emit`'s business.

There is no `hop is None` guard. Callers must not pass one; `render.render_geometry` checks
`ds_hop and ds_hop.src == Space.SHARED` before calling, because the accumulator op-class has an
empty `hops` list. A future caller that forgets will get an `AttributeError` on `hop.is_bulk`, which
is a fine failure mode but is worth knowing.

##### 6.8.4 `sizing.operand_tile_bytes(theta, op) -> int`

```
operand_tile_bytes(theta, op)
    = geometry.presence_tiles(theta, op) * op.frag_elems * op.elem_bytes * theta.lanes
```

The **shared-memory bytes for this operand's whole staged tile, across the wave**: tiles touched per
chunk, times elements per lane per tile, times bytes per element, times the lane count.

It carries the same presence-derived correction as `operand_buffer_regs` and for the same reason: the
previous `free_tiles × k_tiles` form over-counted any operand broadcast over the reduction. For A and
B — the only operands with a shared staging hop today — the value is unchanged by the fix.

The one production consumer is `emit._copy_inst`, which computes the byte size of one cooperative
movement as

```
size = Σ over fused members of ( operand_tile_bytes(theta, member) // max(1, member.split) )
```

Two details of that line matter. **Each member divides by its own split**, not by a group-wide one:
a fused movement may pair a split member with an unsplit one, so a region instance carries
`tile/split` bytes from the split member and the *whole* tile from the unsplit member. And the
members are **summed**, because a fused movement is one instruction moving both members' bytes.
Getting either wrong changes only a size annotation on the IR node, not the emitted instruction —
but that annotation is what a downstream consumer would use to reason about bandwidth, so it should
stay honest.

Sharp edge: `theta.lanes` defaults to 32 on the `Theta` dataclass. A hand-built θ that forgets to
set it gets a wave-32 byte count regardless of the target.

#### 6.9 How the sizes reach the register allocator and the `.set` table

This subsection answers a question the module itself cannot: given that `operand_footprint_regs`
produces a VGPR count, what actually allocates registers? The answer is that **it does not**, and
the path that does is worth tracing in full, because it is the one place where a mismatch between
the decoder's model and the emitter's naming becomes an assembler failure on generated text.

##### 6.9.1 The naming contract

The GIR backend names each register generation of an operand with a symbol of the form

```
vgprValu<tensorChar>_X<slot>_I<iui>
```

where `slot = rate_index mod W_g` — the rotation slot the decoder assigned, modulo the group's
rotation width. Those symbols must exist in the kernel's `.set` table, which is emitted from a
per-tensor buffer count. So the table must define `X0 .. X{W-1}` for **exactly the same `W`** the
decoder used when it computed the slot. If the table is short by one, the emitter writes a symbol
nothing defines and the assembler fails on text that was generated successfully.

##### 6.9.2 The path, function by function

```
KernelWriter._loopModelTheta(kernel)          # builds (theta, S) ONCE, caches by kernel name
        │
        ├─► KernelWriter.loopModelRegBuffers(kernel)  -> { tensorChar : W }
        │        for each operand whose LAST hop lands in the register space:
        │            W = max over groups g != SHARED_GROUP of  S.get(op.name, g)
        │            widths[op.name] = max(1, W)
        │
        ├─► states.loopModelRegBufferWidths = widths        (in _initKernel)
        │   states.numVgprBuffer = max(scaffold_count, *widths.values())
        │        │
        │        └─► the numVgprBufferA/B -> valuBlocks -> numVgprValu sizing,
        │            the numVgprValuPack* sizing, and macroAndSet's `numBi`,
        │            which is what EMITS the `.set` table
        │
        └─► KernelWriter._loopModelGirProgram(kernel) -> the GIR program that
                 names X0..X{W-1} using the very same S
```

Three properties of that path are deliberate and fragile enough to state explicitly.

**(a) The width comes from `S`, not from `sizing`.** `loopModelRegBuffers` reads
`S.get(op.name, g)` directly and takes a `max` over the groups. It does not call
`operand_footprint_regs`, `operand_generations`, or anything else in this module. That is correct
for its purpose — it needs the *number of X indices*, which is a max over groups, not a sum over
groups and certainly not a product with the fragment width — but it does mean the `SHARED_GROUP`
exclusion is written a second time (the first being `operand_generations`, section 6.6.1). Those two
exclusions are independent copies of one rule.

**(b) A `max` over groups, not a sum.** An operand with several register groups needs
`max_g W_g` distinct X indices, not `Σ_g W_g`: the groups share the X axis and are separated from
each other by their *tile offset* within the fragment, not by the slot. So the mxfp8 A of
section 6.5.4, with `lo:2` and `hi:1`, needs `X0` and `X1` — two indices — while its footprint is
192 registers. The two numbers answer different questions and neither can be derived from the other
without `frag_regs` and the fan.

**(c) It grows the scaffold's count, never shrinks it.** The generator's own count is

```
numVgprBuffer = LoopIters                    if ClusterLocalRead   (the default)
                PrefetchLocalRead + 1        otherwise
```

and the decoder's width is folded in with `max`, for two separate reasons. The first is
correctness in the decoder's favour: clamping `W` *down* to the scaffold's count would be wrong,
not merely tight, because `W` is bounded below by the post-write-after-read live peak — at four
reduction substeps with a K-innermost order the peak is 4, meaning four generations are needed at
one instant, and cutting the ring below that is an unrescuable race between simultaneously-live
inputs. The allocator follows the schedule; the schedule does not follow the allocator. The second
is coverage in the scaffold's favour: regions the GIR fork does **not** own still emit from the
generator's own code (the tail loop and the edge kernels are unimplemented under this path), so the
scaffold's count remains the right floor for those. Over-allocating a buffer costs registers;
under-allocating produces an undefined symbol.

**(d) The two consumers must share one θ.** `loopModelRegBuffers` runs from kernel initialization,
long before the GIR program is built. If it built its own θ and the GIR construction built another,
the widths sized here and the slots named there could come from two different objects.
`_loopModelTheta` therefore caches `(theta, S)` keyed on the kernel name and both consumers read the
cached pair. The practical consequence for anyone editing the parameter bridge is that **every fact
θ depends on must be readable at the time of the first call** — which is why the bridge reads
`Solution` keys rather than generator state that is assigned later.

##### 6.9.3 The divergence that motivated the whole path

On the default configuration the scaffold count and the decoder width already agree at every
reduction depth (`LoopIters` equals the substep count equals `W` under the unroll width policy), so
nothing was visibly wrong for a long time. They diverge exactly when clustered local reads are
forced off, which the solution validator does when the requested local prefetch depth reaches the
iteration count — and in the same breath it forces that depth to 0. The scaffold count then
collapses to `1` while θ still rotates the full substep count of slots, so the emitter names `X1`
with no `.set` behind it. The concrete reproducer recorded in the source is a reduction depth of 64
(two loop iterations) with a requested local prefetch of 2.

##### 6.9.4 What `operand_footprint_regs` is for, then

Given (a), the footprint formula's only role today is **observability**: the `vgpr` column of the
derived-geometry dump, which a developer reads beside the emitted assembly to sanity-check that the
schedule is not asking for an implausible register budget. It is not a budget check, it does not
gate anything, and no failure path consults it.

That is a defensible split of responsibilities — the allocator needs a *naming width*, the human
needs a *total* — but it leaves the total unvalidated. A cheap and worthwhile addition for a future
maintainer: have the kernel generator compare `Σ_operands operand_footprint_regs(theta, op, S)`
against the register budget it actually allocates, and emit a note (not a rejection) when the two
differ by more than the accumulator and scratch can explain. That single check would have caught the
reduction-region double count of section 6.5.6 the first time a reduction-axis split was run.

#### 6.10 Complexity, and where the compile-time cost sits

Every function in this module is cheap. The table gives the asymptotic cost and the practical value
of each `n`, measured against the shipping vocabulary (6 canonical axes, at most 5 operands, at most
4 register groups, extents in `{1, 2, 4, 8}`).

| Function | Cost | Practical `n` |
|---|---|---|
| `free_tiles`, `k_tiles`, `presence_tiles`, `_region_count` | `O(#inner modes)` | ≤ 6, usually 4–5 |
| `frag_regs`, `load_regs`, `MmaShape.count`, `group_regs` | `O(1)` | — |
| `mma_shape` | `O(#operands + #inner modes)` | ≤ 11 |
| `operand_buffer_regs`, `operand_tile_bytes`, `plan_transfers` | `O(#inner modes)` | ≤ 6 |
| `operand_generations` | `O(#depth-map rows for this operand)` | ≤ 5 |
| `operand_footprint_regs`, arms 1–2 | `O(#groups + #inner modes)` | ≤ 10 |
| `operand_footprint_regs`, arm 3 | dominated by `resident_free_tiles` | see below |

The only non-trivial one is arm 3, through `theta.resident_free_tiles`. That function enumerates
the full inner traversal — `T = Π extents` steps, materialized as a list of coordinate dicts — then
unrolls it three times and, for each of the `T` positions of the steady iteration, scans every live
interval. So the cost is `O(T)` to build the step list plus `O(T × G)` for the overlap scan, where
`G` is the number of distinct free-tile generations over three iterations (bounded by `3 × free
tiles`). With `T ≤ 64` and free tiles ≤ 8 on shipping shapes that is a few thousand integer
comparisons — invisible.

**Where the cost would actually appear.** Nowhere in a normal build, for two reasons. First, the
whole decoder runs **once per kernel**, not per instruction, and the `(theta, S)` pair is cached.
Second, `operand_footprint_regs` — the expensive one — is only called by the debug renderer, so a
production build never evaluates it at all. If you are profiling kernel generation and this module
appears, something is calling it in a loop; look for the caller, not for a faster formula.

**If it ever does matter**, in order of value:

1. **Memoize `theta.resident_free_tiles` per `(id(theta), op.name)`.** It is pure and it rebuilds
   the entire step list on each call. A dictionary on the `Theta` object, cleared nowhere because
   `Theta` is effectively immutable after construction, is a five-line change.
2. **Hoist `_inner_steps`.** Both `resident_free_tiles` and the group live-peak computation build
   the same step list independently. Building it once per θ and passing it in removes the
   duplication (`derive_S` already threads a `steps` list through the group functions for exactly
   this reason; `resident_free_tiles` is the one that does not).
3. **Replace the `O(T × G)` overlap scan with a sweep.** Sort interval endpoints and take a running
   maximum: `O(G log G)`. Only worth it if `T` grows by an order of magnitude, which would require
   a much larger unrolled body than any shipping shape.

None of these are worth doing speculatively. Item 1 is the only one with a plausible trigger (a
future sizing consumer that calls the footprint per operand per candidate solution during
autotuning).

#### 6.11 The unit tests, as a contract

Three tests in `Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py` exercise this module. They are small, and each encodes
a specific historical failure; that is the reason to keep them in exactly their current form.

**`test_mxfp8_two_rate_derivation`** — the derivation anchor. Builds θ from the `mxfp8_derive`
fixture, derives `S`, and asserts

```
(S.get("A","lo"), S.get("A","hi")) == (2, 1)
operand_footprint_regs(th, th.op("A"), S) == 192
operand_footprint_regs(th, th.op("B"), S) == 256
```

The ordering is the point: the widths are asserted *before* the footprints, so a regression in
`theta.group_width` and a regression in the arm-2 combination produce different failure messages.
This is the only test of `operand_footprint_regs` in the tree, and it covers **arm 2 only** —
neither the accumulator arm nor the majority arm 3 (section 6.5.5) has a test. That is the largest
coverage hole in the module and the first thing to fix if you touch the footprint.

**`test_an_operand_BROADCAST_over_the_reduction_does_not_pay_for_it`** — the presence-derived
correction, described in full in section 6.8.1. It asserts the partition identity, the
`operand_buffer_regs` identity, and the *size of the old error*, with a non-vacuity guard on
`k_tiles > 1`.

**The depth-map disagreement test** (in the same file, exercising `DepthMap.get` and
`groups_of`) — not a `sizing` test, but it constrains `operand_generations` transitively: it
establishes that folding per-region rows raises rather than picks when they disagree.

Two tests that are *not* about `sizing` but pin quantities this module reads, and which will break
if you change the fragment partition semantics:

* `test_readahead_prologue_per_group_dr` computes the expected grouping-mode value set as
  `range(gm_extent // len(groups))` — the same equal-partition assumption, in the read-ahead
  construction rather than the sizing (section 6.7.4 point 5).
* `test_per_hop_presence_REPRODUCES_the_two_hand_rolled_expressions_it_replaced`, in `geometry`,
  pins `hop_broadcast`, on which every `presence_tiles`-derived count in this module rests.

#### 6.12 Sharp edges, weaknesses and dead code — the honest list

Collected in one place, most consequential first.

1. **`_region_count` counts reduction-axis region modes, and `theta._rate_broadcast` does not**
   (section 6.5.6). A reduction-axis region split is charged twice: once inside `W`, once as
   `region_count`. Measured at 384 / 512 registers for a fixture whose fragments are 128 registers
   wide rotating 2 deep. Not observable in generated code because the footprint is dump-only, but
   the two functions cannot both be right.
2. **`operand_footprint_regs` has no production consumer** (section 6.2, 6.9.4). It looks like the
   register-budget authority and is not; the authority is `S` read directly. The consequence is that
   the formula has no oracle and drifts silently.
3. **Arm 3 is the majority path but is documented as a blocked side case** (section 6.5.5). 43 of 54
   fixture observations take it. Its docstring wording will mislead the next reader.
4. **Arms 2 and 3 treat residency differently** (section 6.6.3). Arm 2 charges the full fan; arm 3
   charges the loop-order-derived resident window. Changing `VgprPartition` from 1 to 2 therefore
   changes the reported footprint by more than the partition explains.
5. **`operand_generations` is dead** (section 6.6.1) while being exported as public API.
6. **`group_regs`'s proration is untested and truncates** (section 6.6.2). Every shipping arm-3
   fragment has `parts == (1,)`, so the division is never exercised with a non-trivial split.
7. **Two packing rules exist.** `geometry.frag_regs` prefers an elements-per-register recast;
   `load_regs` always uses a byte ceiling. They agree wherever the element size divides the register
   size, which is everywhere today.
8. **`plan_transfers` does not guard `hop is None`.** The accumulator has no hops; callers must
   check.
9. **`theta.lanes` defaults to 32**, so `operand_tile_bytes` silently assumes a wave width on a
   hand-built θ.

#### 6.13 Advice for extending this module

Concrete, in the order a future change is most likely to arrive.

**Adding a new hop kind.** `plan_transfers` currently branches on `hop.is_bulk` and nothing else,
which mirrors `geometry.hop_broadcast`'s two-way split (bulk spans everything; per-lane spans its
quantum). If a partial cooperative mover appears — one that spans two of four axes — do **not** add
a third branch here. Make `hop_broadcast` derive the spanned-axis set the same way `quantum_axes`
derives one, so the hop's presence shrinks correctly, and then `plan_transfers`'s per-lane arm gives
the right count with no change at all: `presence_tiles` will already have dropped the spanned axes.
Adding a branch here would be the third derivation of one rule.

**Making the footprint account for the movement quantum.** A wide load that covers two tiles merges
them into one presence point, so `presence_tiles` already drops the absorbed axis and
`operand_buffer_regs` already counts fewer instructions' worth of registers. But the *footprint* is
built from `frag_regs × fan`, which does not consult the quantum at all — and a broadcast quantum
(two tiles mapping onto the **same** slot) genuinely occupies fewer registers than two tiles. If you
need that, the right factor is the distinct-slot count the quantum map exposes, applied to the fan
term, not to `frag_regs`. Do not try to fold it into `frag_regs`: that field is the width of one
fragment and is stamped on IR nodes as a def/use width, so shrinking it would desynchronize the
producer and the consumer.

**Adding a second output operand, or an epilogue.** Arm 1 assumes exactly the accumulator shape: one
live value per output tile, held across the whole reduction, no ring. An epilogue store path gives
the same op-class a reverse trajectory and hops, at which point `op.is_output` no longer implies "no
ring" and arm 1's early return becomes wrong. The right change then is to test for *the absence of a
rotating placement* rather than for the role — i.e. dispatch on whether the operand has any register
rate-group rows in `S` — which is a strictly more honest predicate and happens to give the same
answer today.

**Making the footprint authoritative.** If you want the register allocator to consume this module
rather than reading `S` itself, the missing pieces are: (i) resolve the reduction-region question of
section 6.5.6; (ii) give arms 2 and 3 a common residency story; (iii) add the accumulator and arm-3
tests; and only then (iv) change `loopModelRegBuffers` to derive the naming width from the same
place. Do (i)–(iii) as separate, individually-validated changes — the footprint currently has no
consumer that would catch a mistake, so each step must carry its own test.

**Caching.** If a future autotuner evaluates thousands of candidate schedules and calls the
footprint per candidate, memoize `theta.resident_free_tiles` first (section 6.10 item 1); it is the
only super-constant cost in the module and it is trivially pure.

**What breaks if you change things.**

* Change `frag_regs`'s packing rule and you change `Load.size_regs` in the emitted IR and the GIR
  register `Ref` width simultaneously — they read the same function, so they stay consistent, but
  every golden assembly file changes.
* Change `presence_tiles` and you change both the instruction counts and the byte sizes, and
  `emit._copy_inst`'s movement size with them.
* Change `operand_footprint_regs` and you change one column of a debug dump. Nothing else.
* Change `MmaShape`'s field order and you break `mma_shape`'s positional construction from
  `geometry.wmma_grid`'s tuple — the one place in this module where a tuple's positions are relied
  on rather than named.

#### 6.14 Summary of definitions covered

| Symbol | One line |
|---|---|
| `MmaShape` | frozen `(m_tiles, n_tiles, k_tiles)` compute grid for one reduction chunk |
| `MmaShape.count` | product of the three, i.e. matmul instructions per chunk |
| `free_tiles` | forward to `geometry.free_tiles`: tiles the operand fans over on its own free axes |
| `k_tiles` | forward to `geometry.k_tiles`: reduction substeps per chunk, a schedule-level constant |
| `frag_regs` | forward to `geometry.frag_regs`: registers one fragment occupies per lane |
| `operand_generations` | sum of register-group depths, excluding the shared ring row; **no callers** |
| `group_regs` | one reuse group's share of `frag_regs`, prorated by slot count |
| `operand_footprint_regs` | physical VGPRs per lane: accumulator arm, grouping-mode arm, residency arm |
| `_region_count` | product of extents of the operand's region modes present in `ord` |
| `resident_free_tiles` | forward to `theta.resident_free_tiles`: loop-order-derived live free-tile peak |
| `operand_buffer_regs` | registers loaded per chunk = `presence_tiles × frag_regs` |
| `load_regs` | registers moved by one per-lane instruction = vector width packed into registers |
| `operand_tile_bytes` | shared bytes for the whole tile across the wave, presence-derived |
| `plan_transfers` | instructions per chunk: `hop.split` if bulk, else buffer-regs ÷ load-regs |
| `mma_shape` | builds `MmaShape` from `geometry.wmma_grid` |

### 7. `placement.py` — presence, strides, read-ahead and peel

`placement.py` is the second-largest module in the package (1,401 lines, 45 definitions — only
`emit.py`, at 1,406 lines, is longer). It is a library
of **pure derivations**: given a schedule point `theta` and a depth map `S`, every function here
answers one geometric question about *where* an op-class's instances sit in the loop nest and
*which rotating-buffer name* each one touches. Nothing here mutates state, allocates a node, or
emits IR. `emit.py` is the only large consumer; `ledger.py`, `render.py` and the
downstream GIR lowering each read a handful of the same functions (`sizing.py` is *not* a consumer —
it imports only `geometry` and `theta`), and the whole point of the
module existing as a separate file is that **all of them read the same one**.

#### 7.0 How this module is split across sections 7, 8 and 9, and which treatment is primary

Because it is large and thematically layered, this report splits `placement.py` across three
sections, and the split is **not** a partition of the 45 names — it is one catalogue plus two
thematic treatments that deliberately revisit some of the same functions from a different angle.
An earlier revision of this report carried three *different* and mutually contradictory ownership
tables here, in 8.1 and in 9.0. The table below is the single correct one and is reproduced
verbatim at the head of sections 8 and 9.

* **Section 7 is the catalogue.** It walks the file roughly in source order and gives every name a
  short reference entry: signature, what it computes, cost. It is the section to read when you have
  a symbol and want to know what it does.
* **Section 8 is the time-structure deep dive.** The peel, the cross-level boundary term, the two
  rotating rings, and the read-ahead prologue's closed form — each with the history, the failure
  modes, the measurements and the tests.
* **Section 9 is the reach-and-admissibility deep dive.** How far a read-ahead spills into the next
  reduction chunk, which side of a trip's reads a shared copy is emitted on, whether a hardware
  instruction may merge several tile coordinates, and the downstream Mark-placement policy. It also
  restates the peel and boundary term as *reference entries* keyed to their consumers, because the
  quantum and reach arguments depend on them.

| Family | Names | **Primary treatment** | Also treated in |

| Addressing | `_ord_strides` | §7.3.1 | — |
| Presence | `_presence` | §7.4 | — |
| Home level and level naming | `op_class_level`, `_substep_level_name`, `_substep_mode`, `_has_values` | §7.5, §7.6 | §9.4 (restated with the empty-presence case the emitter hits) |

The name columns above sum to 45, which is exactly the definition inventory for `placement.py`; no
name is left to an adjacent module and none is counted twice.

**A maintenance warning that follows from the "also treated in" column.** Four functions —
`readahead_prologue`, `_peel_depths`, `PeelDepths` and `boundary_hoists` — have a pseudocode
rendering in more than one place. That is a real cost, and it has already bitten once: the §7.15
rendering of `_peel_depths` used to drop the source's `chunk is not None` guard that §9.5.4 kept, so
the two disagreed on a schedule point with no reduction chunk. Both are correct as of this revision.
If you change one of those four functions, **grep this report for its name and update every hit**;
the primary treatment alone is not enough.

#### 7.1 The problem this module solves

The emitter needs to place instructions. Everything it needs to place one reduces to five
questions, and this module is the single answer to each:

1. **At which loop level does this op-class live?** — its *home level*. A read of `A` under
   `ord = K·M·N` varies over `K` and `M` but not `N`, so it is emitted at `M`, not at `N` and not
   at the outer chunk. `placement.op_class_level`.
2. **Which coordinate does a given instance carry?** — the tuple of presence-mode indices, possibly
   *shifted* if the read runs ahead of its consumer. `placement._presence` gives the axis list,
   `placement._shifted_coord` gives the shifted index per axis.
3. **Which rotating-buffer name does it write or read?** — the register ring slot
   (`placement._rate_slot`, `placement._shifted_rate_slot`) and the shared ring generation
   (section 8's `_read_placement`).
4. **How far ahead of its consumer may it run, and what must the prologue pre-issue so that the
   steady body is self-sustaining?** — `placement.group_readahead_depth`,
   `placement._readahead_shift`, `placement.readahead_prologue`.
5. **How many peel steps does the software pipeline need, at which levels?** —
   `placement._peel_depths`, `placement.boundary_hoists`.

The invariant that governs the whole file is stated in different words in a dozen docstrings and is
worth putting once, plainly:

> **Every fact that two consumers both need is computed by exactly one function, and both call it.**

That is not style advice; it is the module's central bug-avoidance mechanism. The recurring failure
shape in this package is *two derivations of one rule that agree on the common case and diverge on a
degenerate one*. Concretely, and each of these actually shipped and had to be repaired:

* the read-ahead prologue and the steady advance derived the depth separately, so a group whose
  steady advance was clamped to 0 still had its prologue primed at the requested depth — the pipe
  was filled once and then never refilled (`placement.group_readahead_depth`'s docstring calls this
  "a Shape-A prologue paired with a Shape-B steady");
* the peel depth and the drain's read-ahead suppression window each converted the *requested* depth
  to whole chunks with their own denominator, while the steady body issued the *clamped* one — eight
  local reads silently disappeared at a deep local-prefetch setting with the hazard ledger still
  reporting "all discharged" (#284, `placement.readahead_reach`);
* three call sites each filtered the mode set inline before handing it to `placement._ord_strides`,
  which *renumbers whatever set it is given*, so one site's radix silently differed from the others'
  (`placement.reload_modes`'s docstring: "one function is the fix for that class of bug, independent
  of what the function returns").

So when reading this file, treat a function that looks like a one-line filter as load-bearing: its
value is that it has exactly one definition site, not that the body is interesting.

#### 7.2 Vocabulary this section uses without redefining

Section 1 already defines: schedule point / `theta` (1.1), op-class and role (1.2), presence and
broadcast (1.3), levels / `ord` / inner-vs-outer / reduction chunk (1.4), step and flat position
(1.5), retime `off` (1.6), the four obligation kinds (1.7), the two rings and the width band
`[L, R]` (1.8), the movement quantum (1.9), storage regions and fusion (1.10), rolled emission
(1.11). The additional vocabulary *introduced by this module* is defined where it first appears
below: **home level**, **ord stride**, **rate mode**, **rate slot**, **reload mode**, **free
sibling**, **broadcast fan**, **`dr` vs `dr_g`**, **Shape A / Shape B**, **advance / shift**,
**chunk reach `r`**, **in-place refill**, **peel vector `M_ℓ`**, **boundary hoist**.

#### 7.3 Addressing: the flat position and `_ord_strides`

**Concept.** The core is address-opaque — it never computes a byte offset. What it *does* need is a
total order on the points of the inner (statically unrolled) traversal, because "run `d` steps
ahead" is only meaningful against such an order. `Theta.ord` is a permutation of the loop modes
(section 1.4), so the traversal over any *subset* of those modes is a monotone mixed-radix counter:
the innermost mode of the subset advances fastest with stride 1, the next one out has stride equal
to the innermost's extent, and so on. That is the whole of the addressing model.

**Definition (ord stride).** For a mode set `Q ⊆ inner_modes`, ordered outer→inner by `ord`,

```
stride_Q(m) = Π extent(m')  over all m' ∈ Q strictly inner to m in ord
N_Q         = Π extent(m')  over all m' ∈ Q
```

and the **flat position** of a coordinate `c` is `P = Σ_{m ∈ Q} stride_Q(m) · c[m]`, ranging over
`[0, N_Q)`.

##### 7.3.1 `_ord_strides(theta, modes=None) -> (dict, int)`

Computes exactly the two quantities above. `modes` is an optional iterable of *mode names*; when
supplied, `theta.inner_modes()` is filtered down to those names first, preserving `ord` order.
Returns `(strides, N)` where `strides` maps mode name → `stride_Q(m)` and `N` is `N_Q`.

```
_ord_strides(theta, modes):
    im = [m for m in theta.inner_modes() if modes is None or m.name in modes]   # outer→inner
    coef = 1
    for m in reversed(im):          # innermost first
        strides[m.name] = coef
        coef *= m.extent
    return strides, coef
```

**The `modes` argument is the entire point of the function, and the reason it must not be
inlined.** A read's flat position must be computed over *its own presence modes only*. A broadcast
mode carries identical data across all its values, so it must not advance the position: including
it inflates `P`, and once its extent exceeds 1 the inflated `P` bounces the shared-buffer index
back and forth instead of crossing it once (the docstring calls this "the WT>1 failure" — it
appears whenever `MIWaveTile` exceeds 1 on the broadcast axis). Conversely, *narrowing* the set
renumbers every stride: hand `_ord_strides` a set with one mode removed and the remaining strides
change, so a caller that narrows locally silently decomposes on a different radix from its peers.
This is why `placement.reload_modes` exists as a named function rather than as an inline
comprehension at the two sites that need the narrowed set (section 7.10.3).

**Complexity.** `O(|inner_modes|)` per call, with `|inner_modes|` between 3 and 6 on every shipping
configuration (a three-axis `ord` like `KMN`, or a six-axis one like `KMNMNK` once the macro-tile
and unroll splits are applied). It is called several times per emitted read instruction and once
per read inside `_readahead_shift`, `_read_placement`, `_broadcast_fan`'s oracle test and the
prologue; total calls per kernel are in the low hundreds. It is *not* cached and does not need to
be. If a future `ord` grows to tens of modes — it will not, `ord` is a permutation of tiling axes —
the obvious fix is to memoize on `(id(theta), frozenset(modes))`, but the practical value of `n`
makes that pointless today.

**Sharp edge.** `strides` is a plain `dict`, and several consumers iterate it to build an `Expr`
term tuple (`cterms = tuple((name, coef) for name, coef in strides.items())` in
`placement._shifted_coord`, `placement._shifted_rate_slot` and section 8's `_read_placement`). Those
consumers therefore depend on Python's dict insertion order, which here is *innermost-first* because
the loop above walks `reversed(im)`. Nothing downstream reads the order semantically — `Expr.eval`
sums the terms — but a reader comparing two rendered expressions will see innermost-first term
order, which is the reverse of the `ord` order printed everywhere else. That is cosmetic, not a
defect, but it has confused readers of the dump.

#### 7.4 Presence: `_presence`

**Concept.** *Presence* (section 1.3) is the set of inner axes an op-class's instances actually vary
over; the complement is its broadcast set. `placement._presence(theta, op)` answers this **for the
operand's `→ register` read hop specifically** — not for the operand in general and not for its bulk
copy. Presence is a per-hop fact: a bulk cooperative copy that moves a whole tile in one instruction
varies over *no* inner axis and therefore sits at the outer chunk level, while the same operand's
per-lane read varies over the free tiles and the reduction substeps.

```
_presence(theta, op):
    hop = the first non-bulk hop of op whose dst is REGISTER, else None
    ns  = geometry.broadcast_axes(theta, op)        if hop is None
          geometry.hop_broadcast(theta, op, hop)    otherwise
    return [m.name for m in theta.inner_modes() if m.name not in ns]
```

The return value is a **list of names in `ord` order, outer→inner**, and every consumer relies on
that: `op_class_level` takes `pres[-1]` as the home level, `_ord_strides` re-derives strides from
it, `readahead_prologue` splits it at the substep axis.

**The derivation is delegated, deliberately.** `_presence` computes nothing itself; it asks
`geometry.hop_broadcast` (section 2.2.3) "what does *one instance of this hop* not vary over" and
subtracts. `geometry` is the one owner of that arithmetic, and the docstring records that this
function and `hop_broadcast` had previously drifted apart because each re-derived the subtraction.
Two facts flow in through `geometry`:

* **the data broadcast** — `A[m,k]` is constant over `n`. For an *agent-served* region axis
  (section 1.3) the axis is also broadcast for every data consumer, because a wave reads, computes
  and accumulates entirely inside its own region; `geometry.broadcast_axes` folds
  `theta.agent_served_modes()` in at one point so the read coord, the free-mode list, the register
  naming and the footprint cannot disagree about it.
