* **the movement quantum** — the axes one *instruction* spans (section 1.9). If a single wide
  local-data load covers two adjacent tiles of `M_split`, then `M_split` is absent from that hop's
  presence, because the two tiles are one presence point: one step, one generation.

**The quantum subtraction is half of a pair and must never be applied alone.** The docstring states
both halves and the measured cost of each half in isolation:

* subtract the axis here, and it disappears from `Load.coord`; `ir.Load.quantum` then records *how
  many* coordinates the one instruction fills, and the downstream lowering
  (`Lowering/loopir_to_gir._quantum_coords`) re-inserts the axis to emit that many register
  definitions — one instruction, several defs.
* apply the subtraction **without** the expansion and every non-leader consumer loses its reaching
  definition: measured at 34 failing tests, reported as "32 consumer(s) read a location the arm
  never writes".
* apply the expansion **without** the subtraction and the axis appears twice in one coordinate:
  measured at 492 failing tests.

Also note the ordering requirement encoded in the docstring: `resolve_quantum` (section 9) must have
run first, i.e. the hop must already carry its supplied quantum. While the quantum axis set is empty
this function returns exactly the historical per-tile answer, so the feature is off-by-default-safe.

**Cost.** One `geometry` call plus a filter over `inner_modes`; `O(|inner_modes|)`. It is called
very frequently — inside `reload_modes`, `_broadcast_fan`, `chunk_reach`, `op_class_level`,
`readahead_prologue`, `emit.read_inst`, `emit.nest` — with no memoization. `geometry.hop_broadcast`
itself does a little set arithmetic over the fragment's broadcast list. If profiling ever shows
decode time mattering (it does not today; a whole kernel decodes in single-digit milliseconds), the
first thing to cache is `(theta, op) -> presence tuple`, because it is the single hottest pure
function in the module and `theta` is a frozen dataclass.

#### 7.5 Home levels: `op_class_level`

**Concept (home level).** The *home level* of an op-class is the loop level at which the emitter
places its node — the innermost level whose index the op-class's instances vary over. The rule is
"placed by its own presence set", and the reason it has a named function rather than an inline
`pres[-1]` is that the three roles answer it differently and one of them (copy) is not answered by
the read presence at all.

```
op_class_level(theta, op, role):
    chunk = theta.reduction_chunk_name()
    if role == COPY:
        rm = first of op.region_modes that is an INNER mode, else None
        return rm if (rm is not None and op.split > 1) else chunk
    pres = _presence(theta, op)
    return pres[-1] if pres else chunk
```

* **read** — the innermost mode of the read hop's presence; the reduction chunk when presence is
  empty.
* **copy** — the *region* mode when the movement is region-split (one instruction per region, so
  the copy sits one level deeper and `emit.copy_insts` rolls it under a `Loop(region_mode)`),
  otherwise the reduction chunk, because a coarse bulk copy has empty inner presence.
* **store** — treated like a read. No store op-class exists yet; the epilogue is unmodelled (#116).

Returns `None` for an op-class with no level at all, which only happens for a hand-built `theta`
carrying no outer mode.

**Empty presence is reachable and legal**, and this is the case a reader is most likely to
mis-assume away. When a supplied quantum spans every axis a read still varies over, presence is `[]`
and the op-class is emitted once per chunk. `op_class_level` returns the chunk there, and `emit.nest`
has a dedicated emission site for exactly that — without which the read is emitted *zero* times.
That was a real defect: an MX scale read whose quantum emptied its presence vanished from the
emitted kernel entirely (#275).

**Its second consumer is the boundary hoist.** `boundary_hoists` (section 7.16.3) needs to know
whether an offset sits at a level *outer to the op-class's own home*, which is what distinguishes a
cross-level relocation from ordinary prefetch — so `op_class_level` is not merely an emitter
convenience. `emit.py` records that its local `read_level` map and this function must stay the same
derivation; a duplicated `pres[-1] if pres else None` in `emit` differed from `op_class_level` in
exactly the empty-presence case.

#### 7.6 Naming the reduction substep: `_substep_level_name`, `_substep_mode`, `_has_values`

Three tiny helpers, all of which have caused a shipped defect, which is why each has its own name.

##### 7.6.1 `_substep_level_name(theta) -> str | None`

The **name** of the innermost reduction inner mode — the level that `off(read, substep)` (the local
read prefetch depth) is keyed on. Used purely as a dictionary key into `Theta.off_map`, by
`readahead_reach`, `copy_must_be_first`, `chunk_crossing_violations`, `hop_quantum_axes` and the
ledger. Returns `None` when there is no reduction inner mode at all.

```
_substep_level_name(theta) = name of the last mode of theta.inner_modes() (ord order)
                             whose name is in theta.reduction_names(), else None
```

Note it does **not** filter on extent. That is intentional: it must return the level `off` is
*stored* under, and `translate` stores the offset under whatever the innermost reduction level is
called, degenerate or not.

##### 7.6.2 `_substep_mode(theta) -> Mode | None`

The innermost reduction inner mode **with extent > 1**, falling back to the innermost reduction mode
outright when every one is degenerate. Unlike `_substep_level_name` this returns a `Mode` object,
because the callers need its `extent` (`n_s`) as well as its name.

This is the axis at which both the read-ahead prologue (`readahead_prologue`) and the steady advance
(`_readahead_shift`) split `ord` into `[OUTER… | substep(n_s) | INNER…]`. Both used to take the
innermost reduction mode outright, which is the same axis whenever the reduction is a single mode.
It stops being the same axis when a reduction-axis region split re-factors the unroll depth as
`K_split × K_inner` and `K_inner` collapses to extent 1 while remaining innermost in `ord`: the
split then happened at an axis with no values, `n_s` came out as 1, and the prologue primed one
substep where the steady body consumed two — so the first compute instruction of the second substep
read a register generation nothing had loaded. Measured 2026-08-18 at a reduction-axis split of 2
with local prefetch depth 1 under the two K-innermost loop orders: 192 of 1152 configurations
failed, and *exactly* those two order words. K-outer orders were unaffected because there the
substep factor is `min(dr, n_s)` and `dr = 1` clamped to the same 1 either way — which is why the
defect selected on the loop order and on nothing else.

The fallback matters too: a kernel with no non-degenerate reduction substep at all keeps its old
answer rather than losing its ring entirely.

##### 7.6.3 `_has_values(modes) -> bool`

`any(m.extent > 1 for m in modes)`. Used to test whether the `ord` block inner to the substep is
"empty". The subtlety it encodes: *empty* here is a statement about the **traversal**, not about the
mode list. A block consisting only of extent-1 modes is traversed exactly once, just as an empty
block is, so it must take the same branch. Testing `not inner_block` instead asks a question about
how `theta` happened to *factor* the axes, which is not a scheduling fact. Both
`readahead_prologue._one_group` and `_readahead_shift` call it, and they must agree — this is the
"same split point" invariant that makes the prologue and the steady advance two halves of one rule.

#### 7.7 The register ring: rate modes and rate slots

**Concept (rate mode, rate slot).** A register *reuse group* is a partition of a fragment's values
that rotates through `W` register names (section 1.8). The **rate modes** of a group are the inner
axes that group actually cycles distinct values over. The **rate slot** is the mixed-radix index
over those modes, taken mod `W` — i.e. the symbolic name of the rotating register the instance
touches. Both are per `(operand, group)`.

##### 7.7.1 `_rate_modes(theta, op, group) -> [(name, extent), …]`

The inner modes not in `theta._rate_broadcast(theta, op, group)` **and of extent > 1**, in `ord`
order.

`theta._rate_broadcast` (section 4) is the "two-map reading": a group's rate-broadcast set is its
own fragment broadcast axes, **plus** the fragment's `grouping_mode` (sibling values of the grouping
mode select a *different* part, so that mode does not reload a single group), **plus** the operand's
**free** region modes (a free region split is a spatial storage partition, not a reload). A
*reduction*-axis region mode deliberately stays in the rate: its two regions are successive substeps
of one tile held in one group, so excluding it would make the group constant over the only axis it
actually reloads on. That exclusion was tried and cost 1152/1152 correctness failures at a
reduction-axis split, because the rate `R` collapsed from 2 to 1, `W` followed, and every read got
slot 0 — two regions loaded into the same register pair and whichever landed last won.

**Why extent-1 modes are dropped.** A degenerate mode is nullspace for everything: its coordinate is
always 0 and its radix is 1, so dropping it cannot change the mixed-radix index or the group's rate
product. It is dropped anyway because `_reduction_rate_mode` takes the **innermost** reduction rate
mode, and a degenerate mode would shadow the real substep axis — the same `K_split(2) × K_inner(1)`
shape as above. Dropping it also stops the "several reduction rate modes" guard from firing on a
pair that is really one axis.

##### 7.7.2 `_rate_slot(theta, op, group, d) -> Expr`

The rotation slot expression for a group of width `d`:

```
_rate_slot(theta, op, group, d):
    if d <= 1: return cst(0)                       # single buffer, no rotation
    rm = _rate_modes(theta, op, group)             # outer→inner
    if not rm: return cst(0)
    coef = 1; terms = []
    for (name, ext) in reversed(rm):               # innermost is the fastest radix
        terms.append((name, coef)); coef *= ext
    return Expr(mod=d, terms=tuple(reversed(terms)))
```

The result is `ir.Expr` in its mixed-radix `terms` form: `(Σ coef·var) mod d`. It is symbolic — the
IR stays rolled, and `Expr.eval(env)` concretizes it only when the renderer unrolls or the lowering
resolves a specific iteration.

**The correction this encodes.** An earlier form used the single innermost *presence* mode as the
rotation axis. That is wrong whenever the innermost presence mode is a sibling selector — a
free-axis region index, say — which is nullspace for the rate and must not drive the ring. Using the
group's rate modes, in mixed radix, is the general answer and degenerates to the old one whenever
there is exactly one rate mode.

##### 7.7.3 `_reduction_rate_mode(theta, op, group) -> (name, extent) | None`

The single **innermost reduction** rate mode of a group: filter `_rate_modes` down to names in
`theta.reduction_names()` and take the last. This is the substep axis the read-ahead shifts along
and wraps out of into the reduction chunk. Returns `None` when the group has no reduction rate mode
— which is a real case (a group whose rate is purely a free fan), and every caller handles it by
declining to read ahead.

The docstring records the current restriction: the shipping configurations have exactly one
reduction rate mode per group (`K_inner`), and a group with several would need a mixed-radix flat
shift. `_shifted_rate_slot` (section 7.11) has since implemented exactly that general form, so this
"innermost only" selection is now used to answer *"is there a reduction axis at all, and what is its
stride and extent"* rather than to be the whole rotation — but note that `_readahead_shift` still
multiplies by the stride of this **one** mode, so a genuine two-reduction-rate-mode *advance* is
still single-axis. That is a real, currently-latent limitation and section 7.18 lists it.

#### 7.8 Read-ahead, from first principles

This is the heart of the module. A reader who knows classical software pipelining but not this code
should read this subsection before any of the functions.

##### 7.8.1 The shape of the problem

The main loop's inner nest issues, for each point of the traversal, a set of register **reads**
(shared memory → register) and the **compute** instruction that consumes them. Issued naively, each
read is immediately followed by a wait for its own completion and then by its consumer: the machine
stalls for the full local-memory latency at every step.

The standard repair is *software pipelining*: hoist each read `d` steps earlier in the traversal, so
that at step `i` the machine issues the read for step `i + d` and computes on data that arrived `d`
steps ago. Three things then have to be arranged, and all three are what this family computes.

1. **Capacity.** Data for step `i + d` and data for step `i` must live in *different* registers, or
   the hoisted read destroys the value its own consumer is about to use. So the group's rotation
   width `W` must be at least the number of simultaneously live generations.
2. **A prologue.** The steady body only sustains the pipeline; something must *fill* it. Before the
   first steady step, the reads for steps `0 … d−1` must already have been issued. That set is the
   read-ahead prologue.
3. **A drain.** At the end, the steady body's read-ahead would run off the end of the loop's data.
   Those trailing reads must be suppressed (or the loop's last `d` steps peeled and emitted without
   them).

The decoder does not simulate this. Every one of the three is a **closed form** over `(ord, tile,
off, S)`, and the module's design bet is that a closed form which several consumers share cannot
drift, whereas three simulations will.

##### 7.8.2 The one number: `dr` versus `dr_g`

Two depths exist and confusing them is the single most productive source of bugs in this file.

* **`dr`** — the **requested** depth. It is `off(read, substep)`, the user-facing local-prefetch
  parameter as it reaches `theta`. It is per op-class, not per group.
* **`dr_g`** — the **derived** depth actually used, per **register group**. It is what the emitter
  issues, what the prologue primes, what the ledger files obligations against, and what every
  chunk-counting consumer must read.

`dr_g` is the request cut down by one width clamp and two structural vetoes:

```
dr_g(op, group) = 0                                  if fan(op) > 1                     [veto 1]
                  0                                  if a free sibling is outer to the
                                                        reduction the group rotates over [veto 2]
                  max(0, min(dr, W_g − 1))           otherwise
```

where `W_g = S.get(op.name, group)` is the group's rotation width from the depth map, `fan` is
`_broadcast_fan` (section 7.9) and the free-sibling test is `_sibling_outer_to_reduction`
(section 7.10). The function is `placement.group_readahead_depth`.

**The `W_g − 1` clamp is the capacity requirement made concrete.** With look-ahead depth `d`, the
group holds `d + 1` live generations at the peak: the one the current compute consumes, plus the `d`
in flight. A rotation of `W` names can hold `W` generations, so `d + 1 ≤ W`, i.e. `d ≤ W − 1`.
Requesting more is not merely wasteful — it is a race, because the hoisted read overwrites a name a
later compute still needs.

**Shape A and Shape B.** The consequence of one derived depth is that a group has exactly two
self-consistent configurations, never a mixture:

| | `dr_g ≥ 1` — **Shape A** (prefetch) | `dr_g = 0` — **Shape B** (in place) |
|---|---|---|
| read placement | hoisted ahead of its consuming compute | issued in place, one line before its own compute, with a completion wait between |
| prologue | non-empty (and rounded up to the first tile's full reduction extent when the `ord` block inner to the substep is valueless) | **empty** |
| steady advance | non-zero | **0** |
| ledger | `readahead-residency` rows for the primed coordinates; a `rotation-WAR` on the refill | an `inplace-WAR` that the issue-order refinement discharges by deferral |

Mixing them is the failure the whole `dr_g` refactor exists to prevent: a Shape-A prologue paired
with a Shape-B steady primes the pipe once and then never re-primes it. That was this decoder's
actual state before `group_readahead_depth` existed — the prologue ran at the global `dr` while the
steady advance ran at 0 — and `test_prologue_depth_equals_steady_advance_shape_a_or_b` in
`Tensile/Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py` now sweeps the whole configuration matrix asserting
`bool(shift) == bool(prologue)` per operand.

##### 7.8.3 Why `L` must be derived from `ord`

The width band is `[L, R]` (section 1.8): `R` is the reload rate and `L` is the live-peak floor.
`L` is the thing that decides whether a hoist is legal, and the crucial property is that **`L`
depends on the loop order, not only on the depth**. The closed form the module implements is

```
L(p) = (dr_g + 1) + [1 if the broadcast fan of p is non-trivial]
```

and the second term is a pure `ord`/presence predicate — see `_broadcast_fan` next. Two operands of
the *same* kernel with the *same* requested depth can therefore have different floors purely because
of where their broadcast axes sit in `ord`. That is why `dr_g` is per operand *and* per group, and
why a single global "PLR depth" is not a sufficient model.

The requirement `W ≥ L` is a race condition, not a performance heuristic: `W < L` means two
simultaneously live values are assigned one register name. Since `W` is fixed by the width search in
`theta.build_S`, the decoder satisfies `W ≥ L` by **lowering `dr_g`**, which is the only free
variable left at this point.

#### 7.9 Veto 1 — the broadcast fan: `_broadcast_fan`

**Definition (broadcast fan).** For an op-class `p` with presence set `pres(p)`:

> `fan(p)` = the product of extents of the modes that are **(a)** not in `pres(p)`, **(b)** of
> extent > 1, and **(c)** outer, in `ord`, to **every** mode of `pres(p)`.

Operationally: `fan(p)` is the number of times `p`'s entire register name space is re-traversed
before any one of its values dies.

```
_broadcast_fan(theta, op):
    pres = set(_presence(theta, op))
    if not pres: return 1
    inner = [m.name for m in theta.inner_modes()]          # ord order, outer→inner
    first = min(inner.index(n) for n in pres)              # position of the outermost presence mode
    fan = 1
    for n in inner[:first]:                                # strictly outer to ALL of pres
        if n not in pres and extent(n) > 1:
            fan *= extent(n)
    return fan
```

`fan(p) > 1` forces `dr_g = 0` at **any** width and any substep count. The reason is structural
rather than arithmetic: if the operand's whole name space is walked again before the current
generation dies, then a read-ahead write lands on a name that a *later* consumer in the same fan
still needs, for **any** advance distance. No amount of extra width and no reordering rescues it —
it is a simultaneous-input race, not an anti-dependency that an issue-order refinement can defer.

**The "outer to *every* mode" quantifier is the load-bearing part**, and the docstring gives the
worked example that separates the two operands of a three-axis order. Under `ord = M·N·K`:

* `A` has presence `{M, K}` and is broadcast over `N`. But `N` sits *between* `M` and `K`, so it is
  not outer to `M ∈ pres(A)`. `fan(A) = 1`. `A` is re-read at each `n` into the same register name,
  but with the *same value* — harmless.
* `B` has presence `{N, K}`, is broadcast over `M`, and `M` is outer to both `N` and `K`.
  `fan(B) = extent(M)`. `B`'s whole name space is re-traversed once per `m`, so `B` loses its
  read-ahead.

Under `KMN` / `KNM` the broadcast mode is interleaved with the presence modes and is never outer to
all of them, so neither operand qualifies and both keep read-ahead. The weaker reading — "broadcast
over *some* mode outer to the reduction" — zeroes *both* operands of `MNK`, which is measurably
wrong.

**The `extent > 1` clause is a guard, not a live branch.** `translate` drops degenerate modes when
it builds `theta` from parameters, so a parameter-derived `theta` never carries an extent-1 inner
mode and the clause never fires on the shipping path. It is kept because `theta.inner_modes()` makes
no such promise and a hand-built `theta` (the multi-group work, #118) can carry one; a broadcast mode
of extent 1 re-traverses nothing and therefore cannot force a second live generation. Dropping the
clause would zero `dr_g` for a degenerate free fan, which is the *rescuable* in-place case
(section 7.11), not a race. `test_broadcast_fan_ignores_a_degenerate_mode` covers it directly by
mutating a mode's extent, because no parameter configuration can reach it.

**The independent oracle.** `test_broadcast_fan_predicate_agrees_with_the_walk` in
`Tensile/Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py` is the strongest test in this file and is worth describing,
because it is the pattern a future change to this predicate must reuse. Its helper
`_name_space_walk` performs a **direct live-range simulation** on the joint
`(free-tile, rotation-slot)` register-name space over three consecutive chunks of the `ord`
traversal, judging the middle one. At each step the read writes name `(P + shift) mod names` and the
leaf's compute consumes name `P`; a write onto a name whose surviving consume is **strictly later**
is the unrescuable race (`"clobber"`), while a write whose only surviving consume is at the **same**
leaf is the rescuable write-after-read (`"inplace"`). The test then asserts, over the whole
order × wave-tile × split × prefetch matrix, that `fan > 1` holds **iff** the walk says `"clobber"`.
Because the oracle is an independent simulation and not a second call into `placement`, a `dr_g`
derivation that is merely self-consistent cannot pass it. A companion test,
`test_readahead_advance_never_clobbers_across_the_matrix`, asserts the weaker but broader property
that the *derived* advance never produces a `"clobber"` anywhere in the matrix.

#### 7.10 Veto 2 — free siblings: `_free_siblings`, `_sibling_outer_to_reduction`, `reload_modes`

**Definition (free sibling).** A **region** mode of the operand that sits on a **free** (non-reduction)
axis. Its values enumerate *storage-disjoint siblings* — different fragments of the macro-tile — not
successive generations of one fragment. A **reduction**-axis region split is deliberately *not* a
sibling: its two regions are successive substeps of one tile held in one group.

##### 7.10.1 `_free_siblings(theta, op) -> tuple`

```
_free_siblings(theta, op):
    red   = set(theta.reduction_names())
    named = tuple(r for r in op.region_modes if r not in red)
    if named or op.free_split <= 1:
        return named                       # the normal answer
    # the split is live but its region mode is gone from ord
    inner = [m.name for m in theta.inner_modes()]
    mine  = {op.free_mode, op.fragment.grouping_mode}
    return tuple(n for n in inner if n in mine and n not in red)[:1]
```

The first branch is the shipping answer: name the operand's free region modes. The second branch is
a **fallback anchored on storage rather than on a label**, and the reason it exists is a genuine
sharp edge (#245). `region_modes` answers the question by *naming a mode*, so it is only as durable
as that mode's presence in `ord`. When a region axis's extent collapses to 1 it is dropped by
`translate._canonical_ord`, which empties `region_modes` and **silently releases this veto** — and
with it `dr_g = 0`, so the read-ahead carry comes back. Measured when that happened: at a six-axis
order with a split of 1, one MX scale operand's four read acts split across blocks, the first drain
step emitted **zero** scale loads and the prologue fetched a tile a stage early. Re-imposing the veto
on the renamed axis took the reported violations from 2 to 0. The split is a fact about *storage*, so
the veto keys on `op.free_split` — an integer that survives the mode being dropped — and names the
**outermost** of the operand's own surviving free modes, because that is the position
`_sibling_outer_to_reduction` compares against and because the region axis it replaces was itself
outer to the in-region fan.

The fallback is unreachable on the shipping tree: while the region mode survives in `ord`,
`region_modes` is non-empty and the first branch returns exactly what it always did — verified
byte-identical emission.

##### 7.10.2 `_sibling_outer_to_reduction(theta, op) -> bool`

Is one of `op`'s free siblings **outer**, in `ord`, to the reduction axis the group rotates over?

```
_sibling_outer_to_reduction(theta, op):
    names = [m.name for m in theta.inner_modes()]
    red   = _reduction_rate_mode(theta, op, op.fragment.groups()[0])
    if red is None or red[0] not in names: return False
    ri = names.index(red[0])
    return any(s in names and names.index(s) < ri for s in _free_siblings(theta, op))
```

Note it consults **group 0** for the reduction rate mode. That is an accepted approximation: every
group of one fragment shares the same reduction axis in every reachable configuration, but it is a
place a future multi-group change must revisit (section 7.18).

**Why this configuration forbids the hoist outright.** A cross-tile read-ahead needs two things and
this arrangement supplies neither:

1. *The advance cannot reach the next tile.* The sibling is a storage-disjoint group, so the shift
   must not carry through it — it **bounds** the shift, which then rolls the chunk coordinate
   instead of crossing into the neighbour.
2. *The prologue cannot prime the other sibling either.* The prologue's outer factor is "the first
   coordinate of `pres ∩ OUTER`", i.e. region 0 alone. So sibling 1's leading substep is primed by
   nothing and advanced to by nothing.

Either shape alone would be a mixture; the available consistent answer is in-place, `dr_g = 0`, empty
prologue, refill ordered after the vacating read.

##### 7.10.3 `reload_modes(theta, op) -> [name, …]`

`[m for m in _presence(theta, op) if m not in _free_siblings(theta, op)]` — the modes the group
actually **reloads** over, which is the traversal the steady shift walks. It is *not* the same set as
presence, and keeping the two apart is the whole content of this function:

* **presence** answers "where is this op-class emitted, and what does the prologue enumerate". A
  free-axis region sibling genuinely *is* in the presence set, contributes its `ord` position, and
  contributes its first coordinate to the prologue.
* **reload** answers "what radix does the steady advance decompose on". A sibling selects a
  different group's band, not a later generation of this group, so the shift must not carry through
  it. A shift that walked past it would target the neighbouring sibling's register — a slot no future
  generation of the advancing group ever occupies.

Reduction axes and a genuinely reloaded free fan stay in the reload set. That is what keeps a
reduction-axis split's two-axis `K_split × K_inner` register rotation intact (#254); an earlier
attempt excluded `op.region_modes` wholesale and regressed exactly there, 12 unit failures all on
that rotation.

**Why it is a function and not an inline filter** — repeating the point from section 7.3 because
this is the canonical instance. `_ord_strides` renumbers whatever mode set it is handed, so narrowing
at one call site silently changes that site's radix while the others keep the old one. `emit.py`
states the invariant that breaks: *the same `shift` drives the register slot and the shared source
generation, so the three cannot drift*. Three sites each calling `_presence` independently cannot
honour that by construction. When the exclusion was tried inline, the observed failure was
"compute reads `A` buffer X0 tile 1, which no read in scope has filled" at one order and
symmetrically on `B` at the mirrored order.

**The two halves.** Excluding the sibling from the traversal is necessary but not sufficient:
when the sibling is *outer* to the reduction the group cannot read ahead at all, which is veto 2.
Enabling `reload_modes`' exclusion alone regressed 16 of 168 sweep cells (the two orders with an
outer free split, at local-prefetch depth 1); with both, the sweep is clean. Turning the exclusion
*off* entirely gives 0 failing cells in the checker but emits kernels that are wrong on hardware —
so the checker alone is not a sufficient gate for this property, which is worth knowing before
"simplifying" it.

#### 7.11 The derived depth and the advance

##### 7.11.1 `group_readahead_depth(theta, op, group, dr, S) -> int`

The formula given in section 7.8.2, in the order the code applies it: bail at `dr == 0`; return 0 if
`_broadcast_fan > 1`; return 0 if `_sibling_outer_to_reduction`; else
`max(0, min(dr, S.get(op.name, group) - 1))`.

**Both vetoes must live here, not in `_readahead_depth`.** This is the per-group derivation that
*both* shapes read: `readahead_prologue` calls it directly per group, and `_readahead_depth` takes a
min over it. Putting a veto in the min alone zeroes the steady advance while the prologue keeps
priming — exactly the Shape-A-prologue/Shape-B-steady mixture, and the test that catches it reports
"steady advance 0 but 1 prologue reads".

Callers: `readahead_prologue`, `_readahead_depth`, `readahead_reach`, `copy_must_be_first`,
`chunk_crossing_violations`, `ledger.build_ledger`, `emit._read_groups`, `render.render_geometry`.
That fan-out is the
justification for the function existing.

`test_dr_g_anchors_from_the_floor` pins the derivation per order so a future rewrite cannot silently
change *which* operand keeps its look-ahead:

```
KMN, KNM        A:1  B:1     # no broadcast mode outer to a whole presence set
MNK, MKN        A:1  B:0     # M outer to all of pres(B)
NMK, NKM        A:0  B:1     # mirrored
KMN with dr=2   A:1  B:1     # the width clamp is real: min(dr, W_g−1) = 1 at W_g = 2
KMN with dr=0   A:0  B:0
```

##### 7.11.2 `_readahead_depth(theta, op, dr, S, groups=None) -> int`

`min(group_readahead_depth(...) for g in groups or op.fragment.groups())`, or 0 for an empty
selection. This is `dr_g` **for one read instruction**: one `Inst` carries one advance, so a read
covering groups of differing depth must take the shallowest.

In practice the min is over a uniform-depth subset, because `emit._read_groups` splits the read first
whenever the depths differ: it partitions the fragment's groups into the `dr_g ≥ 1` set and the
`dr_g == 0` set and emits one instruction for each. That split keys on the **derived** depth, not on
`W_g > 1` — width is only one of the two ways a group reaches Shape B, and keying on width alone
left a fan-vetoed group inside the hoisted instruction while its own advance was 0.

**`min` here, `max` in `readahead_reach` — do not unify them.** Both files say so explicitly and the
reason is that they answer different questions. A per-instruction shift must not exceed the
*shallowest* group's rotation, or that group races. A peel depth or a drain suppression window must
cover the *deepest* group, or a later step's reads are dropped. Section 7.13 gives the measured cost
of getting the second one wrong.

##### 7.11.3 `_readahead_shift(theta, op, dr, S, groups=None) -> (shift, strides, n_pres, ext)`

**Definition (advance / shift).** The steady read-ahead expressed in **flat ord-position units over
the group's reload modes**:

```
substep_factor = n_s                    if the ord block strictly INNER to the substep has no values
                 min(dr_g, n_s)         otherwise
shift          = substep_factor · stride_reload(reduction rate mode)
```

The four-tuple returned is `(shift, strides, n_pres, ext)`:

* `shift` — the advance, `0` when the op does not read ahead;
* `strides` — the per-**reload**-mode ord strides (the dict from `_ord_strides(theta, reload_modes)`);
* `n_pres` — the product of those extents, i.e. `N` over the reload traversal;
* `ext` — `{mode name: extent}` over **all** inner modes (not just the reload ones), used by
  `_shifted_coord` to take the final modulus per axis.

`strides`, `n_pres` and `ext` are returned even in the no-advance case, because callers still need
them to build unshifted coordinates and the shared source generation.

```
_readahead_shift(theta, op, dr, S, groups):
    pres            = reload_modes(theta, op)
    strides, n_pres = _ord_strides(theta, pres)
    ext             = {m.name: m.extent for m in theta.inner_modes()}
    red             = _reduction_rate_mode(theta, op, op.fragment.groups()[0])
    dr_g            = _readahead_depth(theta, op, dr, S, groups)
    if not dr_g or red is None or red.name not in strides:
        return 0, strides, n_pres, ext
    substep  = _substep_mode(theta)
    inner_of = inner modes strictly inner to `substep` in ord
    factor   = red.extent if not _has_values(inner_of) else min(dr_g, red.extent)
    return factor * strides[red.name], strides, n_pres, ext
```

Three separate corrections are baked into those five lines, and each was a shipped defect.

**(a) The advance is a flat-position shift, not a bump of the reduction coordinate.** Bumping the
reduction index alone wraps *inside* the current tile and never reaches the next one, so every tile
after the first got its leading substep one compute instruction late. Multiplying by the reduction
mode's stride *within this operand's traversal* is what carries the advance out of the reduction axis
and into the free modes.

**(b) When the `ord` block inner to the substep is valueless, the factor is the full `n_s`, not
`dr_g`.** That is the K-innermost family of orders (`…M·N·K`). There the read-ahead discharges at
**tile** granularity: leaf 0's read-ahead must target the *next free tile's* first substep, not the
*current* tile's second substep — which the prologue has already loaded. Advancing by `dr_g` there
re-reads a value that already exists, i.e. a double issue with no second producer. For a K-outer
order the reduction mode is outermost in the traversal, the factor is `min(dr_g, n_s)`, and the
formula reduces exactly to the old `dr`-bump — so those orders are unchanged by construction.

**(c) The traversal is the *reload* set, not the presence set.** This is the free-sibling exclusion
of section 7.10 applied to the radix. Only this function's radix narrows; `readahead_prologue` keeps
the full presence set. The overflow that used to land in the neighbouring region now rolls the
reduction-chunk coordinate instead, which is a shared-buffer residency question the chunk-crossing
rule already models (section 7.13).

The measured failure that pinned (c) is worth reproducing because it shows how narrowly this
selects. At an fp8 shape with macro-tile 64×64×256, wave tile [2,2], vector width 2, one global and
one local prefetch, and a free-axis region split:

```
KMN     A: shift=2  strides={M_inner:1, M_split:1, K_inner:2}   reduction has the TOP stride
KMKNMN  A: shift=1  strides={M_inner:1, K_inner:1, M_split:2}   reduction at stride 1
```

Under `KMN` the advance cannot reach `M_split`; under every six-letter interleaved order the
reduction sits *inward* of the split, so the first advance carries into the region axis. On hardware
the three interleaved orders failed at local-prefetch 1 and passed at 0 and at `KMN`; the mismatch
was exactly one wave-tile of `A` (with vector width 2 interleaving the two wave-tiles at row
granularity, the even rows of one band were wrong and every odd row plus the whole `N` axis was
clean).

**Note the split point is shared with the prologue.** `_readahead_shift` computes `inner_of` from
`_substep_mode(theta)`, the same helper `readahead_prologue` uses. Two halves of one rule: the steady
body only sustains what the prologue primed, so they must divide `ord` at the same axis.

##### 7.11.4 `readahead_is_inplace(theta, op, dr, S, groups=None) -> bool`

`shift != 0 and shift % max(1, n_pres) == 0`.

**Definition (in-place refill).** The advance lands on name `(P + shift) mod n_pres`; when
`shift ≡ 0 (mod n_pres)` that is name `P` — the very name the co-located compute instruction is
reading. This is a **write-after-read**, not a capacity violation: the post-write live peak of such
a group is 1, and the correct response is an issue-order deferral (emit the refill *after* the
vacating read), not a smaller `dr_g`.

Demoting instead is a real cost: with a degenerate free fan, `n_pres` collapses to `n_s` and the
valueless-inner-block advance of `n_s` wraps exactly, every time — so wave tile [1,1] would lose its
read-ahead entirely for no correctness reason.

The consumer is `ledger.build_ledger`, which turns a true result into the `inplace-WAR` obligation
that the issue-order refinement `sigma_c.order_sigma_c` keys on. `W_g == 1` is the other,
already-handled route into the same case. `test_wrapping_advance_is_inplace_not_a_veto` pins the whole chain: it builds the
wrapping geometry (wave tile [1,1], `MNK`, depth 1), asserts `shift % n_pres == 0`, asserts
`readahead_is_inplace`, asserts the ledger tags it `inplace-WAR`, and then asserts the *emitted*
steady body places that read after the compute that vacates the register.

##### 7.11.5 `_shifted_coord(m, shift, strides, n_pres, ext) -> Expr`

The read-ahead-shifted coordinate along one presence mode `m`:

```
_shifted_coord(m, shift, strides, n_pres, ext):
    if m not in strides:                 # a sibling-enumerating mode, outside the traversal
        return Expr(var=m)               # IDENTITY — it keeps its own coordinate
    cterms = tuple(strides.items())
    return Expr(carry=(cterms, shift, strides[m]), mod=ext.get(m, 1))
```

The `Expr` produced evaluates to `((P + shift) // stride(m)) mod extent(m)` where
`P = Σ stride(m')·idx(m')`. That is the re-decomposition that makes the advance **carry between
modes**: overflow out of the reduction mode lands in the next free-mode tile, and overflow past
`n_pres` is the reduction-chunk crossing that the shared source generation models.

Note `n_pres` is accepted but not used in the body — it is part of the four-tuple contract so that
callers can pass the tuple through unpacked, and removing it would churn six call sites for nothing.
That is a mild wart, not a defect.

**The sibling branch returns an identity, and that is not the same as returning `None`.** A
sibling-enumerating mode is outside the traversal, so its coordinate must be *unshifted* — the
sibling this read belongs to is fixed by its grid position and the advance happens inside it. The
caller in `emit.read_inst` writes
`(m, _shifted_coord(...)) if shift else (m, None)`, using `None` for the **whole-op** no-shift case,
where the walker supplies every coordinate itself. Returning `None` for a *single* mode inside a
shifted op instead **drops** that coordinate, and the region-1 reads vanish; measured as "compute
reads `A` buffer X0 tile 1, which no read in scope has filled" at `MKN` with a 2×2 region split and
local prefetch 1. `Expr(var=m)` — "whatever the enclosing loop says, carried through unchanged" — is
the right answer.

##### 7.11.6 `_shifted_rate_slot(theta, op, group, shift, strides, d) -> Expr | None`

The rotation slot **of the shifted position**: the group's mixed-radix rate index evaluated at
`P + shift` instead of at `P`, mod `d`.

```
_shifted_rate_slot(theta, op, group, shift, strides, d):
    rm = [(n, e) for n, e in _rate_modes(theta, op, group) if n in strides]
    if not rm: return None
    fields, coef = [], 1
    for (name, ext) in reversed(rm):                    # innermost is the fastest radix
        fields.append((coef, strides[name], ext)); coef *= ext
    return Expr(digits=(tuple(strides.items()), shift, tuple(reversed(fields))), mod=d)
```

`ir.Expr`'s `digits` field is exactly this shape: `(terms, add, ((coef, div, ext), …))` evaluating to
`Σ coef · (((add + Σ c·env[m]) // div) mod ext)`. So each rate mode contributes its own **digit** of
the shifted position, at its own radix, and the digits recombine into the rate index.

**It used to be one digit.** The earlier form substituted the single reduction rate mode's shifted
coordinate for the whole slot and *refused* when a group had more than one reduction rate mode,
because a sum of floor-divided coordinates had no `Expr` shape. Adding `digits` to `Expr` made the
general form expressible, so the refusal is gone (#254). Two properties make it safe to apply
unconditionally:

* with **one** rate mode it reduces to exactly the old expression whenever `W == extent(m)`, which
  holds for every group under the `unroll` width policy — i.e. every reachable configuration. Where
  they differ (`W < extent(m)`) the digit form is the correct one, because the slot is
  `rate_index mod W` and `rate_index` is the digit, not the raw quotient.
* the digits are taken over **all** rate modes, matching `_rate_slot`. Substituting only the
  reduction mode's digit silently dropped a free rate mode's contribution for any fragment that keeps
  its fan in the rate (i.e. has no `grouping_mode`).

Returns `None` when the group has no rate mode inside this operand's reload traversal, and the caller
(section 8's `_read_placement`) then keeps the unshifted slot.

#### 7.12 The read-ahead prologue

##### 7.12.1 `readahead_prologue(theta, op, dr, S=None) -> [dict, …]`

**Concept.** The set of register reads the prologue must pre-issue so that the steady body is
self-sustaining. Returns a **list of coordinate dicts** `{inner-mode-name: value}` over `op`'s
presence — one dict per read the prologue owes. Order is generation order (outer factor, then
substep, then inner combination), but no consumer depends on the order; both `emit.fill_reads` and
`ledger`'s `readahead-residency` rows iterate the list as a set.

**The closed form.** Split `ord` at the reduction substep axis `ik` of extent `n_s`, giving
`ord = [OUTER… | substep(n_s) | INNER…]`. Then

```
prologue(p) = { first coord of pres(p) ∩ OUTER }
            × { leading min(dr_g, n_s) substeps, or ALL n_s if the ord INNER block is valueless }
            × { pres(p) ∩ INNER }
```

Three independent factors, each intersected with `pres(p)` so a broadcast axis drops out. **No leaf
simulation.** The intersection is why `A` and `B` can have different prologue *arity* under the same
order — the trap that a leaf simulation walks straight into.

The three worked families the unit tests pin (`test_readahead_prologue_lemma3d`, at `dr = 1`,
`n_s = 2`, wave tile 2×2, coordinates written as `k`/`m`/`n` with an index):

| order | `A` prologue | `B` prologue | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `KMN` (K-outer) | `{(k0,m0), (k0,m1)}` | `{(k0,n0), (k0,n1)}` | substep factor `min(dr,n_s) = 1`; the INNER factor is each operand's **own** presence axis |
| `MNK` (K-inner) | `{(k0,m0), (k1,m0)}` | `{(k0,n0), (k1,n0)}` | INNER block empty ⇒ full `n_s` substeps, at each operand's first outer tile |
| `MKN` (K in the middle) | `{(k0,m0)}` | `{(k0,n0), (k0,n1)}` | **different arity** — `A` is broadcast over `N` so it has no INNER factor; `B` has the `N` fan |

`test_readahead_prologue_substep_saturates_with_dr` pins the substep factor growing with `dr` up to
the `n_s` ceiling, and `test_readahead_prologue_empty_without_dr` pins `dr = 0 ⇒ []`.

**Algorithm, with the per-group structure.**

```
readahead_prologue(theta, op, dr, S):
    if not dr:            return []
    pres = set(_presence(theta, op));      if not pres: return []
    sub  = _substep_mode(theta);           if sub is None: return []
    inner_block = ord modes strictly inner to sub
    OUTER = [m in ord before sub, m.name in pres]
    INNER = [m in inner_block,    m.name in pres]
    n_s   = sub.extent

    if S is None:                          # no depth map: cannot derive dr_g
        return _one_group(dr, None, None)
    groups = op.fragment.groups()
    if op.fragment.grouping_mode is None or len(groups) <= 1:
        return _one_group(group_readahead_depth(theta, op, groups[0], dr, S), None, None)
    # width-split fragment: UNION over groups, each at its own dr_g over its own value subset
    out, seen = [], set()
    for g in groups:
        dr_g          = group_readahead_depth(theta, op, g, dr, S)
        gm, gm_vals   = _group_value_range(theta, op, g)
        for c in _one_group(dr_g, gm, gm_vals):
            if key(c) not in seen: seen.add(key(c)); out.append(c)
    return out
```

##### 7.12.2 `readahead_prologue._one_group(dr_g, gm_name, gm_vals)` (closure)

Builds the three-factor set for **one** group at depth `dr_g`, restricting the grouping mode (if the
fragment is group-split) to that group's own value subset. `dr_g <= 0` returns `[]` immediately —
that is the Shape-B answer, and it is what makes a single-group Shape-B fragment prologue nothing.

```
_one_group(dr_g, gm_name, gm_vals):
    if dr_g <= 0: return []
    n_sub       = n_s if not _has_values(inner_block) else min(dr_g, n_s)
    outer_fixed = {m.name: 0 for m in OUTER}                  # "the first coord" — index 0
    inner_combos = cartesian product over INNER of _vals(m)   # [{}] when INNER is empty
    for gmo in (gm_vals if the grouping mode is in OUTER else [None]):
        for s in range(n_sub):
            for ic in inner_combos:
                yield {**outer_fixed, **({gm_name: gmo} if gmo is not None else {}),
                       sub.name: s, **ic}
```

Note the grouping mode may be either an INNER mode or an OUTER one. In the INNER case `_vals`
restricts it; in the OUTER case the `outer_fixed` value 0 is overridden per group value by the `gmo`
loop. This dual handling is why the closure takes the grouping mode by name rather than filtering
outside.

##### 7.12.3 `readahead_prologue._one_group._vals(m)` (nested closure)

One line: return `gm_vals` when `m` is the grouping mode, else `range(m.extent)`. Trivial, but it is
the only place the group's value subset is injected into the INNER factor.

##### 7.12.4 `_group_value_range(theta, op, group) -> (mode_name, [values]) | (None, None)`

The **value subset** of the grouping mode that a register group owns. A group is a partition of the
grouping tile-mode's values; the current partition is **equal**, so group `i` owns
`[i·part, (i+1)·part)` where `part = free_extent(grouping_mode) // len(groups)`. Returns
`(None, None)` when the fragment is not group-split (no grouping mode, or a single group).

Uneven partitions are unimplemented and are an accepted exception recorded elsewhere in the package
(#166); if you add one, this function and `sizing`'s footprint arithmetic are the two places that
assume equality.

**Why per-group at all.** `test_readahead_prologue_per_group_dr` is the anchor: on a fragment with
groups `{lo: W=2, hi: W=1}`, only `lo` reaches `dr_g = min(dr, W−1) = 1`; `hi` is single-buffered and
gets `dr_g = 0`, so its refill is the in-place write-after-read and it contributes **nothing** to the
prologue. The test asserts that `A`'s prologue covers exactly `lo`'s grouping-mode values, and — as a
non-vacuity guard — that the `S = None` call *does* include `hi`'s values, i.e. that the depth map is
what restricts it.

**The `S = None` fallback is a deliberate degradation, and a trap.** Without a depth map the function
cannot derive `dr_g`, so it primes at the requested `dr` for the *whole* operand. That is wrong for
any Shape-B group. It exists because some callers (older tests, and the renderer before it was
wired) have a `theta` but no `S`. Every production caller passes `S`. If you are adding a new caller,
pass `S`.

**Reading "per-group" as "only when width-split" was itself a bug.** A single-group fragment can be
Shape B too — that is exactly the fan-vetoed operand of a K-innermost order, which has no width split
at all. The single-group branch above therefore still routes through `group_readahead_depth`.

#### 7.13 Crossing into the next chunk: reach, copy order, and the shared-buffer coupling

The substep read-ahead is **not confined to its own reduction chunk**. Once the reduction substep is
outer to the operand's inner free fan (or the fan is exhausted), the top `shift` positions have
nowhere sideways to carry, and the advance rolls the *chunk* coordinate. Crossing is the rule, not a
special case: the carry out of the presence traversal into the chunk index is correct, and what the
crossing costs is **shared buffering**, not a different slot formula.

##### 7.13.1 `chunk_reach(theta, op, dr_g) -> int`

**Definition (chunk reach `r`).** How many whole reduction chunks the substep read-ahead of one
group reaches into.

```
sub  = innermost reduction inner mode                (by name, degenerate or not)
fan  = Π extent(m) over pres(op) modes INNER to sub
span = extent(sub) · fan                             # distinct reads in one chunk
r    = ((span − 1) + dr_g · fan) // span
```

`dr_g <= 0 ⇒ 0`, and `sub is None ⇒ 0`. Note the argument is `dr_g`, the **derived** depth: every
caller computes it first and passes it in, so this function is a pure formula with no depth-map
access of its own.

`test_chunk_reach_is_the_distance_over_the_span_and_saturates_at_the_level` exercises it as a
pure function, including at `dr > n_s`, and states the property that matters for reviewers:
algebraically `r = 1 + (dr_g·fan − 1) // (n_s·fan)`, so **inside the reachable domain `dr_g ≤ n_s`
the second term is always 0 and `r == 1` for every `dr_g ≥ 1`, regardless of `fan`**. That makes the
`fan` factor *vacuous in the reachable domain*: a mutant that drops `fan` from the numerator passes
every parameter-derived test, and only a direct out-of-domain probe distinguishes it. The test exists
to be that probe. Do not "simplify" `fan` away on the evidence of a green suite.

##### 7.13.2 `readahead_reach(theta, S=None) -> int`

The **envelope** over read op-classes and their groups:

```
readahead_reach(theta, S):
    if S is None: S, _ = build_S(theta)
    sub = _substep_level_name(theta);  if sub is None: return 0
    best = 0
    for op in theta.operands where the last hop is SHARED → REGISTER:
        dr = theta.off_at(op.name, READ, sub);  if dr <= 0: continue
        for g in op.fragment.groups():
            best = max(best, chunk_reach(theta, op, group_readahead_depth(theta, op, g, dr, S)))
    return best
```

This is **the one** derivation of "how many whole chunks the substep read-ahead crosses into", shared
by the two consumers that count chunks: the chunk-level peel depth (`_peel_depths`) and the drain's
read-ahead suppression window (in `emit`). It takes `max` over groups, deliberately opposite to
`_readahead_depth`'s `min` (section 7.11).

**Why it exists (#284), with the numbers.** Both chunk-counting consumers used to compute
`ceil(dr / n_s)` on the **raw request**. Measured 2026-08-21 on a bf16 shape, wave tile [2,2],
`n_s = 2`, two global prefetch stages, with the clustering option off so the request actually reaches
`theta`:

* At local prefetch 3, `dr_g` clamps to 1 (`W_g = 2`), so the steady advance and the drain guard are
  the depth-1 ones — but the raw `ceil(3/2) = 2` widened the **drain suppression window** from 1 step
  to 2, so the second-to-last drain step also guarded away read-ahead reads that the last drain
  step's leading compute instructions consume. Emitted local-read count: 62 at depth 1, 62 at depth 2,
  **54** at depth 3 — eight local reads silently gone against an unchanged 36 compute instructions,
  with the hazard ledger reporting empty and no warning. With this function: 62, matching depths 1
  and 2.
* At local prefetch ≥ 5, the same raw form drove the chunk peel to 3/4/5 while the copy's chunk offset
  stayed 2 — extra unrolled drain steps and a raised short-arm threshold for a pipeline depth that does
  not exist. With this function the peel stays 2.

**Two claims the docstring explicitly refuses to make**, and a future maintainer should refuse them
too:

* *"the new form is a closed-form rewrite of the old line."* Three different denominators were in
  play: the peel used the maximum reduction-inner extent, `emit` used the reduction rate mode's
  extent, and `chunk_reach` uses the innermost reduction-inner extent. They coincide on 100% of the
  shipping matrix but differ in **form** on 47% of it, so the equality is a measured coincidence.
* *"new ≤ old always, since `dr_g ≤ dr` and ceiling is monotone."* Two ceilings with different
  denominators are not comparable that way. What *is* true is measured: over every `theta` in all
  three shipping configuration files the two agree except where the width clamp fires (69,108 of
  69,108 `_peel_depths` calls and 11,518 of 11,518 drain builds identical; 152/152 fp8 and 404/404
  MX-scaled fp8 kernels byte-identical). One unrealized **widening** case exists in principle —
  `n_s = 1`, substep extent 2, `dr = dr_g = 2` gives old 1, new 2 — which the width search pins away
  today but which nobody has excluded in general.

`S = None` derives the depth map itself via `theta.build_S`; pass `S` when you already have one,
because `build_S` is by far the most expensive call in the package.

##### 7.13.3 `copy_must_be_first(theta, op, S) -> bool`

Must this operand's shared copy be emitted **before** this trip's reads?

The copy issued in trip `iter` fills chunk `iter + off(copy, chunk)`, whose ring slot is
`(iter + off) mod S_shared`. This trip **reads** chunks `iter … iter + r`. Which relation the copy
has with those reads is decided by which of them its slot lands on:

```
off == r    the copy fills the very chunk the read-ahead crosses into      → RAW → copy FIRST
off != r    the copy's slot collides with a chunk read EARLIER in the trip
            (or with none at all)                                          → WAR → copy LAST
```

Implementation: take `r` as the max of `chunk_reach(theta, op, group_readahead_depth(...))` over the
operand's groups, and return `r >= 1 and theta.off_at(op.name, COPY, chunk) == r`.

The two shipping points both sit at `S_shared = 2, r = 1` and go **opposite** ways, which is the
whole content of the rule:

```
one global prefetch stage   off=1  slot (iter+1)%2   trip reads iter, iter+1 → the CROSSING read → first
two global prefetch stages  off=2  slot (iter+2)%2   trip reads iter, iter+1 → the CURRENT  read → last
                                   = iter%2
```

**The regression this pins.** An earlier version returned `S_shared > r`, which is `True` for both
points and therefore emitted the two-stage case copy-first: the copy then overwrote the buffer the
trip was still consuming. That is a write-after-read violation and it miscompared on hardware
wherever the steady body actually runs — reduction extent 256 for the two-stage case (peel 2), while
the one-stage case (peel 1) had already shown it at 128.

The paired tests are `test_copy_order_follows_which_chunk_the_copy_fills` (asserts `r`, the
predicate, and membership in `copy_first_operands`, over the four `(global stages, local depth)`
combinations) and `test_emitted_steady_body_puts_the_copy_where_the_predicate_says`, which asserts
the same thing on the **emitted** steady body. The second test is the one that would have caught the
regression: the predicate and the emitted order were consistent *with each other* and both wrong, so
a test of either alone passes, and only pinning the two shipping points against each other bites.

##### 7.13.4 `copy_first_operands(theta, S) -> frozenset`

`{op.name for op in theta.operands if op has a → shared hop and copy_must_be_first(theta, op, S)}`.
This is the input the issue-order refinement consumes: it decides which copies lead this trip's
reads. A one-line aggregation, but it is the seam — the refinement never calls `copy_must_be_first`
itself.

Known gap (#213): a fusion group whose members disagree about copy order is currently resolved by an
`any()` at the consumer rather than rejected. It cannot arise on the shipping parameter path (fused
members share their offsets), but it is unguarded.

##### 7.13.5 `chunk_crossing_violations(theta, S) -> [(op, dr_g, r, off_copy, required), …]`

The **shared-ring companion** to the register floor: the register floor sizes the register buffering
the read-ahead needs; this sizes the **shared** buffering it needs. A chunk `c` is copied in steady
trip `c − off(copy, chunk)`, so the copy of chunk `iter + r` precedes the read that wants it only if
it was issued in an earlier trip.

```
for each operand with a → shared hop:
    dr = off(op, READ, substep level)
    for each group:
        dr_g = group_readahead_depth(...);   r = chunk_reach(theta, op, dr_g)
        if r <= 0: continue
        need = r      if copy_must_be_first(theta, op, S)     # copy-first: same-trip fill is fine
               r + 1  otherwise                               # copy-last: needs an earlier trip
        if off(op, COPY, chunk) < need: record and break       # one report per operand
```

Returns `[]` when `theta` is emittable. Violating the coupling is not a tuning wart: the first steady
trip reads a shared buffer never written, and every later trip reads the copy issued *after* it in
the same body. The hazard ledger catches this by construction at walk time; this closed form lets the
decoder prune invalid `(dr, off(copy))` combinations up front instead.

**The conditional `+1` is the correction.** An earlier version demanded `r + 1` unconditionally, and
would have rejected the shipping one-stage point (`S_shared = 2`, `off(copy) = 1`, `r = 1`), which is
emittable and correct. The `+1` is demanded only in the copy-last case, where copy-first would
overwrite a slot the current trip still reads — it is a placement fact, not a fixed inflation of the
offset.

#### 7.14 Ring depth: `_prefetch_depth`

```
_prefetch_depth(theta, op) = theta._shared_depth(theta, op)
```

A one-line forwarder, and the docstring is emphatic about why it forwards rather than computing:
the shared ring size the copy rotates through **must** equal `theta`'s own `_shared_depth`, so that
the emitted copy slot modulus matches the depth map and the rotation write-after-read the ledger
files. Using `off` here instead would alias generations `iter` and `iter + off`.

`theta._shared_depth` reads the operand's **buffer count** (a target fact), not the prefetch depth.
The two coincide at the common double-buffered, two-stage setting, which is why deriving
`S_shared = off` passed everything until the one-stage case: there the kernel still has 2 shared
blocks while `off` is 1, a depth-1 ring has no rotation, and the decoder emitted **no** buffer swap
at all while the kernel's addressing kept alternating — so every copy overwrote the buffer being
read. `test_shared_depth_is_the_buffer_count_not_the_prefetch_depth` and `test_pgr1_emits_the_lds_swaps`
pin both sides of that coincidence.

The function survives as a name because the downstream lowering imports it
(`Lowering/loopir_to_gir.py` uses it to size a generation ring) and because `emit` calls it when
building the copy placement. It is re-exported through `decoder.py`.

#### 7.15 The peel: `PeelDepths` and `_peel_depths`

**Concept.** A pipelined loop of trip count `T` with retime depth `M` decomposes into an `M`-step
prologue, a steady region of `T − M` trips, and an `M`-step drain. The decoder needs to know `M` — and
the key correction encoded here is that **`M` is a vector, one entry per level, not an integer**.

##### 7.15.1 `class PeelDepths` (frozen dataclass)

The one source of truth for the peel construction in `emit.build_ir`.

| field | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `per_level` | `{level name: M_ℓ}` | only levels with `M_ℓ > 0`, in `ord` order (outer→inner) |
| `offs` | `{(op name, role, level): δ}` | the per-op-class offsets each `M_ℓ` is the max of — per op-class because the peel is **staggered** by each op-class's own `δ`, not by the level's max |
| `dr` | `int` | the substep read-ahead **request**, `max off(read, substep)`, kept separate because the whole read-ahead family is expressed in substeps, not chunks |
| `chunk` | `str \| None` | the reduction-chunk level's name, `None` for a `theta` with no outer level |
| `reach` | `int` | `r`, the **derived** chunk reach (`readahead_reach`) |
| `deferrals` | `{(op, role, level): δ}` | the **negative** entries, kept apart and never folded into `M_ℓ` |

`dr` versus `reach` is the distinction of section 7.8.2 surfacing at the top level: `dr` is the
request, `reach` is what the emitter actually issues, and every consumer that counts **chunks** must
read `reach`.

`deferrals` deserves its own note. The retime matrix is typed non-negative: `off` maps
(op-class × level) to a natural number and the schedule move *sets* the entry rather than subtracting
from it, so a negative `off` is ill-typed, not merely unmodelled. **Deferral still exists and needs
no negative**: it is a *positive* `off` on a **reverse-trajectory** op-class (an epilogue store),
which gets the reflected peel — trailing instances hoisted forward into the successor iteration,
prologue and drain swapped. Direction comes from the trajectory sense, not from the sign. Negative
entries are therefore **recorded rather than dropped** so that `emit._check_peel_is_emittable` can
refuse them with a real message instead of silently building something.

###### 7.15.1.1 `PeelDepths.depth(level) -> int`

`int(self.per_level.get(level, 0))`. `0` means that level needs no peel.

###### 7.15.1.2 `PeelDepths.M` (property) -> int

`self.depth(self.chunk)` — the depth **at the reduction chunk**, the one level `emit.build_ir` can
currently emit a peel region for. A coarser outer level's peel needs a loop construct that does not
exist yet (#113).

###### 7.15.1.3 `PeelDepths.peeled_levels() -> list`

`list(self.per_level)` — every level that *wants* a peel, outer→inner. More than one entry means the
`theta` asks for a nested peel. This exists so that `M` and the full requirement cannot silently
disagree: a coarser level's peel is **refused**, not dropped.

###### 7.15.1.4 `PeelDepths.copy_off() -> dict`

`{op name: δ}` for the **copy** op-classes at the reduction chunk. This is the staggered-peel input
`emit.build_ir` walks: copy `p` is present in ramp step `t` iff `off_p >= M − t`, and in drain step
`t` iff `off_p <= M − 1 − t`. `test_per_op_class_peel_offsets_stay_staggered` pins that two operands
with different global prefetch depths keep their own `δ` while `M` is the max.

##### 7.15.2 `_peel_depths(theta) -> PeelDepths`

```
_peel_depths(theta):
    red     = theta.reduction_names()
    chunk   = theta.reduction_chunk_name()
    substep = innermost inner mode whose name is in red        # by name, degenerate or not
    offs, deferrals = {}, {}
    for op in theta.operands:
        if op.hops and trajectory_sense(op) == REVERSE:  raise ValueError(...)
        for hop in op.hops:
            for m in theta.ord:
                d = theta.off_at(op, hop.role, m.name)
                if   d > 0: offs[(op.name, hop.role, m.name)] = d
                elif d < 0: deferrals[(op.name, hop.role, m.name)] = d
    per_level = {m.name: max(δ over offs at that level) for m in theta.ord, if any}
    dr    = max(off(op, READ, substep) over shared→register reads, default 0)   # clamped ≥ 0
    reach = readahead_reach(theta) if dr else 0
    if reach and chunk is not None and reach > per_level.get(chunk, 0):
        per_level[chunk] = reach
    per_level = re-sorted into ord order
    return PeelDepths(per_level, offs, dr, chunk, reach, deferrals)
```

**`M_ℓ = max` over every op-class carrying an offset at `ℓ`** — copies *and* a slab-level read
offset, which the `(op-class, level)` key (#209) is what makes expressible at all. The defect this
replaces is named in the docstring: *a decoder that keys peel depth only on the innermost outer level
silently drops every coarser-level offset* — which is exactly what this function did when it read
`off_at(op, reduction_chunk_name())` and returned a scalar.

At the reduction chunk the substep read-ahead also contributes, converted to whole chunks. It is
added to the chunk's max rather than entered into `offs`, because it is a **reach**, not an offset at
the chunk — entering it into `offs` would make it show up in `copy_off()` and in `boundary_hoists`,
neither of which it belongs to.

**Both guards on the bump are load-bearing.** `reach and …` skips the whole clause at `dr == 0`,
where `reach` is 0 and the bump would be a no-op anyway; `chunk is not None` is the one that matters,
because `reduction_chunk_name()` returns `None` on a schedule point with no reduction chunk (every
K axis absorbed into the movement quantum, so `n_s == 1` and the chunk mode drops out of `ord`).
Without it, `per_level[None] = reach` writes a level nobody can name, `PeelDepths.peeled_levels()`
then yields `None`, and `emit.build_ir` tries to peel a loop level with no `Mode`. This is the
rendering that used to omit the guard; section 9.5.4 gives the same function again in its reference
form, and the two are now identical modulo layout.

**The reverse-trajectory refusal is deliberate and should not be softened.** Everything downstream
reads `hop.role`, which is keyed on `(src, dst)` alone and therefore cannot tell a forward read from
a store round trip's read-back leg. A reverse-trajectory op-class needs the *reflected* peel, which
is not emitted (#116) — so `_peel_depths` raises rather than silently peeling it forward, which is
what a role-keyed peel would do and what makes this a latent defect rather than a missing feature.

Every level **name** is derived from `theta` — outer levels from `theta.outer_modes()`, the substep
from the innermost reduction inner mode. There are no string literals.

`test_peel_depth_is_per_level_not_one_integer` pins the whole structure on the reference
configuration: `per_level == {"iter": 2, "K_inner": 1}`, `depth("nope") == 0`, `M == 2`,
`chunk == "iter"`, `copy_off() == {"A": 2, "B": 2}`, `dr == 1`.

#### 7.16 The cross-level boundary term

**Concept (boundary hoist).** When an op-class carries an offset at a level **outer** to its own home
level, the offset does not merely shift *which* data the instances fetch — it **relocates** the
leading `δ` instances of the inner nest across the enclosing loop's back edge, out of the current
outer iteration and into the **drain of the previous** outer iteration (equivalently, at the first
outer iteration, into the outer prologue). This is a determinate relocation: the moved instances are
exactly inner-coordinates `[0, δ)` of the current outer tile.

##### 7.16.1 `class BoundaryHoist` (frozen dataclass)

One instance of that relocation. Fields: `op` and `role` (the op-class whose instances relocate),
`level` (the outer level whose offset does the hoisting), `home` (the op-class's own emission level,
strictly inner to `level`), `delta` (how many leading inner-nest instances move) and `coords` (those
instances, as concrete presence-coordinate dicts in `ord` order).

##### 7.16.2 `_leading_inner_coords(home, delta) -> tuple`

`tuple({home: i} for i in range(max(0, delta)))` — the relocated instances. The inner coordinate is
the **home** level's own index, because that is the level whose instances the outer offset relocates,
so the set is simply its leading `δ` values.

##### 7.16.3 `boundary_hoists(theta, pd) -> [BoundaryHoist, …]`

Walks `pd.offs` and applies three conditions, all necessary, returning the survivors sorted by
(level position in `ord`, op name, role):

1. **`level` is an OUTER level.** Only an outer (runtime-trip) level has the prologue/drain region
   the instances relocate *into*. An offset at an inner, statically-unrolled level crosses no
   boundary — the inner nest has no back edge. That case is the ordinary substep read-ahead, whose
   reach into the next chunk is already modelled by `chunk_reach` and `readahead_prologue` and whose
   "peel" is absorbed into the unroll.
2. **`home` is strictly INNER to `level` in `ord` order.** `home == level` is the ordinary staggered
   peel (a copy prefetching its own chunk level), not a relocation.
3. **`home` is itself an OUTER (looped) level.** This is the discriminator, and it is the condition
   the first implementation omitted.

Condition 3 is worth spelling out because cases 1–2 alone do not separate the two shapes:

* **home OUTER** — an offset at a coarser outer level whose op-class's home is the *enclosed* loop.
  The op-class has a whole enclosed iteration space per outer trip, and `δ` of those iterations'
  instances move into the previous trip's drain. That is the next-tile prefetch of a persistent /
  grid-stride loop: a genuine relocation.
* **home INNER** — a copy whose chunk offset is set and whose home is its *region* mode (a
  region-split copy, home unrolled). The op-class has a fixed unrolled fan per trip and every member
  of it stays in the trip; `δ` shifts which **chunk** the instances fetch, not which trip they are
  issued in. That is ordinary global prefetch.

Without condition 3, `boundary_hoists` flagged **every shipping region-split kernel** and refused to
emit them. `test_region_split_copy_is_NOT_a_cross_level_boundary_term` is the regression: it builds a
region-split configuration, asserts the precondition that makes it *look* like a boundary term
(`op_class_level(th, A, COPY) == "M_split" != reduction_chunk_name()`), asserts the verdict is `[]`,
and then emits the kernel.

**It is empty for every `theta` the parameter path builds today.** `translate` sets a copy offset at
the chunk (home = the chunk itself, or a region mode that is inner and unrolled) and a read offset at
an inner level. It becomes non-empty the moment a coarser outer level exists — the persistent /
grid-stride tile loop, #113. The positive-side tests build such a `theta` by mutation
(`_theta_with_persistent_level`, which prepends a `Mode("gtile")` to `ord` and sets
`off[("A", COPY, "gtile")]`), because no parameter expresses one yet. They assert:

* `pd.depth("gtile") == 1` and `pd.peeled_levels()` names all three levels — so the peel *vector* is
  what records the coarser request;
* exactly one hoist, with `(op, level, home, delta) == ("A", "gtile", "iter", 1)` and
  `coords == ({"iter": 0},)`;
* `emit_mainloop` raises `NotImplementedError` — the term is **refused, not dropped**.

That last assertion is the point of the whole mechanism. Silently dropping the coarser offset would
produce a schedule that ignores it and still reports an empty hazard ledger — the one failure mode
the certificate exists to rule out. `test_a_deeper_coarser_off_relocates_proportionally_many_instances`
adds that `delta` is the offset itself, not 1.

#### 7.17 Complexity, cost, and where to optimize

Let `A` = number of operands (2–4: `A`, `B`, and up to two scale operands), `G` = register groups per
fragment (1–2), `I` = inner modes (3–6), `L` = levels in `ord` (4–7), and `n_pres` = the product of
presence extents (2–16 on shipping shapes; the prologue enumerates a subset of it).

| function | cost | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `_ord_strides`, `_presence`, `_rate_modes`, `_broadcast_fan`, `_free_siblings`, `_has_values` | `O(I)` | called very often, uncached |
| `_rate_slot`, `_shifted_rate_slot` | `O(I)` | build a small `Expr` |
| `group_readahead_depth` | `O(I)` | plus one depth-map lookup |
| `_readahead_depth`, `_readahead_shift` | `O(G·I)` | |
| `readahead_prologue` | `O(G · n_prologue)` where `n_prologue ≤ n_s · Π extent(INNER ∩ pres)` | the only combinatorial one; ≤ a few dozen dicts in practice |
| `chunk_reach` | `O(I)` | |
| `readahead_reach` | `O(A·G·I)` **plus a full `build_S` when `S` is omitted** | the `S=None` path is the expensive one |
| `copy_must_be_first`, `chunk_crossing_violations` | `O(A·G·I)` | each calls `chunk_reach` per group |
| `_peel_depths` | `O(A·hops·L)` plus one `readahead_reach` | |
| `boundary_hoists` | `O(\|offs\| · L)` | `offs` has ≤ 6 entries |

Nothing here is a bottleneck: a whole kernel decodes in single-digit milliseconds and the dominant
cost in the package is `theta.build_S`'s width search, not this module. The decode result is cached
per kernel name by `KernelWriter._loopModelTheta` precisely because two consumers run at different
times.

**If you nevertheless want it faster**, in descending order of value:

1. **Cache `_presence`.** It is the hottest pure function and is called transitively by almost
   everything else. `theta` is a frozen dataclass, so `functools.lru_cache` on `(id(theta), op.name)`
   works, but prefer an explicit per-decode memo dict threaded through, because `id()` reuse after
   garbage collection is a real hazard and this package has been bitten by `id()`-keyed maps before.
2. **Compute the per-`(op, group)` read-ahead facts once per decode** — `dr_g`, `shift`, `strides`,
   `n_pres`, the reload set — into a small immutable record, and have `readahead_prologue`,
   `_readahead_depth`, `_read_placement`, `chunk_reach`, `copy_must_be_first`,
   `chunk_crossing_violations` and `emit._read_groups` read *that*. This is the natural next step of
   the same "one derivation" discipline the module already follows: today those seven call sites each
   recompute the chain from `theta`. The record is also the right place to hang the currently-implicit
   invariant `bool(shift) == bool(prologue)`.
3. **Pass `S` everywhere.** The `S=None` branches of `readahead_reach` and `readahead_prologue` each
   trigger or approximate a `build_S`; the reach one is an outright `build_S` call inside
   `_peel_depths`, which is itself called several times per decode. Threading the already-built `S`
   through `_peel_depths` would remove the single largest avoidable cost in this file.

#### 7.18 Weaknesses, sharp edges and dead code

Named honestly, because naming them is the point:

* **`_ = None` at module scope** (just above `resolve_quantum`) is dead. It exists only to give the
  preceding 25-line comment block — the record of four rejected attempts to *derive* the movement
  quantum inside the core — a statement to attach to. Harmless, but it will confuse a reader and a
  linter; the comment would be better as a module-level string constant or moved into
  `resolve_quantum`'s docstring.
* **`_sibling_outer_to_reduction` consults group 0** for the reduction rate mode
  (`op.fragment.groups()[0]`), and so does `_readahead_shift` and section 8's `_read_placement`. Every
  reachable fragment has one reduction axis shared by all groups, so this is correct today; it is a
  silent assumption that a genuinely heterogeneous multi-group fragment (#118) would violate.
* **`_readahead_shift` still advances along a single reduction axis.** `_shifted_rate_slot` was
  generalized to recombine every rate mode's digit (#254), but the *advance* is still
  `factor · stride(one reduction rate mode)`. A group with two genuinely non-degenerate reduction
  rate modes would need a mixed-radix advance. No shipping configuration has one — the two-axis
  rotation ships with one of the two axes degenerate — but the asymmetry between the slot (general)
  and the advance (single-axis) is a real latent gap.
* **`_shifted_coord` takes `n_pres` and ignores it.** Contract convenience, not a bug.
* **`readahead_prologue(S=None)` silently primes at the request.** Correct only for a
  uniformly-Shape-A operand. Production callers all pass `S`; a new caller that forgets will
  reintroduce the prologue/steady mixture with no error.
* **`chunk_reach`'s `fan` factor is vacuous in the reachable domain** (section 7.13) — a reviewer
  will be tempted to delete it and every parameter-derived test will agree. Do not.
* **`copy_first_operands` cannot express disagreement inside a fusion group** (#213).
* **`_peel_depths` raises for any reverse-trajectory op-class**, so the whole epilogue/store side of
  the model is unreachable (#116). That is deliberate refusal, not an oversight, but it means no test
  in this file exercises the `store` branch of `op_class_level`.
* **`boundary_hoists` is dead on the parameter path** — always `[]` — and its positive tests build
  `theta` by dataclass mutation. It is exercised, but only synthetically, so the *shape* of a real
  persistent-level `theta` (#113) has never been checked against it.
* **`readahead_reach`'s one unrealized widening case** (`n_s = 1`, substep extent 2, `dr = 2`) is
  documented and unexcluded.

All of these live in `Tensile/Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py`, the main test file for the decoder
(`test_gir.py` and `gir_fixtures.py` also import `LoopModel`). `placement.py` is its most-tested
target (20 direct references). Grouped
by what they pin:

Two patterns in this suite are worth copying when adding a test here. First, **an independent
oracle** (`_name_space_walk`) rather than a second call into the code under test. Second, **pinning
two configurations against each other** — the copy-order pair — because a predicate and its consumer
can be mutually consistent and both wrong.

### 8. `placement.py` (continued) — peel depths, wrap lead and the rings

#### 8.1 What this half of the module owns

`placement.py` is the package's largest pure-derivation module, and this report treats it in three
sections. **Section 7.0 carries the canonical family-by-family split, with the primary treatment
marked for each family; that table governs, and this subsection only expands the four families this
section is primary for.** Section 7 is the catalogue — every name, with a short reference entry, in
source order. Section 9 is the reach-and-admissibility deep dive. This section is the time-structure
deep dive, and it is the primary treatment of four things:

1. **The peel depth vector.** How many straight-line copies of the loop body have to be emitted
   before the steady region (the *prologue*) and after it (the *drain*), per loop level. Owned by
   `placement.py:PeelDepths` and `placement.py:_peel_depths`.
2. **The cross-level boundary term.** What it means for an op-class to carry a retime offset at a
   level *outer* to the level it is emitted at, why that is a *relocation of instances across a
   loop back edge* rather than an ordinary prefetch, and why the decoder currently refuses it.
   Owned by `placement.py:BoundaryHoist`, `placement.py:_leading_inner_coords` and
   `placement.py:boundary_hoists`.
3. **The two rotating rings** — the shared/LDS ring that turns once per reduction chunk, and the
   register ring that turns inside the unrolled body — and the single rule `slot = coordinate mod
   S` that both obey with different coordinates and different moduli. The vocabulary is fixed in
   section 1.8; this section gives the mechanics, the failure modes, and the way the peel depth and
   the ring depth are *different numbers that coincide on the shipping configuration*.
4. **The read-ahead prologue**, the closed-form set of register reads that must be issued before
   the steady body so that a read running `d` substeps ahead of its consumer has something to read.
   Owned by `placement.py:_group_value_range` and `placement.py:readahead_prologue` (with its two
   nested helpers).

Along the way this section explains one derivation that lives *outside* `LoopModel` but is a direct
consumer of `PeelDepths.M`: the **TDM wrap lead** in `gir_to_rocisa.py:GirToRocisa._wrap_lead`. It
is documented here because it is the sharpest illustration of why `M` has to be the schedule's own
number and not a number calibrated against the code generator, and because the historical defect it
encodes — *the single-buffered prefetch case is degenerate, so a rule fitted to it generalises
wrongly* — recurs three separate times in this module.
