Nothing in this section is address-aware. Every quantity below is an integer count of loop
iterations, buffer slots, or traversal steps.

#### 8.2 The peel: what it is and why the depth is a vector

##### 8.2.1 The decomposition, from first principles

Take a loop of trip count `T` over the reduction chunk axis, whose body contains two op-classes: a
bulk copy `c` that stages one chunk of an operand from global memory into shared memory, and a read
`r` that pulls that chunk from shared memory into registers for the matmul. If both run in the same
iteration, the read waits on the copy and the pipeline has no overlap at all.

Retiming (section 1.6) fixes that. Setting `off(c, chunk) = δ` means: *the copy instance belonging
to chunk `i` is issued during iteration `i − δ`*. The loop body now issues the copy for a chunk `δ`
iterations in the future, and reads the chunk that was copied `δ` iterations ago. That is the whole
of software pipelining, expressed as one integer.

The cost is that the loop no longer starts and ends cleanly:

* Iterations `−δ … −1` do not exist, but their copies do — the copies for chunks `0 … δ−1` have to
  be issued *before* the loop. That block of `δ` straight-line steps is the **prologue** (the source
  also calls it the *ramp*).
* Symmetrically, the last `δ` iterations would issue copies for chunks `T … T+δ−1`, which are out of
  range. Those iterations must run with the copy removed, and they cannot be part of the loop body
  because the loop body is one piece of code. That block is the **drain**.
* What is left — `T − δ` iterations in which every op-class is present — is the **steady region**,
  and it is the only part that is a real loop.

The decomposition is only valid when there are enough iterations for it: `T` must exceed the peel
depth, or the prologue and the drain overlap and the "steady" region has negative length. The
emitter therefore guards the whole three-part structure with a runtime predicate `T > M` and emits a
separate, fully unpipelined arm for the other case (section 9 covers that arm; `emit.py` calls it
the *short* or *degenerate* arm). `M` is the name this package gives the peel depth.

Two refinements make the picture accurate rather than merely illustrative.

**The peel is staggered, not uniform.** Different op-classes may carry different `δ`. If `A`'s copy
has `off = 1` and `B`'s has `off = 2`, then the prologue is 2 steps deep (the max), but step 0 must
issue only `B`'s copy and step 1 must issue both. The rule the emitter uses is *`copy_p` is present
at prologue step `t` iff `off_p ≥ M − t`*, and in the drain, *iff `off_p ≤ M − 1 − t`* — deepest
first in, deepest first out. That is why `PeelDepths` keeps the per-op-class offsets alongside the
per-level maximum: the maximum sizes the region, the individual offsets populate it.

**A reverse-trajectory op-class gets the mirrored peel.** An op-class running *toward* the matmul
(a copy, a read) is hoisted *backward* in time by a positive offset — that is prefetch. An op-class
running *away* from it (an epilogue store) is hoisted *forward* — that is deferral, and its
prologue and drain swap places. The direction is read from the op-class's trajectory sense
(section 1.2), never from the sign of `off`. This matters here because `_peel_depths` refuses
outright when it sees one; see 8.2.5.

##### 8.2.2 Why the depth is a vector and not an integer

The retime matrix is indexed by (op-class, level), so *any* level can carry an offset, not just the
reduction chunk. A schedule with a persistent outer tile loop (a grid-stride level enclosing the
reduction loop, tracked as #113) can retime a copy on that outer level: fetch the *next output
tile's* first chunks while still finishing this tile. A read can carry an offset on the reduction
substep level — that is the local-prefetch read-ahead. All three are offsets; all three imply a
peel; and they are peels of *different loops*.

Collapsing them to one integer is a specific, named defect: **a decoder that keys the peel depth
only on the innermost outer level silently drops every coarser-level offset**. Silently is the
operative word. The emitted tree would be structurally well formed, the obligation ledger would walk
it and come back empty, and the certificate that is supposed to prove the schedule hazard-free would
certify a schedule that is not the one requested. That is exactly what this function used to do: it
read `off_at(op, reduction_chunk_name())` and returned an `int` (#210).

So `_peel_depths` returns a small immutable record with a per-level map, and every consumer that
wants "the depth" has to say *of which level*.

##### 8.2.3 `PeelDepths` — the record

`placement.py:PeelDepths` is a frozen dataclass with six fields. It is constructed in exactly one
place (`placement.py:_peel_depths`) and is read-only everywhere else.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `per_level` | `{level_name: int}` | `M_ℓ = max over op-classes of off(p, ℓ)`, containing **only** levels with a positive depth, in `ord` order (outer→inner). |
| `offs` | `{(op_name, role, level_name): int}` | Every strictly positive offset the schedule point carries, per op-class. This is the *staggered* input; `per_level` is its per-level max. |
| `dr` | `int` | The substep read-ahead **request**: `max over read op-classes of off(read, substep)`. Kept separate because the whole read-ahead family counts in substeps, not in whole chunks. |
| `chunk` | `str \| None` | The name of the reduction chunk level, or `None` for a hand-built schedule point that carries no outer level at all. |
| `reach` | `int` | `r`, the **derived** number of whole reduction chunks the read-ahead the emitter actually issues crosses into. Distinct from `dr`; see 8.2.6. |
| `deferrals` | `{(op_name, role, level_name): int}` | Every **negative** offset. Recorded, never folded into `per_level`, and non-empty means the emitter refuses. |

Four accessors:

* `PeelDepths.depth(level)` — `M_ℓ` for one level, `0` if that level carries no offset. A plain
  `dict.get` with an `int()` coercion. Every consumer that needs a depth goes through this rather
  than indexing `per_level`, so asking about a level with no peel is a legal question with a
  well-defined answer instead of a `KeyError`.
* `PeelDepths.M` (property) — `self.depth(self.chunk)`, the depth at the reduction chunk. This is
  *the* `M` the emitter peels, because the reduction chunk is the only level whose prologue/drain
  region the emitter can currently build. It is deliberately a narrow accessor rather than the whole
  story, and it sits next to `peeled_levels()` so that the two cannot silently disagree.
* `PeelDepths.peeled_levels()` — the list of every level with `M_ℓ > 0`, outer→inner. More than one
  entry means the schedule point *wants* a nested peel. `emit._check_peel_is_emittable` compares
  this list — *filtered to the OUTER levels* — against `{chunk}` and raises `NotImplementedError` when
that filtered set is non-empty (an inner, statically-unrolled level never triggers it), naming the extra
  levels and their depths in the message. The pairing of a narrow `M` with a wide
  `peeled_levels()` is the structural device that converts the old silent drop into a loud refusal.
* `PeelDepths.copy_off()` — `{op_name: δ}` filtered to `role == COPY and level == chunk`. This is
  the staggered-peel input the emitter walks: at prologue step `t` it emits `copy_p` iff
  `off_p ≥ M − t`; at drain step `t` iff `off_p ≤ M − 1 − t`.

The `copy_off()` filter is worth reading as a statement of a limitation rather than a convenience.
Because it selects `role == COPY`, a **read** offset sitting at an outer level contributes to
`M_ℓ` (so the guard predicate, the prologue length, the steady bound and the drain step count all
move) but is applied to nothing: every read instruction keeps its unshifted slot. That is a
half-application — neither the requested schedule nor a refusal — and it is caught by an explicit
check in `emit._check_peel_is_emittable` rather than here, for a reason given in 8.3.4.

##### 8.2.4 `_peel_depths` — the algorithm

```
_peel_depths(theta) -> PeelDepths:
    red      = theta.reduction_names()                 # {names of reduction modes}
    chunk    = theta.reduction_chunk_name()            # the outer reduction level, or None
    substep  = innermost inner mode whose name is in red      # or None

    offs, deferrals = {}, {}
    for op in theta.operands:
        if op.hops and trajectory_sense(op) is REVERSE:
            raise ValueError(...)                      # see 8.2.5
        for hop in op.hops:
            for m in theta.ord:                        # EVERY level, outer -> inner
                d = theta.off_at(op, hop.role, m.name)
                if d > 0:   offs[(op.name, hop.role, m.name)] = d
                elif d < 0: deferrals[(op.name, hop.role, m.name)] = d

    per_level = {}
    for m in theta.ord:                                # ord order preserved by insertion
        vals = [d for (_, _, lvl), d in offs.items() if lvl == m.name]
        if vals: per_level[m.name] = max(vals)

    dr    = max(off_at(op, READ, substep) for op in shared->register read op-classes)
    dr    = max(0, dr)
    reach = readahead_reach(theta) if dr else 0        # DERIVED, not ceil(dr / n_substeps)
    if reach and chunk and reach > per_level.get(chunk, 0):
        per_level[chunk] = reach
    per_level = reorder per_level into ord order       # the chunk bump can break insertion order

    return PeelDepths(per_level, offs, dr, chunk, reach, deferrals)
```

Three details in that sketch are load-bearing.

*The level names are derived, never spelled.* `chunk` comes from `Theta.reduction_chunk_name` and
`substep` from the innermost reduction inner mode. Every other consumer of "which level is the
chunk" — `theta._shared_depth`, `placement._read_placement`, `emit.build_ir`'s `outer_var` — goes
through the same accessor, so the peel depth, the shared ring depth and the emitted loop axis cannot
key off different levels. A literal `"iter"` anywhere in this chain would reintroduce that
possibility.

*The iteration is over `theta.ord`, i.e. every level.* Both outer (looped) and inner (unrolled)
levels are scanned. An inner level's `M_ℓ` is real and is recorded — `off(read, substep)` gives the
substep level one — but it needs no prologue/drain *region*, because an inner level is statically
unrolled and its peel is absorbed into the unroll. The read-ahead family realises it instead
(8.6). The scoping to outer levels happens at the consumer, in
`emit._check_peel_is_emittable`, not here; `_peel_depths` reports what the schedule point says.

*The final reordering pass is not cosmetic.* `per_level` is built by insertion in `ord` order, but
the `reach` bump can raise the chunk's entry after the fact, and if the chunk had no entry before
the bump it would be appended last — out of order. `peeled_levels()` promises outer→inner, and at
least one consumer (`emit`'s refusal message, and any future nested-peel builder) depends on that
ordering to know which level encloses which. The rebuild costs one pass over `theta.ord`.

##### 8.2.5 Two refusals inside a derivation function

`_peel_depths` is a pure derivation and yet it raises. Both raises are deliberate and both encode a
defect that was previously silent.

**Reverse trajectory.** The loop over operands starts by testing `trajectory_sense(op) == REVERSE`
and raising `ValueError` with the operand's hop chain in the message. The reason is a *role/sense
mismatch* that would otherwise look correct. A hop's role is derived from its `(src, dst)` spaces
alone, so in an epilogue store round trip `register → shared → register → global`, the middle leg
is classified `read` — identical in role to a main-loop operand read, and opposite in trajectory.
Everything downstream of this function keys on the role. So a reverse-trajectory op-class would be
given the *forward* peel: prefetched backward when it should be deferred forward, prologue and
drain the wrong way round. Refusing here converts a latent miscompile into a missing feature with a
message that says which feature (#116, the unmodelled epilogue; #212, the per-hop/per-op-class
distinction that made the test expressible).

**Negative offsets.** The retime matrix is typed non-negative: `off : (op-class × level) → ℕ`, and
the `retime` schedule move *sets* the entry rather than subtracting from it, so no legal move can
reach a negative value. A negative entry is therefore *ill-typed*, not merely unmodelled. The
temptation is to read a negative offset as "defer by |δ|", and the reason that is wrong is the
point of 8.2.1's second refinement: deferral is a *positive* offset on a *reverse-trajectory*
op-class, and the direction comes from the trajectory sense. If negatives were allowed to mean
deferral, the model would have two encodings of one fact and they would drift.

`_peel_depths` does not raise on a negative — it *records* it in `deferrals` and leaves
`per_level` untouched — so that the error can be reported with the full list of offending entries.
`emit._check_peel_is_emittable` raises `ValueError` with a message containing "negative off is
ill-typed" when `deferrals` is non-empty. The split exists so that a caller doing analysis (the
renderer, a future search) can inspect a malformed schedule point without an exception.

The contract is pinned by `test_loopmodel.py:test_a_negative_off_is_rejected_as_ill_typed`, which
mutates a valid schedule point's `off_map` to put `off(A:read, iter) = −1`, then asserts three
things: the entry lands in `deferrals` and nowhere else; `depth("iter")` is still `2`, i.e. a
negative offset does not perturb `M_ℓ`; and every value in `offs` is strictly positive. Only then
does it assert the emitter's raise. The test's own docstring notes that it deliberately puts the
deferral on an existing read op-class rather than building a store, because the store's
`register → global` hop has no completion class yet — the test is about the *sign*, not about
stores.

##### 8.2.6 The reach bump: the request is not the realisation

The last thing `_peel_depths` does before returning is raise the chunk's depth to `reach` if
`reach` is larger. This is the one place where a *substep-level* quantity influences a *chunk-level*
peel, and getting it wrong cost eight silently dropped local reads.

The mechanism: a read carrying `off(read, substep) = dr` fetches the register value it will need
`dr` substeps in the future. Near the end of a chunk's substeps there is no "future" left inside the
chunk, so the read reaches into the *next* chunk's data. How many whole chunks it crosses into is
`r`, computed by `placement.py:chunk_reach` per group and enveloped over groups by
`placement.py:readahead_reach` (both covered in the previous section). If the read-ahead reaches `r`
chunks forward, the loop's drain must be at least `r` steps deep — otherwise the last steady
iteration issues reads for chunks that no drain step ever consumes, or worse, consumes chunk data
that no step ever loaded.

So `reach` participates in `M`. It is a *reach*, not an offset at the chunk, which is why it is
folded into `per_level[chunk]` by a max rather than entered into `offs`: `offs` is the staggered
input, and there is no copy op-class whose stagger position this quantity describes.

The defect this shape replaces (#284) is that the bump used to be `ceil(dr / n_substeps)` computed
from the raw **request** `dr`. The request and the realisation differ whenever the register width
band clamps a group: the actually-issued advance is `dr_g = max(0, min(dr, W_g − 1))`, zeroed
outright by two structural vetoes. A request deeper than the rotation can hold reaches no further
than the rotation does. Two consumers were reading the request:

* the chunk-level peel here, which grew `M` to 3, 4 and 5 at local-prefetch depths of 5, 8 and 10
  while the copy's own offset stayed at 2 — extra unrolled drain steps, and a raised `T > M`
  threshold, for a pipeline depth that does not exist;
* the drain's read-ahead suppression window in `emit`, which at local-prefetch depth 3 widened from
  1 step to 2 and therefore guarded away the read-ahead reads that the *last* drain step's leading
  matmuls consume. Measured on a bf16 NT kernel with a 16×16×32 matmul instruction, a 2×2 wave tile
  and `DepthU` 64: 62 emitted `ds_read`s at prefetch depths 1 and 2, **54** at depth 3, against an
  unchanged 36 matmuls — eight local reads gone, with an empty obligation ledger and no warning.

Both now read `PeelDepths.reach`, which is derived from `readahead_reach`, which runs the clamp per
group before converting to chunks. `PeelDepths.dr` stays the raw request because its other
consumers (`readahead_prologue`, `_readahead_shift`) each derive their own per-group depth from it;
only the *chunk count* has to be pre-derived, and pre-deriving it once here is what stops the two
chunk-counting consumers from disagreeing.

There is an honest caveat, recorded in `readahead_reach`'s docstring and worth repeating: the new
form is **not** a closed-form rewrite of the old one. Three different denominators are in play (the
max reduction-inner extent, the rate-mode extent, and the innermost reduction-inner extent), and
they coincide on 100% of the shipping configuration matrix but differ in *form* on 47% of it. Nor
is "new ≤ old, since `dr_g ≤ dr` and `ceil` is monotone" a proof — two ceilings with different
denominators are not comparable that way. What is established is measurement: across every schedule
point in all three shipping kernel configurations the two agree except where the width band clamps
(69,108 of 69,108 `_peel_depths` calls and 11,518 of 11,518 drain builds identical; 152 of 152 fp8
and 404 of 404 MX-fp8 kernels byte-identical). One *widening* case exists in principle —
`n_s = 1, s_sub = 2, dr = dr_g = 2` gives old 1, new 2 — which the width derivation pins away in
every logged case but which nobody has excluded in general. A future developer who changes the
substep factorisation should re-run that comparison rather than assume it still holds.

##### 8.2.7 Who consumes `PeelDepths`, and what each takes

| Consumer | Reads | Uses it for |
|---|---|---|
| `emit._check_peel_is_emittable` | `peeled_levels()`, `depth()`, `offs`, `deferrals` | Four refusals: extra outer peel level; read offset at an outer level; cross-level boundary term; negative offset. |
| `emit.build_ir` | `copy_off()`, `dr`, `M` | The prologue's `M` straight-line steps with staggered copies; the steady loop bound `iter < T − M`; the drain's `M` steps with the mirrored stagger; the `T > M` guard predicate; the drain's `Bind(iter = T − M + t)`. |
| `emit`'s drain builder | `reach` | The read-ahead suppression window: at drain step `t`, suppress the read-ahead iff `t ≥ M − max(1, reach)`. |
| `ledger.build_ledger` | `dr` (via `_peel_depths(theta).dr`) | Feeds `readahead_prologue` to enumerate the read-ahead residency obligations. |
| `render.render_geometry` | `dr` only | The read-ahead depth request it hands to `group_readahead_depth` for the per-group read-mode column of the derived-geometry dump. It surfaces no other field of the record — not the peel vector, not `reach`. |
| `Lowering/loopir_to_gir.py` | `copy_off()`, `dr`, `M` | Re-derives the same three quantities when lowering the tree to the SSA form, from the same function, so the two cannot disagree. |

The last row is the reason `_peel_depths` is exported through `decoder.py`'s re-export shim despite
the leading underscore: the lowering needs the *same* numbers the emitter used, and importing the
one function is strictly safer than recomputing them.

##### 8.2.8 The peel contract, as the tests state it

Two unit tests in `Tensile/Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py` pin the record's shape, and both are
regression tests for the collapse described in 8.2.2.

`test_peel_depth_is_per_level_not_one_integer` builds a schedule point from a bf16 parameter dict
(16×16×32 matmul instruction, 2×2 wave tile, `DepthU` 64, 2-byte elements, `KMN` loop order, global
prefetch 2, local prefetch 1) and asserts the whole record at once:

```
pd.per_level == {"iter": 2, "K_inner": 1}     # BOTH levels carrying an offset
pd.depth("iter") == 2 and pd.depth("K_inner") == 1 and pd.depth("nope") == 0
pd.M == 2 and pd.chunk == "iter"
pd.copy_off() == {"A": 2, "B": 2}
pd.dr == 1
```

The `depth("nope") == 0` clause is the accessor's total-function property: an unknown level is a
legal question. The presence of `"K_inner": 1` beside `M == 2` is the vector property: the inner
level's depth is *recorded* even though `build_ir` peels only the chunk.

`test_per_op_class_peel_offsets_stay_staggered` sets a per-operand global prefetch depth (`A` at 1,
`B` at 2) and asserts `copy_off() == {"A": 1, "B": 2}` alongside `M == 2`. One line each for the two
halves of the staggered peel: the level's max sizes the region, each op-class keeps its own depth.
Without the per-op-class map, `A`'s copy would be emitted at prologue step 0 (one step too early,
harmless) or `B`'s at step 1 (one step too late, and it lands *after* the step that reads it).

A third test lives with the emitter but belongs to the same contract:
`test_degenerate_arm_resets_off_at_and_inside_the_peeled_level` pins that the `T ≤ M` arm resets
every offset at and inside the peeled level to zero, so that the short arm is `T` unpipelined
iterations, each of which copies and reads its own chunk. This is the reflection of the peel rule:
a fully-peeled level has no pipeline left to run.

#### 8.3 The cross-level boundary term

##### 8.3.1 The concept

Every op-class has a **home level**: the loop level at which its instruction is emitted, i.e. the
innermost level whose iteration index the instruction varies over. `placement.py:op_class_level`
computes it (previous section): the innermost presence mode for a read, the region mode for a
region-split copy or the reduction chunk for a coarse one, and the reduction chunk as the fallback
when the presence set is empty.

An op-class's offset normally sits *at its own home level*. `off(copy, chunk) = 2` on a copy whose
home is the chunk means "this copy runs two iterations of its own loop ahead" — ordinary prefetch,
handled entirely by the staggered peel of 8.2.

Now consider an offset at a level **outer** to the op-class's home. Suppose there is a persistent
outer loop over output tiles (`gtile`) enclosing the reduction loop (`iter`), and the copy — whose
home is `iter` — carries `off(copy, gtile) = δ`. What does that mean? The copy has a whole *enclosed
iteration space* per `gtile` trip: `T` instances, one per reduction chunk. Retiming it on `gtile`
says the leading `δ` of those instances belong to the *previous* `gtile` trip. They must be emitted
in the previous outer iteration's drain (or, on the very first outer iteration, in the outer
prologue).

That is a **determinate relocation of a specific, enumerable set of instances across a loop back
edge**, and it is qualitatively different from prefetch. Prefetch changes *which data* an instance
of a loop body touches, and every instance stays in its iteration. A boundary hoist changes *which
iteration* an instance is issued in, and the instances that move are exactly `[home-coord 0 .. δ)`
of the current outer tile. This report calls it the **cross-level boundary term**.

##### 8.3.2 `BoundaryHoist` — the record

`placement.py:BoundaryHoist` is a frozen dataclass carrying one such relocation:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `op` | The operand name whose instances relocate. |
| `role` | Which hop of that operand (`copy`, `read`, `store`) — the op-class key's second component. |
| `level` | `ℓ_outer`, the level whose offset does the hoisting. Must be an *outer* (runtime-trip) level: the relocation target is "the drain of the previous `ℓ_outer` iteration", and only a looped level has a prologue/drain region to relocate into. |
| `home` | The op-class's own emission level, strictly inner to `level`. `home == level` is the ordinary staggered peel, not a relocation. |
| `delta` | δ, how many leading inner-nest instances move. |
| `coords` | Those instances, as a tuple of concrete coordinate dicts in `ord` order. |

`placement.py:_leading_inner_coords(home, delta)` builds the `coords` tuple and is the module's most
trivial helper: `tuple({home: i} for i in range(max(0, delta)))`. The relocated instances are
enumerated by the *home* level's own index, because the home level is precisely the level whose
instances the outer offset relocates; so the set is its leading δ values, `{home: 0} … {home: δ−1}`.
The `max(0, delta)` guard makes a non-positive δ produce an empty tuple rather than raising, which
matters only for defensive callers since `boundary_hoists` only ever passes entries drawn from
`PeelDepths.offs` (all strictly positive).

The coords are materialised rather than left as a range because the eventual emitter for this
construct has to *place* those instances, and placing them means binding a concrete coordinate. Two
tests pin exactly this: one asserts `h.coords == ({"iter": 0},)` at δ = 1, the other
`({"iter": 0}, {"iter": 1}, {"iter": 2})` at δ = 3 — "δ instances relocate, not one; the count is
`off(p, ℓ_outer)` itself".

##### 8.3.3 `boundary_hoists` — three conditions, all necessary

```
boundary_hoists(theta, pd) -> [BoundaryHoist]:
    names = [m.name for m in theta.ord]          # outer -> inner
    outer = {m.name for m in theta.outer_modes()}
    out = []
    for (opname, role, level), delta in pd.offs.items():
        if level not in outer:            continue   # (1)
        home = op_class_level(theta, theta.op(opname), role)
        if home is None or home not in names: continue
        if names.index(home) <= names.index(level): continue   # (2)
        if home not in outer:             continue   # (3)
        out.append(BoundaryHoist(op, role, level, home, delta,
                                 _leading_inner_coords(home, delta)))
    return sorted(out, key=(ord-position of level, op, role))
```

**Condition 1 — `level` must be an outer level.** The relocation target is a prologue/drain region,
and only a looped level has one. An offset at an inner (statically unrolled) level crosses no
boundary: the inner nest has no back edge, so there is nothing to cross. That case is the ordinary
substep read-ahead, whose reach into the next chunk is modelled by `chunk_reach` and whose "peel" is
absorbed into the unroll and realised by `readahead_prologue`.
`test_an_inner_level_off_is_not_a_boundary_term` pins both halves of this: `depth("K_inner") == 1`
(the inner level's `M_ℓ` *is* recorded) and `boundary_hoists(...) == []` (but it is not a
relocation), followed by a successful `emit_mainloop`.

**Condition 2 — `home` must be strictly inner to `level` in `ord` order.** `home == level` is the
ordinary staggered peel — a copy prefetching on its own chunk axis. A home *outer* to the offset's
level is not expressible by any move and does not arise; the index comparison rejects it anyway.

**Condition 3 — `home` must itself be an outer (looped) level.** This is the discriminator, and it
is the one that took a regression to find. Under conditions 1 and 2 alone, two structurally
identical situations are conflated:

* *home outer* — `off(copy, gtile)` with home `iter`. The op-class has a whole enclosed **iteration
  space** per outer trip, and δ of those iterations' instances move into the previous trip's drain.
  A relocation.
* *home inner* — `off(copy, iter)` for a **region-split** copy, whose home is the region mode
  `M_split`, an inner unrolled axis. The op-class has a fixed unrolled fan per trip and every member
  of that fan stays in the trip; δ shifts which *chunk* the instances fetch, not which trip they are
  issued in. That is ordinary global prefetch.

The second bullet is not hypothetical: it is every shipping region-split kernel. The first
implementation of `boundary_hoists` omitted condition 3 and therefore reported a boundary term for
all of them, and since the emitter refuses on a non-empty hoist list, it refused to emit them.
`test_region_split_copy_is_NOT_a_cross_level_boundary_term` is the regression, and it is written to
be non-vacuous: it asserts `A.split > 1` ("fixture must actually be region-split for this test to
mean anything"), then asserts the *precondition that makes it look like a boundary term*
(`op_class_level(th, A, COPY) == "M_split" != th.reduction_chunk_name()`), then the verdict
(`boundary_hoists(...) == []`), then that `emit_mainloop` still succeeds. Reading only the verdict
line would not tell you the test could still pass if the fixture stopped being split.

The result is sorted by (ord position of `level`, op name, role) so the output is deterministic and
outer levels come first — the order in which a future nested-peel builder would have to process
them.

The canonical positive case has no parameter-path fixture, because no TensileLite parameter
expresses a persistent level yet. `test_loopmodel.py:_theta_with_persistent_level` builds one by
mutation: it takes a normal bf16 schedule point, adds `off[("A", COPY, "gtile")] = δ` to the retime
map, and prepends `Mode("gtile")` to `ord` via `dataclasses.replace`. The test then asserts
`depth("gtile") == 1`, `depth("iter") == 2`, `peeled_levels() == ["gtile", "iter", "K_inner"]`,
exactly one hoist with `(op, level, home, delta) == ("A", "gtile", "iter", 1)`, and finally that
`emit_mainloop` raises `NotImplementedError` matching `"boundary term|peel at outer level"`. Its
docstring states the point of the second half: *silently dropping it would produce a schedule that
ignores the coarser offset and still reports an empty ledger — the one failure mode the certificate
exists to rule out.*

##### 8.3.4 Why the read-at-outer-level refusal is not in this function

`emit._check_peel_is_emittable` carries a *separate* refusal for a `read` op-class holding an offset
at an outer level, and a reader might reasonably ask why it is not folded into `boundary_hoists`.
The answer is that condition 3 is load-bearing for the region-split copy and cannot be loosened.

A read whose home is the substep, carrying `off(read, iter)`, satisfies conditions 1 and 2 and fails
condition 3 — its home is an inner unrolled mode. By the definition in 8.3.1 it *is* a cross-level
boundary term. But so is the region-split copy, by exactly the same test, and that one is ordinary
prefetch on the shipping path. The distinction between them is **per role**: a copy's ordinary
prefetch level *is* the chunk, while a read's is the substep. So the narrow refusal belongs where it
can name the role, which is the emitter's check; the shared predicate keeps condition 3 and stays
conservative in the direction that does not reject live kernels.

The failure the emitter's extra check prevents is the half-application described in 8.2.3: the read
offset inflates `M_ℓ` (moving the guard, the prologue depth, the steady bound and the drain step
count) while `copy_off()`'s `role == COPY` filter means no read instruction is actually shifted. The
ledger then certifies empty over a schedule that is neither the requested one nor a refusal. It is
unreachable from the parameter path — `translate` sets only `off(copy, chunk)` and
`off(read, substep)`, each at that op-class's own home level — so this is a latent defect closed
before it could become shipping, found by a systematic audit rather than by a failure (recorded as
audit deviation D1).

##### 8.3.5 What has to happen for this to become emittable

Everything needed to *describe* a boundary hoist exists; what is missing is the enclosing loop to
relocate into. Concretely, a future developer landing the persistent/grid-stride level (#113) has
to:

1. make `emit.build_ir` recursive over `peel.peeled_levels()` instead of peeling the single chunk
   level, so each looped level gets its own prologue/steady/drain triple;
2. for each `BoundaryHoist`, emit the `coords` instances into the *enclosing* level's drain (and
   into the enclosing prologue on the first outer trip) instead of at the top of the inner nest;
3. extend the obligation ledger so the relocated producer and its unmoved consumer are still paired
   — the relocation crosses a back edge, so the residency obligation becomes loop-carried across
   the outer level, not just the inner one;
4. delete the corresponding refusal in `emit._check_peel_is_emittable`, level by level, rather than
   all at once. The refusal is written to name the levels it is refusing precisely so that it can be
   narrowed incrementally.

Nothing in `boundary_hoists` needs to change for that work; it already reports the full set.

#### 8.4 The TDM wrap lead — a downstream consumer of `M`, and the degeneracy trap

`PeelDepths.M` leaves this package and reappears in the backend, in
`Lowering/gir_to_rocisa.py:GirToRocisa._wrap_lead`. It is described here, in the peel-depth section,
because it is the clearest available demonstration of two things this module depends on: that `M`
must be *the schedule's own number*, and that the single-buffered prefetch configuration is
**degenerate** for every rule of this shape, so a rule calibrated on it generalises wrongly.

##### 8.4.1 What the wrap is

The bulk global-memory descriptor for an operand walks forward one reduction chunk at a time: after
copying chunk `c`, an increment adds one `DepthU` stride to the address. To avoid every workgroup
hammering the same memory channel at the same time, the kernel *staggers* the starting chunk: a
workgroup begins at some chunk `S ∈ [0, T)` rather than at 0, walks up to chunk `T − 1`, and then
must **wrap** back to chunk 0 and continue up to `S − 1`. Over `T` copies it visits each chunk
exactly once.

The wrap is realised inside one increment. On the wrap increment the address must move by
`inc − T·inc` (back to the tensor base) instead of by `inc`; the backend keeps that quantity in a
per-operand `WrapU` scalar pair and selects between `WrapU` and the plain stride with a compare.
The compare is against the loop counter:

```
wrap this increment  iff  LoopCounterL + lead == StaggerUIter,    StaggerUIter = S + pf
```

`pf` is a small constant the code generator adds when computing `StaggerUIter` (2 for global
prefetch depths below 3), and `lead` is the quantity `_wrap_lead` computes. The class constant
`GirToRocisa._STAGGER_PF_CONST = 2` names `pf` rather than inlining it, so that lifting the
rejection of prefetch depth ≥ 3 surfaces in one place.

Why a `lead` is needed at all: the loop counter is a single runtime register with one value per
trip, but the increments are *not* all issued in the trip whose number the counter holds. Prologue
increments run before the loop starts; a steady increment runs in a trip but advances the descriptor
to a chunk the *next* trip will copy. Each increment therefore lives in a different frame from the
counter, and `lead` is the shift that brings the compare into the frame the increment actually runs
in. Passing 0 for a peel increment puts the wrap on the wrong iteration, and the staggered address
walks off the end of the tensor.

##### 8.4.2 The derivation

The wrap must fire on the increment that takes the address from chunk `T − 1` to chunk `T`, i.e. on
increment number `n` where `S + n = T`, i.e. `S = T − n`.

Under the SSA lowering's copy-then-advance convention (each copy is followed by the increment that
moves the descriptor past it), the two phases have different frames:

* **Prologue.** Increment `#n` targets chunk `n`, and it runs before the loop, at
  `LoopCounterL = T`. It exists for `n ≤ M`. Substituting into `ctr + lead == S + pf` with
  `ctr = T` and `S = T − n`:
  `T + lead == T − n + pf`, so `lead = pf − n`.
* **Steady.** The increment in steady trip `v` is increment number `M + v + 1`, and it runs at
  `LoopCounterL = T − v`. With `n = M + v + 1` and `S = T − n`:
  `(T − v) + lead == T − (M + v + 1) + pf`, so `lead = pf − M − 1`. The `v` cancels — the steady
  lead is a **constant**, which it must be, since one instruction is emitted for all steady trips.

Writing `to_chunk` for the chunk the increment targets (`n` in the prologue, and anything greater
than `M` in the steady body), the two cases combine into one closed form:

```
lead = pf − min(to_chunk, M + 1)
```

Both inputs are the schedule's own: `to_chunk` comes from the SSA dataflow analysis that placed the
increment, and `M` is `PeelDepths.M`. Nothing is calibrated against the code generator's control
flow. `_wrap_lead` is a `classmethod` taking `(to_chunk, M)` and returning
`cls._STAGGER_PF_CONST - min(to_chunk, M + 1)`; `_emit_gr_inc` calls it once per increment and
passes the result to the backend primitive as `wrapLead`.

**A negative lead is correct, not a sign error.** At global prefetch depth 2 (`M = 2`, `pf = 2`) the
steady lead is `2 − 3 = −1`: a steady increment under copy-then-advance runs one chunk *behind* the
counter's frame, so the compare shifts the other way. The backend cannot encode a negative literal
in a scalar add, so it emits a subtract instead — which is why the emitting code has an explicit
sign branch, with the negative case commented as intentional.

##### 8.4.3 Why the single-buffered case is degenerate

Tabulate the closed form for the two shipping prefetch depths (`pf = 2`):

| | prologue, `to_chunk = 1` | prologue, `to_chunk = 2` | steady |
|---|---|---|---|
| global prefetch 1 (`M = 1`) | +1 | 0 | 0 |
| global prefetch 2 (`M = 2`) | +1 | 0 | −1 |

At `M = 1` the prologue lead and the steady lead **coincide at 0** after the first increment. The
whole steady column collapses onto a value that several unrelated rules also produce. Consequently
*any rule fitted to global prefetch 1 says nothing about global prefetch 2*.

Three calibrated rules were shipped in sequence before the closed form landed (#188):

1. `lead = M − to_chunk`;
2. `lead = 1 if phase == "prologue" else 0`;
3. `lead = 1 if to_chunk == 1 else 0`.

Each was written against the prefetch-1 configuration, each passed its prefetch-1 tests, and each
gives the prefetch-2 steady increment a lead of 0 instead of −1. That is not a small numeric error:
the wrap then fires one increment early, `WrapU` subtracts a whole tensor's worth of stride from an
address that had not yet reached the end, and the kernel reads out of bounds and segfaults.

This is the same degeneracy that bit `placement.py:copy_must_be_first` (previous section): the old
predicate `S_shared > r` is true for both prefetch depths, while the real rule is `off == r`, and
the two disagree exactly at prefetch 2. And it is the same shape as the shared-ring depth bug
recorded in `theta.py:_shared_depth`, where deriving `S_shared = δ` agrees with the operand's real
buffer count at prefetch 2 and diverges at prefetch 1. Three instances, one lesson:

> **Any rule involving the peel depth, the prefetch depth, or the counter frame must be checked
> against at least two prefetch depths, and the test must pin them against each other. A test of
> either alone passes with the wrong rule.**

`test_gir_to_rocisa.py:test_wrap_lead_is_derived_from_the_peel_depth` is parametrised over exactly
that: three `M = 1` rows and four `M = 2` rows in one table, with the docstring stating "the `M = 2`
rows are the ones with content".

##### 8.4.4 The oracle that settled it

Agreement between a formula and a test written from the same derivation proves nothing. The test
that settled the wrap lead —
`test_gir_to_rocisa.py:test_wrap_lead_makes_every_stagger_start_cover_the_chunks_exactly_once` — is
an *independent simulator*. It replays the emitted copy/advance sequence for every peel depth in
`{1, 2}`, every trip count `T` from `M + 1` to 11, and every stagger start `S ∈ [0, T)`, applying
the wrap exactly as the backend does, and requires that the copied chunks are a permutation of
`0 … T−1`:

```
chunk, copied = S, []
for i in range(T):                        # copy-then-advance
    copied.append(chunk)
    ctr  = T if i < M else T - (i - M)    # the counter's value at this advance
    lead = _wrap_lead(i + 1, M)
    wrap = (ctr + lead == S + pf)
    chunk = chunk + 1 - T if wrap else chunk + 1
assert sorted(copied) == list(range(T))
```

It consults only the formula's *output*, so a wrong rule shows up as a duplicated or out-of-range
chunk rather than as agreement with itself. Two details in that eight-line simulator were themselves
wrong on the first attempt and are worth flagging to anyone who rewrites it: the wrap shifts the
chunk by `1 − T` (the increment is `inc − T·inc`), not by `−T`; and the copy/advance order in the
steady body differs between the two lowering paths, so the simulator has to model the one the SSA
lowering emits, not the one the older code generator emits.

The general lesson for this package: **for any closed form that indexes a rotating structure, write
a simulator whose success criterion is a structural property of the whole schedule (a permutation, a
covering, a non-overlap) rather than a value comparison against the formula.** The read-ahead
prologue in 8.6 has the same character and would benefit from the same treatment; today it is
checked only against enumerated expectations.

##### 8.4.5 A neighbouring quantity that is *not* derived

`_emit_gr_inc`'s comments are careful to distinguish the wrap lead from a second small integer that
also shifts a prefetch-related compare and that is **not** derivable from the schedule. The code
generator's `StaggerUIter = S + pf` uses its own pipeline convention, and `pf` is chosen by a flat
positional rule (`1 if global prefetch < 3 else global prefetch − 1` for the prologue group, and 0
everywhere in the steady body). An earlier version computed that quantity as `M − to_chunk` with a
special case, which agrees with the code generator on every reachable configuration — but only by
coincidence, since it is chunk arithmetic dressed up as a derivation for a quantity that is not
derived from the schedule at all. The current code names it a calibration in the comment and pins it
with `test_gir_to_rocisa.py:test_prefetch_index_still_matches_the_scaffolds_own_constant`, which
reads the code generator's source and asserts the literal rule text. That is the right treatment for
a genuine calibration: make it break loudly when the thing it is calibrated against moves.

The distinction matters when reading this code: `_wrap_lead` is derived and its test is an oracle;
the neighbouring constant is calibrated and its test is a source-text pin. Do not upgrade the second
into the first without an oracle.

#### 8.5 The two rings

##### 8.5.1 One rule, two coordinates

Section 1.8 introduced the two rotating buffer sets. Their mechanics are one rule applied twice:

```
slot = coordinate mod S
```

What differs is *which coordinate advances* and *what one rotation means*.

| | shared / LDS ring | register ring |
|---|---|---|
| Rotating coordinate | the reduction chunk index | the mixed-radix index over the group's **rate modes** |
| Modulus | `S_shared`, from `theta._shared_depth` via `placement._prefetch_depth` | `W`, the group width from `theta.group_width`, stored in the depth map |
| Turns once per | outer-loop trip (a chunk) | pass through the group's rate-mode traversal inside the unrolled body |
| Depth-map key | `(op, region, "shared")` | `(op, region, group_label)` |
| Built by | `placement._read_placement`'s `src_slot` (for the reading side) and the copy's slot expression in `emit` (for the writing side) | `placement._rate_slot`, per group, inside `_read_placement` |
| A "generation" is | one chunk's worth of an operand in one buffer | one filling of one register name |

Both slots are emitted as symbolic `Expr` objects, not integers, so the tree stays rolled: one node
per op-class per level with a slot expression whose value depends on the loop coordinate. The
renderer evaluates them for a partial unroll; the backend resolves them to physical names.

##### 8.5.2 The shared ring: rotation across the outer back edge

The shared ring is the one that turns on the *trip* level. Its slot is `chunk mod S_shared`, and
`_read_placement` builds it as `Expr(var=outer_var, mod=S_shared, carry=...)` where `outer_var` is
`Theta.reduction_chunk_name()` — derived, never a literal, and the *same* accessor `_peel_depths`
and `theta._shared_depth` use, so the peel depth, the ring depth and the emitted loop axis can never
key off different levels.

`placement.py:_prefetch_depth(theta, op)` is the module's accessor for that modulus. It is a
one-line delegation to `theta._shared_depth`, and the delegation is the point: the docstring states
that it **must** equal what the depth map holds, because the emitted copy's slot modulus and the
rotation anti-dependency recorded in the obligation ledger both key on this number. Deriving it
independently here — for instance from `off` — would alias generations `iter` and `iter + off` onto
one slot and quietly overwrite live data. The function exists so that the emitter has a named,
greppable way to ask for the shared ring depth without importing a private from `theta`, and so that
any future divergence has exactly one place to happen.

What `theta._shared_depth` itself returns is worth restating here because it is a peel-adjacent trap
of the same family as 8.4.3. The depth is **the operand's own buffer count** (`op.lds_buffers`, a
target fact supplied from outside), not the retime depth `δ`. Deriving `S_shared = δ` was a real
bug: `δ` and the buffer count coincide at the common double-buffered global-prefetch-2 setting, so
every test agreed; at global prefetch 1 against the same double-buffered allocation they diverge —
the model said 1, the kernel had 2 — and a depth-1 ring has no rotation, so the decoder emitted **no
buffer swap at all** while the kernel's addressing, its second LDS offset block and its memory token
all still alternated. Every copy then overwrote the buffer being read. A `0` buffer count falls back
to `δ`; that fallback is retained only for hand-built schedule points in tests and is the trap for
anything that knows the real number.

There is deliberately **no** `S ≥ δ` assertion in `_shared_depth`. The coupling is per *placement*,
and on this target `off(copy, chunk)` is not the LDS placement's retime depth — the global read
lands in registers and the LDS write is a separate, serialized step. A single-LDS-buffer kernel with
global prefetch 2 is a shipped configuration, i.e. a real kernel with `S_shared = 1 < δ = 2`.
Asserting the inequality against the global prefetch depth rejects it. A genuine check belongs
against the local-write offset once the write side is modelled (#116).

**What one rotation means on this ring:** advancing the chunk by one moves every subsequent copy and
read to the next buffer, and after `S_shared` chunks the ring returns to the first buffer — which is
still being read by nothing, if the schedule is correct, because the reader of that generation
finished `S_shared` chunks ago. The hazard this creates is the rotation anti-dependency: the copy
that refills slot `s` must not issue before the last read of the previous occupant of slot `s`. When
`S_shared` equals the retime depth exactly (the tight, feasible case) that anti-dependency binds in
the *same* trip, which is why the issue-order refinement in section 7 has to place those copies
after the reads rather than trusting a wait.

##### 8.5.3 The register ring: rotation inside the unrolled body

The register ring turns much faster. A register *group* is a partition of an operand's register
fragment into a set of names that are reused as the unrolled body walks its inner traversal
(section 1.8). The coordinate that advances is not a single mode but the **mixed-radix index over
the group's rate modes**, and `placement.py:_rate_slot(theta, op, group, d)` builds it:

```
_rate_slot(theta, op, group, d):
    if d <= 1: return cst(0)                       # width 1 = in place, no rotation
    rm = _rate_modes(theta, op, group)             # [(name, extent)], ord order outer->inner
    if not rm: return cst(0)
    coef, terms = 1, []
    for (name, ext) in reversed(rm):               # innermost mode is the fastest radix
        terms.append((name, coef)); coef *= ext
    return Expr(mod=d, terms=reversed(terms))      # sum(coef_m * idx_m) mod d
```

The rate modes come from `placement.py:_rate_modes`: the inner modes the group is *not* constant
over, of extent greater than 1, in `ord` order. Two exclusions carry weight. Dropping the modes the
group is constant over is what stops a *sibling selector* — an axis that picks which of several
co-resident values is used, without generating new values — from driving the ring; the rotation must
be indexed by the modes that actually produce distinct values. Dropping extent-1 modes is formally a
no-op (their coordinate is always 0 and their radix 1) but is done explicitly because
`_reduction_rate_mode` takes the *innermost reduction rate mode*, and a degenerate axis would shadow
the real substep axis: under a reduction-axis region split, `DepthU` re-factors as
`K_split(2) × K_inner(1)` and the innermost reduction mode becomes the extent-1 one. The read-ahead
would then shift along an axis with no values.

**What one rotation means on this ring:** the group's `W` names are written and consumed in a cycle
inside the unrolled body. `W` is searched in a derived band `[L, R]` (section 5.3): below the live
peak `L` two simultaneously-live values share a name, which is a race; above the reload rate `R` the
extra names are never reached, which is waste. The corresponding hazard is per group, which is why
`_read_placement` takes an optional `groups` argument: an operand whose groups have different widths
is read by more than one instruction, each carrying only the slots it writes, because the
anti-dependency that bounds how early a group may be refilled is per group too.

The special case `W = 1` is *in-place refill*: the group has one name, so the refill writes exactly
the name the current consumer reads. `_rate_slot` returns the constant 0 and there is no rotation to
speak of; safety comes from *ordering* (the refill must be emitted after the consumer), not from
capacity. That is the register-side analogue of the tight shared ring, and it is handled by the same
issue-order refinement.

##### 8.5.4 Why two rings and not one map

It is tempting to think of "the buffering" as one number per operand. The package deliberately does
not:

* the two rings rotate on **different coordinates** — one on a runtime trip index, one on a
  compile-time-unrolled traversal — so a single modulus would have to be reinterpreted per consumer;
* their depths come from **different sources** — the shared depth is a target fact (how many LDS
  buffers the allocation reserves), while the register width is searched inside a derived band;
* the register footprint is a **product of orthogonal factors** (regions × groups × width), and
  merging the shared depth into it would turn a product into an unrelated sum.

`theta.DepthMap` holds both as different *rows* of one map, keyed `(op, region, group)` with the
sentinel group label `SHARED_GROUP = "shared"` for the LDS ring. Callers that mean "a register
group" must exclude that label — a small sharp edge, and the reason `derive_S` and `build_S` are
separate functions: `derive_S` produces only the register rows, `build_S` adds the shared row on top
and returns `(S, floor)` so that reporting can show the pure derived register floor beside the final
map.

The three-part key (rather than `(op, group)`) exists because a region-split tile is **two
placements of one operand**, and the depth is indexed by the placement. `DepthMap.get` without a
region does *not* silently pick one: if per-region rows exist and disagree it raises, because
collapsing a per-placement fact to per-operand is precisely the class of bug the key was introduced
to prevent (#212). When the rows agree — today's equal-partition case — the collapse is well defined
and it answers. `DepthMap.regions_of` gives a per-placement consumer the enumeration to iterate
instead of assuming one placement per operand.

##### 8.5.5 The ring depth versus the peel depth

These are two different numbers that the shipping configuration makes equal, and the module's
comments say so in three places. Both are "how deep is the pipeline", but:

* `M` (peel depth) counts **iterations of the loop that must be peeled**. It is a max over retime
  offsets, plus the read-ahead reach.
* `S_shared` (ring depth) counts **buffers**. It is the operand's allocation.

At global prefetch 2 with double-buffered LDS both are 2. At global prefetch 1 with double-buffered
LDS, `M = 1` and `S_shared = 2`. At global prefetch 2 with a single LDS buffer, `M = 2` and
`S_shared = 1`. The last case is a shipped configuration, and it is the reason the emitter's copy
slot expression cannot assume `M ≤ S_shared`: the comment at the copy-slot construction notes that a
rotation anti-dependency becomes a real obligation exactly when `M > d`, and that claiming one
unconditionally would be wrong.

A future developer merging these two quantities "because they are both the pipeline depth" will pass
every test on the default configuration and break the two off-diagonal ones. Both off-diagonal
configurations are in the shipping test matrix; run them.

#### 8.6 The read-ahead prologue

##### 8.6.1 The problem

A register read carrying `off(read, substep) = dr` fetches, at traversal step `P`, the value that
step `P + dr` will consume. That is a shift along the flat traversal, and it makes the steady body
self-sustaining: each step reads one step further ahead than it consumes, so the register pipe stays
`dr` deep forever. But it is only self-sustaining once it is *primed*. On entry to the steady region
the first `dr` steps' values have to already be in registers, because nothing in the steady body
loads them — the steady body's read at step 0 loads the value for step `dr`.

The **read-ahead prologue** is that priming: the set of register reads that must be issued before
the steady body starts. It is a set of coordinates over the operand's presence modes, and the
emitter turns each coordinate into one read instruction placed in the prologue.

Two properties make this harder than "issue the first `dr` reads".

*It is per-operand.* Operands have different presence sets, so the coordinate spaces differ, and the
number of instances differs. With the reduction axis in the middle of the loop order (`M·K·N`), `A`
is present on `M` and `K` and broadcast over `N`, giving one prologue read; `B` is present on `N`
and `K`, giving a whole `N`-fan. A "simulate the first `dr` leaves of the traversal" implementation
gets this wrong because the traversal is shared while the presence sets are not.

*It is per-group and per-realisation.* The depth that is actually issued is the clamped per-group
`dr_g`, not the request. A group with `dr_g = 0` prologues nothing and refills in place. Priming a
group whose steady advance is 0 is the named failure mode: *the pipe is primed and then never
re-primed*, so the first pass through the unrolled body reads the primed values and every subsequent
pass reads a name nothing rewrote.

##### 8.6.2 The closed form

The construction is a **product of three independent factors**, each intersected with the operand's
presence set, with no leaf simulation anywhere. Split the inner-mode list at the reduction substep
axis `ik` (the innermost reduction inner mode with more than one value, from
`placement.py:_substep_mode`), of extent `n_s`:

```
ord (inner part) = [ OUTER… | substep(n_s) | INNER… ]

prologue(p) = { the FIRST coordinate of pres(p) ∩ OUTER }          (a single tile: all zeros)
            × { the leading  min(dr_g, n_s)  substeps,
                or ALL n_s substeps if the ord INNER block is empty }
            × { every coordinate of pres(p) ∩ INNER }
```

The middle factor's two cases are the subtle part. When there are inner modes below the substep
axis, the read-ahead advances through *those* first, so only `min(dr_g, n_s)` substeps are entered
before the shift is consumed. When the substep axis is innermost (`INNER = ∅`), a single step of the
read-ahead moves a whole substep, so the entire `n_s` range must be primed — and that factor is
independent of `dr_g` beyond being non-zero. The two shapes are visible in the parametrised test
`test_readahead_prologue_lemma3d`, which pins three loop orders at `dr = 1, n_s = 2` and a 2×2 wave
tile:

| order | `A` prologue | `B` prologue | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `KMN` (K outer) | `{k0m0, k0m1}` | `{k0n0, k0n1}` | `min(dr, n_s) = 1` substep; the inner factor is each operand's own presence fan |
| `MNK` (K inner) | `{k0m0, k1m0}` | `{k0n0, k1n0}` | `INNER = ∅` → full `n_s` substeps; the outer factor is the single first tile |
| `MKN` (K middle) | `{k0m0}` | `{k0n0, k0n1}` | **different arity** — `A` is broadcast over `N`, `B` over `M` |

The `MKN` row is the per-operand-presence point and the reason a leaf simulation was rejected. A
companion test, `test_readahead_prologue_substep_saturates_with_dr`, raises `dr` to 2 on `MKN` and
shows the substep factor growing to the `n_s` ceiling: `A` becomes `{k0m0, k1m0}` and `B` becomes
the full `2 × 2` product. `test_readahead_prologue_empty_without_dr` pins `dr = 0 → []`.

The docstring's comment about the earlier version is a useful warning: the test this replaced
hard-asserted the fill as `read_subs == {0}`, which is correct for the `KMN` order by accident and
is the wrong general model — the same "right for the default configuration, silent elsewhere" shape
as 8.4.3.

##### 8.6.3 `_group_value_range` — which values a group owns

`placement.py:_group_value_range(theta, op, group)` answers "if this fragment is split into register
groups, which values of the grouping mode does *this* group own?"

```
_group_value_range(theta, op, group) -> (mode_name, [values]) | (None, None):
    gm     = op.fragment.grouping_mode
    groups = op.fragment.groups()
    if gm is None or len(groups) <= 1:  return (None, None)     # not group-split
    ext       = theta.free_extent(gm)
    part_vals = max(1, ext // len(groups))
    i         = index of `group` in groups
    return (gm, list(range(i * part_vals, (i + 1) * part_vals)))
```

A register group is a partition of the grouping tile-mode's *values*, and the partition implemented
here is the **equal** one: group `i` owns `[i·part_vals, (i+1)·part_vals)`. That is an accepted
restriction, not an oversight (#166): uneven partitions are expressible in the vocabulary but
nothing derives them today, and `sizing.py`'s footprint arithmetic makes the same equal-partition
assumption. The `max(1, …)` floor keeps the function total when there are more groups than values,
in which case the ranges overlap — a configuration nothing produces, but one that would silently
double-prime rather than crash. A developer adding uneven partitions must change this function and
`sizing.py` together, and should add a test that the ranges partition `[0, ext)` exactly.

The return shape `(None, None)` for an unsplit fragment is what lets the caller pass the pair
straight through to `_one_group`, which treats `gm_name is None` as "do not restrict anything".

##### 8.6.4 `readahead_prologue` — the driver

```
readahead_prologue(theta, op, dr, S=None) -> [ {mode_name: value}, … ]:
    if not dr:               return []
    pres = set(_presence(theta, op))
    if not pres:             return []
    inner = list(theta.inner_modes())          # ord order, outer -> inner
    sub   = _substep_mode(theta)
    if sub is None:          return []         # no reduction ring -> no read-ahead
    si          = inner.index(sub)
    inner_block = inner[si+1:]                 # ALL modes below the substep, presence or not
    OUTER       = [m for m in inner[:si]  if m.name in pres]
    INNER       = [m for m in inner_block if m.name in pres]
    n_s         = sub.extent

    if S is None:                                        # no depth map: fall back to the request
        return _one_group(dr, None, None)
    groups = op.fragment.groups()
    if op.fragment.grouping_mode is None or len(groups) <= 1:
        return _one_group(group_readahead_depth(theta, op, groups[0], dr, S), None, None)
    out, seen = [], set()                                # width-split: union over groups
    for g in groups:
        dr_g              = group_readahead_depth(theta, op, g, dr, S)
        gm_name, gm_vals  = _group_value_range(theta, op, g)
        for c in _one_group(dr_g, gm_name, gm_vals):
            if key(c) not in seen: seen.add(key(c)); out.append(c)
    return out
```

Four things to note about the driver.

**`inner_block` is computed over *all* modes below the substep, while `INNER` is that list filtered
to the presence set.** The unfiltered list is what decides the middle factor's two cases via
`_has_values(inner_block)`: whether a full-`n_s` prime is needed is a property of the *traversal*,
not of this operand's presence. The filtered list is what supplies the third factor's coordinates.
Conflating them would make one operand's broadcast change another's substep count.

**The single-group branch still derives.** It calls `group_readahead_depth` for the sole group
rather than using `dr`. Reading "per-group" as "only when width-split" is exactly the bug this
branch exists to prevent: a single-group fragment can be a zero-depth (in-place) shape too — that is
the operand of a K-innermost loop order whose whole register-name space is re-traversed before any
value dies, which has no width split at all. Before this branch, the fill ran at the global `dr` for
a group whose steady advance was already 0.

**The `S is None` fallback uses the raw request.** It exists for callers with no depth map (the
renderer, and the older tests that pass a literal `dr`). It is documented as a fallback and it is
*wrong* in the sense that it over-fills a clamped group; the test
`test_readahead_prologue_per_group_dr` asserts precisely this difference and uses it as its
non-vacuity guard: on an MX-fp8 fragment split into `{lo: W=2, hi: W=1}`, the depth-map call yields
only `lo`'s grouping-mode values `[0, part)`, while the no-`S` call yields the whole fan — "confirm
`S` changes it". New code should always pass `S`.

**The union across groups is de-duplicated by sorted-items key.** Two groups can generate the same
coordinate when the grouping mode is not in the coordinate at all (an unsplit axis), so the union
would otherwise double-emit reads. Deduplication preserves first-seen order, which keeps the emitted
prologue deterministic across runs — worth keeping if this is ever rewritten with a `set`.

##### 8.6.5 `_one_group` and `_vals` — the three-factor product for one group

`readahead_prologue._one_group(dr_g, gm_name, gm_vals)` is the closure that materialises the product
for one group at one depth, restricting the grouping mode to that group's values when the fragment
is split:

```
_one_group(dr_g, gm_name, gm_vals):
    if dr_g <= 0: return []                                   # Shape B: no read-ahead at all
    n_sub       = n_s if not _has_values(inner_block) else min(dr_g, n_s)
    outer_fixed = {m.name: 0 for m in OUTER}                  # factor 1: the FIRST tile
    inner_ranges = [ [(m.name, v) for v in _vals(m)] for m in INNER ]
    inner_combos = [dict(c) for c in product(*inner_ranges)] or [ {} ]
    outer_gm     = [m for m in OUTER if m.name == gm_name]    # the grouping mode may be OUTER
    for gmo in (gm_vals if outer_gm else [None]):
        for s in range(n_sub):                                # factor 2: the substeps
            for ic in inner_combos:                           # factor 3: the inner fan
                yield {**outer_fixed, **({gm_name: gmo} if gmo is not None else {}),
                       sub.name: s, **ic}
```

`readahead_prologue._one_group._vals(m)` is the innermost helper: for a mode `m` in the `INNER`
factor it returns `gm_vals` if `m` is the grouping mode and `range(m.extent)` otherwise. Two lines,
and the only place the group restriction enters the inner product.

The `outer_gm` loop exists because the grouping mode is not guaranteed to be inner to the substep.
Under some loop orders the axis a fragment is grouped on sits in the `OUTER` block, where the first
factor would otherwise pin it to 0 for every group — and every group would then prime the same
coordinate, with group `hi`'s values never primed at all. So when the grouping mode is in `OUTER`,
the loop iterates its owned values and overwrites the pinned 0. When it is not, the loop runs once
with `gmo = None` and the pinned first tile stands.

`_one_group`'s `dr_g <= 0` early return is the enforcement of the one-shape rule stated in the
driver's docstring: **a zero-depth group prologues nothing and its steady advance is 0 — one shape,
not a mixture.** Pairing a primed prologue with a zero steady advance, or an unprimed prologue with
a non-zero advance, are the two ways to break it, and the reason they cannot happen is structural
rather than disciplinary: `ledger.build_ledger` derives the read-ahead residency obligations from
*this* function and `emit.fill_reads` emits from *this* function, so the two sides read one
derivation. Suppressing one side alone is what previously left obligations undischarged.

##### 8.6.6 The prologue's obligations, and the test that checks them

The read-ahead prologue generates a fifth obligation kind, `readahead-residency`, which is carried
in the ledger but deliberately excluded from the set of kinds that become `Await` markers
(section 1.7). It is a *structural* requirement — "these coordinates must have been read before the
steady body" — not a wait, so it is checked directly against the emitted tree.

`test_gate_catches_missing_readahead_prologue_fill` is the negative test for that gate: it is
parametrised over loop orders, removes the prologue fill, and requires the whole-tree check to
report the missing coverage rather than passing. A second test at the emit level takes the derived
`dr` from `_peel_depths` and then reads the **emitted tree** rather than calling
`readahead_prologue` again — its inline comment says why: re-calling the shared helper would compare
a function against itself. That is the same independent-oracle discipline as 8.4.4, applied one
layer up.

#### 8.7 Complexity, and where the compile-time actually goes

All the quantities below are tiny by asymptotic standards; what matters is the *constant* and how
many times each function is called per kernel, because kernel generation runs these derivations once
per candidate solution and a library build has thousands of candidates.

Let `P` = number of operands (2 for a plain GEMM, up to 4 with MX scale operands), `H` = hops per
operand (1 or 2), `L` = levels in `ord` (the reduction chunk plus the inner modes; 4 to 7 in
practice), `G` = register groups per operand (1 or 2), and `I` = points of the inner traversal (the
product of the inner modes' extents; 4 to 64 typically, up to a few hundred at large wave tiles).

| Function | Complexity | Practical `n` | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `_leading_inner_coords` | O(δ) | δ ≤ 3 | allocates δ single-key dicts |
| `PeelDepths.depth` / `.M` | O(1) | — | one dict lookup |
| `PeelDepths.peeled_levels` | O(L) | ≤ 7 | list of dict keys |
| `PeelDepths.copy_off` | O(\|offs\|) | ≤ 8 | linear filter, rebuilt on every call |
| `_peel_depths` (scan) | O(P·H·L + L·\|offs\|) | ~50 dict ops | the per-level max rescans `offs` per level |
| `_peel_depths` (reach) | one `readahead_reach`, which builds the **whole depth map** | see below | dominant term |
| `boundary_hoists` | O(\|offs\|·L) | ~50 | `names.index` is a linear scan, done twice per entry |
| `_group_value_range` | O(G) | ≤ 2 | |
| `readahead_prologue` | O(G · output size), output ≤ `n_s · Π extents over INNER` | 2–32 coords | plus O(output log output) for the de-dup key |

**The dominant term is not in this section's code.** `_peel_depths` calls
`readahead_reach(theta)` with no depth map, and `readahead_reach` therefore calls `build_S(theta)`
itself. `build_S` runs `derive_S`, which computes a group width per group, which computes a live
peak by enumerating the inner traversal three times over (a cyclic interval-overlap over three
unrolled iterations). That is `O(P·G·I)` with a non-trivial constant, and it is the single most
expensive derivation in the package.

`_peel_depths` is called roughly five times per kernel: once in `emit.build_ir`, twice inside
`ledger.build_ledger` (once for the rotation/in-place WAR rows built from `S.depths`, and once for
the read-ahead residency rows),
once in `render.render_geometry` when the dump is enabled, and once in `Lowering/loopir_to_gir.py`.
Each of those calls rebuilds the depth map from scratch, and every one of those call sites
**already has an `S` in hand** — `emit.emit_mainloop` computes it and passes it to `build_ir`, which
passes it to `build_ledger`.

**Concrete, low-risk improvement.** Give `_peel_depths` an optional `S` parameter and forward it:

```
def _peel_depths(theta, S=None):
    ...
    reach = readahead_reach(theta, S) if dr else 0
```

`readahead_reach` already accepts `S` and only derives one when it is `None`. Threading it from the
four call sites that have it removes four full depth-map builds per kernel with no behavioural
change, and it removes a class of latent inconsistency: today, if a caller's `S` differed from a
freshly derived one (it cannot today, but `build_S` reads target facts and could become
configuration-dependent), the peel depth would be computed against a different map than the one the
emitter uses.

**A second, larger improvement if that is not enough.** Memoize the whole `(theta) → (S, PeelDepths)`
pair once per kernel and pass the pair down. `Theta` is a frozen dataclass but contains lists, so it
is not hashable; the cache therefore has to be an explicit object owned by the caller rather than an
`lru_cache`. `KernelWriter` already caches the `Theta` per kernel for exactly this reason, so the
natural home is next to that cache. Do **not** reach for an `id()`-keyed module-level dict — that
pattern was removed from `emit.py` once already and the replacement was an explicit result object.

**Micro-optimisations that are not worth doing.** Rescanning `offs` per level in `_peel_depths`
(O(L·|offs|) instead of one grouped pass) and the double `names.index` in `boundary_hoists` are both
visible in the source and both operate on collections with fewer than ten elements. Changing them
buys nothing measurable and costs readability. Leave them.

#### 8.8 Sharp edges, weaknesses and dead ends

**Four spellings of "the substep axis" coexist in `placement.py`, and two of them differ on purpose.**

Three are listed below. The fourth is inside `chunk_reach` (`placement.py:57-59`), which open-codes
the same scan as `_substep_level_name` but keeps the `Mode` rather than its name — so it cannot
call that helper unchanged, and merging the third spelling alone does *not* finish the job.

* `placement.py:_substep_level_name` — the innermost reduction inner mode, *by name*, regardless of
  extent. This is the level the retime offset is *stored on*: `translate` writes
  `off(read, substep_level)` keyed on the innermost reduction inner mode's name.
* `placement.py:_substep_mode` — the innermost reduction inner mode **with extent > 1**, falling
  back to the innermost outright when all are degenerate. This is the axis the traversal is *split
  at* by `readahead_prologue` and by the steady read-ahead shift.
* An **inline copy** of the first, inside `_peel_depths`, spelled out rather than calling
  `_substep_level_name`.

The first two differ deliberately, and the difference was a measured bug: with a reduction-axis
region split of factor 2 and local prefetch 1 under the K-innermost loop orders, `DepthU` re-factors
as `K_split(2) × K_inner(1)` and the innermost reduction mode has extent 1. Splitting the traversal
there gave `n_s = 1`, so the read-ahead prologue primed one substep where the steady body consumes
two, and the first matmul of the body read a register generation nothing had loaded — 192 of 1152
configurations, selecting on the loop order and on nothing else, because the K-outer orders clamp to
the same value either way. `_substep_mode` exists to fix that; `_substep_level_name` must *not* be
changed to match it, because it names the key an offset is stored under.

The third spelling is straightforwardly redundant and should call `_substep_level_name`. It is
byte-identical today, which is the dangerous state: the pattern that produces most of the defects in
this package is *two places computing one fact, agreeing on the common case, diverging on the
degenerate one*. Merging it is a one-line change with no behavioural risk.

**`PeelDepths` is frozen but not deeply immutable.** `per_level`, `offs` and `deferrals` are plain
dicts. `dataclasses.frozen=True` prevents rebinding the fields, not mutating what they point at, and
the class is consequently unhashable. Nothing mutates them today. If a future consumer wants to
cache on a `PeelDepths`, freeze the dicts (`types.MappingProxyType`, or tuples of pairs) first
rather than adding an `__hash__`.

**`copy_off()` rebuilds its dict on every call.** `emit.build_ir` calls it once and binds the
result; `Lowering/loopir_to_gir.py` does the same. If a future consumer calls it inside a loop over
prologue steps, hoist it — the filter is linear in `offs` and `offs` is rebuilt from nothing each
time.

**`PeelDepths.M` is a narrow accessor beside a wide record, and that is deliberate.** A reader who
sees `peel.M` may reasonably assume it is "the" peel depth of the schedule. It is the depth *at the
reduction chunk*, and the only reason it is safe to use as though it were the whole story is that
`emit._check_peel_is_emittable` refuses any schedule point where `peeled_levels()` names an extra
outer level. If that refusal is ever relaxed without making `build_ir` recursive, `M` silently
becomes wrong again. Treat the refusal and the accessor as one unit.

**The `reach` bump has one unexcluded widening case.** As recorded in 8.2.6, the derived reach and
the old request-based `ceil` agree on the entire measured matrix, but the comparison is empirical,
not proved, and a configuration with `n_s = 1`, a two-value substep factorisation and `dr_g = 2`
would widen the peel by one step. The width derivation pins that away in every logged case. A
developer who changes the reduction-axis factorisation should re-run the comparison across the three
shipping kernel configurations rather than assume it still holds.

**`boundary_hoists` is correct and reports nothing.** It returns `[]` for every schedule point the
parameter path can currently build, because `translate` only ever sets an offset at the op-class's
own home level. It is exercised solely by hand-built fixtures. That makes it *unverified against
reality* in a way the rest of this section is not: the three conditions are pinned by tests, but the
`coords` it produces have never been consumed by an emitter. When #113 lands, expect the coordinate
*shape* to need revision before the conditions do — in particular, a hoist whose home level is
itself nested (two enclosed loops) needs a coordinate per enclosing level, and
`_leading_inner_coords` produces a single-key dict.

**The `S is None` path of `readahead_prologue` produces a wrong answer, on purpose.** It over-fills
any clamped group. It exists for callers that genuinely have no depth map, and it is directly
asserted by a test as the *contrast* case. Any new caller must pass `S`. If the remaining
no-`S` callers can be converted, make the parameter required and delete the branch — that removes a
way to be silently wrong.

**No independent oracle exists for `readahead_prologue`.** Its tests enumerate expected coordinate
sets for three loop orders and two depths. That catches a wrong formula for those shapes but not a
wrong *model*. The structural property to test would be the one the wrap lead's oracle uses: simulate
the steady body's advance from the primed state and require that every register generation a matmul
consumes was written by exactly one read, across every loop order and every group width. That
simulator does not exist and would be the highest-value test to add to this module.

**Dead-ish code.** `PeelDepths.peeled_levels()` has exactly one consumer (`_check_peel_is_emittable`)
and `PeelDepths.reach` has exactly one (the same check's neighbour in `emit`'s drain builder,
`dr_iters = peel.reach`; the geometry renderer reads `_peel_depths(theta).dr`, not `.reach`).
Neither is dead, but both are one-consumer fields that would be easy to drop by accident
during a refactor; the emitter's refusal message is the only thing standing between a dropped
`peeled_levels()` and the silent-drop defect returning.

#### 8.9 If you are about to change something in this half of the module

A short checklist distilled from the defects above.

1. **Changing the peel depth?** Regenerate the emitted assembly for global prefetch 1 *and* 2, and
   for a single-LDS-buffer configuration. Prefetch 2 with double buffering makes the peel depth, the
   shared ring depth and the retime depth all equal to 2, so it validates nothing about their
   relationship. The two off-diagonal configurations are in the shipping matrix.
2. **Changing anything that counts chunks?** Ask whether the input is the *request* (`PeelDepths.dr`,
   `off(read, substep)`) or the *realisation* (`PeelDepths.reach`, `group_readahead_depth`). Chunk
   counters take the realisation; per-instruction shifts take the per-group realisation; only the
   read-ahead family's own internals take the request, and each derives its own clamp.
3. **Changing `boundary_hoists`' conditions?** Condition 3 is load-bearing for region-split copies,
   which are on the shipping path. Run the region-split fixture and check that
   `emit_mainloop` still succeeds, not just that the hoist list is what you expect.
4. **Adding a level?** The peel depth is already per-level; the emitter is not. Adding a level that
   carries an offset will trip `_check_peel_is_emittable` with a clear message rather than
   miscompile — that is the intended behaviour, and the fix is to make `build_ir` recursive, not to
   widen the check.
5. **Adding an op-class with a reverse trajectory (an epilogue store)?** `_peel_depths` refuses on
   sight. Implement the mirrored peel (prologue and drain swapped, instances hoisted forward) before
   removing the refusal, and note that hop roles cannot distinguish a forward read from a store's
   read-back leg — the trajectory sense is the only discriminator.
6. **Touching the register ring?** The width band, the rate modes and the in-place case interlock:
   `W = 1` means no rotation and safety by ordering, `W < L` is a race, `W > R` is waste, and a
   zero-depth group must prologue nothing *and* advance by nothing. Change one and check all four.
7. **Writing a test for a closed form that indexes a rotating structure?** Write a simulator with a
   structural success criterion (a permutation, a covering, a non-overlap), not a value comparison
   against the formula. The wrap lead's permutation oracle is the model to copy.


---

### 9. `placement.py` (continued) — marks, quantum admissibility and hazards

#### 9.0 Scope of this section, and the coverage split across sections 7–9

`placement.py` is the largest core module (1401 lines, 45 definitions). It is documented in three
consecutive sections because it holds three genuinely different bodies of work that happen to share
