a file. This section is the **reach-and-admissibility** deep dive: how far a read-ahead reaches in
whole reduction chunks, which side of a trip's reads a shared copy is emitted on, whether a hardware
instruction is allowed to merge several tile coordinates into one movement, and — as reference
entries keyed to the consumers that live here — how deep each level's software-pipeline peel is and
which op-class instances an outer offset relocates across a loop boundary. It closes with the
downstream Mark-placement policy that turns this section's legal *ranges* into points.

**The canonical split is the table at 7.0, and it is reproduced here verbatim.** The split is *not*
a partition of the 45 names into three disjoint boxes — section 7 is a catalogue that gives almost
every name a short reference entry, and sections 8 and 9 are thematic treatments that revisit some
of those names in depth. An earlier revision of this report stated the split three different and
mutually incompatible ways, here and at 7.0 and 8.1; this is the reconciled version.

| Family | Names | **Primary treatment** | Also treated in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Addressing | `_ord_strides` | §7.3.1 | — |
| Presence | `_presence` | §7.4 | — |
| Home level and level naming | `op_class_level`, `_substep_level_name`, `_substep_mode`, `_has_values` | §7.5, §7.6 | §9.4 (restated with the empty-presence case the emitter hits) |
| Register rate slots | `_rate_modes`, `_rate_slot`, `_reduction_rate_mode` | §7.7 | §8.5.3 (as the register ring's slot rule) |
| Read-ahead vetoes | `_broadcast_fan`, `_free_siblings`, `_sibling_outer_to_reduction`, `reload_modes` | §7.9, §7.10 | — |
| Read-ahead depth and shift | `group_readahead_depth`, `_readahead_depth`, `_readahead_shift`, `readahead_is_inplace`, `_shifted_coord`, `_shifted_rate_slot` | §7.11 | §13.3 (from the emitter's side) |
| Read-ahead prologue | `readahead_prologue` (+ nested `_one_group`, `_one_group._vals`), `_group_value_range` | **§8.6** | §7.12 (catalogue entry) |
| Read placement | `_read_placement` | **§8.5** | — |
| Chunk reach and copy order | `_prefetch_depth`, `chunk_reach`, `readahead_reach`, `copy_must_be_first`, `copy_first_operands`, `chunk_crossing_violations` | **§9.1–§9.3** | §7.13, §7.14 (catalogue entries) |
| The peel | `PeelDepths` (+ `depth`, `M`, `peeled_levels`, `copy_off`), `_peel_depths` | **§8.2** | §7.15 (catalogue entry), §9.5 (reference restatement) |
| Cross-level boundary term | `BoundaryHoist`, `_leading_inner_coords`, `boundary_hoists` | **§8.3** | §7.16 (catalogue entry), §9.6 (reference restatement) |
| Movement quantum | `resolve_quantum`, `quantum_tile_cap`, `_generation_map`, `hop_quantum_axes`, `_divisors`, `_uniform_over` | **§9.8** | — |
| Downstream consumer of `M` | `gir_to_rocisa.py:GirToRocisa._wrap_lead` (not in this file) | §8.4 | — |
| Downstream realisation of the marks | `Lowering/gir/passes/placement.py:PlacementPass` (not in this file) | §9.7 | — |

The name columns sum to 45, so the three sections together account for every name the definition
inventory lists for `placement.py`, with no name left to an adjacent module and none double-counted.
Two names are read across the boundary — `_substep_level_name` is called from the read-ahead family
as well as from this section, and `_read_placement` (primary at 8.5) is called from this section's
`_generation_map` — so a reader chasing one of those will cross a section boundary once.

##### 9.0.1 A naming collision worth knowing about before you grep

There are **two** files called `placement.py` in this tree, in different packages, doing different
jobs, and the emphasis of this section touches both:

* `Tensile/LoopModel/placement.py` — the subject of sections 7–9. It computes *where in the
  loop nest an op-class lives* and *how far in time it reaches*. It is pure, address-opaque, and
  emits nothing.
* `Tensile/Lowering/gir/passes/placement.py` — a GIR pass (`PlacementPass`) that resolves *where
  inside a basic block a pointer-mutating instruction is inserted*. It is 56 lines and its whole
  content is a policy choice.

They are unrelated as code, but they are two halves of one idea: a scheduling fact has a **legal
range**, not a single correct point, and the decision of where inside the range to land is
**policy**. §9.7 documents the GIR `PlacementPass` policy in full — earliest for descriptor
changes, midpoint for the read pointer, one mark per incoming path — because that policy is the
direct downstream realization of the time structure this section derives, and because a maintainer
who greps `placement.py` will hit both files and needs to know which one answers which question.

##### 9.0.2 The three questions this section answers

1. **How far ahead does the read-ahead reach, in whole reduction chunks?** (`chunk_reach`,
   `readahead_reach`.) This single integer, called `r`, sizes the shared-memory buffering, sets the
   chunk-level peel depth, and drives the drain's read-ahead suppression window.
2. **What is the peel, per level?** (`PeelDepths`, `_peel_depths`, `BoundaryHoist`,
   `boundary_hoists`, `op_class_level`.) The peel is a *vector* over levels, not an integer, and an
   offset at a level outer to an op-class's own home level is a *relocation* rather than a peel.
3. **Which merges of tile coordinates into one instruction are admissible?** (`resolve_quantum`,
   `quantum_tile_cap`, `_generation_map`, `hop_quantum_axes`, `_divisors`, `_uniform_over`.) This
   is the movement-quantum question of section 1.9, and the honest answer the module reached — after
   four failed attempts to derive the quantum inside the core — is that the core must not decide it
   at all.

Each of the three carries at least one historical defect that reached hardware, and each of those
is reproduced in place below, because the defect is usually the clearest statement of what the
invariant is.

#### 9.1 Chunk reach — how far a substep read-ahead spills into the next chunk

##### 9.1.1 The problem

Section 1.6 introduced the two retime offsets the shipping parameter path sets:
`off(copy, chunk)`, the global prefetch depth, and `off(read, substep)`, the local prefetch depth
written `dr`. The second one is a *substep* offset: the register read for reduction substep `s` is
issued during substep `s − dr`. There is a temptation to think of that as confined inside one
reduction chunk, since the substep axis is an inner (statically unrolled) axis of the chunk.

It is not confined. The traversal is a monotone mixed-radix counter over `ord` (section 1.4), so
advancing the *flat* position by `dr` substeps carries out of the substep digit into whatever digit
sits outside it. When the substep is the outermost digit of the operand's own presence traversal,
or when the digits inner to it are exhausted, the carry lands on the reduction-chunk coordinate:
the read reaches into the *next chunk's* shared buffer. This is not an edge case — it is the normal
behaviour of the last `dr` positions of every trip, and it is why the shared source slot
(`_read_placement:src_slot`, §8) is written with a carry term rather than as a constant per trip.

`chunk_reach` is the one derivation of *how many whole chunks* that carry crosses. The integer it
returns is called `r` everywhere in this package.

##### 9.1.2 `placement.py:_prefetch_depth`

A three-line forwarding function, but a load-bearing one:

```
_prefetch_depth(theta, op) = theta._shared_depth(theta, op)
```

It answers "how many shared-ring generations does this operand's copy rotate through", i.e.
`S_shared`. It exists so that `emit.py` and `Lowering/loopir_to_gir.py` — both of which import it by
name — cannot reach for a different number. The docstring states the invariant explicitly: this
**must equal** `theta._shared_depth`, and the tempting alternative of using `off(copy, chunk)`
instead is a real defect. If the modulus used to compute the emitted copy's slot expression differs
from the modulus the depth map allocated with, generations `iter` and `iter + off` alias onto one
buffer and the rotation-WAR obligations in the ledger are filed against the wrong slot. The import
is done lazily inside the function body (`from .theta import _shared_depth`), but **not** to break a
cycle: `placement` already imports from `theta` at module scope (`placement.py:23`), and `theta`
never imports `placement`, so the same import would work at module level. The laziness here is
stylistic — the same distinction section 11 draws for `ledger.py`'s lazy `placement` imports.

**Complexity** O(1) plus whatever `_shared_depth` costs (a small max over the operand's offsets).
**Extension advice** if you ever add a second shared-like ring (a global-to-global staging buffer,
for instance), do not add a parameter here — add a second named accessor, so the grep
`_prefetch_depth` continues to mean exactly one ring.

##### 9.1.3 `placement.py:chunk_reach` — the closed form

Inputs: `theta`, an operand `op`, and `dr_g` — the operand's **derived** per-group read-ahead depth
(the clamped one, `group_readahead_depth`, §8), not the requested `dr`. Output: a non-negative
integer `r`.

```
chunk_reach(theta, op, dr_g):
    if dr_g <= 0:                       return 0        # no read-ahead, no crossing
    inner  = theta.inner_modes()                        # ord order, outer -> inner
    sub    = innermost mode of `inner` whose name is a reduction mode
    if sub is None:                     return 0        # no reduction substep axis at all
    pres   = set of presence mode names of op
    fan    = product of extent over the modes of `inner` strictly INNER to `sub`
                                        that are in pres(op)
    span   = extent(sub) * fan                          # distinct reads of op in one chunk
    return ((span - 1) + dr_g * fan) // span
```

The three quantities have direct meanings:

* `fan` — how many *presence* positions of this operand sit inside one substep. For an operand
  whose only free axis is inner to the substep, this is that axis's extent; for an operand whose
  free axes are all *outer* to the substep, it is 1.
* `span` — the number of distinct read positions of this operand in one chunk. Advancing the flat
  position by `span` is exactly one chunk.
* `dr_g * fan` — the read-ahead expressed in flat-position units rather than substeps. One substep
  of advance moves `fan` flat positions.

The formula is then the standard "how many multiples of `span` does a window of length `span` shifted
by `dr_g*fan` touch": `floor(((span−1) + shift) / span)`.

##### 9.1.4 What the unit test pins, and the mutant it kills

`Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py:test_chunk_reach_is_the_distance_over_the_span_and_saturates_at_the_level`
is unusually careful and worth reading before touching this function. Algebraically the closed form
is `1 + floor((dr_g·fan − 1) / (n_s·fan))` where `n_s = extent(sub)`. The design constraint on the
substep read-ahead is `dr ≤ n_s` — the offset lives on a loop level whose trip count is `n_s`, so a
deeper request has nothing to prefetch from. Inside that bound the second term is identically zero,
so:

> **`r == 1` for every `dr_g ≥ 1`, regardless of `fan`.**

That is a genuinely useful fact — the substep read-ahead reaches exactly one chunk ahead and never
more, on every configuration reachable from parameters. It is also a trap: **the `fan` factor is
vacuous in the reachable domain.** A mutant that deletes `fan` from the numerator passes every
parameter-derived test that can be written. The test therefore probes `dr = n_s + 1`
out-of-domain, where `fan = 2, n_s = 2` gives `span = 4` and `(3 + 3·2)//4 = 2`, while a fan-less
numerator would give `(3+3)//4 = 1`. Keep that assertion if you refactor: it is the only thing
standing between this formula and a silent simplification.

**Complexity** O(|inner_modes|) per call, with `|inner_modes|` between 3 and 6 on the shipping
matrix. It is called inside two nested loops (over operands, over register groups) from at least
four places, so the total is still trivially small.

##### 9.1.5 `placement.py:readahead_reach` — the envelope, and the request-vs-realization defect

`chunk_reach` answers for one operand and one register group. `readahead_reach(theta, S=None)`
takes the **maximum** over every shared→register read op-class and every one of its register
groups:

```
readahead_reach(theta, S):
    if S is None:  S, _floor = theta.build_S(theta)
    sub = _substep_level_name(theta)
    if sub is None: return 0
    best = 0
    for op in theta.operands:
        if op's last hop is not SHARED -> REGISTER:  continue
        dr = theta.off_at(op.name, READ, sub)
        if dr <= 0: continue
        for g in op.fragment.groups():
            best = max(best, chunk_reach(theta, op, group_readahead_depth(theta, op, g, dr, S)))
    return best
```

Two properties of this function are load-bearing and easy to get wrong.

**It is a `max`, and the per-instruction depth is a `min`.** `_readahead_depth` (§8) takes the
*minimum* over groups; `readahead_reach` takes the *maximum*. Both are correct for their consumer
and they must not be "unified":

* A **peel depth** and a **suppression window** must cover the *deepest* group. Too small, and the
  drain guards away reads a later drain step still consumes.
* A **per-instruction shift** must not exceed the *shallowest* group's rotation width. Too large,
  and the read names a register the rotation cannot hold.

**It is built from the derived depth, never the request.** `group_readahead_depth` computes
`dr_g = max(0, min(dr, W_g − 1))` and zeroes it outright under two structural vetoes (a broadcast
fan greater than one, and a free-axis region sibling that sits outer to the reduction axis). So a
request deeper than the rotation can hold reaches no further than the rotation actually does.

The second property exists because of a measured defect (#284). With a bf16 NT kernel, MI shape
[16,16,32], wave tile [2,2], `DepthU` 64 (so `n_s = 2`), two-deep global prefetch, and the
scheduling mode that routes through the pass-based optimizer, a local-prefetch request of 3 is
clamped to `dr_g = 1` because the group's rotation width `W_g` is 2. Everything in the read-ahead
family therefore emitted the depth-1 schedule — but the two chunk-counting consumers were computing
`ceil(dr / n_s) = 2` off the **raw request**. That widened the drain's read-ahead suppression window
from one step to two, so the second-to-last drain step also suppressed reads that the last drain
step's leading matmuls consumed. Emitted local-read count: 62 at request 1, 62 at request 2, **54**
at request 3 — eight local reads silently gone against an unchanged 36 matmuls, with the obligation
ledger reporting *empty* and no warning printed. At requests of 5 and above the same raw form drove
the chunk peel `M` up to 3, 4 and 5 while `off(copy, chunk)` stayed at 2, producing extra unrolled
drain steps and a raised short-loop threshold for a pipeline depth that did not exist.

##### 9.1.6 Why the fix is not "the same integer with a different symbol"

The docstring goes out of its way to refuse an attractive simplification, and the refusal is
correct. It is tempting to claim that `((span−1) + dr_g·fan)//span` "reduces to `ceil(dr_g / n_s)`,
which is the old expression with the request swapped for the realization" — i.e. that the only
change was `dr → dr_g`. Three *different denominators* were in play across the old call sites:

* `_peel_depths` divided by the **maximum** reduction-inner extent;
* the drain builder in `emit.py` divided by `_reduction_rate_mode`'s extent;
* `chunk_reach` divides by the **innermost** reduction-inner extent, weighted by `fan`.

Those coincide on 100% of the shipping configuration matrix but differ in *form* on 47% of it. The
equality is a measured coincidence, not an identity, and a future shape can separate them.

Likewise the monotonicity argument "new ≤ old always, since `dr_g ≤ dr` and `ceil` is monotone" is
**not a proof**: two ceilings with different denominators are not comparable that way. What is
actually established is measured, over every schedule point in all three shipping configuration
files: 69,108 of 69,108 `_peel_depths` calls and 11,518 of 11,518 drain builds produced identical
results, and the generated kernels were byte-identical (152 of 152 fp8, 404 of 404 MX-scaled fp8).
One *widening* case exists on paper and is currently unreachable — `n_s = 1`, substep extent 2,
`dr = dr_g = 2` gives old 1 and new 2 — pinned away today only because the derived width `W_g` is 2
in every logged case. Nobody has excluded it in general. **If you see the peel depth grow after a
change to the width band, this is the first place to look.**

##### 9.1.7 The `S = None` convenience, and its compile-time cost

`readahead_reach(theta)` with no depth map derives one itself by calling `theta.build_S(theta)`.
That is convenient (the function is called from `_peel_depths`, which does not otherwise need `S`)
and it is the single most expensive thing in this section: `build_S` runs the whole width-band
search (section 4.4) over every operand and group. `_peel_depths` calls it once per invocation, and
`_peel_depths` is itself called from `emit.build_ir`, `ledger`, `render` and `loopir_to_gir`.

**Concrete advice for a future developer wanting to make this faster.** Three options, in
increasing order of effort:

1. **Thread `S` through.** Every caller of `_peel_depths` except one already holds a depth map from
   `build_S`. Adding an optional `S=None` parameter to `_peel_depths` and forwarding it to
   `readahead_reach` removes the redundant search with no semantic change. This is the obvious win
   and nothing blocks it.
2. **Memoize `build_S` on the schedule point.** `Theta` is a frozen dataclass, and the derived
   depth map is a pure function of it. A module-level `functools.lru_cache` keyed on `id(theta)` is
   wrong (identity reuse after garbage collection), but a cache stored *on* the theta object at
   construction — a lazily-populated private field — is safe because the object is immutable.
3. **Cache `readahead_reach` itself.** It is a pure function of `(theta, S)`; the shipping value is
   almost always 0 or 1. This is the smallest change but saves the least, because the cost is in
   `build_S`, not in the envelope loop.

None of these is a correctness matter. Kernel generation is dominated by assembly emission, and the
whole schedule decode is a small fraction of it; measure before optimizing.

#### 9.2 Copy-first versus copy-last — the σ_c input

##### 9.2.1 Concept

Within one steady trip the emitter issues, among other things, the operand's global→shared bulk copy
and that operand's shared→register reads. Their relative order is not free. Two mutually exclusive
relationships are possible and they demand *opposite* orders:

* If the copy issued in this trip fills the very chunk that *this trip's* read-ahead reaches into,
  the reads are **consumers** of the copy. That is a true dependency (a `crossing-RAW`, section
  1.7), and the copy must be issued **first**.
* Otherwise the copy's shared slot collides with a chunk this trip read *earlier* (or with nothing
  at all). That is an anti-dependency — the copy would overwrite data the trip is still consuming —
  so the copy must be issued **last**.

The decision is per operand, it is computed once per `build_ir` call, and it is handed to every σ_c
invocation — the issue-order refinement implemented in `sigma_c.py` — as a set of operand names.

##### 9.2.2 `placement.py:copy_must_be_first` — the predicate and its derivation

```
copy_must_be_first(theta, op, S) -> bool:
    chunk = theta.reduction_chunk_name()
    if chunk is None:                       return False   # legacy theta, no outer level
    dr = theta.off_at(op.name, READ, _substep_level_name(theta))
    r  = max over groups g of chunk_reach(theta, op, group_readahead_depth(theta, op, g, dr, S))
    return r >= 1 and theta.off_at(op.name, COPY, chunk) == r
```

The derivation, stated as the docstring states it: the copy issued in trip `iter` fills chunk
`iter + off`, whose shared slot is `(iter + off) mod S_shared`. This trip *reads* chunks `iter`
through `iter + r`. Which relationship the copy has with those reads is decided by **which of them
its slot lands on**:

| Condition | The copy's slot is | Relationship | Order |
|---|---|---|---|
| `off == r` | the crossing chunk the read-ahead reaches into | RAW | copy **first** |
| `off != r` | a chunk read earlier this trip, or none | WAR, or nothing | copy **last** |

Worked at the two shipping points, which both have `S_shared = 2` and `r = 1` and which go
**opposite** ways:

```
one-deep global prefetch   off=1   slot (iter+1) mod 2   trip reads iter, iter+1
                                   -> lands on the CROSSING read  -> copy FIRST
two-deep global prefetch   off=2   slot (iter+2) mod 2 = iter mod 2
                                   -> lands on the CURRENT read   -> copy LAST
```

##### 9.2.3 The defect this replaced, and why it is the canonical example

An earlier version of this predicate returned `S_shared > r`. That is `2 > 1`, i.e. **True**, at
*both* shipping points — so the two-deep-prefetch kernels were emitted copy-first, and the copy then
overwrote the shared buffer the trip was still consuming. It miscompared on hardware as soon as the
steady body actually ran (`T − M ≥ 1` steady trips): `K = 256` for the two-deep case, where `M = 2`.
The one-deep case, where `M = 1`, had already shown the same class of error at `K = 128`.

The reason a plausible predicate went wrong is worth stating in general terms, because it is the
dominant bug shape in this package: **"when the shared depth equals the reach" describes when
copy-first *fails within* the `off == r` branch. It is not a standalone predicate for choosing the
branch.** A condition lifted out of its branch and promoted to the top of the decision is True on
the common case and wrong on the sibling.

Two tests pin it, and the pairing is the point:

* `test_copy_order_follows_which_chunk_the_copy_fills` — parametrized over four
  (prefetch depth, local prefetch) combinations, asserting `r`, `copy_must_be_first`, membership in
  `copy_first_operands`, and that `chunk_crossing_violations` is empty (both points are emittable).
* `test_emitted_steady_body_puts_the_copy_where_the_predicate_says` — walks the **emitted** steady
  body from `build_ir`, extracts the sequence of copy/read movements, and asserts the first one.

The second test exists because "the predicate and the emitted order were consistent with each other
and both wrong": a test of either alone passes. Pinning the two shipping points *against each other*
is what makes the pair bite. If you add a third shipping prefetch depth, extend both.

##### 9.2.4 `placement.py:copy_first_operands`

```
copy_first_operands(theta, S) -> frozenset[str]
    = { op.name : op has some hop with dst == SHARED
                  and copy_must_be_first(theta, op, S) }
```

The σ_c input. `emit.build_ir` calls it exactly once and passes the frozen set to every
`_order_sigma_c` call, so the ordering decision is derived once per schedule point and cannot drift
between the prologue, the steady body, the drain and the degenerate short-loop arm. Returning a
`frozenset` rather than a list is deliberate: the set is captured in a closure and read many times,
and immutability makes accidental mutation by a caller impossible.

**Known sharp edge (#213, still open).** A fused movement group (section 1.10) whose members
disagree — one member wants copy-first, another copy-last — is resolved by `any()` on the consumer
side rather than being rejected. One cooperative instruction cannot be both first and last, so a
mixed group silently gets one member's answer. It is unreachable on the shipping path because every
fused group's members share their prefetch depth, but nothing enforces that. If you widen fusion,
make this a refusal.

#### 9.3 `placement.py:chunk_crossing_violations` — admissibility of the (dr, off) pair

##### 9.3.1 Concept: the shared-buffering companion to the register floor

The read-ahead needs two kinds of buffering, and they are sized by two different derivations:

* **Register buffering** — the live-peak floor `L` bounds the rotation width from below
  (section 1.8, section 4.4). Too narrow and two live values share one register name.
* **Shared buffering** — the copy must have run *early enough* that the chunk the read-ahead
  reaches into is already resident. That is a constraint relating `off(copy, chunk)` to `r`.

`chunk_crossing_violations` is the closed form of the second one. It returns a list of tuples
`(operand_name, dr_g, r, off_copy, required)` — one entry per violating operand — and the empty list
means the schedule point is emittable in this respect.

##### 9.3.2 Why the bound has two forms

A chunk `c` is copied in steady trip `c − off(copy, chunk)`. Given the refill-after-read freeze
(the default rule that a copy sits *after* the reads it might overwrite), the copy of chunk
`iter + r` precedes the read that wants it **only if it was issued in an earlier trip**. Naively
that gives `off(copy, chunk) ≥ r + 1`.

But the `+1` is only demanded in the copy-**last** case. When `copy_must_be_first` holds, the copy
is issued *ahead of* this trip's reads, so being issued in the same trip is enough and `off ≥ r`
suffices. Hence:

```
need = r      if copy_must_be_first(theta, op, S)
       r + 1  otherwise
violation iff off(copy, chunk) < need
```

An earlier version used `r + 1` unconditionally and would have rejected the shipping point
`S_shared = 2, off(copy) = 1, r = 1` — a configuration that is emittable and correct. The `+1` is a
**placement fact about σ_c**, not a fixed inflation of the offset, and that phrasing is the thing to
remember: any rule that mentions "one extra trip" is probably conditional on which side of the reads
the copy sits.

##### 9.3.3 The algorithm

```
chunk_crossing_violations(theta, S) -> list[(name, dr_g, r, off_copy, need)]:
    chunk = theta.reduction_chunk_name();  if None: return []
    bad = []
    for op in theta.operands:
        if no hop of op has dst == SHARED:      continue   # no shared residency to size
        dr = theta.off_at(op.name, READ, _substep_level_name(theta))
        for group in op.fragment.groups():
            dr_g = group_readahead_depth(theta, op, group, dr, S)
            r    = chunk_reach(theta, op, dr_g)
            if r <= 0:                          continue
            off_copy = theta.off_at(op.name, COPY, chunk)
            need = r if copy_must_be_first(theta, op, S) else r + 1
            if off_copy < need:
                bad.append((op.name, dr_g, r, off_copy, need));  break   # one report per operand
    return bad
```

The `break` after the first violating group is deliberate: the message is diagnostic, and listing
every group of a many-group fragment would bury the operand-level fact. If you ever need per-group
detail, add a second function rather than removing the break — several callers format this list
directly into an error string.

##### 9.3.4 Why a closed form at all, when the ledger would catch it

The obligation ledger catches this by construction: a read whose producing copy has not been issued
yet has no discharging producer, and the whole-tree gate reports it. So `chunk_crossing_violations`
is strictly redundant with the ledger *as a correctness check*.

It exists because it lets the decoder **prune invalid `(dr, off(copy))` combinations up front**,
instead of discovering them at ledger-walk time. The difference matters for two reasons. First,
error quality: a closed-form rejection can say "operand A, derived read-ahead 1, reach 1, prefetch
depth 1, needs 2", whereas a ledger failure says "obligation X is undischarged" and leaves the
reader to reconstruct why. Second, cost: the ledger walk is over the whole emitted tree, and a
schedule search that evaluates many candidate points wants to reject the bad ones before emission.

The failure mode being prevented is not a tuning wart. If the bound is violated, the *first* steady
trip reads a shared buffer that was never written, and every later trip reads the copy that was
issued after it in the same body. Both produce wrong numerics, not slow ones.

**Complexity** O(#operands × #groups × |inner_modes|), with all three factors small (2–4 operands,
1–2 groups, 3–6 modes). It calls `copy_must_be_first` inside the group loop, which recomputes the
same `max` over groups — a small quadratic that nobody has needed to remove. If profiling ever
points here, hoist `copy_must_be_first` out of the loop; the value does not depend on `group`.

#### 9.4 Level naming — where an op-class lives

Two small functions answer "which loop level is this?" and both are single-derivation points that
replaced multiple divergent call sites.

##### 9.4.1 `placement.py:_substep_level_name`

```
_substep_level_name(theta) -> str | None:
    red = theta.reduction_names()
    sub = innermost mode of theta.inner_modes() whose name is in red
    return sub.name if sub is not None else None
```

The **innermost reduction inner mode** — the level that `off(read, substep)` is keyed on. Returns
`None` for a schedule point with no reduction inner axis at all (a degenerate hand-built theta;
every parameter-derived point has one). Callers must handle `None`: `readahead_reach` returns 0,
`copy_must_be_first` passes `None` straight into `off_at`, which misses every key and yields 0.

It reads `reversed(inner_modes())` rather than filtering-and-taking-last for no reason other than
economy; the two are identical. The reason it is a function rather than an inlined expression is
that four call sites in this file, plus one in `ledger.py`, all need it — `emit.py` does NOT; it
carries its own re-derivation of the same fact, `_reduction_inner_mode` — and an earlier
round of this work had two of them computing it as `reduction_modes()[-1]` (which is *not* the same
thing when a reduction mode is outer).

##### 9.4.2 `placement.py:op_class_level` — the home level

This is the canonical answer to "at which loop level is this op-class emitted?", and the term for
it in this report is the op-class's **home level**.

```
op_class_level(theta, op, role) -> str | None:
    chunk = theta.reduction_chunk_name()
    if role == COPY:
        inner = { m.name for m in theta.inner_modes() }
        rm    = first mode of op.region_modes that is an inner mode, else None
        return rm if (rm is not None and max(1, op.split) > 1) else chunk
    pres = _presence(theta, op)
    return pres[-1] if pres else chunk
```

By role:

* **read** — the innermost mode of its presence set; the reduction chunk when the presence set is
  empty. An operand whose presence has been emptied (every axis broadcast away, or absorbed into a
  movement quantum) is emitted once per chunk.
* **copy** — the **region mode** when the movement is actually region-split (`split > 1` and the
  region mode is an inner mode), which places the copy one level deeper, one instruction per
  region; otherwise the reduction chunk, because a bulk cooperative copy has an empty inner presence
  set (section 1.3).
* **store** — falls through the `read` branch, i.e. the innermost of its presence set. No store
  op-class exists yet; the epilogue is unmodeled (#116).

Returns `None` only for a legacy schedule point carrying no outer mode and an empty presence, which
no parameter path produces.

**Why this matters beyond bookkeeping.** The home level is the second input the cross-level boundary
term needs (§9.6): *an offset at a level outer to an op-class's home is what relocates its instances
across the enclosing boundary*. Before `op_class_level` existed, `emit.copy_insts` hardcoded the
copy level to the reduction chunk (#164) — which is right for a bulk copy and wrong for a
region-split one — and `emit.py` computed the read level inline. The comments in `emit.py` record
that "the two answers have always been the same, and now there is one of them".

**Sharp edge.** The `region_modes` lookup uses `getattr(op, "region_modes", ())`, a defensive
default for operands built before that field existed. Every current construction path sets it. If
you are hardening this module, that `getattr` is safe to turn into a direct attribute access, and
doing so would make a missing field a loud error rather than a silent "copy sits at the chunk".

#### 9.5 The peel, per level

*Reference restatement.* The primary treatment of the peel — the decomposition from first
principles, the two refusals inside a derivation function, the reach bump, the consumer list and
the test contract — is 8.2. This subsection restates the data structure, its four accessors and
the builder as a self-contained reference, because 9.1's reach argument and 9.6's boundary term
both key on `PeelDepths` and a reader working through this section should not have to page back.
The two renderings of `_peel_depths` are checked against each other; if you change the function,
change both (7.0).

##### 9.5.1 Concept: the peel is a vector, not an integer

Section 1.6 and the peel decomposition (section 6.3) establish that a pipelined loop of trip count
`T` with retime depth `M` becomes an `M`-step prologue, a steady region of `T − M` trips, and an
`M`-step drain. The subtlety this subsection is about is that `M` is **per level**:

> For each level `ℓ` that carries an offset, `M_ℓ = max over op-classes p of off(p, ℓ)`. A level
> with `M_ℓ = 0` needs no peel; a level with `M_ℓ > 0` gets its own prologue and drain of depth
> `M_ℓ`.

and the defect that replaces:

> A decoder that keys peel depth only on the innermost outer level silently drops every
> coarser-level offset.

That was exactly what this code did before: it read `off_at(op, reduction_chunk_name())` and
returned one integer. Any offset at a coarser outer level — the persistent / grid-stride tile loop
that #113 will add — was invisible, and the emitted schedule would ignore it *and still report an
empty obligation ledger*, which is the one failure mode the certificate exists to rule out.

##### 9.5.2 `placement.py:PeelDepths` — the data structure

A frozen dataclass with six fields, and the discipline of the whole peel construction lives in
keeping them apart.

| Field | Shape | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `per_level` | `{level_name: M_ℓ}` | Only levels with `M_ℓ > 0`, in `ord` order (outer → inner). |
| `offs` | `{(op_name, role, level_name): δ}` | The per-op-class positive offsets each `M_ℓ` is the max of. Per-op-class because the peel is **staggered** by each op-class's own δ, not by the level's max. |
| `dr` | `int` | The substep read-ahead **request**, `max over reads of off(read, substep)`. |
| `chunk` | `str \| None` | The reduction-chunk level's name, or `None` for a legacy point. |
| `reach` | `int` | `r`, the **derived** chunk reach (`readahead_reach`). |
| `deferrals` | `{(op_name, role, level_name): δ}` for δ < 0 | The negative half of the retime matrix, kept apart and never folded into `M_ℓ`. |

Three of these distinctions are the entire content of three separate historical defects:

* **`dr` versus `reach`.** `dr` is what the schedule point *asks for*; `reach` is how many whole
  chunks the advance the emitter *actually issues* crosses into. They differ whenever the width band
  clamps a group. Every consumer that counts **chunks** must read `reach`; every consumer that works
  in **substeps** (the read-ahead prologue, the steady shift) derives its own per-group depth from
  `dr`. Reading `dr` where `reach` belongs is the eight-lost-local-reads defect of §9.1.5.
* **`per_level` versus `offs`.** The level's maximum sizes the *region* (how many prologue and drain
  steps exist); each op-class's own δ decides *which* of those steps that op-class appears in. An
  emitter that staggers by the max issues every copy in every ramp step.
* **`offs` versus `deferrals`.** See §9.5.4.

##### 9.5.3 The four accessors

* **`PeelDepths.depth(level) -> int`** — `M_ℓ` for one level, 0 when absent. Total: an unknown level
  name returns 0 rather than raising, which is what the callers want (they ask about levels that may
  not carry an offset).
* **`PeelDepths.M -> int`** (a property) — `depth(self.chunk)`, the depth at the reduction chunk.
  This is the one level `emit.build_ir` currently peels, because a coarser outer level's peel needs
  an enclosing `Loop` node that does not exist yet (#113). The docstring is careful about why this
  is a *property* rather than the only stored number: `peeled_levels()` reports every level that
  *wants* a peel, so `M` and the set of wanted peels cannot silently disagree — the emitter checks
  the second and refuses when it exceeds the first.
* **`PeelDepths.peeled_levels() -> list`** — every level with `M_ℓ > 0`, outer → inner (dict
  insertion order is `ord` order by construction). More than one entry means the schedule point asks
  for a nested peel.
* **`PeelDepths.copy_off() -> {op_name: δ}`** — the staggered-peel input `build_ir` walks, filtered
  to `role == COPY and level == chunk`. The emitter's ramp rule is "copy for operand *p* is present
  in ramp step *t* iff `off_p ≥ M − t`", and in the drain "iff `off_p ≤ M − 1 − t`". Note that this
  filter is exactly why an `off(read, chunk)` entry is **accepted, deepens the peel, and is applied
  to nothing** — see §9.5.5.

##### 9.5.4 `placement.py:_peel_depths` — the builder

```
_peel_depths(theta) -> PeelDepths:
    red     = theta.reduction_names()
    chunk   = theta.reduction_chunk_name()
    substep = innermost inner mode whose name is in red

    offs, deferrals = {}, {}
    for op in theta.operands:
        if op.hops and trajectory_sense(op) == REVERSE:
            raise ValueError(...)                       # see below
        for hop in op.hops:
            for m in theta.ord:
                d = theta.off_at(op, hop.role, m.name)
                if   d > 0: offs[(op.name, hop.role, m.name)] = d
                elif d < 0: deferrals[(op.name, hop.role, m.name)] = d

    per_level = { m.name : max(d for entries at level m.name)
                  for m in theta.ord if any entry at that level }

    dr    = max over shared->register reads of off_at(op, READ, substep), floored at 0
    reach = readahead_reach(theta) if dr else 0
    if reach and chunk is not None and reach > per_level.get(chunk, 0):
        per_level[chunk] = reach
    per_level = re-sorted into ord order            # the chunk bump can break insertion order
    return PeelDepths(per_level, offs, dr, chunk, reach, deferrals)
```

Every level name is **derived from the schedule point** — outer levels from `outer_modes()`, the
substep from the innermost reduction inner mode. There are no string literals, which is what makes
a renamed or added level work without touching this function.

##### 9.5.5 The three refusals `_peel_depths` participates in

`_peel_depths` itself raises once; the other two refusals are raised by
`emit._check_peel_is_emittable` from the structure `_peel_depths` builds. All three are refusals
rather than best-effort emissions, and the reason is uniform: a half-applied offset produces a
schedule that ignores what was asked for *and still certifies an empty ledger*.

**(a) Reverse trajectory — raised here.** If any operand's trajectory sense is `REVERSE` (an
epilogue store round-trip), `_peel_depths` raises `ValueError` immediately. The reasoning in the
comment is the important part and is easy to lose:

> The **sense** is per op-class; the **role** is per hop. Everything below reads `hop.role`, which is
> keyed on `(src, dst)` alone and therefore cannot tell a forward read from a store round-trip's
> read-back leg.

A reverse-trajectory op-class needs the *reflected* peel — trailing δ instances hoisted **forward**
into the successor iteration, prologue and drain swapped. That is not emitted (#116). Building it
the forward way is what keying on the role alone would do, and it would *look* correct while being
backwards. Refusing turns a latent defect into a missing feature.

**(b) A read offset at an outer level — raised in `emit`.** `off(read, chunk)` is expressible (it is
a distinct key from `off(copy, chunk)` precisely because the map is keyed by op-class, section 1.6)
and `_peel_depths` records it in `offs`, so it folds into `M_ℓ` and moves the guard, the prologue
depth, the steady bound and the drain step count. But `build_ir` staggers over `copy_off()`, which
filters `role == COPY`, so every read instruction keeps its **unshifted** slot and source slot.
Neither the requested schedule nor a refusal — half-applied, with the ledger reporting empty.
`emit._check_peel_is_emittable` refuses it by name.

The comment in `emit.py` explains why that check is *there* and not in `boundary_hoists`: this is a
cross-level boundary term by definition, but `boundary_hoists` drops it on its third condition
(§9.6.3), and that condition is load-bearing for the region-split copy that ships today. The
distinction is per-role — a copy's ordinary prefetch level *is* the chunk, a read's is the substep —
so the narrow refusal belongs where it can name the role.

**(c) A peel at a coarser outer level — raised in `emit`.** `peeled_levels()` reports every level
wanting a peel; any outer level other than the chunk gets a `NotImplementedError` naming the levels
and their `M_ℓ`. Inner levels are explicitly *not* refused: an inner level's `M_ℓ` is real
(`off(read, substep)` gives the substep level one) but needs no prologue/drain **region**, because
an inner level is statically unrolled and its peel is absorbed into the unroll — primed by
`readahead_prologue`, sustained by `_readahead_shift`, ended by the drain's suppression guard.

##### 9.5.6 Deferral is not a negative offset

The retime matrix is typed non-negative: `off : (op-class × level) → ℕ`. The `retime` schedule move
*sets* the entry rather than subtracting from it, so no legal sequence of moves reaches a negative
value. A negative entry is therefore **ill-typed**, not merely unmodeled, and `_peel_depths` records
it in `deferrals` — separately, so it can be rejected with a real message — rather than dropping it
or letting it perturb `M_ℓ`.

Deferral, the thing an epilogue store actually wants (issue |δ| iterations *later*), needs no
negative number. It is a **positive** offset on a **reverse-trajectory** op-class, which gets the
reflected peel. Direction comes from the trajectory sense, never from the sign.

`test_a_negative_off_is_rejected_as_ill_typed` pins all three halves: `deferrals` captures the
entry, `depth("iter")` is unperturbed at 2, `offs` holds only positive values, and
`decoder.emit_mainloop` raises with the message `negative off is ill-typed`. It deliberately puts
the negative offset on an existing read op-class rather than on a store, because the store hop has
no completion-class mapping yet and the test is about the sign, not about stores.

##### 9.5.7 Tests, and what they fix in place

* `test_peel_depth_is_per_level_not_one_integer` — two-deep global prefetch plus one-deep local
  prefetch gives `per_level == {"iter": 2, "K_inner": 1}`, `depth("nope") == 0`, `M == 2`,
  `chunk == "iter"`, `copy_off() == {"A": 2, "B": 2}`, `dr == 1`. It asserts the *whole* structure,
  which is the right shape for a test of a summary object.
* `test_per_op_class_peel_offsets_stay_staggered` — with a per-operand prefetch depth override
  (operand A at 1, operand B at 2), `copy_off() == {"A": 1, "B": 2}` while `M == 2`. This is the
  test that would catch a regression to "stagger by the level max".

**Complexity.** `_peel_depths` is O(#operands × #hops × |ord|) for the offset scan — at most about
`4 × 3 × 7 = 84` dictionary lookups — plus one `readahead_reach`, which is the real cost because of
the `build_S` call inside it (§9.1.7). It is called at least four times per kernel from independent
entry points (`emit.build_ir`, `ledger`, `render`, `loopir_to_gir`), each rebuilding the depth map.
Threading `S` in is the single highest-value cheap optimization in this section.

#### 9.6 The cross-level boundary term — offsets that relocate rather than peel

*Reference restatement.* The primary treatment — what the relocation means, why it is not a
prefetch, why the decoder refuses it and what lifting the refusal requires — is 8.3. This
subsection gives the record and the three conditions again as a reference entry, because the
quantum admissibility argument at 9.8 uses the same coordinate enumeration.

##### 9.6.1 Concept

Everything in §9.5 assumes the offset sits at the op-class's *own* home level: a copy prefetching
its own chunk level, a read prefetching its own substep level. That is the ordinary staggered peel.

A different thing happens when an offset sits at a level **outer to** the op-class's home:

> When `off(p, ℓ_outer) = δ > 0` for an op-class `p` whose home level is inner to `ℓ_outer`, the
> outer offset hoists `p`'s leading δ instances of the inner nest **out of** the current `ℓ_outer`
> iteration and **into the drain of the previous** `ℓ_outer` iteration — equivalently, at the first
> outer iteration, into the outer prologue. This is a determinate relocation: the δ instances are
> exactly inner-coordinates `[0 .. δ)` of the current outer tile.

This is a **relocation**, not a peel: the instances do not get replicated into ramp steps, they move
bodily into a different loop iteration's drain region. The canonical case is the persistent /
grid-stride tile loop: a copy whose home is the reduction-chunk loop, retimed on an enclosing
`gtile` loop, prefetches the *next output tile's* first δ chunks during this tile's drain.

##### 9.6.2 `placement.py:BoundaryHoist` — the record

A frozen dataclass with six fields describing one such relocation:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `op`, `role` | The op-class whose instances relocate. |
| `level` | `ℓ_outer` — the level whose offset does the hoisting. Must be an **outer** (runtime-trip) level, because the relocation target is "the drain of the previous iteration of this level", and only an outer level has a prologue/drain region to relocate into. |
| `home` | The op-class's own emission level, strictly **inner** to `level`. `home == level` is the ordinary staggered peel, not a relocation. |
| `delta` | δ — how many leading inner-nest instances move. |
| `coords` | Those instances, as concrete presence-coordinate dictionaries in `ord` order. |

##### 9.6.3 `placement.py:_leading_inner_coords` and `placement.py:boundary_hoists`

`_leading_inner_coords(home, delta)` is the trivial helper that materializes the relocated set:

```
_leading_inner_coords(home, delta) = tuple({home: i} for i in range(max(0, delta)))
```

The inner coordinate is the **home level's own index**, because that is the level whose instances
the outer offset relocates, so the set is simply its leading δ values. The `max(0, ...)` makes a
non-positive δ produce the empty tuple rather than raising, which keeps the function total.

`boundary_hoists(theta, pd)` enumerates every boundary term the schedule point carries, outer level
first, from a previously-built `PeelDepths`:

```
boundary_hoists(theta, pd) -> list[BoundaryHoist]:
    names = [m.name for m in theta.ord]                 # outer -> inner
    outer = { m.name for m in theta.outer_modes() }
    out = []
    for (opname, role, level), delta in pd.offs.items():
        if level not in outer:                 continue   # (1)
        home = op_class_level(theta, theta.op(opname), role)
        if home is None or home not in names:  continue
        if names.index(home) <= names.index(level): continue   # (2)
        if home not in outer:                  continue   # (3)
        out.append(BoundaryHoist(op=opname, role=role, level=level, home=home,
                                 delta=delta, coords=_leading_inner_coords(home, delta)))
    return sorted(out, key=(index of level in ord, op, role))
```

**Three conditions, all necessary.** They are the whole content of the function and each one is
answering a different confusion:

1. **`level` is an outer level.** Only an outer (runtime-trip) level has the prologue/drain region
   the instances relocate into. An offset at an inner, statically unrolled level crosses no
   boundary — the inner nest has no back edge. That case is the ordinary substep read-ahead, whose
   reach into the next chunk is modelled by `chunk_reach` and whose warm-up is
   `readahead_prologue`. Pinned by `test_an_inner_level_off_is_not_a_boundary_term`: the substep
   level's `M_ℓ` is still recorded as 1, but `boundary_hoists` returns `[]` and emission proceeds.

2. **`home` is strictly inner to `level` in `ord` order.** `home == level` is the ordinary staggered
   peel — a copy prefetching its own chunk level — and `home` outer to `level` is not a relocation
   in this direction at all.

3. **`home` is itself an outer (looped) level.** This is the discriminator that separates the
   canonical case from ordinary prefetch, and conditions 1–2 alone do not separate them:

   * *home outer* — e.g. `off(copy, gtile)` with home `iter`. The op-class has a whole **enclosed
     iteration space** per `gtile` trip, and δ of those iterations' instances move into the previous
     trip's drain. A relocation.
   * *home inner* — e.g. `off(copy, iter)` for a **region-split** copy, whose home is the region
     mode `M_split`. The op-class has a fixed unrolled fan per trip and every member of it stays in
     the trip; δ shifts which **chunk** the instances fetch, not which trip they are issued in. That
     is ordinary global prefetch.

##### 9.6.4 The regression condition 3 exists for

`test_region_split_copy_is_NOT_a_cross_level_boundary_term` is explicit that this is history, not a
hypothetical: **the first implementation of `boundary_hoists` omitted condition 3 and flagged every
shipping region-split kernel, refusing to emit them.** The test builds a region-split point, asserts
the fixture is genuinely split (`A.split > 1` — a non-vacuity guard), asserts the precondition that
makes it *look* like a boundary term (`op_class_level(th, A, COPY) == "M_split"`, which is not the
reduction chunk), then asserts the verdict is `[]` and that emission still succeeds.

##### 9.6.5 The positive case, built by mutation

No TensileLite parameter expresses a persistent outer level yet, so the positive test builds one by
`dataclasses.replace`: it prepends a `Mode("gtile")` (extent 0, hence outer) to `ord` and adds
`off[("A", COPY, "gtile")] = δ`.

`test_a_coarser_outer_off_is_a_boundary_term_and_is_REFUSED_not_dropped` then asserts two things,
and the second is the point:

* the term is **derived** — `pd.depth("gtile") == 1`, `pd.depth("iter") == 2`, three peeled levels,
  exactly one hoist with `(op, level, home, delta) == ("A", "gtile", "iter", 1)` and
  `coords == ({"iter": 0},)`;
* `decoder.emit_mainloop` **raises** `NotImplementedError`. Silently dropping the term would produce
  a schedule that ignores the coarser offset and still reports an empty ledger.

`test_a_deeper_coarser_off_relocates_proportionally_many_instances` pins that δ instances relocate,
not one: at δ = 3 the coords are `({"iter": 0}, {"iter": 1}, {"iter": 2})`.

##### 9.6.6 State, cost and extension

`boundary_hoists` is **empty for every schedule point the parameter path builds today**, because
`translate` sets only `off(copy, chunk)` — whose home is the chunk itself, or a region mode that is
inner and unrolled — and `off(read, substep)`, whose level is inner. It becomes non-empty the moment
a coarser outer level exists.

**Complexity** O(|offs| × |ord|) because of the two `names.index(...)` linear scans per entry;
`|offs|` is at most a few dozen and `|ord|` at most about seven, so this is noise. If a future
schedule point ever carries hundreds of offsets, precompute `{name: index}` once outside the loop —
that is the only change needed.

**What to do when #113 lands.** The three conditions stay; what changes is the consumer. Today
`emit._check_peel_is_emittable` turns a non-empty result into a refusal. The emitter will instead
need to (a) build the enclosing `Loop` for `ℓ_outer`, (b) emit its own prologue and drain of depth
`M_{ℓ_outer}`, and (c) place each `BoundaryHoist.coords` entry into the *previous* outer iteration's
drain region, or into the outer prologue at the first iteration. `coords` already gives exactly the
instance set to move, so the structure is designed for that use; nothing in `boundary_hoists` should
need to change.

**Sharp edge to be aware of.** `boundary_hoists` iterates `pd.offs.items()`, whose order is
insertion order (operand, then hop, then `ord`). The result is explicitly re-sorted by
`(ord index of level, op, role)`, so the output is deterministic. Keep that sort: two of the
downstream consumers format the list into an error message, and a nondeterministic message defeats
the golden-output comparisons used to validate that codegen is unchanged.

#### 9.7 Mark placement policy — the downstream realization

This subsection documents `Tensile/Lowering/gir/passes/placement.py`, the namesake pass named in
§9.0.1. It belongs here because the policy it implements is the direct realization of the time
structure §9.1–§9.6 derive, and because the three rules it encodes — *descriptor changes earliest*,
*read-pointer swap at the midpoint*, *one mark per incoming path* — are each the answer to a
question this section has already set up.

##### 9.7.1 Concept: a Mark has a legal range, not a point

Downstream of the schedule decoder, the loop nest is lowered into a static-single-assignment control
flow graph (GIR). Two physical registers in that graph are *mutated* rather than re-derived:

* the **shared-memory read pointer** — one register holding the base address the register reads use.
  Advancing to the next generation of the rotating shared ring is a **swap** of that pointer.
* the **bulk-copy descriptor** — the register (or register pair) describing the global source of the
  cooperative copy. Advancing it to the next chunk is a **gr_increment**; switching which buffer it
  writes is also a descriptor mutation.

An instruction that performs one of these mutations is called a **Mark**. The insight the design
turns on is that a Mark does not have one correct position: a read-pointer swap from generation
`gen_from` to `gen_to` may legally sit **anywhere after the last access that uses `gen_from` and
before the first access that uses `gen_to`**. Baking a fixed body index into the analysis that
discovers the Mark is *premature realization* — the mistake an earlier hand-rolled walker made.

So the lowering is split into three layers, deliberately mirroring the shape used by the assembly
optimizer's wait-count and liveness passes:

1. a **region analysis** returns a plan of `PendingMark`s; the IR is untouched;
2. a **placement** stage picks a concrete point inside each region; the IR is still untouched;
3. a single **apply** pass inserts each Mark before its resolved anchor — the only IR mutator.

`Lowering/gir/region.py` defines the vocabulary: a `Region(block, after, before, policy)` where
`after` and `before` are **opaque anchors** (a body node, or the sentinels `BLOCK_ENTRY` /
`BLOCK_EXIT`), and a `PendingMark(mark, region, anchor)` whose `anchor` is `None` until the
placement stage fills it. A region may span a block edge — after a node in a predecessor, before a
node in a successor — which is how a cross-block swap is expressed with no single index.

##### 9.7.2 `Lowering/gir/passes/placement.py:PlacementPass`

The pass is 56 lines and has four definitions.

**`PlacementPass.run(prog, am)`** — iterates `prog.pending` and sets `pm.anchor = self._resolve(...)`
for each pending mark. Returns the empty tuple, meaning **no IR mutation**. That return value is the
pass framework's contract for "I changed no nodes", and it is what lets the pass run before the
verifier without the verifier needing to re-derive anything.

**`PlacementPass._resolve(prog, region)`** — the policy, in six lines:

```
_resolve(prog, region):
    body = prog.block(region.block).body
    lo = _slot(body, region.after,  opening=True)    # first legal slot
    hi = _slot(body, region.before, opening=False)   # one past the last legal slot
    if hi < lo:  return (region.block, region.before)     # malformed window: use stated bound
    idx = lo + (hi - lo)//2   if region.policy == MIDPOINT   else   lo
    return (region.block, body[idx] if idx < len(body) else BLOCK_EXIT)
```

**`PlacementPass._slot(body, anchor, opening)`** — converts an opaque anchor into an integer index.
`BLOCK_ENTRY` is slot 0; `BLOCK_EXIT` is `len(body)`; a body node maps to `i+1` when it is the
*opening* bound (place strictly **after** it) and to `i` when it is the closing bound (place
strictly **before** it). An anchor not found in the body falls back to 0 for the opening bound and
`len(body)` for the closing bound — i.e. the widest window — which is total but silent; see the
sharp edges below.

The anchor returned is expressed as "the node to insert *before*", because the apply pass inserts
before its anchor. So "immediately after node X" is expressed as "before the node following X", and
`BLOCK_EXIT` when X ends the body. This double negative is the one genuinely confusing part of the
file and is worth re-reading before changing an index.

##### 9.7.3 Rule 1 — every descriptor change goes EARLIEST

`region.EARLIEST` means: land immediately after `region.after`, the access whose use of the
descriptor this supersedes.

**Why it is right.** The descriptor feeds the bulk load. Every cycle between the descriptor update
and the load that consumes it is *overlap* — cycles in which the address arithmetic has already
retired and the memory pipeline can start. Pushing the update as early as the window allows
maximizes that overlap and costs nothing, because the window's lower bound is precisely the last
instruction that needed the old value.

**Why the same rule covers both descriptor mutations.** The advance (`gr_increment`) and the
buffer switch (the copy-hop swap) mutate the same physical resource and feed the same consumer.
Giving them different policies would mean two updates to one register landing at different points
in a window, which serializes them for no reason. The memory note that records this policy states
it as one rule covering "gr_inc AND the TDM swap", and the source states it the same way. Treat any
future proposal to split them as a red flag: it means someone has found the two windows to differ,
and the right response is to ask why, not to add a policy.

**What breaks under the alternative.** The pass *used to* return `region.before` for every Mark and
let the apply pass insert before it — the **latest** legal point — under a method that was actually
named `_earliest_legal`. That is a full window's worth of lost overlap on every descriptor update,
in a loop body where the bulk load is the longest-latency operation present.

There is an important sequencing note here: the fix was only *safe* once the windows were real.
While `region.after` was an underived `BLOCK_ENTRY` placeholder rather than a value computed by the
dataflow solver, "earliest" meant "block entry", which is before the last use of the old descriptor
value and therefore wrong. The policy change and the analysis rewrite had to land in that order.
Anyone tempted to sharpen a placement policy should check the same thing first: **is the window
bound derived, or is it a placeholder?**

##### 9.7.4 Rule 2 — the shared read-pointer swap goes at the MIDPOINT

`region.MIDPOINT` means: land midway between the last use of `gen_from` and the first use of
`gen_to`.

**Why it is not the descriptor rule.** The read pointer is bounded by **two different resources**.
Its lower bound is the last read that still needs the old generation; its upper bound is the first
read that needs the new one. Both bounds are real consumers with real latency, so slamming the swap
to either edge creates a dependency stall against that edge's consumer:

* at the earliest point, the swap issues immediately after the last old-generation read, and the
  address arithmetic contends with the load pipeline still draining those reads;
* at the latest point, the swap issues immediately before the first new-generation read, so that
  read waits on the pointer update with nothing to hide it.

The midpoint puts independent work on both sides. It is a heuristic, not a proof, and the source is
honest about that: the argument in the docstring is that the region is "bounded by two DIFFERENT
resources, so it is not the descriptor rule and must not be slammed to either edge".

**Why the policy travels with the Region and not with the pass.** This is the structural point. The
policy field lives on `Region`, so the analysis that *discovers* the window also declares what kind
of mutation it is. A single global policy in `PlacementPass` would be wrong, because the right
answer differs by what the Mark mutates — and the two analyses (`swap_regions`, `gr_increment`) run
independently and produce both kinds. Putting the policy on the pass would force the pass to
re-derive the mark's kind from the mark itself, duplicating a fact the analysis already knows.

##### 9.7.5 Rule 3 — one Mark per incoming path

The third rule is not in `PlacementPass` at all; it is in the analysis that produces the pending
marks, `Lowering/gir/analyses/value_placement.py:ValuePlacementSolver`. It is stated here because it
is the rule most often got wrong, and because it is what makes the first two rules sound.

**The problem.** One physical register must hold a specific value at each access, and a Mark is the
only thing that changes it. The requirement is:

> exactly one def on **every** path between two accesses that need different values, and none
> anywhere else.

On a straight-line body that is trivial. On a control-flow graph with joins — and the lowered loop
nest has several: the steady loop header joins the prologue and the back edge, the drain chain joins
the loop exit and the short-loop arm — it is not.

**Why edges, and why this replaced a backward walk.** Placing the def **on an edge** makes the
requirement structural: an edge is traversed exactly once per path through it, so no reasoning about
domination or double emission is needed. A hand-rolled backward walk that hops predecessors until it
finds an access has to *prove* those properties and cannot, because it has no fixpoint — on any join
or multi-path region it silently answers for one path. It also moves defs that the value analysis
already assumed were elsewhere, so the emitted code stops matching the propagation that justified it.

**The two fixpoints.** The solver is the classic code-motion pair, specialized to a single register
(so there is no expression to hash and no redundancy to eliminate — only placement):

```
AVAIL  (forward)   avail_out[b] — the value the register holds LEAVING b:
                   the requirement of b's last access, or a pass-through when b has none.
ANTIC  (backward)  antic_in[b]  — the value required ENTERING b:
                   the requirement of b's first access, or the meet over successors.

a def is needed   on edge p->b  iff  avail_out[p], re-expressed in b's frame != antic_in[b]
                  inside b      between consecutive accesses whose requirements differ
```

The lattice is three-valued: `BOTTOM` (nothing reaches or demands here yet), a concrete value, and
`TOP` (a genuine conflict). `value_placement.meet` is the standard one — `BOTTOM` is the identity,
equal values agree, disagreement is `TOP` — and `TOP` is **reported, never silently resolved**.

The dependency between the two fixpoints runs one way only, so there is no circularity: `solve`
runs `antic()` first and hands the result to `avail(antic)`, which consults it through `_exit_want`
to decide the post-def value a block LEAVES; the demand entering a block is fixed by its own
accesses or its successors', and the edge def is what reconciles them. (The module docstring still
says the two are independent; the signature `avail(self, antic)` is the truth.)

**Where "one Mark per incoming path" comes from.** `ValuePlacementSolver.solve` emits three
disjoint kinds of def, and the *exit def* is the one that realizes the rule:

* **intra-block** — between consecutive accesses in one block whose requirements differ;
* **exit def** — at block `b`'s end, when every successor agrees on a value `b` does not already
  hold (`_exit_want` returns that single agreed value, or `None` if the successors disagree or none
  demands anything). Its `Placement` carries `at_exit=True`, meaning it sits on **every** edge
  leaving that block;
* **head def** — at `b`'s start, when what actually arrives differs from what `b` demands, which
  happens exactly when a predecessor could not place an exit def because *its* successors
  disagreed.

At a join with several predecessors arriving with different values, the fix is therefore **one exit
def in each predecessor** — one Mark per incoming path — and *not* one Mark at the join. A single
Mark at the join cannot be right: there is one register, and it would have to hold a different
"from" value depending on which edge arrived.

The solver enforces exactly that. The head-def branch is guarded by `len(preds) <= 1`; with more
than one predecessor it calls `on_conflict("critical-edge", ...)`, which the callers raise on. That
is the honest answer: a def on edge `p→b` is realizable at the end of `p` when `p` has one
successor, or at the head of `b` when `b` has one predecessor, and when **neither** holds the edge
must be *split*. Splitting is reported rather than resolved by picking a side, because picking a
side executes the def on a sibling path.

**The two refinements that made this survive contact with the real graph**, both worth knowing:

* *An ambiguous value nobody consumes is not a conflict.* When the arriving value is `TOP` but
  `antic` is `BOTTOM`, no consumer on any path from here ever reads the register, so two
  predecessors may leave it at different values with nothing able to observe the difference.
  Measured case: the folded short-loop entry makes the first drain block a join for the global-read
  address, where the prologue leaves chunk 2 and the loop leaves chunk 3 — but the drain issues no
  copies, so the demand is `BOTTOM` and neither value is used. Reporting that as an unsplittable
  critical edge asks the caller to reconcile a dead value.
* *A def placed at a block's exit changes the value leaving it.* The forward fixpoint propagates
  `leave` (post-def), not `body_out` (pre-def). Propagating the pre-def value makes the successor
  re-derive the same transition and emit a **second** def for it — a real double emit, which an
  accessless-block test catches.

**Frames.** Values are compared only after `edge_delta(p, b)` re-expresses them, so a block whose
chunk frame differs — the drain runs in a different chunk origin than the steady body — is directly
comparable. The `modulus` parameter makes the domain the integers mod the ring size for a rotating
pointer, and `None` leaves it the integers for a monotonically advancing address. That single
parameter is what lets the same solver serve the read pointer (a ring) and the copy descriptor (a
monotone address).

##### 9.7.6 Sharp edges in `PlacementPass`, and how to extend it

* **The malformed-window fallback is silent.** When `hi < lo` — the closing bound precedes the
  opening bound, which can only happen if the analysis produced an inconsistent region — `_resolve`
  returns `(region.block, region.before)`, i.e. it honours the stated closing bound and drops the
  opening one. That is a defensible recovery (the closing bound is the correctness-critical one:
  landing before the first new-generation use is what makes the swap take effect in time), but it is
  **not reported**. If you are chasing a mark that landed impossibly early, add a diagnostic here
  first.
* **`_slot`'s not-found fallback is also silent** and widens the window to the whole block. Both
  fallbacks exist because the anchor is opaque and a region may legitimately name a node in a
  different block. A stricter version would take the region's block into account and assert.
* **`_resolve` is a `classmethod` and `_slot` a `staticmethod`** with no state read from `self`. The
  pass carries no configuration. If you add a policy, add it as a new constant in
  `Lowering/gir/region.py` alongside `EARLIEST` and `MIDPOINT` and a new branch in the `idx =`
  expression — do **not** add a constructor argument, because the whole point of the design is that
  the policy travels with the region.
* **The midpoint is an integer bisection of the *node list*, not of a cost model.** Two nodes that
  take wildly different numbers of cycles count the same. If a future scheduling target makes that
  matter, the right change is to pass a per-node weight function into `_resolve` and bisect the
  cumulative weight; the region vocabulary needs no change.
* **Complexity** is O(|body|) per pending mark because `_slot` linearly scans the body for the
  anchor node, and it is called twice per mark. With `P` pending marks and a body of `B` nodes this
  is O(P·B). On the shipping matrix `P` is a handful (one read-pointer swap and one or two
  descriptor updates per block) and `B` is in the low hundreds, so it is negligible. If it ever is
  not, build one `{id(node): index}` dictionary per block before the loop — that turns it into
  O(B + P).

#### 9.8 The movement quantum — admissibility, and why the core does not decide it

##### 9.8.1 Recap of the abstraction

Section 1.9 defines the **movement quantum**: a description of how an op-class's *tiles* merge into
the instructions that move them, given as **two expressions over the tile coordinate**:

```
carrier(t)  ->  which instruction carries tile t  (tiles sharing a carrier are ONE movement)
slot(t)     ->  which position inside that instruction's destination holds t
```

`ir.QuantumMap` holds those two expressions and provides `carrier_of(t, env)`, `slot_of(t, env)`,
`group(t, extent, env)` (the carrier preimage — the coordinates one instruction serves) and
`regs(t, extent, env)` (the count of distinct slots over that group, which is how a wide load
differs from a sub-agent broadcast: counted, never declared). `ir.identity_quantum()` is
`carrier(t) = t, slot(t) = 0` — one tile per instruction, always admissible, and `None` means
exactly that.

The structural consequence, which is what makes this a *scheduling* fact rather than an addressing
one, is:

> The coordinates inside one quantum are **one presence point**, hence one step and one generation.
> An axis absorbed into a quantum is therefore subtracted from that hop's presence set, and the
> merged movement cannot straddle a generation **by construction** — `ord` orders modes, and no
> reordering can get inside a single presence point.

That subtraction is performed by `geometry.quantum_axes`, called from `geometry.hop_broadcast`. It
derives the spanned axes *from the supplied map* rather than accepting a parallel list of axis names:
an axis is spanned exactly when varying that axis alone never changes the carrier. The
innermost-first behaviour falls out of that constancy test instead of being imposed — at wave tile 2
with a region split the degenerate inner axis means a 2-tile load fills the region axis and that is
what gets absorbed, while at wave tile 4 the same load fills the inner axis and the region axis stays
present, because tiles 0 and 2 then have different carriers.

##### 9.8.2 The decision: supplied, never derived in the core

The quantum is an **input** to the schedule point, with the same standing as the depth map `S`:
a per-placement value computed outside and reasoned over structurally inside. The reason is the
address-opacity rule of section 1.1 — which tiles one instruction covers is a consequence of the
address layout and the emitter's folding behaviour, and the core has no way to see byte adjacency
and must not pretend to. So the pairing is computed where the layout is known (in `KernelWriter.py`,
from target facts, surfaced through the bridge as the `ReadQuantum` entry of the parameter dict) and
enters the schedule point already translated into contraction semantics: *which tile coordinates
form one quantum*.

`theta.Hop.quantum` carries the `QuantumMap`; `None` means the identity merge.

##### 9.8.3 The four attempts to derive it in the core, and why each is wrong

`placement.py` carries a comment block, immediately before `resolve_quantum`, recording four
derivations that were tried and removed. They are reproduced here because they are the most
compressed statement available of where the core's authority ends. Each was attempted during
2026-08-19/20.

1. **Scan the free modes for an axis that "looks contiguous."** This is address-thinking in
   disguise: contiguity is a property of the address map, which the core cannot see. Concretely, at
   wave tile [2,2] the scan lands on the region axis and starts issuing verdicts about the
   region/cross-wave question — a separate problem with a separate treatment.
2. **Test whether the paired coordinates share a generation, and narrow when they do not.** This
   tests the *un-quantized* schedule, which is not the one being emitted. Absorbing the axis is what
   *makes* the coordinates one presence point; asking whether they would have shared a generation
   without the absorption answers a counterfactual, and answering "no" throws away the wide load the
   layout exists to serve.
3. **Refuse the geometry when the pair straddles a storage region.** Regions of one chunk share a
   generation, so the merge is admissible; the region question is the producer-set question (a read's
   producer is a *set* of writers, section 1.7), not a quantum question.
4. **Split an axis to *create* the pair.** The pairing is not the schedule point's to choose — it is
   determined by the layout, and manufacturing it would produce a schedule the emitter cannot
   realize.

Two of these had been *implemented* and shipped verdicts. The residue of that period is the code in
§9.8.6, which is now unreachable.

##### 9.8.4 `placement.py:resolve_quantum` — the live entry point

```
resolve_quantum(theta, S=None) -> {operand_name: QuantumMap}
    = { op.name : h.quantum
        for op in theta.operands for h in op.hops
        if not h.is_bulk and h.dst == REGISTER and h.quantum is not None }
```

A **reporting and validation step, not a derivation.** `translate` fills `Hop.quantum` from the
parameter dict (which the bridge fills from the target's layout and folding behaviour), and this
surfaces it for logging and tests. It is filtered to per-lane hops that land in registers, because a
bulk cooperative copy already spans every inner axis by definition and a quantum on it would be
meaningless.

`S` is **accepted and unused**. That is deliberate and documented: the decode driver
(`emit.build_ir`) calls a sequence of per-placement steps with a uniform `(theta, S)` signature, and
making this one differ would make the call site read as if it were a different kind of step. It is a
small, disclosed cost — a reader who greps for `S` here will find a dead parameter and needs the
docstring to know why.

**Where it is called.** `emit.emit_mainloop` — the decode driver — calls `resolve_quantum(theta, S)`
once, immediately after `build_S` and before `build_ledger`, and **discards the result**; the value
itself is consumed by tests and by the observability dump. The call is a cheap assertion that the
map is well-formed and reachable at emission time, and the comment beside it restates the
"supplied, not derived" rule so that a reader of the driver does not go looking for a derivation.
`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:test_a_SUPPLIED_quantum_reaches_the_hop_unchanged_under_every_loop_order`
asserts, for each loop order, both that `hop.quantum is q` (the schedule point carries the supplied
map verbatim) and that `resolve_quantum(th) == {"MXSA": q}`. The load-bearing property being pinned
is that *the emitted grouping cannot vary with the loop order* — which is the whole reason the
quantum lives outside.

The surrounding tests in that file pin the rest of the contract: with no target facts, no hop
carries a quantum and the default is one tile per instruction
(`test_the_quantum_defaults_to_ONE_TILE_when_nothing_supplies_it`); the supplied map propagates all
the way to the emitted span and the absorbed-axis set
(`test_the_quantum_reaches_the_emitted_span_end_to_end`); and a **region difference is not a quantum
violation** (`test_a_REGION_difference_is_not_a_quantum_violation`), which is attempt 3 above kept
as a regression test after the derivation was removed, because the chunk-versus-region distinction
survived the code that motivated it.

##### 9.8.5 `placement.py:quantum_tile_cap` — the target bound

```
quantum_tile_cap(theta, op, hop) -> int:
    if hop.is_bulk or not hop.vector_elems:   return 1     # "whole fragment" = one tile
    frag = max(1, int(op.frag_elems))
    return max(1, int(hop.vector_elems) // frag)
```

How many of the operand's free tiles **one instruction of this hop could carry**, read off the
target. `Hop.vector_elems` is the instruction's element payload per lane; `Operand.frag_elems` is
the element count of one (free-tile, substep) fragment per lane. Their ratio is a tile count. These
are the same two numbers the instruction-count and register-footprint derivations already divide
(`sizing.load_regs`, `sizing.plan_transfers`), read here for the *axis* question instead of the
*count* question.

The framing in the docstring is the useful one: this is the **domain the target offers**, exactly as
the register budget is the domain the depth map is searched in. Which part of that domain the loop
order actually permits is a separate question, answered by `hop_quantum_axes`.

A hop with `vector_elems == 0` means "whole fragment", i.e. one tile, hence a cap of 1 and no merge.
A bulk hop returns 1 for a different reason: it already spans everything.

**Status: unreachable.** Nothing outside `placement.py` calls `quantum_tile_cap`, and inside the
file its only caller is `hop_quantum_axes`, which is itself unreachable. See §9.8.9.

##### 9.8.6 `placement.py:_generation_map` — the decoder's own answer, enumerated

```
_generation_map(theta, op, S, dr) -> ({coord_key: (generation, register_slots)}, pres_modes):
    pl    = _read_placement(theta, op, S, dr=dr)          # the read's symbolic Placement
    pres  = theta.presence_modes(op)                      # ord order
    chunk = theta.reduction_chunk_name()
    for combo in itertools.product(*[range(max(1, m.extent)) for m in pres]):
        env  = {chunk: 0} | {mode.name: value for mode, value in zip(pres, combo)}
        gen   = pl.src_slot.eval(env)                     # the shared generation
        slots = tuple(s.eval(env) for _group_label, s in pl.slots)
        out[ tuple(zip(names(pres), combo)) ] = (gen, slots)
    return out, pres
```

**What it computes.** For every point of the operand's read presence, the shared-ring generation the
read's data lives in, and the register slots the read writes. The dictionary key is a tuple of
`(mode_name, value)` pairs in `ord` order, which makes it hashable and printable.

**The invariant that makes it worth having.** The generation is `_read_placement`'s own `src_slot`
expression — `(chunk + (P + shift) // N_pres) mod S_shared`, where `P` is the flat presence position
and `shift` the read-ahead advance — **evaluated per coordinate, not re-derived**. That is the whole
point of the function: an admissibility question about generations must be decided against the
