1. hoist one `regions = _region_bodies(tree)` and share it across the four arms (a two-line change,
   ~4× on this function);
2. fuse arms (b), (b3) and (b2) into a single pass over each region body — they all scan the same
   instruction list and differ only in what they record;
3. build the per-kind ledger index (`war_ops`, `cross_ops`, `inplace`, `ra_obls`) once at the top
   instead of four separate comprehensions.

None of these change behaviour, and none are worth doing until a profile says so.

`build_ledger` is the cheaper half and does not warrant caching; `emit_mainloop` already calls it
once. Note, though, that `emit.build_ir` calls `build_ledger` **again** internally (to build the
await index by consume site), so the ledger is constructed twice per decode. That duplication is
harmless because the function is pure — the two results are equal by construction — but it is the
obvious place to pass the already-built ledger in if the call ever becomes expensive.

#### 11.11 Design choices, alternatives, and advice for extending

##### 11.11.1 Why a ledger at all, rather than emitting waits directly

The alternative is the obvious one: have the emitter attach a wait wherever it knows one is needed,
and skip the bookkeeping. That is what the decoder did before the ledger existed, and it has two
failure modes the ledger removes.

* **Silent omission.** If the emitter forgets a wait, nothing notices. With a ledger, "the hazard
  exists" and "the hazard is discharged" are computed by two different functions from two different
  inputs (the schedule point versus the emitted tree), and their disagreement is a build-time
  error. Every negative test in section 11.9.2 is a case where the emitter *could* be wrong and the
  gate is what says so.
* **No place to put a structural requirement.** The read-ahead residency is not a wait at all — it
  is "the prologue must contain this read". Without an obligation record there is nowhere to state
  it, and it degenerates into a comment.

The cost of the ledger is that it is a *second* model of the same facts and can therefore drift
from the first. The mitigation used throughout is to derive both from one function:
`readahead_prologue` feeds both the ledger row and the emitted fill; `movement_units` feeds both
the ledger's producer identity and the downstream token; `_peel_depths` and `group_readahead_depth`
feed both the reach and the advance. Where that discipline is not possible, a test pins set
equality (section 11.5.4).

##### 11.11.2 Why the gate checks position and not just coverage

Because the target backend re-derives synchronization from the emitted def-use order. Coverage
alone is a statement about the *marker*; the backend consumes the *order*. Two schedules with
identical markers and inverted order compile to different (and one of them wrong) synchronization.
Arms (b), (b2) and (b3) exist entirely for that gap, and all three were added after a
coverage-passing tree miscompiled on hardware.

The honest weakness of the position arms is that they are **structural, not semantic**: they check
the relative index of two instructions in a flattened list. They do not know which *generation*
each instruction touches. Arm (b2)'s two documented gaps are both consequences of that, and the
principled fix — carry the generation on the instruction and quantify per generation — is a real
piece of work, not a tweak.

##### 11.11.3 Concrete advice for a future maintainer

**Adding a new obligation kind.** Four places, in this order:

1. `ir.RAW_KINDS` or `ir.WAR_KINDS` — otherwise `ir.is_war` raises when the emitter classifies it,
   which is by design (a new kind must not default). If the kind is *not* a wait (like
   `readahead-residency`), leave it out and be prepared to handle it explicitly in the two places
   that iterate all kinds.
2. `build_ledger` — a new pass minting the rows, placed so the deduplicating `set` sees it.
3. `emit._consume_role` — which emitted instruction discharges it, as an `(operand, role)` pair;
   or, if it is structural, an explicit `continue` like the read-ahead residency's.
4. `check_ledger_discharged` — a new arm if it needs a position check, since arm (a) covers only
   the counter class.

Then write the negative test **first**: construct the broken tree and confirm the new arm fires.
Every arm in this file that lacks such a test is an arm that has been vacuous at some point.

**Adding a region dimension to the endpoints (#217).** The depth map key already carries `region`
and `build_ledger` already reads it. The blocker is downstream: the memory tokens and hazard classes
must be keyed by region at the same time, or region-0 obligations pair against region-agnostic
discharges. Do the token side first, then the endpoint side, then the gate's `war_ops` /
`cross_ops` / `inplace` key tuples, all in one change.

**Making the gate faster.** See section 11.10. Sharing one `_region_bodies` result is the whole
win; nothing else is close.

**Making `discharge_once` general.** Widen `produces` to `isinstance(op, Load) and op.dst == dep.at
and <token match>`. That subsumes the current copy-only test and closes the latent register-hop gap
measured in section 11.6.3 before a future flattening exposes it.

**Do not** replace the `kind` string with an enum unless you also update the downstream consumers
that read `Await.kind` as a string (the assembly emitter's diagnostic tags and the hazard-edge
renderer). The string is load-bearing across a package boundary.

##### 11.11.4 Sharp edges, dead code and honest weaknesses, collected

* **`Space.SHARED == SHARED_GROUP == "shared"`.** `Endpoint.at` overloads one string across three
  namespaces (space, group label, site) and is disambiguated only by `kind`. Section 11.2.4.
* **`discharge_once` is scoped to copies by `produces`, but `MERGEABLE` is scoped by kind.** The two
  scopes do not coincide; the mismatch is currently unreachable. Section 11.6.3.
* **`Branch` handling in `discharge_once`, `walk_insts` and `_region_bodies` is dead.** The emitter
  never produces a `Branch`; the arms are kept for vocabulary completeness.
* **`_region_bodies.flat` inlines only `Cond.then`.** A guard with a populated false arm inside a
  trip would have its instructions excluded from every position check. Section 11.7.3.
* **The degenerate short-loop arm gets no region**, so no position arm inspects it. Coverage does
  apply. Section 11.7.3.
* **Arm (b2)'s `consumed` set is never reset**, so only the first refill of a slot per body is
  checked; and it is an existential where the correct test is a per-generation universal. Both
  stated in the source, both unreachable today, both needing a width-split in-place fixture
  (#262).
* **`region` is read from the depth map key in pass 2 and then ignored.** Deliberate; see above.
* **`build_ledger` is called twice per decode** (once by `emit_mainloop`, once inside
  `build_ir`). Harmless because pure, but a reader tracing the call graph should know.
* **The gate never checks an address**, never checks that the ledger is complete, and is
  generation-blind on the read-after-write side. Section 11.1.

##### 11.11.5 The shared-hop ledger, in one paragraph

Because it is the piece most often reasoned about, here is the whole shared-memory story in one
place. For an operand staged through shared memory, the ledger carries up to three rows about that
one ring: a **residency** saying the reads must wait for the copy (arm (a) covers it, and
`emit._site_awaits` attaches the wait to the read); a **write-after-read** saying the refilling copy
must not clobber a buffer whose readers have not finished, labelled with the *vacating read's*
completion class and classified in-place or rotation by whether the refill lands on the buffer this
trip is reading (arm (b) checks the in-place case's position, last-read-before-first-refill); and,
when this trip's read-ahead crosses into the chunk this trip's own copy fills, a **chunk-crossing
read-after-write** demanding the opposite order (arm (b3)). The write-after-read points at the
*previous* trip's readers; the crossing read-after-write points at *this* trip's. An operand is
never subject to both position demands, and the coupling that guarantees it is
`off(copy, chunk) ≥ r + 1` in the copy-last case, checked in closed form by
`placement.chunk_crossing_violations`.


---

### 12. `emit.py` — the emission driver

`emit.py` is the largest module in the package (1406 lines) and the only one with a fan-in of six:
it imports `ir`, `theta`, `sizing`, `geometry`, `ledger`, `placement` and `sigma_c` and consumes
each as a pure derivation. Everything else in the core answers *one* question; `emit.py` is the
place where the answers are assembled into a tree.

This section covers the driver and the loop nest — how a schedule point plus a depth map becomes a
rolled LoopIR tree, how the three pipeline stages are laid out, how the loop nest is constructed
over the inner modes, and how each op-class is placed at the level its presence names. Section 13
continues with the remaining machinery of the same file.

#### 12.1 What the module is for

**Concept.** The input is a schedule point `theta` (section 1.1) and the derived depth map `S`
(section 1.8). The output is a *rolled region tree*: a nested structure of `Loop`, `Peel`, `Bind`,
`Cond` and `Inst` nodes in which

* every op-class (section 1.2) appears **once per pipeline stage**, at the loop level its presence
  set names — never once per iteration;
* every rotation index is a symbolic `Expr` over loop-mode names, not a resolved integer;
* every hazard the ledger enumerated is discharged by a named `Await` attached to the instruction
  that consumes the produced value;
* the software-pipeline structure — prologue peel, steady loop, drain peel, and a degenerate
  short-trip arm — is explicit in the node types rather than implied by an annotation.

Node count is therefore `O(#op-classes × #levels)` and is independent of the runtime trip count.
The renderer (`render.py`) performs a partial unroll as a *view*; the stored tree stays rolled.

**Two public entry points.** `emit.py:emit_mainloop` is the driver a caller uses; `emit.py:build_ir`
is the tree builder it calls, exported separately because the unit tests and the observability dump
want the tree without the gate. Everything else in the file is either a module-level helper
(`_check_peel_is_emittable`, `_scope_of`, `_reduction_inner_mode`, `_read_quantum`, `loop_shape`) or
a **closure defined inside `build_ir`**. There are 30 of the latter, and the nesting is not
incidental: they close over `theta`, `S`, the peel depths, the await index, the two mode lists and
the copy-metadata side table, all of which are computed once per decode. Making them module-level
functions would mean threading eight parameters through every call, and two of them (`_copy_meta`,
`awaits_by_site`) are mutable state whose lifetime is exactly one `build_ir` call.

**The one module-level constant.** `emit.py:_SINGLE_ROLE` is the string `"w0"`, the issuing agent
stamped on `Inst.agent` at every `Inst` the emitter builds. It does **not** reach `Loop.role`: no
`Loop(...)` in `emit.py` passes `role`, so a freshly built loop takes `ir.Loop`'s own hardcoded
default (`ir.py:588`, `role: str = "w0"`) and the two rebuilders propagate the existing `n.role` —
changing `_SINGLE_ROLE` would move `Inst.agent` alone. An unspecialized kernel is the single-agent special case; a *specialized* kernel — one that gives
different agents different roles, so that (say) one wave issues only copies while the others compute
— would derive this per instance from `theta.rho` and grow one subtree per role. `theta` carries
`rho` for exactly that purpose, but nothing reads it yet (section 19.6 records why), so the constant
stands in for the derivation. Its value is a single name rather than a literal repeated at each of
the four `Inst(...)` construction sites, which is the whole reason it exists.

**Vocabulary used without redefinition.** This section assumes the terms defined in section 1:
schedule point, op-class, role, presence and broadcast set, inner-versus-outer level, the reduction
chunk, retime (`off`), the four obligation kinds, the two rotating rings, the movement quantum,
storage regions, fusion, and rolled emission with named dependencies. The one term this section
adds is **stage**: one of the four straight-line or looped regions the emitter produces —
`prologue`, `steady`, `drain`, and the degenerate `short` arm.

#### 12.2 `emit_mainloop` — the driver

**Concept.** `emit_mainloop(theta)` is the whole decode. It takes a schedule point and returns a
dictionary; it raises rather than returning a tree it cannot certify. It is re-exported as
`decoder.emit_mainloop` and as `LoopModel.emit_mainloop`, and is called from exactly three places
outside the tests: `KernelWriter.py` (to obtain the tree that codegen walks),
`Lowering/loopir_to_gir.py` (to obtain the tree it converts to GIR), and `bridge.kernel_to_ir_text`
(`bridge.py:232`, the observability dump, which reads `ledger_empty`, `n_obl` and `undischarged`
off the same return dict).

**Algorithm.**

```
emit_mainloop(theta):
    loop      = loop_shape(theta)                  # ord contiguity report (12.3)
    S, floor  = build_S(theta)                     # the depth map + the register floor
    resolve_quantum(theta, S)                      # surface the supplied movement quantum
    ledger    = build_ledger(theta, S)             # every hazard, symbolic per op-class
    ir        = build_ir(theta, S)                 # the rolled tree (12.4 onward)
    ir        = discharge_once(ir)                 # drop an Await a predecessor already made
    undischarged = check_ledger_discharged(ledger, ir)
    defects   = validate_loopir(theta, ir, S, undischarged=undischarged)
    if defects: raise ValueError("... structural gate failed ...", + a theta fingerprint)
    if not loop["clean"]: theta.notes.append(<explanatory note>)
    return {"S", "floor", "ir", "ledger", "ledger_empty", "undischarged",
            "n_obl", "loop", "tensor_per_kiter"}
```

**Why this order.** Four of the eight steps could in principle move, and each is pinned:

* `build_S` runs **before** `build_ledger` and `build_ir` because both consume `S`. `build_S` is
  pure, and it is also called independently by the kernel writer during register sizing, which
  happens earlier in wall-clock time than emission; because it is pure the two calls agree by
  construction rather than by caching discipline.
* `resolve_quantum` runs before the ledger. It does not *derive* the quantum — the quantum is
  supplied on the hop by the addon layer (section 1.9) — it only surfaces and validates it, so that
  a quantum that would straddle two buffer generations is reported at the point where the schedule
  is still intact.
* `discharge_once` runs **before** `check_ledger_discharged`. `discharge_once` removes an `Await`
  that a preceding instruction on the same path already established, so running it first means the
  gate checks the boundary that is actually emitted rather than a redundant restatement of it. If
  the order were reversed, the gate would pass on a tree, and then the tree would be edited.
* `validate_loopir` runs last and **raises**. The comment at that site records that the checker was
  written as "the permanent structural gate" and then, for a long time, was called by nothing but
  the unit tests. Wiring it in is what turns a decoder bug into a build failure instead of a wrong
  kernel at runtime.

**The failure message carries a fingerprint, and that is a deliberate ergonomic choice.** The raise
formats `ord`, the whole `off_map`, and the per-input register widths into the message:

```python
_shape = "ord=[%s] off=%s S_reg=%s" % (
    ",".join(m.name for m in theta.inner_modes()),
    dict(getattr(theta, "off_map", {}) or {}),
    {op.name: dict(S.groups_of(op.name)) for op in theta.operands
     if getattr(op, "role", "input") == "input"})
```

The reason is recorded in place: this raise executes inside a parallel worker during a whole-matrix
build, so the traceback alone says "a kernel" and nothing about *which*. Loop order, peel depth and
register width are the three axes every gate failure so far has turned on, so a reader can
reconstruct the failing cell from the log without a rebuild. The `getattr` defaults make the message
formatter total — a fingerprint that itself raises while formatting a failure would be worse than no
fingerprint.

**The return dictionary.** Nine keys, and their consumers differ:

| Key | Meaning | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| `S` | the depth map | the kernel writer's register sizing, the renderer |
| `floor` | the derived register live-peak floor | the renderer's geometry table |
| `ir` | the rolled tree | codegen and the GIR lowering |
| `ledger` | the full obligation list | the renderer, the ledger/GIR cross-check |
| `ledger_empty` | `not undischarged` | the tests' one-line certificate |
| `undischarged` | the obligations with no discharge | the gate, the renderer |
| `n_obl` | `len(ledger)` | dump headers |
| `loop` | the `loop_shape` report | the dump, and the note below |
| `tensor_per_kiter` | instruction counts per reduction substep | the dump |

`ledger_empty` is the property every scenario test asserts: **every hazard the schedule creates has
a named discharge in the emitted tree.** It is not a proof of correctness — the ledger is symbolic
per op-class and generation-blind, which section 8 explains and which the degenerate-arm defect
(12.14.4) exploited — but an empty ledger plus a passing structural gate is the strongest machine
check the package makes.

**The non-contiguity note is a note, not a rejection.** When `loop["clean"]` is false, the driver
appends a sentence to `theta.notes` and continues. This is a reversal of an earlier position and the
reversal is the interesting part; it is described with `loop_shape` immediately below.

#### 12.3 `loop_shape`, `loop_shape._key`, `loop_shape._lbl` — the ord contiguity report

**Concept.** A steady loop body is *uniform* when one straight-line body, repeated, expresses every
iteration. That fails when a role's inner modes are **non-contiguous** in `ord`. Concretely: an
order whose modes read `[m, n_hi, k, n_lo]` splits the N fan around the reduction step, so the
body before the K step and the body after it are not the same body. The tree can still be emitted —
see below — but the shape is different, and knowing which shape you are in is worth reporting.

**The partition key is presence-derived, with no axis-letter literal.** For each inner mode, the key
is the *frozen set of input operand names present on that mode*:

```
_key(mode_name) = frozenset{ op.name  for op in theta.operands if op.is_input
                                       and mode_name in theta.presence(op) }
```

A reduction mode is present on every input, so its key is `{A, B}` (or all inputs, whatever they are
called); a free mode belonging to one operand's tile has that operand's singleton key. Contiguity of
this key sequence in `ord` is the test, and because the key is a *set of operand names* rather than
an `m`/`n`/`k` letter, the test generalizes to any operand count, any number of free axes and any
naming.

```
seq   = [_key(m.name) for m in theta.inner_modes()]     # ord order
split = [ k for k in unique(seq)
            if the positions of k in seq are not a contiguous run ]
return {"clean": not split, "roles": [_lbl(k) for k in seq],
        "split_roles": [_lbl(k) for k in split]}
```

`loop_shape._lbl(k)` is the display helper: it renders a key as its sorted operand names joined with
`+`, or `-` for the empty key (a mode no input is present on). It is explicitly *not* branch logic —
the decision is made on the frozensets, and `_lbl` exists so that the report a human reads says
`"B"` rather than `frozenset({'B'})`.

**Complexity.** `O(#inner modes × #inputs)` for the keys plus `O(#inner modes²)` for the contiguity
scan, with `#inner modes ≤ 8` and `#inputs ≤ 4` on the shipping vocabulary. Irrelevant.

**A live stale docstring — flagged here because this is the document a maintainer reads.** The
`loop_shape` docstring says, in capitals, that `emit_mainloop` "CONSULTS this and REJECTS a
clean=False ord (raises)". **The code does not raise.** `emit_mainloop` records a note on `theta`
and proceeds. The docstring describes a policy that was reversed: a non-contiguous role *is*
emittable, because a read that is invariant over an enclosing mode is issued once under an explicit
first-touch guard (12.13), which is exactly what that guard is for. The reversal was validated
end-to-end on the `MKNMKN` order at a wave tile of `[4,4]`: one read per distinct presence
coordinate, no duplicates, the GIR verifier clean, the ledger empty. The multi-sub-body steady
region that would hoist those guards into the loop *structure* instead of testing them per iteration
is a cost refinement, and it now exists too (`_peel_first_touch`, 12.13) — so even the cost argument
has largely been paid. **Fix the docstring; do not restore the raise.**

**Reachability, so the reader knows this is not a hypothetical.** `loop_shape` returns
`clean=False` for the `MKNMKN` and the interleaved `KMKNMN` loop orders at a wave tile of `[4,4]`.
Those same orders read `clean=True` at `[2,2]` — not because the order changed but because the
split/inner mode pair collapses to extent 1 and is dropped from `ord` entirely. That is a
general sharp edge worth internalising: **degenerate extents change the shape of `ord`, so a
property measured at a small wave tile may not be the property that holds at a large one.**

#### 12.4 `build_ir` — the tree builder, and its preamble

**Signature and contract.** `build_ir(theta, S) -> list[node]`. The returned list is the root of the
tree; with a non-zero peel depth it is a single-element list holding the peel-validity `Cond`, and
with a zero peel depth it is the bare stage list. It has no side effects on `theta` (the only
mutation of `theta` in the whole module is the note `emit_mainloop` appends). It is deterministic
and pure given `(theta, S)`.

The body executes in one pass, in this order:

```
 1  _copy_first  = copy_first_operands(theta, S)     # which copies must lead their reads
 2  _copy_meta   = {}                                # id(Inst) -> (level, nregions, spans, enum)
 3  copy_ops     = operands whose first hop lands in SHARED
 4  peel         = _peel_depths(theta);  off, dr, M = peel.copy_off(), peel.dr, peel.M
 5  outer_var    = theta.reduction_chunk_name("iter")
 6  _check_peel_is_emittable(theta, peel, outer_var)
 7  ledger       = build_ledger(theta, S);  awaits_by_site = index it by consume site
 8  all_inner / inner                                # the two mode lists (12.7)
 9  reads        = operands whose last hop lands in REGISTER;  scale = len(reads) > 2
10  read_level   = {op: op_class_level(theta, op, READ)}
11  _wmma_pres / leaf_mode                           # the matrix instruction's level (12.7)
12  _units       = theta.movement_units();  the fuse-group off guard
13  ... the closures ...
14  iter_body / loop / pro / drain / sbody / the root Cond
```

Steps 1–12 are derivations; step 14 is the assembly. Everything between is closure definition.

**Step 1, `_copy_first`.** `placement.copy_first_operands(theta, S)` returns the set of operands
whose shared copy must be emitted **before** the reads rather than after them. The default position
is *copies last*: a copy refills a shared buffer, so it must follow the reads that vacate that
buffer. The exception is a copy whose chunk *this trip's read-ahead reaches into* — then the copy is
a true producer for those reads and must lead. The predicate lives in `placement`, is computed once
here, and is handed to every `_order_sigma_c` call, so the ordering rule cannot be re-derived
differently in the steady body, the drain and the prologue.

**Step 2, `_copy_meta` — an `id()`-keyed side table, and the honest reason it exists.** It maps
`id(inst)` to the tuple `(level, n_regions, spans, enum)` for each copy instruction. The comment
states the constraint plainly: the issue-order refinement must see the copies as *individual
movements* so it can classify each one, while the tree wants them *nested* under region loops. Those
two facts cannot travel on the same node, because the nest replaces the node. So the metadata rides
on a table keyed by object identity, scoped to a single `copy_insts` → `_order_sigma_c` hand-off.

This is the one place in the package where object identity is load-bearing, and it has two
consequences a maintainer must know. First, **any transformation that copies a node loses its
metadata** — which is why `_nest_copy_runs` is documented as idempotent-safe: an already-nested node
is simply not in `_copy_meta`, so a second pass leaves it alone. Second, **the table is never
cleared between phases**, so it accumulates entries for every phase's copies within one `build_ir`
call; that is harmless because keys are fresh object ids, but it does mean the table's size is
`O(#copies × #phases)` rather than `O(#copies)`. A cleaner design would attach the tuple to a
dedicated field on `Load` (there is precedent: `Load.coord` and `Load.part` already carry structural
position), and a future refactor should do that; the counter-argument at the time was that the field
would be meaningful only between two adjacent calls and would then be dead weight on every consumer
of the IR.

**Step 4, the peel depths.** `placement._peel_depths(theta)` returns a `PeelDepths` record carrying
`per_level` (the peel depth `M_ℓ` for each level), `offs` (the per-op-class retimes that produced
them), `dr` (the read-ahead depth), `chunk`, `reach`, and `deferrals` (any negative entries). Three
of its fields are unpacked here into local names used throughout the builder:

* `off = peel.copy_off()` — a dict from operand name to that operand's copy retime **at the chunk
  level**. This is the staggering input: prologue and drain steps include a copy only when its own
  `off` says it belongs there.
* `dr = peel.dr` — the read-ahead depth in substeps.
* `M = peel.M` — the peel depth **at the reduction chunk**, i.e. the number of prologue steps, the
  number of drain steps, and the constant in the steady bound `iter < T − M`.

`peel.copy_off()` filters to `role == COPY and level == chunk`. That filter is the reason
`_check_peel_is_emittable` has to reject a *read* offset at an outer level — see 12.5.

**Step 5, `outer_var`.** The reduction chunk's name, obtained from `theta.reduction_chunk_name`
with the legacy fallback `"iter"` for a hand-built schedule point that has no outer mode at all.
This one string is used for: every synthesized `Loop.mode`, every `Peel.mode`, every `Bind.mode`,
the copy slot's base variable, and the generation qualifier on every read's residency dependency.
Section 1.4 records why it is centralized: before it was, three call sites took the first outer mode
and two took the last, which are the same answer while there is exactly one outer level and silently
different the moment a coarser one exists.

#### 12.5 `_check_peel_is_emittable` — four refusals, and why refusing beats emitting

**Concept.** The peel is a *vector*: every level with a non-zero peel depth wants its own
prologue and drain. `build_ir` can emit a peel for exactly **one** level, the reduction chunk,
because a coarser level's prologue and drain would have to sit inside an enclosing loop for that
level — and that loop (a persistent, grid-stride tile loop) does not exist yet. The natural
temptation is to emit the chunk-only peel anyway and ignore the coarser retimes.

That is precisely the failure mode the whole certificate machinery exists to rule out. A decoder
that keys peel depth only on the innermost outer level **silently drops** every coarser retime, and
because the ledger is built from the same schedule point, the resulting tree **still reports an
empty obligation ledger**. The output is a schedule that is not the one requested, wearing a valid
certificate. So this function raises, loudly, with the derived facts in the message.

**Signature.** `_check_peel_is_emittable(theta, peel, chunk)`. Returns `None`; raises
`NotImplementedError` (three cases) or `ValueError` (one case). Called once, from `build_ir`,
immediately after the peel depths are derived and before any node is constructed.

**The four checks, in order.**

*(a) A peel wanted at a coarser outer level.*

```
outer = {m.name for m in theta.outer_modes()}
extra = [lvl for lvl in peel.peeled_levels() if lvl in outer and lvl != chunk]
if extra: raise NotImplementedError(... with {lvl: peel.depth(lvl)} ...)
```

The scoping to **outer** levels is the load-bearing part of this check. An *inner* level's peel
depth is real — a read retimed by one substep gives the substep level a depth of one — but an inner
level is statically unrolled, so its peel is absorbed into the unroll and realized by the read-ahead
family rather than by a region: the prologue fill primes it, the steady shift sustains it, and the
drain's suppression guard ends it. Only an outer level needs a region this emitter cannot build.

*(b) A read retime at an outer level.* This is the subtlest of the four and the docstring devotes
half its length to it. The retime matrix is indexed by op-class × level for *every* op-class, and
the staggered peel's input is copies **and** a chunk-level read offset. The emitter honours neither:
`_peel_depths` folds such an entry into the level's peel depth — so the validity guard, the prologue
depth, the steady bound and the drain step count all move — while the only thing `build_ir` staggers
over is `peel.copy_off()`, which filters to copies at the chunk. Every read instruction keeps its
unshifted rotation slot and unshifted shared source slot. **Half-applied: neither the requested
schedule nor a refusal, and the ledger certifies empty.** So it is refused, with the offending
entries named.

The docstring also explains *why the check lives here and not in the shared boundary-term
derivation*. `placement.boundary_hoists` — which finds retimes at a level outer to an op-class's own
home level — drops this case on its third condition (`home not in outer`). That condition is not a
bug: it is what keeps the **region-split copy** legal, whose home is a region mode (an inner mode)
while its retime sits at the chunk. That pairing is the ordinary copy prefetch and is on the
shipping path. Loosening the shared predicate would refuse live kernels. The distinction is
per-role — a copy's ordinary prefetch level *is* the chunk, a read's is the substep — so the narrow
refusal belongs at a site that can name the role, and that site is here.

*(c) A genuine cross-level boundary term.* `placement.boundary_hoists(theta, peel)` returns records
`(op, role, level, home, delta, coords)` describing retimes that would relocate the leading `delta`
inner-nest instances of an op-class across an enclosing loop boundary — into the *previous* outer
iteration's drain. That relocation is not emitted, so it is refused with each hoist spelled out
("`off(A:copy, gtile)=1` relocates the leading 1 instance(s) of home level `iter`").

*(d) A negative retime.* `peel.deferrals` collects any entry with a negative value.

```
if peel.deferrals: raise ValueError("negative off is ill-typed: ...")
```

The retime matrix is typed over the non-negative integers, and the schedule-space move that sets a
retime *assigns* rather than subtracts, so no move can reach a negative entry. **Deferral — issuing
`|d|` iterations later, which is what an epilogue store wants — is not a negative offset.** It is a
*positive* retime on a **reverse-trajectory** op-class (section 1.2), which gets the mirrored peel:
the steady region runs over `[0, T−d)` with the trailing `d` instances hoisted forward into the
successor iteration, prologue and drain swapped. The direction is read off the op-class's
trajectory sense, never off the sign of the number. So `off(C, STORE, gtile) = 1` is the deferred
store and it is an ordinary positive entry.

**Reachability.** None of the four fires from the shipping parameter path: `translate` sets only
`off(copy, chunk)` and `off(read, substep)`, each of which is that op-class's own home level. They
fire for a hand-built schedule point, and check (a) will stop firing, level by level, as the
persistent-loop level lands. This is deliberate: the checks are **latent, not shipping**, and they
exist so a latent case cannot *become* shipping silently.

**Test coverage.** `test_loopmodel.test_a_coarser_outer_off_is_a_boundary_term_and_is_REFUSED_not_dropped`
builds a schedule point with an added persistent level, asserts that `boundary_hoists` derives
exactly one hoist with the right `(op, level, home, delta)` and relocated coordinate set, and then
asserts `pytest.raises(NotImplementedError)` from `emit_mainloop`. Its sibling
`test_a_deeper_coarser_off_relocates_proportionally_many_instances` pins that the relocated instance
count is the retime itself, not one. `test_an_inner_level_off_is_not_a_boundary_term` pins the
scoping in (a): the substep level's peel depth is recorded, `boundary_hoists` returns empty, and
emission proceeds. `test_a_negative_off_is_rejected_as_ill_typed` installs a `-1` read retime by
`dataclasses.replace` on the off map, checks that `_peel_depths` files it under `deferrals` and that
it does **not** perturb the level's peel depth, and then pins the `ValueError`.

**Advice for a future developer.** These are four separate `raise` statements with four separate
messages and no shared structure. If a fifth appears, resist adding it inline: the right shape is a
list of `(predicate, message_builder)` pairs so the messages stay uniform and a caller can ask
"which of these would fire" without catching an exception. More importantly, when the persistent
level lands, **do not delete check (a) — narrow it.** The value of the check is that it names
exactly the levels the emitter cannot express; as that set shrinks, the check should shrink with it.

#### 12.6 The await index — one derivation from the ledger to every `Await`

**Concept and invariant.** The obligation ledger is the *single source of truth for every wait*. The
emitter never hand-authors an `Await` at a construction site; instead it indexes the ledger by
**consume site**, and each instruction asks the index for its own site's obligations. The invariant
is therefore: **every `Await` in the emitted tree is derived from exactly one ledger obligation, and
carries that obligation's producer endpoint, completion class and kind.** The gate afterwards checks
the converse — that every obligation has a discharge.

A *consume site* is the pair `(operand, role)` naming the emitted instruction that must wait.

##### 12.6.1 `_consume_role(ob)`

Maps one obligation to its consume site.

```
if ob.kind == "RAW-residency":
    # X@shared is consumed by the READ; X@register by the matmul
    return (ob.consumer.op, "read" if ob.consumer.at == Space.SHARED else "wmma")
# a *-WAR's consumer is the REFILLER
return (ob.consumer.op, "copy" if ob.consumer.at == "shared" else "read")
```

The asymmetry is the content: a true dependency is consumed by whoever *reads* the value, an
anti-dependency by whoever *overwrites* it. So the four shapes are

| Obligation | Producer | Consume site | Completion class |
|---|---|---|---|
| RAW `A@shared` | the copy | `("A","read")` | the copy's counter |
| RAW `A@register` | the read | `("A","wmma")` | the read's counter |
| WAR `A:shared:refill` | the vacating read | `("A","copy")` | the read's counter |
| WAR `A:g0:refill` | the vacating matmul | `("A","read")` | the read's counter |

**The one exclusion, and the bug it fixes.** A `readahead-residency` obligation is `continue`d over
when the index is built. Its edge — the prologue read at a coordinate must complete before the
matmul at that coordinate issues — is the *same* edge the matmul's ordinary register residency
already discharges, and the obligation's real content is a **structural** requirement on the
prologue: the prologue must pre-issue that read. That is checked directly against the prologue body
by the ledger gate, not turned into a wait.

The historical defect is worth stating because it shows how a bucketing key can fan out. The kind
used to be bucketed like a WAR, which filed it under the **read** — the obligation's *producer*,
not its consumer. And because the bucket key is only `(operand, role)`, **every** coordinate's
obligation then landed on **every** read of that operand. The visible result: a prologue read
awaited its own residency, and each steady read carried one spurious wait per read-ahead
coordinate.

##### 12.6.2 `_scope_of(theta, ob, opname)`

The synchronization **scope** a discharge must reach: `"wave"` (the same agent, so program order
suffices) or `"block"` (across agents, so a memory-ordering barrier is needed).

```
if ob.kind in ("inplace-WAR", "RAW-residency"):
    return "block" if theta.agent_distributed(opname) else "wave"
return "wave"
```

*Why `inplace-WAR` goes block-scoped when the movement is agent-distributed.* The in-place case is
the one where the refill writes the very slot the current consumer reads, so the buffer is refilled
by only the subset of agents that wrote it while it is read by **all** of them. Program order relates
nothing across those two sets, so the anti-dependency is live and needs a selector whose scope
reaches the agents involved. The required strength is specific: a **memory-ordering** barrier that
orders the read's completion before the refill's write; a bare execution-only barrier leaves the
hazard live. That requirement travels with the scope to the backend.

*Why `RAW-residency` was added to the same branch (a correction, not an extension).* The bullet
this replaced argued that a residency's consumer awaits a completion *class*, which is not an
agent-relative fact — "the counter says the bytes landed regardless of which agent moved them".
That is **false for a per-wave counter, which is the only kind the target has.** A wait instruction
retires *this* wave's outstanding loads and says nothing about another wave's. Under a cooperative
fill each agent issues its own part of the slab and then every agent reads the whole tile, so a
reader waiting on its own counter has no edge at all to the writer that actually filled the bytes it
is about to read.

*Why `rotation-WAR` deliberately stays wave-scoped.* The rotating case is the one where the refill
writes a *different* slot from the one being read, i.e. the ring depth already holds a slot nobody
is reading this trip. The remedies for a cross-agent anti-dependency are alternatives — a
proc-scoped selector **or** a spare slot — and the depth has already supplied one. Widening its
scope would emit a barrier per trip for an obligation that is already discharged.

**`scope` is currently inert, and this report must not overstate it.** Its only consumer downstream
is a diagnostic tag inside a comment string in the final emission stage; the function that actually
emits a barrier never receives it. The barrier that makes these kernels correct today comes from a
narrower mechanism in the lowering that probes the shared-memory ring rotation directly. So the
correction above changes what the *model* believes and provably not one emitted byte. Making `scope`
load-bearing is tracked work and has to be measured against an over-synchronization budget before it
lands. `test_loopmodel.test_a_cross_agent_RAW_residency_is_BLOCK_scoped_not_wave` pins the model
fact.

##### 12.6.3 `_bulk_hop(op)`

`next((h for h in op.hops if h.is_bulk), None)` — the operand's cooperative whole-tile hop, or
`None`. Trivial in code and not trivial in intent: it identifies the copy hop **by its mover kind
rather than by position**. A direct-to-register operand's `hops[0]` is a `global→register` per-lane
read, and asking *that* hop a copy-placement question gets a confident wrong answer — it names a
reduction axis where a region axis belongs. Four call sites use it (`_region_note`,
`_region_mode_of`, `_enum_axes`, `_group_region_modes`) and each of them is a placement question.

##### 12.6.4 `_region_note(opname)`

Under the *per-region completion granularity* toggle (`theta.per_region_completion`), a movement
that was cut into storage regions yields one completion per region rather than one for the whole
tile — so a read of region `j` should name region `j` and leave the others in flight. This helper
returns **the region mode's name**, or `None` when the toggle is off or the operand has no bulk hop.

```
if not theta.per_region_completion: return None
h = _bulk_hop(operand named opname)
if h is None: return None
return first mode name in theta.presence_modes(op, h)   # empty when the tile is not split
```

Three things are worth noting. First, the note is a **mode name, not a value**: the read is rolled
at its presence level, so the value is supplied when the tree is unrolled. Second, the ledger entry
stays symbolic per op-class — only the emitted discharge point is instance-named; the ledger is
deliberately an `O(1)`-per-op-class safety check, not a per-instance enumeration. Third, the
"is it split" test is asked **of the hop's presence** rather than reconstructed from `op.split` and
`op.region_modes`. The copy hop's presence set names the region axis precisely when the tile is
split and is empty otherwise, so the two-field reconstruction and the presence query are the same
one question — and asking it once means they cannot disagree.

##### 12.6.5 `_group_labels(opname)`

`set(op.fragment.groups())` for the named operand, or the empty set if there is no such operand or
it has no fragment. It exists so that `_site_awaits` can tell a **register-ring** anti-dependency
(whose producer endpoint is a register group label) from a shared-ring one (whose producer endpoint
is a space name) without a string-shape test.

##### 12.6.6 `_site_awaits(opname, role, kiter_note=None, groups=None)`

The one constructor for `Await` tuples. Inputs: the consume site, an optional generation qualifier,
and an optional restriction to a subset of register groups. Output: a tuple of `Await` nodes.

```
obs = awaits_by_site[(opname, role)]
mv  = movement_name(theta, opname)          # the fused movement, or the bare name
if mv != opname: obs += awaits_by_site[(mv, role)]

for ob in obs:
    if groups is not None and is_war(ob.kind) \
       and ob.producer.at in group_labels(opname) and ob.producer.at not in groups:
        continue                                    # another split's register-ring WAR
    quals = (kiter_note, region_note(opname)) if ob.kind == "RAW-residency" else ()
    emit Await(dep     = ob.producer.qualified(*quals),
               counter = ob.counter,
               scope   = _scope_of(theta, ob, opname),
               kind    = ob.kind,
               note    = "refill WAR: slot vacated by prior read" if is_war(ob.kind)
                         else f"{opname} resident")
```

**Three mechanisms, each with a measured motivation.**

*Fusion lookup.* A fused cooperative movement owes **one** obligation, not one per member, so the
ledger keys such an obligation by the *movement* (a tuple of member names) rather than by any single
operand. Every member consumes that same object, so a member's consume site must resolve to its own
per-op-class obligations **plus** the movement's. `ledger.movement_name` returns the bare name when
there is no fusion, and the second lookup would then be the same key — hence the `!=` guard, without
which an unfused kernel would double-count every obligation.

*Group restriction.* When an operand's read is split into two instructions because its register
groups have different rotation shapes (12.11.2), each half must carry only the anti-dependency of
the slot **it** overwrites. Without the filter each half would wait on the other half's vacating
read — a self-inflicted serialization between two instructions that are supposed to be independent.
The filter is narrow by construction: it applies only when `groups` is given, only to
anti-dependencies, and only when the producer endpoint is recognisably a register group label of
this operand. Obligations that are not register-ring anti-dependencies — the residency, the shared
ring — are carried by **every** split, which is correct: both halves read the same shared buffer.

*Generation qualifiers.* A residency's dependency name is suffixed with the generation the consumer
reads (the chunk, passed in as `kiter_note`) and, under the per-region toggle, with the region note.
Anti-dependencies get no qualifier: the slot they name is the whole content of the obligation.

**Complexity.** `O(#obligations at this site)` per call, and it is called once per emitted
instruction, so `O(#instructions × #obligations-per-site)` per decode. Both factors are small
(single digits and low tens respectively). The dictionary index is built once.

**Sharp edge.** The bucket key is `(operand, role)` and *not* the coordinate. That is intentional —
the ledger is symbolic per op-class — but it means **an obligation filed at a site fans out to every
instruction at that site**. The read-ahead residency exclusion above exists precisely because
something was filed at a site where it fanned. If you add an obligation kind, ask first: *is this a
fact about the op-class, or about one instance?* If it is about one instance, it does not belong in
this index.

#### 12.7 Two mode lists: `all_inner` versus `inner`

This is the single most consequential three lines in the module, and getting the distinction wrong
produces a tree that is *structurally* valid and *semantically* replicated.

```python
_agent_served = theta.agent_served_modes()
all_inner = [(m.name, m.extent) for m in theta.inner_modes()]
inner = [(n, e) for (n, e) in all_inner if n not in _agent_served]
```

**Concept.** Section 1.3 introduced the third class of inner axis. An **agent-served** axis is one
traversed by the *agents* rather than by the coordinate: when the wave grouping places wave `w`
entirely inside storage region `w`, each wave sees exactly one region, so nothing a wave *reads* or
*computes* varies over the region axis. But the cooperative bulk copy still walks every region — it
is one instruction serving all of them, or one instruction per region issued by the group as a
whole. So the axis is real for the copy and absent for the read and the matmul.

The two lists encode exactly that:

* **`all_inner`** — every inner mode, in `ord` order. **Copies iterate this list.**
* **`inner`** — `all_inner` minus the agent-served modes. **Reads and the matmul iterate this list.**

`inner` is used for: the read/compute nest walk (`build_level` indexes `inner[li]`), the ord-position
map `pos` used by the first-touch derivation, the matmul's coordinate tuple, and the copy filing
level's ordinal comparison. `all_inner` is used for: the copy nest's sort order **and its extent
map**.

**The failure mode when a read/compute site uses `all_inner`.** A `Loop` is emitted over the
agent-served axis inside the read/compute nest. Nothing in its body varies over it. Every read and
every matmul instance is therefore emitted `extent` times — one per storage region — where one
instance is correct. The tree passes the structural gate (it is a perfectly well-formed nest), the
ledger is unaffected (obligations are per op-class, and the op-classes are all still present), and
the defect surfaces only as duplicated instructions downstream.

**The failure mode when the copy nesting helper uses `inner` — and it must use `all_inner` for BOTH
the order and the extents.** `_nest_copies` (12.11.3) does two things with a mode list: it *sorts*
the levels it will build into `ord` order, and it *looks up each level's extent* to set the emitted
`Loop.trip` and to compute the presence stride on enclosing levels. If it used `inner`:

* **The order lookup fails outright.** `levels.sort(key=order.index)` raises `ValueError: <mode> is
  not in list` the moment a copy is filed at an agent-served axis — which is exactly the
  configuration that creates one. Not a silent wrong answer, but a crash in a code path that only
  the agent-served configuration reaches, i.e. one that a matrix run over the common shapes never
  exercises.
* **The extent lookup splits into a hard failure and a silent one, and the silent half is worse.**
  `ext = dict(all_inner)`; the region loop is emitted as `Loop(mode=m, trip=ext[m], ...)`, a HARD
  subscript — so with `inner` an agent-served level raises `KeyError` there, a crash like the sort
  above it, not a silent trip of 1. The silent half is `_axis_stride`, which *does* use the
  defensive `ext.get(g, 1)`: with the agent-served axis missing it silently reads `1`,
  the computed stride collapses, every enclosing-level presence guard evaluates to "present at every
  value", and the first-touch guard that should restrict a coarse movement to one value of an axis
  disappears.

The source states the rule in one comment — *"The COPY nests over EVERY ord level — including the
agent-served ones the read/compute nest dropped. Both the sort order and the extent map need the
full list"* — and the "both" is the operative word. A partial fix that uses `all_inner` for the
sort and `inner` for the extents is the silent-wrong-answer version.

**Where else the distinction bites.** `_copy_meta`'s filing level is chosen with
`_ordpos = {n: i for i, (n, _e) in enumerate(inner)}` and `_ordpos.get(a, -1)`, i.e. from the
**reduced** list with a default. That is a genuine inconsistency with the rest of the copy path and
a live sharp edge: a copy enumerated by two axes, one of which is agent-served, will compare the
agent-served axis at position `-1` and therefore file the movement at the *other* axis even if the
agent-served one is inner to it. The nest still wraps both loops (the levels come from the
enumeration axes, not from the filing level), so the emitted count is right; what moves is which
`Loop` directly contains the instruction. No shipping configuration has a copy enumerated by an
agent-served axis *and* another axis simultaneously, so this has never fired. **If you add one,
change `_ordpos` to index `all_inner` and re-run the region-walk tests** — the copy path's rule is
"the full ord", and this is the one line that does not follow it.

#### 12.8 Placing each op-class: `read_level`, and the matmul by presence

##### 12.8.1 `reads`, `copy_ops`, `scale`

Three presence-derived operand partitions, each defined with no name literal:

```
copy_ops = [op for op in theta.operands if op.hops and op.hops[0].dst == Space.SHARED]
reads    = [op for op in theta.operands if op.hops and op.hops[-1].dst == Space.REGISTER]
scale    = len(reads) > 2
```

`reads` covers both the two-hop `shared→register` form and the one-hop direct-to-register form; a
direct-to-register operand has no separate copy and awaits on the load counter. The accumulator has
no input trajectory in the main loop, so it falls out of `reads` automatically. `scale` marks the
presence of extra elementwise/broadcast operands beyond the two matmul inputs — again derived by
counting, with no format-name test.

##### 12.8.2 `read_level` — one derivation, and the empty-presence case

```python
read_level = {op.name: op_class_level(theta, op, READ) for op in reads}
```

`placement.op_class_level` states the rule: **the innermost mode of the op-class's presence set;
the reduction chunk when the presence set is empty.**

This used to be re-derived inline as `_presence(theta, op)[-1] if _presence(theta, op) else None`.
The two agree on every non-empty presence set and diverge on exactly the empty one, where the
canonical helper says "the chunk" and the inline version says `None`. `None` matches no mode at the
emission site (`read_level[op.name] == mode`), so **the read was emitted zero times, in every
block**.

*Why empty presence is reachable at all.* The movement quantum is subtracted from the hop's presence
set (section 1.9): the coordinates inside one instruction are one presence point, so an axis one
instruction spans is absent. When the quantum spans every axis the read still varies over, the
presence set is legitimately empty and the operand is read exactly once per enclosing chunk.

*The measurement.* On an MX-scaled fp8 block at a reduction depth of 128 — where the reduction inner
mode has extent 1 and drops out of `ord` — with a vector width of 1 on both inputs, which is the
only case for which the addon layer supplies a read quantum for the scale operands, the scale
operand's presence set is empty and **no scale read appears in the prologue, the steady body, any
drain step or the short arm**. The operand is copied to shared memory and never read into registers.
It surfaced as two unrelated-looking failures with one cause: an in-place anti-dependency on the
scale operand reported undischarged (the anti-dependency has no read to discharge it, because the
read does not exist), and, at a shallower prefetch, a complaint that the short-trip path could not
be emitted in either shape with four unserved consumers. Reduction depths of 256 and 512 pass,
because the reduction inner mode survives the subtraction. The `nest` head-emission site (12.12.3)
is the other half of this fix.

##### 12.8.3 `leaf_mode` — placing the matrix instruction by presence, not by nest depth

This is the second emphasized topic, and it is a two-part story: a rule that was wrong, and a
correction that was itself wrong on the first attempt.

```python
_wmma_pres = ({m for o in theta.output_operands() for m in theta.presence(o)}
              | set(theta.reduction_names()))
leaf_mode = next((m for m, _e in reversed(inner) if m in _wmma_pres),
                 inner[-1][0] if inner else None)
```

**Part 1: the rule that was wrong.** `leaf_mode` used to be `inner[-1]` — the innermost level of the
nest, unconditionally. That made the matrix instruction **the one op-class not placed the way every
other op-class is placed**: `read_level` above is an `op_class_level` call, the copy level is a
presence query, and the compute leaf was a nest-depth index.

The two answers had always agreed, which is why it survived. Every inner mode is either in some
output's presence set (a free axis) or is a reduction mode, and the union of those two is every
inner mode, so "the innermost mode in the union" and "the innermost mode" are the same mode. They
come apart exactly when an axis is traversed by an **agent** rather than by the coordinate — the
third axis class from 12.7. Such a mode stays in `ord` because the bulk copy still walks its
regions, while the accumulator does not vary over it, so it is in neither half of the old
two-way classification.

Note the interaction with 12.7: `leaf_mode` is chosen from `inner`, which has already had the
agent-served modes removed. So on today's tree the correction and the old rule still coincide, and
the change was byte-neutral when it landed. Its value is that it will *stop* coinciding correctly
rather than silently the day the mode lists diverge for another reason.

**Part 2: the correction that was wrong on the first attempt — and this is the load-bearing
sentence of the whole subsection.** The obvious presence set for the compute leaf is *the
accumulator's presence set*. That is wrong: **the accumulator does not vary over a reduction mode —
that is what makes it a reduction — but the matrix instruction occurs once per reduction
coordinate**, accumulating into the same registers. Using the output presence alone therefore puts
`leaf_mode` at the innermost *free* axis, which is **outer** to the reduction loop in a K-innermost
order, and the matrix instruction is hoisted clean above the K loop: one multiply-accumulate per
tile instead of `k_tiles` of them. 130 tests failed on exactly that.

Hence the union with `theta.reduction_names()`. Read the set as: *the levels at which a distinct
matmul instance exists* — the axes the accumulator varies over, plus the axes it accumulates over.

**Where it is consumed.** `build_level` appends the matmul to the body of the level whose mode
equals `leaf_mode`, and continues recursing below it for any level the output does not traverse. So
the matmul is not necessarily at the bottom of the nest; there can be loops inside it. That is the
concrete difference from the old rule, expressed structurally.

**The fallback.** `next(..., inner[-1][0] if inner else None)` — if no inner mode is in the presence
union (which requires an accumulator present on nothing and no reduction modes at all), the old
answer is used, and with no inner modes at all `leaf_mode` is `None`, in which case `nest` emits the
matmul directly with no enclosing loop (12.12.3).

**The test is unusually instructive and is worth reading before touching this.**
`test_loopmodel.test_the_wmma_is_placed_by_presence_not_by_the_nests_depth` runs three
configurations and asserts three separate things:

1. that the modes *outside* the presence union are **exactly** the agent-served ones —

   ```python
   assert set(inner) - want == set(served) & set(inner)
   ```

   The test comment records that this guard *fired*, and that firing was its job: it was written to
   fail the day an inner mode stopped being either free-on-the-output or a reduction, i.e. the day
   the two-way classification became three-way. Any *other* mode leaving the presence union is a new
   fact, not this one, and the assertion message says so.
2. that the rule's answer equals the deepest unserved mode — the equivalence that makes the change
   emit-neutral, pinned so that it **fails loudly** the day an axis becomes agent-served, at which
   point a maintainer must re-read the emitted diff rather than assume it.
3. that `build_ir` still produces a non-empty tree for each configuration.

That structure — assert the *reason* the two rules coincide, not just that they coincide — is the
pattern to copy when you change a placement rule that is currently a no-op.

#### 12.9 The copy family — movements, region axes, and one copy instruction

##### 12.9.1 `_units` and the fused-retime guard

```python
_units = {key: (members, nreg) for key, members, nreg in theta.movement_units()}
```

`theta.movement_units()` is the **single authority** for which cooperative movements this schedule
point emits and how many region instances each one has. Both the emitter and the downstream lowering
read it, precisely because deriving it twice invites the two to disagree about how many copies exist
and what a copy's completion granularity is. The key is a tuple of member operand names; the value
is `(members, n_regions)`.

Immediately after, a guard rejects a fused group whose members carry different prefetch retimes:

```python
for _g in theta.fuse_groups:
    _members = [n for n in _g if n in off]
    if len({off[n] for n in _members}) > 1:
        raise ValueError("fuse group ... mixes prefetch offsets ...")
```

A fused group is **one cooperative instruction**, so its members must be co-issued; one instruction
cannot simultaneously move operand X's chunk `iter+off_X` and operand Y's chunk `iter+off_Y`. The
alternative — silently forcing every member to the representative's retime — would emit a schedule
nobody asked for, so the request is rejected with both offsets named and the two repairs suggested
(split the group, or equalize the retimes).

There is a **known unresolved sibling of this guard** worth naming here: a fused group whose members
disagree about *copy-first versus copy-last* is currently resolved by a disjunction rather than
rejected. That is tracked and is not fixed; it is the same class of defect as the retime mix, and if
you are here to harden this area, that is the next one.

##### 12.9.2 `_copy_group(name)`

`next((k for k in _units if name in k), (name,))` — the movement key containing this operand, or a
one-element tuple. A linear scan over a dictionary with at most a handful of keys, called once per
copy operand per phase. Its only role is deduplication: `copy_insts` walks the copy operands and
uses the group key to emit each cooperative movement once rather than once per member.

##### 12.9.3 Three region-axis questions, deliberately kept apart

The single hardest thing to keep straight in this file is that a split movement raises **three
different questions about region axes**, and the source answers each with its own helper because
conflating any two of them has produced a real defect.

| Helper | Question | Answer shape |
|---|---|---|
| `_region_mode_of` | *Which level is this movement filed under?* | one mode name, or `None` |
| `_enum_axes` | *Which axes enumerate this movement's instances?* | the **representative** member's tuple |
| `_group_region_modes` | *Which axes is this movement present on at all?* | the **union** over members |

**`_region_mode_of(member_ops)`** returns the first presence mode of the group representative's bulk
hop, i.e. the mode the copy is filed under for naming purposes. It is read off **the copy hop's own
presence** rather than by reaching for `op.region_modes`: a bulk copy is present exactly on the axes
it does *not* span in one instruction, which for a split tile is the region mode and for an unsplit
one is nothing. Same answer today, but obtained from the presence set that places every other
op-class — so a future hop with a different bulk-ness needs no new branch. It uses `_bulk_hop`, not
`hops[0]`, for the reason in 12.6.3. Members of a fused group may be tiled on *different* region
axes (the pairing is by index), so a heterogeneous group is labelled by one axis; that naming gap is
tracked and is orthogonal to the ordering.

**`_enum_axes(member_ops)`** returns the representative member's own presence-mode tuple, and the
docstring is explicit that union-over-members is wrong **in both directions**:

* *A fused group.* Members are paired **by index** — region `j` of A moves with region `j` of B — so
  A's split axis and B's split axis are **one** index, not a product. Taking the union puts the
  movement under both loops and emits `|A_axis| × |B_axis|` placements for a `|A_axis|`-region
  movement.
* *One operand split on two axes.* A tile cut both on a free axis and on the reduction depth
  genuinely has a product of regions, and **one member carries both axes** — so the
  representative's own tuple *is* the product and both loops must enclose it.

Union-over-members cannot tell these apart because it loses which member contributed what. The
representative's own tuple answers exactly the enumeration question.

**`_group_region_modes(member_ops)`** returns the ordered union of every member's bulk-hop presence
modes. This is the *invariance* question — what the movement is present on, which is what the
first-touch/stride guard needs. The docstring states the failure concretely: a fused group filed
under one member's axis and judged "invariant over the other member's axis" by name inequality would
have its single cooperative load first-touch-guarded to value 0 of that other axis, and the regions
paired with every other value **would never be issued**. That is a wrong kernel, from a one-character
test.

The rule to carry away: **invariance is presence-based, never name-inequality-based.**

##### 12.9.4 `_copy_inst(member_ops, slot, nregions, war=True)`

Builds one movement instruction. Inputs: the member operands of one cooperative movement, the
rotation slot expression for the shared buffer, the movement's region count, and whether the
anti-dependency applies. Output: an `Inst` wrapping a `Load`.

```
h0     = member_ops[0].hops[0]
pl     = Placement(space=SHARED, slots=(("", slot),))
tokens = tuple(op.name for op in member_ops)
size   = Σ over members of  operand_tile_bytes(op) // max(1, op.split)
coord  = tuple((axis, None) for axis in _enum_axes(members))  if nregions > 1 else ()
aw     = dedup-union over members of _site_awaits(op.name, "copy"),
         dropping WAR kinds when war is False
ld     = Load(tokens, h0.src, h0.dst, 0, part=0, n_parts=1, coord=coord, size_bytes=size)
return Inst(op=ld, placement=pl, agent=_SINGLE_ROLE, awaits=aw)
```

Five decisions are recorded at this site and each is a constraint on future edits.

**(a) A token is an op-class name, always — never a synthesized string.** Which storage region a
movement carries is a *coordinate* (`Load.coord`), exactly like every other position in the model.
Encoding the pair `(op-class, region)` as `"A0"` made every consumer re-derive the op-class by
**parsing it back**, and three call sites grew three different string-strippers that disagreed once
there were three or more regions. A region split makes sibling movements of the *same* op-class, so
they must keep sharing its name — the residency obligation is keyed on it.
`test_loopmodel.test_load_tokens_are_theta_op_class_names_never_synthesized` runs over every named
scenario and asserts that every token is a name in `theta.operands`.

**(b) `part`/`n_parts` are not the region count.** They are the intra-tile transfer index and count
of *one* movement, and both are pinned at `0`/`1` because sub-tile transfer fan-out on the copy is
not modelled. A region-split copy already emits **separate** instructions per region; those are
distinct movements, not sub-transfers of one movement. Conflating the two fields is an easy and
tempting error: `nregions` is right there in the signature and is used for nothing but the coordinate
guard.

**(c) The coordinate names every enumerating axis, not just the representative.** `_region_mode_of`
answers "which level does this copy sit at", which is one mode by construction; the coordinate is a
different question — **it must name each axis whose enclosing loop supplies one of its digits**, or
the value that loop supplies is never recorded. The measurement: on a configuration with both inputs
cut two ways on a free axis and two ways on the reduction depth, one operand is enumerated by the
product and the nest correctly wrapped it in both loops, so the right *number* of copies was emitted
(4 for 4 regions) — but every one of them carried only the reduction-axis coordinate. Downstream,
the region resolver reads the coordinate, found no free-axis digit, dropped the movement from its
region-splitting set, and **emitted no region increment at all**: the descriptor never walked that
operand's regions. The independent walk checker skipped it on the same "no flat index" rule and
called the program clean, which is how a 90-cell loop-order sweep passed for weeks on a walk that did
not exist. Two checkers, one blind spot, because both keyed on the same missing field.

**(d) Size is per movement, summed over members.** Each member contributes *its own* per-region
share, `operand_tile_bytes(op) // op.split`, so a region movement of a split member carries a
fraction of the tile while an unsplit member in the same fused group carries the whole thing. This
is what makes a fused group with heterogeneous split counts size correctly.

**(e) Awaits are a real union, not a concatenation.** Because a fused movement's producer identity is
the *movement*, every member's residency obligation resolves to the **same** dependency name, so
concatenating the members' await tuples emitted the identical wait once per member. The dedup key is
`(str(dep), counter, kind, scope)`. The members' anti-dependencies stay distinct — each names the
op-class whose reads vacate that operand's buffer — so the union deduplicates the residency and
keeps both anti-dependencies. The `war=False` path (the prologue) drops anti-dependencies entirely:
a prologue copy fills a buffer nothing has read yet, so there is no vacating read to wait for.

#### 12.10 `copy_insts(phase, t)` — one instruction list per stage step

**Concept.** `copy_insts` is the single generator of shared-fill instructions for **all five**
emission contexts. It returns a flat list of `Inst` (no nesting — the nesting is a separate step,
12.11) and records each instruction's nesting metadata in `_copy_meta`.

```
for op in copy_ops:
    key = _copy_group(op.name)
    if key already emitted: continue
    members = the group's operands;  nreg = _units[key][1]
    o = off[op.name]                      # this movement's prefetch retime
    d = _prefetch_depth(theta, op)        # the shared ring depth this movement rotates through
    slot, present, war = <per-phase, table below>
    if not present: continue
    inst = _copy_inst(members, slot, nreg, war=war)
    spans = _group_region_modes(members) if nreg > 1 else ()
    enum  = _enum_axes(members)          if nreg > 1 else ()
    level = the innermost of `enum` in ord order, or None
    _copy_meta[id(inst)] = (level, nreg, spans, enum)
```

**The five phases.** `t` is the step index within a peel, ranging over `[0, M)`.

| `phase` | slot expression | presence test | anti-dependency |
|---|---|---|---|
| `steady` | `Expr(var=outer_var, mod=d, add=o)` — symbolic `(iter + off) mod d` | always | yes |
| `prologue` | `cst((t + o − M) mod d)` — a concrete ramp buffer | `o ≥ M − t` | **no** |
| `degenerate` | `cst(t mod d)` — this step's own chunk | always | `t ≥ d` |
| `drain_bind` | `Expr(var=outer_var, mod=d, add=o)` — the **steady** symbolic slot | `o ≤ M − 1 − t` | yes |
| `drain` | `Expr(var=f"T-{M−t−o}", mod=d)` — a symbolic tail chunk | `o ≤ M − 1 − t` | yes |

**The stagger is per op-class, not per level.** This is the direct consequence of the retime being
indexed by op-class: the peel ramp brings each movement into the pipe at *its own* depth, not at the
level's maximum. In the prologue a movement appears from step `M − o` onward (deepest first); in the
drain it disappears after step `M − 1 − o` (deepest first again). A configuration where the two
inputs have different prefetch depths is an ordinary schedule point, not a special case.

**The `drain` phase is legacy and `drain_bind` is what runs.** The `else` branch — the symbolic
`T-Δ` tail slot — dates from before drain steps were wrapped in a binding that *defines* the chunk
index. With the binding, a drain step can use the ordinary steady slot expression keyed on the chunk
variable, and the whole schedule shares **one residue timeline** from prologue through steady to
drain rather than having a special tail form. `_drain_step` passes `"drain_bind"`; nothing in the
package passes `"drain"`. **It is dead code.** It is retained because it documents the older shape
and because the branch is `else`, i.e. free; if you delete it, make the final branch raise on an
unknown phase name rather than silently falling through to a symbolic slot nobody validated.

**The `degenerate` phase, and why it is not a special case bolted on.** The short-trip arm emits an
*unpipelined* schedule: every step copies its own chunk and reads it in the same step. The comment
proves the continuity: for a **uniform** retime, `degenerate` is bit-identical to `prologue`, because
`o = M` makes the presence test `o < M − t` false at every `t` and `(t + M − M) mod d == t mod d`.
That equivalence is exactly why every shipping configuration is untouched by the phase existing. It
differs only where the retime is **non-uniform**, and there the ramp is *wrong*: a shallow movement
(retime 1 against a peel depth of 2) is skipped at step 0 and copied at step 1 — landing **after**
the step that reads it, with no steady body to absorb the stagger.

**The `degenerate` anti-dependency is derived from the ring, not assumed.**

```python
war = True if phase not in ("prologue", "degenerate") else (
    phase == "degenerate" and t >= max(1, d))
```

In the short arm each step reads what it copied, so step `t` overwrites a buffer only once an
*earlier step of this same arm* used that slot — that is, once the arm wraps the ring at `t ≥ d`.
The comment names both wrong shortcuts: claiming "no anti-dependency ever" drops a real obligation
when the peel depth exceeds the ring depth (the single-buffered configuration), and claiming "always"
asks the ledger to discharge against a vacating read that does not exist.

**Filing the movement at its innermost enumerating axis.**

```python
_ordpos = {n: i for i, (n, _e) in enumerate(inner)}
_lvl = max(_enum, key=lambda a: _ordpos.get(a, -1)) if _enum else None
```

A movement spanning two axes filed at the **outer** one is enumerated by that axis alone and emits
`extent` copies instead of the product; filed at the **inner** one, both loops wrap it and the
strides on each do the rest. `_region_mode_of` returns the representative, which is the right *name*
but not necessarily the right *level* — which is why the filing level is computed here from `_enum`
and the naming mode is computed there. (This is the one line that indexes `inner` rather than
`all_inner`; see the sharp edge at the end of 12.7.)

`test_loopmodel.test_region_split_copy_is_ROLLED_at_its_region_level` pins the outcome from the
outside: for a split scenario it finds every loop that directly wraps a copy, asserts the loop's mode
is one of that operand's region modes, that its trip equals the operand's split count, that it is an
inner (statically unrolled) level, that the instruction's coordinate names the region **symbolically**
(the loop supplies the value), and — the rolled-emission property — that a split operand emits the
**same number of copy nodes** as an unsplit one. It finishes by asserting the rendered dump shows a
region loop header, because the structural distinction is supposed to be visible.

#### 12.11 Nesting the copies: `_nest_copy_runs`, `_nest_copies`, `_axis_stride`, `_order_sigma_c`

##### 12.11.1 `_order_sigma_c(body)` and the order of the two operations

```python
def _order_sigma_c(body):
    return _nest_copy_runs(_sigma_c_order(body, _copy_first))
```

Two lines, and the order is **not stylistic**. The issue-order refinement classifies a node by
unwrapping it to its **one** movement. A nest holding two operands' copies together has no single
movement, so the classifier returns "not a refill copy" for the whole block and the block silently
stays wherever the skeleton put it — **copies first**, inverting the refill-after-read freeze. This
was measured: doing it the other way round flipped copy-last to copy-first, and the ledger's ordering
arm then reported both shared anti-dependencies undischarged.

So: the refinement orders the copies as **separate** instructions, exactly as it always did, and only
then are contiguous runs folded into the ord nest — a fold that reorders *within* a run and never
across the read/compute boundary the refinement established.

##### 12.11.2 `_nest_copy_runs(body)` and `_nest_copy_runs.flush()`

Folds each **maximal run** of copy instructions in an ordered body into one ord-ordered nest,
leaving everything else in place.

```
out, run = [], []
def flush():
    if run:
        out.extend(_nest_copies([_copy_meta[id(n)] + (n,) for n in run]))
        run.clear()
for n in body:
    if id(n) in _copy_meta: run.append(n)
    else:                   flush(); out.append(n)
flush()
return out
```

`flush` is the trivial inner helper: if the pending run is non-empty, hand it to `_nest_copies` with
each node's metadata tuple prepended, extend the output with the result, and clear the run. It is a
closure rather than a parameter-passing function purely so that `out` and `run` stay in one scope.

**Why runs rather than "all the copies".** Preserving the run structure is what keeps the fold
inside the boundaries the ordering refinement set. If the refinement moved some copies after the
reads and left others before, there are two runs, and each is nested independently; a
whole-body gather would merge them and destroy the ordering decision.

**The invariant this function carries, stated in its docstring as an imperative.** *Every* consumer
of `copy_insts` must call it. The region loop used to be built inside `copy_insts`, so it came for
free everywhere; moving it out (so the refinement can still see individual movements) means **a
caller that forgets it emits copies with no enclosing region loop** — and a copy with no region loop
carries no region coordinate. The measured symptom: the prologue went from four correctly-coordinated
copies to four coordinate-less ones. Today there are three callers — the steady body, each prologue
step, and each drain step — plus the short arm, and all four route through either `_order_sigma_c` or
a direct `_nest_copy_runs` call.

**Idempotence.** A second pass is safe: an already-nested node is a `Loop`, not an `Inst`, so its
identity is not in `_copy_meta` and it is treated as a non-copy and passed through.

##### 12.11.3 `_nest_copies(made)` and `_nest_copies.build(li)`

**Concept.** Order the chunk's copies **by the traversal order, not by operand**, and build exactly
the loop levels the copies need.

**The defect it fixes.** Each op-class used to get its own region loop, appended as siblings, so the
emitted sequence was grouped per operand: `A0 A1 B0 B1`. The traversal order for a split kernel is
`[K_inner, M_split, N_split]`, and walking *that* gives `A0 B0 B1 A1` — which is exactly the order the
**reads** come out in, because reads are placed by `build_level` at their presence level inside the
shared nest. Two different orders over one traversal is not a schedule; the traversal is supposed to
be a single sweep. It was invisible without a split, because unsplit every op-class has exactly one
copy and "grouped by operand" and "ord order" are the same sequence.

**Algorithm.**

```
flat   = [inst for entries whose filing level is None]     # unsplit: hoisted outermost
order  = [name for (name, _e) in all_inner]                # THE FULL ord (12.7)
ext    = dict(all_inner)                                   # THE FULL extent map (12.7)
levels = ordered-unique of the ENUMERATION axes of every entry
levels.sort(key=order.index)
if not levels: return flat                                 # no split: byte-identical to before

build(li):
    m = levels[li];  body = []
    for each entry filed at m:
        node = inst
        for g in reversed(levels[:li]):                    # every ENCLOSING level
            stride = _axis_stride(g, spans, nregions, ext)
            if stride > 1:
                node = Cond(Pred(Expr(var=g, mod=stride) == 0), then=[node], kind="first_touch")
        body.append(node)
    if li+1 < len(levels): body.append(build(li+1))
    return Loop(mode=m, trip=ext[m], outer=False, bodies=[body])

return flat + [build(0)]
```

**Levels come from the enumeration axes, not from the spanned axes.** A fused movement is *present*
on its peer's axis without being *enumerated* by it (12.9.3); making that a level for it emits the
cross product. The two tuples are both in the metadata precisely so this distinction can be made
here.

**The nest is built only over the modes some copy is filed at, never over the full traversal.** A
level no copy is present on would wrap everything in a loop of that extent with every body
first-touch-guarded to iteration 0 — the same instructions, needless structure, and a shape the
downstream region walk then has to see through.

**Presence on an enclosing axis is a stride, and first-touch is its degenerate case.** This is the
generalization that removed a special case. A movement moves `own` regions along axis `g` out of
`ext[g]` values, so it issues every `ext[g] // own` values:

* `own == ext[g]` → stride 1 → **no guard** (present at every value);
* `own == 1` → stride `ext[g]` → the guard `g mod ext[g] == 0`, which over a coordinate ranging
  `[0, ext)` **is** `g == 0` — the classic first-touch guard;
