   those exact literals, and the scale names `MXSA[m,k]` / `MXSB[n,k]` likewise. So the dump is now
   *faithful to the node*, which is what the renderer owes, but the node itself still carries A/B/C
   literals. Fixing the renderer moved the literal one layer up rather than removing it. A reader
   who sees `A[m,k]` in a dump has learned that the node says `A[m,k]`, not that the decoder
   independently derived the name. If you generalise `emit.wmma_inst` to derive these from the
   operand list, this line needs no change.
2. The evaluation guard is `env is not None and hasattr(pl, "at")`, and it calls
   `pl.at(env)` — **without** `keep_unresolved`. So a compute line inside the drain, where the outer
   induction is deliberately unbound, will pin any source slot that references it. In practice the
   register-ring slot never references the outer induction (it rotates on the inner substep), so
   this has no observed effect; but it is the same class of defect that `render_unrolled` fixes for
   the load line, and it is unguarded here. See 15.6.2.

##### 15.4.3 `_one_line(op, placement, env)`

**Signature.** `_one_line(op, placement=None, env=None) -> str`. Four lines of body: a two-way
dispatch, `Load → _load_line`, anything else → `_mma_line`.

**What it is for.** It is called by `render_ir`, by `render_unrolled` and by `render_stream` — three
walkers with three different traversal strategies and three different coordinate frames. Because all
three bottom out here, an instruction's rendered text is a pure function of `(op, placement, env)`
and nothing else, so two views of the same node differ only where their `env` differs. That is what
makes the standard debugging move work: dump the rolled view and the unrolled view of one kernel,
and every textual difference between a node's two renderings is a *frame* difference, never a
formatting one. Inline this into the walkers and that guarantee is gone — which is not hypothetical,
because the two views were separately formatted in an earlier revision and drifted in exactly this
way (the rolled view printed a bare slot expression where the unrolled view printed a resolved
index, and a reader comparing them read the difference as a scheduling difference).

**The dispatch is on the node type, not on a `kind` string, and that is deliberate.** `Load` and
`Mma` are the only two op-class types in `ir.py` (3.4, 3.5), so `isinstance` is exhaustive by
construction and a third type added later fails loudly by rendering as a matmul rather than silently
matching a default branch. An `op.kind`-keyed dict would need a `KeyError` path; the type test does
not.

**Cost.** One `isinstance` per rendered instruction, so `O(1)` per node and `O(nodes)` per dump —
entirely dominated by the string building inside the two callees. It is not on the codegen path at
all: no renderer runs unless a debugging flag is set (15.1).

**Weakness.** The `placement=None, env=None` defaults let it be called with no frame at all, which
both callees then handle by printing symbolic forms. That is genuinely useful in a unit test, but it
also means a walker that *forgets* to thread its `env` produces a plausible-looking dump in the wrong
frame rather than an error. `render_unrolled` had that defect (15.6.2). If you add a fourth caller,
pass `env` explicitly even when it is empty, so that "no frame" is a stated choice.

**Alternative considered.** Making `Load` and `Mma` each carry a `render()` method and dropping this
function. Rejected because it would put target-flavoured vocabulary (`tdm`, `ds_read`, `vgpr`) into
`ir.py`, which is core — the whole reason the renderer is a separate module with a stated exemption
(0.2, 15.2). The dispatch lives here precisely so the naming stays on this side of the boundary.

#### 15.5 `_await_line(aw)` — the discharge points, and why the kind is printed

An `Await` (section 1.11) is a **named** dependency: it says "the value `dep` on completion class
`counter` must be complete, within scope `scope`, before the owning instance issues". It carries no
number — `Await.count` is left at `-1` by construction, because this decoder targets a backend that
re-derives counts from the emitted dataflow.

Format:

```
{'await':8s}{aw.dep}  on {tag}@{aw.scope}{cnt}  <{kind}>{order}   # {aw.note}
```

Real lines:

```
await   A@global:iter  on copy@wave  <RAW-residency>   # A resident
await   A:g0:lastread  on read@wave  <rotation-WAR> [issue AFTER those readers]   # refill WAR: slot vacated by prior read
await   A:shared:lastread  on read@wave  <inplace-WAR> [issue AFTER those readers]   # refill WAR: slot vacated by prior read
```

Column by column:

* **`aw.dep`** — the producer endpoint, formatted by the `Endpoint` dataclass's own `__str__`
  (defined in `ledger.py`, section 8). It reads `op@at` or `op:at:role`, optionally with a
  generation. `A@global:iter` is "operand A's arrival in global-staged form, generation indexed by
  the outer induction"; `A:g0:lastread` is "the last read of A out of register group `g0`". The
  endpoint is a **structured record**, not a formatted string, precisely because four call sites
  once re-split a formatted string with three different rules; the renderer is the one place that
  legitimately turns it back into text.
* **`on {tag}@{scope}`** — `_counter_tag(aw.counter)` and `aw.scope`. Scope is `wave` (same agent —
  program order suffices) or `block` (cross-agent — a memory-ordering barrier is needed). **`scope`
  is currently inert in the model**: nothing downstream branches on it except a diagnostic tag
  string, so read it as documentation of intent, not as a claim about what will be emitted.
* **`{cnt}`** — ` (<= N)` when `aw.count >= 0`, otherwise absent. Since nothing sets it, this never
  appears today. It is left in so that a counter-materialising backend, if one is ever written,
  shows its work in the same dump.
* **`<{kind}>`** — the hazard class. This is the field the audit added, and the rationale is
  scheduling, not readability.
* **`{order}`** — the literal ` [issue AFTER those readers]`, appended exactly when
  `aw.kind` is in the anti-dependency set.
* **`# {aw.note}`** — a free-text note the ledger attached at construction.

**Why the kind must be printed.** Section 1.7 defines four obligation kinds forming a closed set:
`RAW-residency` and `crossing-RAW` (true dependencies — the consumer needs the producer's value) and
`rotation-WAR` and `inplace-WAR` (anti-dependencies — the writer must wait for prior readers). The
two families do not merely *read* differently; they **decide issue order**. An anti-dependency await
means its owning instruction must be issued *after* the readers it names, which is exactly the
refinement that places refill copies last in a body (section 7). Rendering every await identically
made a correctly-ordered body and a wrongly-ordered body produce the same dump, so the one artifact
that could have caught an ordering defect could not distinguish it from a correct schedule.

**Unknown kinds are shown as defects, not smoothed over.** The kind is checked for membership in the
closed set and, if absent, rendered `{kind}!UNKNOWN-KIND`:

```python
kind = aw.kind if aw.kind in OBLIGATION_KINDS else f"{aw.kind}!UNKNOWN-KIND"
order = " [issue AFTER those readers]" if aw.kind in WAR_KINDS else ""
```

That is deliberate and it matches the model's `is_war` predicate, which *raises* on an unknown kind
rather than defaulting to "true dependency". The renderer cannot raise (it must never break a
build), so it does the renderer's equivalent: it makes the anomaly loud in the output. If you ever
see `!UNKNOWN-KIND` in a dump, the fix is in `ir.py` — add the new kind to the RAW or WAR set — and
until you do, every issue-order decision downstream has silently classified it as a true
dependency.

Note the asymmetry between the two membership tests above: the `order` suffix is keyed on the WAR
set directly, so an unknown kind gets no order annotation *and* is flagged. That is the safe
pairing; do not "simplify" it by deriving `order` from the already-flagged `kind` string.

**The fifth kind is not here.** The ledger also constructs `readahead-residency` obligations, which
are *not* in the closed dispatch set: they are a structural requirement that the prologue actually
pre-issue a named coordinate, not a wait. They are skipped when the await index is built, so they
never reach `_await_line` and never appear in the stream views at all. If you are chasing a missing
prologue read, the stream dump will not show you the obligation — you need the ledger, via
`emit_mainloop(theta)["ledger"]`, or the `UNDISCHARGED:` header lines that `kernel_to_ir_text`
prints above the dump.

**Placement of await lines.** Both stream walkers emit an instruction's awaits *immediately before*
the instruction, one per line, at the same indentation. Awaits are therefore attached to the
consumer, never floating. A consequence worth knowing when skimming: a body with heavy
synchronization has more await lines than instruction lines, and the instruction is always the
*last* line of each such group.

#### 15.6 The structure formatters

##### 15.6.1 `_loop_header(node)` — outer versus inner

```python
if node.outer:
    pred = node.trip.render() if hasattr(node.trip, "render") else str(node.trip)
    return f"for {node.mode} while ({pred})"
return f"for {node.mode} in range({node.trip})"
```

`Loop.trip` is a **control edge**, not a display extent (section 3): for an outer, pipelined,
runtime-trip level it is a structured predicate object; for an inner statically unrolled level it is
an integer repeat count. The header spells the two differently on purpose, so the dump distinguishes
"a real back edge whose continuation condition is *this*" from "a fully unrolled level of *this*
many steps":

```
for iter while (iter < T-2):
for K_inner in range(2):
```

`node.outer` is read from the explicit structural flag, never inferred from the trip being symbolic.
The `hasattr(…, "render")` guard is defensive: an outer loop's trip is always a structured
predicate today, and the `str()` fallback exists so a hand-built test IR with a string trip still
renders.

The steady header carries the whole pipeline story in one line. `iter < T-2` says the steady region
runs `T-2` trips out of a runtime trip count `T`, because two chunks were peeled into a prologue and
two into a drain. Cross-check it against the peel-validity guard above it (`if T > 2`) and the
`off (retime, …)` line of the geometry table (`A:copy@iter=2`): all three must agree on the same
`2`, and if they do not, the peel depth and the emitted structure have diverged.

##### 15.6.2 `_subbody_header(node, lo, hi)` — the multi-sub-body form

A loop level may be emitted as a **sequence of sub-loops over disjoint sub-ranges** rather than one
body with a per-iteration predicate. Section 3.12.2 gives the node representation and section 12.3
the derivation that decides when it applies; both cover why the emitter does this, and
the renderer's problem is how to *head* it.

```python
end = hi if hi is not None else node.trip
if hi is not None and hi - lo == 1:
    return f"{node.mode} = {lo}"          # a BINDING: no loop left
return f"for {node.mode} in range({lo}, {end})"
```

A singleton range is a **binding of the mode to that value**, not a loop; anything wider is a real
loop over the sub-range. In the shipping first-touch shape, a level of trip 2 splits into ranges
`[0,1)` and `[1,2)` and *both* are singletons, so the level is fully unrolled and there is no loop
to head at all:

```
M_inner = 0:  # sec 5.1 sub-body
  ... the read, issued once ...
  for N_inner in range(2): ...
M_inner = 1:  # sec 5.1 sub-body
  ... no read: it was hoisted into the m==0 sub-body ...
  for N_inner in range(2): ...
```

**The defect this replaced (provenance: #175) is the archetypal renderer bug.** The header used to
be printed *once*, above all the sub-bodies, as `for m in range(trip):`. A multi-sub-body loop is a
*sequence*, so that header reads as `trip × (bodyA + bodyB)` — it over-counts the level by the
number of bodies. A reader counting instructions off the dump gets exactly twice the true count, and
the arithmetic is self-consistent, so nothing about the dump looks wrong. That is the shape of every
serious renderer defect in this file: not a garbled line, but a *coherent wrong reading*.

##### 15.6.3 `_COND_NOTE` and `_cond_note(cond)` — naming what a guard is

`Cond` nodes carry a **generic `kind`** — backend-agnostic model vocabulary set by the core — plus
an advisory `label` that the core always leaves empty (scaffold naming is a downstream pass's job,
and the structural validator enforces that the core leaves it blank). `_COND_NOTE` maps the four
kinds to a human sentence, and `_cond_note` looks it up, accepting either a `Cond` node or a bare
kind string, and falling back to the raw kind or the word `guard`.

| `kind` | What the guard is |
|---|---|
| `peel_validity` | The software-pipelined path is only reachable when the loop is long enough to fill and drain the pipe. The note explicitly says **the printed predicate is the authority**: the emitter emits a *strict* `T > M`, so the arm runs at `T >= M+1`. |
| `first_touch` | A read that is invariant over an enclosing loop mode is issued once, on that mode's first pass. |
| `readahead_suppress` | On the last drain step the look-ahead read would fetch a chunk that does not exist; this guard drops that substep. |
| `short_step_validity` | Inside the degenerate (too-short-loop) arm, peeled step `t` has a real chunk only when `T > t`. |

**The `peel_validity` note carries a correction that is worth understanding rather than trusting.**
It used to read `T >= peel-depth` while the line directly above it printed `T > 2`. Those are
different conditions, one apart, and the difference is real: the steady region is lowered into a
*post-tested* loop shape whose body always executes at least once, so admitting `T == M` would run
one steady trip computing a chunk the drain also computes. The note now defers to the printed
predicate and states why. If you are diagnosing an off-by-one at the loop boundary, read the
predicate, not the prose.

**A latent trap in how the note is used.** In `render_ir` the `else` arm of *any* `Cond` prints a
fixed comment describing the short-loop case:

```python
L.append(f"{ind}else:  # short-loop (T < peel-depth: prologue meets drain, ...)")
```

That is correct today because `peel_validity` is the only kind the emitter ever gives an `els` arm
to — `readahead_suppress`, `first_touch` and `short_step_validity` are all one-armed. The moment a
second kind acquires an else branch, this line will confidently mislabel it. The fix, if you add
one, is to route the else comment through `_cond_note` with a per-kind else message rather than
hardcoding one; do not remove the comment, because "else" with nothing after it is how a reader
loses track of which arm they are in.

#### 15.7 `render_stream(ir, raw=False, unroll=False)` — the dispatcher

Three lines of code, and a design decision worth recording:

```python
if raw:    return render_ir_raw(ir)
if unroll: return render_unrolled(ir)
return render_ir(ir)
```

Priority is `raw > unroll > rolled`. `raw` and `unroll` are **keyword arguments of this function**,
not command-line switches. The only CLI surface is `--output-loop-ir`, a bare `store_true` with no
view selector, and it always produces the rolled view. The module docstring used to write these as
`--unroll` / `--raw`, which told every reader to pass an option that does not exist; if you want a
different view from a build, you call `render_stream` yourself from a Python shell, or you change
the one call site in `bridge.kernel_to_ir_text`.

**There is no collapse view, and there is nothing left to collapse.** A `--collapse` folder existed
in an earlier design, when the IR enumerated one instruction node per thread/address instance and
identical ones were folded to `(inst) ×N`. Trimming the address/layout algebra out of the core
removed that enumeration entirely: the stored IR is *already* the collapsed form, one node per
op-class per level, with symbolic slot expressions. If per-address expansion is ever re-added, the
IR module's docstring carries a step-by-step recipe for doing it additively, and a collapse view
would come back with it.

#### 15.8 `render_ir(ir)` — the rolled view

**What it is.** The IR exactly as stored: a loop nest with loop headers, each op-class exactly once
at its presence level with its *symbolic* rotation slot, and the named awaits attached to their
consumers. Nothing is enumerated. Node count — and therefore dump length — is proportional to
`#op-classes × #levels` and is **independent of the trip count**.

Header line:

```
# rolled θ-nest IR (the stored IR; render_stream(unroll=True) for the interleaved view) — §5.2
```

The `§5.2` at the end is the source's own shorthand for an external design note; section 0.3 of this
report is the decoder ring that translates every such marker into a claim stated in full here (this
one is: the emitted IR is rolled, one node per op-class per level, node count independent of trip
count, wait counts left to a downstream lowering). The markers survive in the dump text because the
dump is generated from the source docstrings; they require no lookup.

##### 15.8.1 `render_ir.walk(nodes, d)` — the recursion

Indentation is `"  " * (d + 1)`, i.e. every line is indented at least once under the header. The
dispatch, in source order:

```
for node in nodes:
    Loop, single body     -> print _loop_header, recurse at d+1
    Loop, multi body      -> for each (lo, hi, body) from ranged_bodies():
                                 print _subbody_header(node, lo, hi) + "  # sub-body"
                                 recurse at d+1                       [NO enclosing header]
    Branch                -> print "rotate buf = {mode} % {modulus}:"
                             for residue r: print "buf{r}:", recurse at d+2
    Peel                  -> print "# --- PROLOGUE|DRAIN (peel {k} of {mode}, Lemma 1) ---"
                             recurse at d          [SAME depth: a peel is not a scope]
                             (the literal "Lemma 1" in that banner is the source's citation of the
                              peel decomposition: a pipelined loop of trip T with retime depth M
                              splits into an M-step prologue, a steady region of T−M trips and an
                              M-step drain, valid only when T is large enough — stated in full in
                              section 6.3 of this report)
    Bind                  -> print "{mode} = {value.render()}:  # peel-step chunk binding"
                             recurse at d+1
    Cond                  -> print "if {pred.render()}:  # {note}", recurse then at d+1
                             if els: print "else:  # short-loop ...", recurse els at d+1
    Inst                  -> for each await: print _await_line
                             print _one_line(node.op, node.placement)     [env=None]
```

Four points a maintainer will trip over:

1. **A multi-body loop prints no enclosing header.** That is `_subbody_header`'s contract
   (15.6.2): the sub-bodies *are* the level. Adding a wrapper header back is the #175 defect.
2. **A `Peel` does not increase depth.** The prologue and drain bodies sit at the same indentation
   as the steady loop they bracket, under a comment banner. This is a readability choice — the three
   pipeline stages are siblings in time, and nesting the peels one level deeper suggests
   containment that does not exist.
3. **`Inst` is rendered with `env=None`.** That is what makes this the rolled view: `_coord_of`
   takes its `Expr` branch and prints the shifted coordinate as a formula, and `Placement.render`
   prints the raw slot expression rather than a number. The long `((0+(M_inner+K_inner*2+2)//2)%2)`
   strings are not noise: they are the *definition* of the read-ahead, and evaluating one by hand at
   a chosen `(K_inner, M_inner)` is how you check the schedule without trusting the unrolled view.
4. **The `Branch` arm is maintained but dead.** `Branch` is a register-rotation selector — a switch
   on a residue, one arm per buffer — and it renders as `rotate buf = mode % S:` with `buf0:` /
   `buf1:` arms. **No current emitter output contains a `Branch`**: the emitter expresses rotation
   with symbolic slot expressions instead, and the two are interchangeable views of the same fact.
   The handling is kept so that an IR built by hand, or by a future emitter that prefers explicit
   control, still renders. `render_ir`'s docstring says so, because it used to *advertise* "Branch
   arms for register rotation" as something a reader would see.

##### 15.8.2 `_one_line` at the leaves — and the one thing the rolled view cannot show

Because the rolled view never expands a level, it cannot show you *ordering across iterations* —
whether a refill lands before or after the read it overwrites in the trip that actually executes.
For that, and only for that, use the unrolled view. Everything else — presence level, awaits,
advance, slot formulas, guard structure — is more reliable here, because nothing has been resolved
against an invented environment.

#### 15.9 `render_unrolled(ir)` — the interleaved view

**What it is.** A *view* of the rolled IR, not a second IR. The walker carries a live environment
`{mode: index}`, expands every statically-extent level, evaluates the symbolic slot expressions
against that environment, and emits the resulting linear stream. Enumeration lives **only** here;
the stored IR stays rolled. The value of the view is that a step's read and its consuming compute
end up adjacent, so the read/compute interleave — the thing a scheduling defect actually corrupts —
is legible.

Header line:

```
# UNROLLED view (interleaved read;wmma per leaf; a rendering of the rolled IR — §5.3)
```

(The trailing marker is the source docstring's own citation of the emission procedure — build the
rolled nest, refine the issue order, attach the awaits — which sections 12 and 13 of this report
describe in full, with the issue-order refinement itself at section 10. Section 0.3 is the decoder
ring for every such marker; nothing outside this report is needed.)

##### 15.9.1 `render_unrolled.walk(nodes, env, d)` — the recursion, node by node

**`Loop`, outer.** Prints the header with the suffix `  # one iter shown` and recurses into each
body with `env[mode] = 0`, at depth `d+1`. A runtime trip count cannot be unrolled, so the view
shows **one representative iteration**. Two consequences: (a) you are looking at trip 0, so any
per-trip variation (there should be none in a steady body, by construction) is invisible; (b) the
outer branch iterates `node.bodies` directly rather than `ranged_bodies()`, so an outer *multi-body*
loop would lose its ranges. Outer loops are single-body today; if a coarser outer level is ever
emitted with sub-ranges, this is the line to change.

**`Loop`, inner.** For each `(lo, hi, body)` from `ranged_bodies()`, iterate `v` over
`range(lo, end)` where `end = hi if hi is not None else lo + 1`, recursing with `env[mode] = v` at
the **same depth `d`**. Inner levels do not indent — that is what makes the steady body read as a
flat instruction stream rather than a staircase.

**`Branch`.** Two cases, and the second is the subtle one:

```
if node.mode in env:            # an ordinary residue selector
    take arm (env[mode] % modulus)
else:                           # a PINNED-residue branch
    for each (r, arm): recurse with env[mode] = r
```

The second case handles a branch whose arm key *is* the mode's concrete value — a peel-unrolled
reduction substep. Binding `r` into the environment is what makes the nested coordinates and slots
inside that arm evaluate to the right numbers. Without the binding they would all resolve against a
missing name. As noted in 15.8.1, no current emitter output contains a `Branch` at all.

**`Peel`.** Prints `# --- PROLOGUE ---` or `# --- DRAIN ---` (no `k`/mode detail, unlike the rolled
view) and recurses at the same depth.

**`Bind`.** Prints the binding as a *comment* — `# iter = T-1` — and recurses with
`node.bound_env(env)`. That method binds the mode **only if the value is statically resolvable**: a
prologue step's `iter = j − M` is a constant and binds; a drain step's `iter = T − M + t` references
the runtime trip count and does **not** bind, so the drain body stays symbolic in `iter`. This is
the mechanism the next subsection depends on.

**`Cond`.** Evaluates the predicate in the current environment:

```
v = node.pred.eval(env)
if v is None:                 # UNRESOLVED (references a runtime symbol)
    print "if <pred>:  # <note>"; recurse then at d+1
    if els: print "else:";      recurse els at d+1
else:                         # RESOLVED
    recurse only the arm that actually executes, at depth d
```

So a first-touch guard (`M_inner == 0`) and the drain's look-ahead suppression (`k < n_s − dr`)
**disappear** from the unrolled stream, leaving only the instructions that really run — which is
exactly what you want when counting instructions. The peel-validity guard (`T > M`) is runtime, so
it stays as a visible `if`, and the view shows the long-loop `then` path as the representative.

Note that the unresolved `else` prints bare, with no note — unlike the rolled view, which appends
the short-loop explanation. Minor inconsistency; if you fix it, fix it by calling `_cond_note` in
both places.

**`Inst`.** The interesting arm, covered next.

##### 15.9.2 The unbound-induction guard — the defect that invented a buffer index

```python
if node.placement is not None and hasattr(node.placement, "at"):
    pl = node.placement.at(env, keep_unresolved=True)
else:
    pl = node.placement            # a compute node's {operand: Placement} dict, or None
```

`Expr.eval` **substitutes 0 for a name the environment does not carry**. That is the right behaviour
for evaluation on the codegen path, where the environment always closes the expression, and it is a
fabrication anywhere else. The drain body deliberately leaves the outer induction unbound (see
`Bind` above, because the runtime trip count is not a compile-time number), so pinning rendered
*every drain read in the first steady trip's frame*: a line reading `<-lds[buf0]` under a header
reading `# iter = T-1`, with nothing marking the index as invented. A reader diagnosing a
double-buffer swap sees a concrete buffer number and believes it.

The fix has three properties worth preserving:

1. **Opt-in.** `Placement.at` grew a `keep_unresolved` parameter defaulting to `False`. Making the
   behaviour unconditional was tried and broke 409 tests and both codegen paths, because the emitter
   must always receive a concrete placement; handing it a symbolic expression is not a rendering
   question, it is a miscompile.
2. **Per-expression, not per-placement.** `at` decides slot by slot: a slot whose free variables are
   all in the environment is pinned to a number *while preserving its modulus* (so a consumer can
   still read the ring width off `slot.mod`), and a slot that is not is handed back untouched. On a
   single drain read that means the **register** slot stays concrete (`register[buf1]` — the
   schedule really did choose it) while the **shared-source** slot stays symbolic
   (`<-lds[buf(iter+(N_inner+K_inner*2+2)//4)%2]`). Blanking both would hide a number that is real,
   which is the same defect pointing the other way.
3. **The guard lives in the renderer, not in `at`.** `at` is on the codegen path; the renderer is
   the only caller that can be handed an environment which does not close the expression, so it is
   the one that must ask for the lenient mode.

The unit test pins all three: it asserts that some drain shared-source slot stays symbolic, that the
register slot on those same lines is concrete, that the default `at({})` still pins (so the codegen
contract is unchanged), and — the non-vacuity guard — that some *steady* read does render a concrete
shared slot, so the drain assertion is not satisfied by the renderer simply never pinning anything.

#### 15.10 `render_ir_raw(ir)` — the uninterpreted dump

**Purpose.** Debug the *emitter* without the pretty-printer as a confounder. Every other view
applies formatting rules that could themselves be wrong; this one prints `repr()` of the dataclass
and lets you read the fields.

Header: `# raw rolled θ-nest IR (dataclass repr, pre-order)`.

##### 15.10.1 `render_ir_raw.walk(nodes, d)`

Indentation is `"  " * d` (one level shallower than the other two walkers, which use `d + 1`).
Structural nodes get a compact one-line summary rather than a full `repr`, because a `Loop`'s
`repr` would recursively print its whole body and defeat the purpose:

| Node | Line |
|---|---|
| `Loop` | `Loop({mode} trip={rendered trip}{" outer" if outer})`, then, **if multi-body**, a `body {i} [{lo},{hi}):` line per sub-body, each body walked at `d+1` |
| `Branch` | `Branch({mode} % {modulus})`, then `arm {r}:` per residue, walked at `d+2` |
| `Peel` | `Peel({kind} {mode} k={k})`, body at `d+1` |
| `Bind` | `Bind({mode} = {value.render()})`, body at `d+1` |
| `Cond` | `Cond({pred.render()}{" -> "+label if label})  # {note}`, then `then:` / `else:` sub-headers, arms at `d+2` |
| anything else | `repr(node)` — in practice always an `Inst` |

So the `Inst` line is the raw one: the full `Load`/`Mma` dataclass, the full `Placement` with every
`Expr` field spelled out (`var`, `mod`, `add`, `terms`, `digits`, `carry`), the agent, and every
`Await` with its `Endpoint`. One such line runs to about 900 characters. That is the point — it is
the only place `Expr.digits` and `Expr.carry` are visible as structure rather than as a rendered
formula, and the difference matters: `carry` extracts one floor-divided quantity (the look-ahead
rollover into the next chunk) while `digits` extracts several floor-divided digits of one shifted
position and recombines them in mixed radix (what a rotation slot needs when a group cycles over
more than one reduction rate axis). They render similarly and are different mechanisms.

The `Cond` arm is the only place `Cond.label` is printed, as `-> {label}`. The core always leaves it
empty and the structural validator enforces that, so a non-empty label in a raw dump of core output
is itself a defect signal. It is printed for IRs that have already been through the downstream
scaffold-naming pass.

**When to reach for it.** When a stream view shows something you cannot explain and you need to know
whether the renderer or the emitter is responsible. Concretely: a slot expression that renders
oddly; a coordinate whose value you cannot account for; an `Inst` you expected and cannot find (the
raw view will show it in a body you were not looking at); and the `body_ranges` of a multi-body loop,
which the raw view prints explicitly as `[lo,hi)` and the rolled view only implies through the
sub-body header.

**What it still hides.** `Inst.agent` is inside the `repr`, so it *is* there, but no curated view
prints it — see 15.14. And a `Peel`'s `k` may be an expression object, in which case `Peel(... k=…)`
prints the object's `repr`, not a rendered formula; that is an accepted rough edge in a raw view.

#### 15.11 `render_geometry(theta)` — the derived-numbers table

This is the half of the dump that answers "why does the schedule have this shape" rather than "what
is the schedule". It takes a **schedule point**, not an IR, and re-derives every quantity the
emitter used — instruction counts, buffer sizes, ring depths, register footprint, read-ahead shape,
region and agent structure — so that a reader can check each one by hand. Its stated contract, in
its own header comment, is *every number is checkable by hand*, and 15.11.5 records the one time
that contract was broken.

It performs three lazy imports at call time — `theta.build_S`, and `placement._peel_depths` /
`placement.group_readahead_depth`. These are defensive, not cycle breaks: `render.py` imports only
`ir` and `sizing` at module load, so importing it never drags in the whole derivation stack, and the
two `placement` names are private and would be an odd module-level dependency for a renderer.

It calls `build_S(theta)` itself and uses only the first return value (the register/shared depth
map). `build_S` is pure, so this agrees by construction with the copy the emitter built — but note
that the table is therefore **`S`-consistent with the emitter and not derived from the emitted IR**.
If the emitter ever deviated from `S`, this table would not show it. That is a real blind spot and
the reason the two dumps (this one and the stream view) must be read together.

##### 15.11.1 The header block

```
# derived geometry (how the op counts + sizes are computed)
  reg_bytes=4  lanes=32
  levels(ord) = iter(OUTER) · K_inner(x2) · M_inner(x2) · N_inner(x2)   (outer→inner)
    outer(peel/reduction-chunk ring) = ['iter']   inner(register-ring) = ['K_inner', 'M_inner', 'N_inner']
    reduction modes = ['K_inner']   (= inner \ pres(output), §2.1; in ord order)
  off (retime, per op-class×level) = A:copy@iter=2, A:read@K_inner=1, B:copy@iter=2, B:read@K_inner=1
  mma grid: m_tiles=2 n_tiles=2 k_tiles=2  => 8 mma/kiter
```

* **`reg_bytes` / `lanes`** — the two target scalars everything else is scaled by: bytes per
  register, and lanes per agent.

* **`levels(ord)`** — the full outer-to-inner traversal permutation, formatted by the nested helper

  ```python
  def _lvl(m):
      tag = "OUTER" if m.is_outer else f"x{m.extent}"
      return f"{m.name}({tag})"
  ```

  `_lvl` is trivial but it encodes the package's single most load-bearing distinction (section 1.4):
  a level with a statically known extent prints its extent and is unrolled; a level with the
  extent-0 sentinel prints `OUTER` and is a real runtime loop with a back edge, a peel, and the
  shared ring rotating across it. There is no separate "level kind" field — the extent *is* the
  classification — so `_lvl` reads `Mode.is_outer` rather than any tag.

* **The `outer` / `inner` projection line** restates the same split as two lists, so a reader can
  see at a glance which axes carry the peel and which carry the register ring.

* **`reduction modes`** — the inner axes the accumulator is *not* present on: the contraction axes.
  The trailing marker in that line is the source's citation of the presence rule (an op-class is
  present on exactly the axes it varies over; the complement is its broadcast set), stated in full in
  section 1.3 of this report.
  The parenthetical spells the derivation (inner axes minus the output operand's presence) and — the
  part that was fixed — states that the list is **in traversal order**. It used to be `sorted()` over
  a set, which printed `['K_inner','K_split']` directly beneath a `levels(ord)` line reading
  `K_split · K_inner`: two orderings of the same axes, one line apart, with nothing saying they
  differed. A reader deriving a stride from the reduction list got the radices backwards. Every list
  in this block is now in traversal order.

* **`off (retime, per op-class×level)`** — the retime matrix (section 1.6), printed only when
  non-empty, one term per `(operand, role, level) = depth`, sorted. `A:copy@iter=2` means A's
  global→shared copy runs two chunks ahead of the compute that consumes it; `A:read@K_inner=1` means
  A's shared→register read runs one substep ahead. **The `role` component is why the key is a
  triple**: without it, `off(copy, chunk)` and `off(read, chunk)` are the same key, and the read's
  outer-level offset becomes inexpressible. Reading this line is the fastest way to confirm that the
  parameters you set actually reached the model.

* **`mma grid`** — the compute grid for one reduction chunk, from `sizing.mma_shape`: the two input
  operands' free-tile counts and the reduction-tile count, with the product. `8 mma/kiter` should
  equal the number of compute lines in one steady trip of the unrolled view; it is the cheapest
  cross-check between the two halves of the dump.

##### 15.11.2 The footprint legend

```
  footprint = region_count × Σ_part(W_part × |part|) × frag_reg + accum
  #   region_count is the operand's storage-region count (see the `region axes` block below); it is
  #   NOT folded into free_tiles when the region mode is a reduction mode.
```

This is the formula the `vgpr` column implements, and it is printed so the column can be
reproduced. The factors, each orthogonal (section 5 covers the derivation; the point here is that
it is a **product, never a merge** — the fan appears in exactly one factor, which is what prevents
double-counting):

* `region_count` — how many storage-disjoint parts the operand's tile is cut into;
* `W_part` — the rotation width of one register reuse group, i.e. the value `S` stores;
* `|part|` — how many values of the grouping axis that group holds;
* `frag_reg` — registers one fragment occupies per lane;
* `+ accum` — the accumulator, which has no ring at all and costs `free_tiles × frag_reg`.

##### 15.11.3 The per-operand table: every column

```
  operand    role   presence            free k_tiles frag_reg tile_B ds_reads Sldsreg  Wreg  vgpr  readmode(dr_g)
  A        input  K_inner,M_inner       2       2        8   4096        8       2  g0:2    32  g0:prefetch(1)
  B        input  K_inner,N_inner       2       2        8   4096        8       2  g0:2    32  g0:prefetch(1)
  C        output M_inner,N_inner       4       2       16   8192        0       0     -    64  -
```

| Column | Source | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `operand` | `op.name` | The operand (op-class family) name. |
| `role` | `op.role` | `input` or `output`. Derived on the operand, not from a name literal. |
| `presence` | `theta.presence(op)` joined by commas, or `-` | The inner axes **this operand's data** varies over. |
| `free` | `sizing.free_tiles` | Product of extents of the operand's *own free* presence axes (presence minus reduction). |
| `k_tiles` | `sizing.k_tiles(theta)` | Product of extents of the reduction axes. Schedule-global. |
| `frag_reg` | `sizing.frag_regs` | Registers one fragment occupies per lane. |
| `tile_B` | `sizing.operand_tile_bytes` | Shared-memory bytes for one whole tile across the agent: presence-tiles × fragment elements × element bytes × lanes. |
| `ds_reads` | `sizing.plan_transfers(theta, op, last hop)` when that hop's source is shared, else `0` | Per-lane transfer instructions per chunk. |
| `Sldsreg` | `S.get(op.name, "shared", default=0)` | The **shared ring depth**: how many staging buffers the copy rotates through. `0` for an operand with no shared staging. |
| `Wreg` | `{g: S.get(op.name, g)}` for each fragment group, joined `g:W`; `-` for the output | The **register ring width** per reuse group. |
| `vgpr` | `sizing.operand_footprint_regs(theta, op, S)` | The footprint from the legend above. |
| `readmode(dr_g)` | per group, `prefetch(d)` if `d` else `inplace(0)`; `?` if the derivation raised | The read-ahead shape. |

Two structural notes. The row loop iterates `theta.operands`, so an operand present in the schedule
point but not in the emitted IR (there are none today) would appear here and nowhere else. And
`ds_hop = op.hops[-1] if op.hops else None` — the output operand has no hops at all, so its
`ds_reads` and `Sldsreg` are both zero and its `Wreg` is `-`. That is not a gap; the accumulator has
no rotating ring by construction.

##### 15.11.4 Three columns that do not mean what their headings suggest

The table prints three comment lines immediately under the header, because three columns were each
*measured* misleading and the honest fix was to label them rather than to remove them.

1. **`presence` is the OPERAND's presence, not the read hop's.** A movement quantum absorbs an axis
   from the *read hop's* presence only (section 1.9). So this column is identical with and without an
   active quantum, and when one is active it matches **neither** hop: not the copy (bulk, which
   varies only over region axes) and not the read (which has had the quantum's axes subtracted). The
   downstream GIR dump's `spans` field is where the read hop's real presence is visible.

2. **`k_tiles` is a schedule-global constant with no operand argument.** It is repeated verbatim on
   every row — including the output row, which has no reduction hop at all. It is *not* a
   per-operand quantity, and multiplying it into a per-operand footprint is precisely the
   over-counting bug that section 2.2.4 records (the accumulator came out at `4 × 2 × 16 = 128`
   registers for a tile holding 64). Printing it per row is a layout convenience that invites the
   very arithmetic that was wrong.

3. **`ds_reads` counts PER-LANE transfers, the stream views count OP-CLASS fragments.** These are
   different units and the two numbers are not comparable. Concretely on the reference bf16 fixture:
   the table says `ds_reads = 8` for A, while one steady trip of the unrolled stream contains **4**
   A read lines. Both are right. `plan_transfers` computes
   `operand_buffer_regs ÷ load_regs = (presence-tiles × frag_regs) ÷ regs-per-instruction
   = (2 × 2 × 8) ÷ 4 = 8`; the stream shows 4 op-class fragments, each of which takes 2
   instructions because `frag_regs (8) ÷ load_regs (4) = 2`. If you are reconciling the two, the
   ratio you are looking for is `frag_regs ÷ load_regs`, and `load_regs` is not printed — see 15.14.

##### 15.11.5 Reproducing the `vgpr` column by hand — and the legend that did not

This is the worked arithmetic, and it is also the record of a real defect, because the legend that
is supposed to let you do it was wrong for two months.

**On the bf16 fixture, operand A.** `region_count = 1` (no region split). The register fragment has
one group `g0` with `W = 2` (the `Wreg` column). The grouping axis is `M_inner`, extent 2, one part,
so `|part| = 2`. `frag_reg = 8`.

```
footprint(A) = 1 × (2 × 2) × 8 = 32          matches the vgpr column
```

**The accumulator C.** No ring; `free_tiles × frag_regs = 4 × 16 = 64`. Matches.

**On the four-agent scaled-format fixture, operand A** — the case that exposed the bug. There the
row reads `free=2  frag_reg=16  Wreg=g0:2  vgpr=128`, and `region_count = 2` (A is cut into two
storage regions on the `M_split` axis).

```
footprint(A) = 2 × (2 × 2) × 16 = 128        matches
```

The legend used to read `Σ generations(S) × frag_reg(width) × free_tiles + accum`, i.e. it stood
`free_tiles` in for `|part| × region_count`. Those two agree while the region axis is a **free**
axis and diverge the moment it is a **reduction** axis, where the region multiplies on top of the
whole free fan. They also diverge, as here, when the region axis is *agent-served* and therefore
absent from the operand's presence: `free_tiles = 2` (only `M_inner`), so the old legend computes
`2 × 16 × 2 = 64` against a printed 128. **Measured: 16 of 60 operand rows** across the scaled-format
matrix — every operand of every loop order at region-split 2 — printed a `vgpr` the legend
disagreed with by exactly the region factor.

The consequence is the thing to internalise. The header two lines above promises that every number
is checkable by hand. A reader who does the check concludes **the `vgpr` column is wrong** — and
therefore that the register allocator is over-allocating — when in fact the column was right and the
missing factor was a quantity the table did not even display. That is why the corrected legend is
accompanied by a comment pointing at the region block below it, and why `_region_and_agent_lines`
prints the region *count* and not only the axis names.

##### 15.11.6 The ring legends and the `readmode` column

```
  # S_ldsreg = shared reduction-chunk ring depth (S_shared, rotates on the OUTER outer-reduction level);
  #   W_reg = register-ring width per group (rotates on group+substep, two rings)
  #   readmode = per group at the requested dr=1 ... prefetch(dr_g>=1) = read HOISTED ahead of its
  #   consumer, prologue primes it; inplace(dr_g=0) = read issued IN PLACE one line before its own
  #   wmma, prologue empty.  One dr_g drives BOTH, and mixing them is the named defect.
  depth map S (raw): A=[g0:2, shared:2] | B=[g0:2, shared:2]
```

**The two rings are different objects with different rotation axes** (section 1.8), and the legend
exists because the two columns sit adjacent and are otherwise easy to read as one quantity. The
shared ring rotates on the outer reduction chunk (one step per back edge); the register ring rotates
on the group's rate axes inside the unrolled body (several steps per chunk).

**`readmode` is the column the audit added, and the reason is a shipped defect class.** The
per-group derived look-ahead depth is computed here as

```python
dg = group_readahead_depth(theta, op, g, _dr_req, S)
parts.append(f"{g}:{'prefetch' if dg else 'inplace'}({dg})")
```

where `_dr_req = _peel_depths(theta).dr` is the **requested** depth. The distinction between the
request and the derived per-group answer is one of the sharpest edges in the whole package
(section 6), and this column shows the derived one. A group is Shape A (hoisted, prologue primes it,
steady advance non-zero) or Shape B (in place, prologue empty, steady advance zero) — never a
mixture. Two in-place defects shipped because nothing a reader could see distinguished the two: a
Shape-A prologue paired with a Shape-B steady body looked identical to a correct schedule.

**`W_reg` alone does not tell you.** A broadcast fan zeroes the depth at *any* width. That is why
`readmode` is derived through the real function rather than inferred from the `Wreg` column, and why
the legend states, honestly, that **`dr_g = 0` has two independent causes** and a printed zero does
not by itself say which fired:

* the broadcast-fan veto — the operand's whole register name space is re-traversed before any one of
  its values dies, so no look-ahead is admissible at any width;
* the free-sibling veto — a region sibling on a free axis sits outer to the reduction, so the
  advance would carry into a storage-disjoint sibling that nothing primes.

If you need to know which one fired, call `placement._broadcast_fan(theta, op)` directly: `> 1` is
the first veto, otherwise it is the second (or the width clamp, which shows as a nonzero-but-smaller
value than the requested `dr`).

The derivation is wrapped in a bare `try/except` per group, falling back to `g:?`. That is the right
call for a renderer — the alternative is a build-time crash from a diagnostic — but a `?` in this
column is a real signal, not noise: it means the read-ahead derivation raised for that group.
Similarly, `_dr_req` itself is wrapped, defaulting to `0`; a legend reading `at the requested dr=0`
on a kernel you know has local prefetch enabled means `_peel_depths` raised, and the whole `readmode`
column is then reporting a counterfactual.

**`depth map S (raw)`** prints `DepthMap.__repr__`, which groups by operand and shows every
`(region, group) → depth` row: `A=[g0:2, shared:2]` is "A has one register group `g0` of width 2 and
a shared ring of depth 2"; a region-split operand's rows print as `g0@r0:2, g0@r1:2`. This is the
only place a *per-placement* disagreement is visible. The depth map is indexed by the placement, not
by the operand, and asking it for a per-operand answer when the placements disagree **raises** — so
if the `Wreg` column is missing and the raw map shows two different values for one group, that
exception is the reason.

#### 15.12 `_region_and_agent_lines(theta)` — the per-hop asymmetry

The last block of the geometry table, emitted only when there is something to say. It carries three
schedule-point facts that no other line of the table shows, and each was unprintable until the audit
(provenance: #287).

```
  agents = 4   (one tile, 4 cooperating agents; cross-agent obligations are block-scoped)
  A        2 storage region(s) on axes ('M_split',)  free_split=2  load=AGENT  tdm=coord   <-- ASYMMETRIC: the region is an AGENT fact on one hop and a COORDINATE fact on the other
  B        2 storage region(s) on axes ('N_split',)  free_split=2  load=AGENT  tdm=coord   <-- ASYMMETRIC: ...
  MXSA     1 storage region(s) on axes ('M_split',)  free_split=2  coordinate-relative on every hop
  MXSB     1 storage region(s) on axes ('N_split',)  free_split=2  coordinate-relative on every hop
```

**The algorithm.**

```
agents = theta.agents or 1
if agents > 1: emit the agents line
for op in theta.operands:
    rms = op.region_modes ; fsp = max(1, op.free_split)
    if not rms and fsp <= 1: skip this operand entirely
    rel = { hop.kind or f"{hop.src}->{hop.dst}" : bool(hop.region_agent_relative)
            for hop in op.hops }                       # PER HOP
    if the set of values has more than one element:
        who = "  ".join(f"{k}={'AGENT' if v else 'coord'}") + "   <-- ASYMMETRIC: ..."
    else:
        who = "AGENT-relative on every hop" | "coordinate-relative on every hop"
    nreg = max(1, op.split)
    emit f"{op.name} {nreg} storage region(s) on axes {rms}  free_split={fsp}  {who}"
```

**`theta.agents`** — how many agents cooperate on one tile. The model represents an agent only as a
count. Without it printed, a single-agent dump and a four-agent dump of the same shape are
indistinguishable, and the cross-agent obligations that only the latter has look like noise. The
parenthetical states the consequence: those obligations are block-scoped rather than wave-scoped
because program order within one agent does not order anything across agents.

**`Hop.region_agent_relative`, and why it is listed per hop.** A region is *agent-relative* when
which storage region an access touches is a property of **which agent runs it**, not of the
coordinate: two agents executing the same read instruction land in different regions. This flag is
set on the **read hop only**. So within a single operand, the region is an *agent* fact on the read
hop and a *coordinate* fact on the bulk copy hop — the copy walks all the regions, the read sees
one. Collapsing that to one per-operand answer re-introduces exactly the conflation the per-hop
field exists to remove, which is why the two hops are listed separately whenever they disagree, with
an explicit `ASYMMETRIC` marker.

The hop key is `hop.kind or f"{src}->{dst}"`, so on the shipping shapes the line reads
`load=AGENT  tdm=coord` — `load` is the per-lane read, `tdm` is the bulk cooperative mover. Keys are
sorted, so the ordering is stable across runs and the block is diffable.

**Cost on record, and it is the reason this function exists.** A comment in the parameter-translation
layer once justified the claim "the read's region needs the agent-assignment field" by quoting a
checker message about region coverage. Nothing in any dump said the operand was agent-relative, so
nobody could see that the check was asking a *coordinate* question about an *agent* fact. The wrong
premise stood for a day and drove work on a feature that turned out not to be required.

**`Operand.free_split`** — the traversal-order-independent anchor for the free-sibling veto in the
read-ahead derivation. It exists precisely because that veto used to be recovered from
`region_modes`, which drops out of the traversal permutation in degenerate shapes; a reader could not
tell the two situations apart. Printing it is what makes "the sibling veto fired" checkable.

**`op.split` — the region COUNT, not just the axes.** Without it, a line reading
`MXSA region axes ('M_split',)` reads as a split operand, while `MXSA.split == 1` means **one**
storage region — and the downstream GIR dump, which gates its region block on `regions > 1`,
correctly omits `MXSA` entirely. Two dumps of one schedule point disagreeing about whether an
operand is region-split is worse than either being silent. The scaled-format rows above show exactly
this: `MXSA` has one region on an axis that `A` is genuinely split on.

**Non-vacuity, in the test.** The unit test does not merely assert that the word `ASYMMETRIC`
appears. It first computes, from the schedule point itself, the set of operands whose hops actually
disagree, asserts that set is non-empty (so the fixture is really asymmetric), then asserts each such
name is printed — *and* asserts that an operand whose hops **agree** is not labelled asymmetric.
Both directions, or the test passes on a renderer that prints the word unconditionally.

#### 15.13 Worked example — reading one real dump end to end

The fixture is the canonical bf16 kernel used throughout the unit tests: a 16×16×32 matrix
instruction, a per-agent tile of 2×2, a reduction chunk of 64 elements, one agent, global prefetch
depth 2, local prefetch depth 1, and the traversal order reduction-outermost. Everything below is
literal output, produced by calling `render_geometry` and `render_ir` on that schedule point.

A note on the `§` markers that appear in the quoted text: they are the source docstrings' own
shorthand for an external design note, and they reach the dump because the dump is generated from
those docstrings. Section 0.3 of this report is the decoder ring — every marker's claim is stated in
full somewhere in this report, and no lookup outside it is required.

##### 15.13.1 Step 1 — read the geometry header and check the parameters arrived

```
  reg_bytes=4  lanes=32
  levels(ord) = iter(OUTER) · K_inner(x2) · M_inner(x2) · N_inner(x2)   (outer→inner)
    outer(peel/reduction-chunk ring) = ['iter']   inner(register-ring) = ['K_inner', 'M_inner', 'N_inner']
    reduction modes = ['K_inner']
  off (retime, per op-class×level) = A:copy@iter=2, A:read@K_inner=1, B:copy@iter=2, B:read@K_inner=1
  mma grid: m_tiles=2 n_tiles=2 k_tiles=2  => 8 mma/kiter
```

Four things are already established:

* One outer level (`iter`), so one peel and one shared ring. Three inner levels, all extent 2, so
  the unrolled body has `2 × 2 × 2 = 8` leaves.
* `K_inner` is the only reduction axis, so `M_inner` and `N_inner` are the free axes and the
  accumulator is present on exactly those two.
* The requested global prefetch depth of 2 landed as `A:copy@iter=2`, and the local prefetch depth
  of 1 landed as `A:read@K_inner=1`. If a parameter you set is missing from this line, the bridge or
  the translation dropped it, and nothing further downstream will be right.
* 8 compute operations per chunk, which must equal the compute-line count in one steady trip.

##### 15.13.2 Step 2 — check the footprint by hand

```
  A        input  K_inner,M_inner       2       2        8   4096        8       2  g0:2    32  g0:prefetch(1)
  C        output M_inner,N_inner       4       2       16   8192        0       0     -    64  -
  depth map S (raw): A=[g0:2, shared:2] | B=[g0:2, shared:2]
```

`A` has one register group `g0` of width 2, the grouping axis holds 2 values, one region, and 8
registers per fragment: `1 × (2 × 2) × 8 = 32`. `C` is the accumulator: `4 × 16 = 64`. Both match.
The shared ring is depth 2 on both inputs, so the copy alternates between two staging buffers.

`readmode` says `g0:prefetch(1)` — Shape A, the read is hoisted one substep ahead and the prologue
must prime it. Hold on to that: it predicts a non-empty prologue and a non-zero `advance` on every
steady read, and if either is missing, the two halves of the read-ahead have come apart.

##### 15.13.3 Step 3 — the pipeline skeleton

```
  if T > 2:  # peel-validity: enter the software-pipelined body ...
    # --- PROLOGUE (peel 2 of iter, Lemma 1) ---
    ...
    for iter while (iter < T-2):
    ...
    # --- DRAIN (peel 2 of iter, Lemma 1) ---
    ...
  else:  # short-loop (T < peel-depth: prologue meets drain)
```

("Lemma 1" in the peel banners is the source's name for the peel decomposition — a pipelined loop of
trip `T` with retime depth `M` splits into an `M`-step prologue, a steady region of `T−M` trips and
an `M`-step drain, valid only when `T` is large enough. Section 6.3 of this report states it in
full; the banner requires no lookup.)

The peel depth is 2 in three independent places — the guard `T > 2`, the peel banner `peel 2 of
iter`, and the steady back edge `iter < T-2` — and it equals the `A:copy@iter=2` retime from the
geometry table. Those four numbers agreeing is the first invariant to check on any dump. The guard
is a **strict** `>`, so the pipelined arm runs at `T ≥ 3`; the steady region is lowered into a
post-tested shape whose body always runs once, which is why `≥` would compute one chunk twice.

##### 15.13.4 Step 4 — the prologue

```
    iter = -2:  # peel-step chunk binding
      tdm     A                -> shared[buf0]     4096B   # copy
      tdm     B                -> shared[buf0]     4096B   # copy
    iter = -1:  # peel-step chunk binding
      tdm     A                -> shared[buf1]     4096B   # copy
      tdm     B                -> shared[buf1]     4096B   # copy
    await   A@global:iter  on copy@wave  <RAW-residency>   # A resident
    ds_read A[K_inner0,M_inner0] -> register[buf0]<-lds[buf0] 8reg   # read
    ds_read A[K_inner0,M_inner1] -> register[buf0]<-lds[buf0] 8reg   # read
    await   B@global:iter  on copy@wave  <RAW-residency>   # B resident
    ds_read B[K_inner0,N_inner0] -> register[buf0]<-lds[buf0] 8reg   # read
    ds_read B[K_inner0,N_inner1] -> register[buf0]<-lds[buf0] 8reg   # read
```

Read the copy ramp first. Two `Bind` steps pin `iter` to `-2` and `-1` — the copies for the two
chunks that must already be in flight when the steady loop starts — and they land in shared buffers
0 and 1 respectively, i.e. the two slots of a depth-2 ring. The peel is **staggered by each
op-class's own retime**, so with both copies at depth 2 both appear in both steps; with unequal
depths, the shallower op-class would be absent from the earlier step.

Then the read-ahead fill: **four** reads, all at `K_inner0`, covering `M_inner ∈ {0,1}` for `A` and
`N_inner ∈ {0,1}` for `B`. That is the closed-form prologue set — the leading look-ahead substeps
crossed with the operand's free presence axes — not a simulation. Its size is what `readmode`
predicted: depth 1 means one leading substep, so `K_inner0` only. All four land in `register[buf0]`
and read `lds[buf0]`, and none carries `advance=` because these are pinned fills, not hoists.

Every read is covered by a `RAW-residency` await on the copy that filled the buffer it reads, but
**two** awaits appear here rather than four. `emit_mainloop` runs `ledger.discharge_once` over the
tree before anything renders it, `RAW-residency` is one of that pass's mergeable kinds, and both `A`
fills name the same `dep` — so the second `A` await and the second `B` await are dropped as already
established by a preceding instruction on the same path. What survives is one boundary per operand,
because the two operands are two distinct obligations and nothing merges those. (The pre-discharge
`build_ir` tree does carry all four; no dump path renders it.)

##### 15.13.5 Step 5 — the steady body, and evaluating one slot formula by hand

```
    for iter while (iter < T-2):
      for K_inner in range(2):
        M_inner = 0:  # §5.1 sub-body
          await   A@global:iter  on copy@wave  <RAW-residency>   # A resident
          await   A:g0:lastread  on read@wave  <rotation-WAR> [issue AFTER those readers]   # refill WAR: slot vacated by prior read
          ds_read A[K_inner=((0+(M_inner+K_inner*2+2)//2)%2),M_inner=((0+(M_inner+K_inner*2+2)//1)%2)] -> register[buf(0+(M_inner+K_inner*2+2)//2%2)%2]<-lds[buf(iter+(M_inner+K_inner*2+2)//4)%2] 8reg   # read  advance=2
          for N_inner in range(2):
            ...
            wmma    C[m,n][K_inner,M_inner,N_inner] += A[m,k]*B[n,k]  <- A=reg[buf(K_inner)%2], B=reg[buf(K_inner)%2]   # A(k)*B(k)
        M_inner = 1:  # §5.1 sub-body
          ... A read again, then the N loop with NO B read ...
      await   A:shared:lastread  on read@wave  <inplace-WAR> [issue AFTER those readers]   # refill WAR: slot vacated by prior read
      tdm     A                -> shared[buf(iter+2)%2]     4096B   # copy
      await   B:shared:lastread  on read@wave  <inplace-WAR> [issue AFTER those readers]   # refill WAR: slot vacated by prior read
      tdm     B                -> shared[buf(iter+2)%2]     4096B   # copy
```

(The `§5.1 sub-body` tag on the two `M_inner` headers is `_subbody_header`'s marker for the
multi-sub-body form of 15.6.2: a level whose body differs before and after a boundary is emitted as
several sub-loops over disjoint sub-ranges rather than as one body with a per-iteration predicate.
Section 3.12.2 of this report gives the node representation, and 12.3 the `loop_shape` derivation
that decides when a level takes this form.)

**Structure.** `M_inner` is emitted as two sub-bodies over singleton ranges rather than as a loop —
that is the first-touch guard hoisted into the loop *structure*, so `B`'s read (invariant over
`M_inner`) is issued in the `M_inner = 0` sub-body only, and the predicate is not evaluated per
iteration. Count the reads: 2 `A` reads (one per `M_inner`) × 2 `K_inner` values = 4, and likewise
4 for `B`. That matches the unrolled view exactly and is half of the geometry table's `ds_reads = 8`
for the reason in 15.11.4.

**The refill copies are last, and their awaits say why.** The two `tdm` lines sit at the very end of
the trip, each preceded by an `inplace-WAR` await naming the last read that vacates the buffer, with
the explicit `[issue AFTER those readers]` tag. Reading the tag is how you check the issue-order
refinement did its job: with a shared ring depth equal to the copy's retime depth, the refill writes
the very slot the trip is still reading, so it must follow every read of it. Move those two lines
above the reads and the kernel is wrong; nothing else in the dump would look different.

**Now evaluate one line by hand.** Take the `A` read at `K_inner = 0`, `M_inner = 0`, in steady trip
`iter = 0`. The shared sub-expression is `P = M_inner + K_inner*2 + 2 = 2` — the flat traversal
position over `A`'s reload axes, advanced by the look-ahead shift of 2.

| Field | Formula in the dump | Evaluated |
|---|---|---|
| coordinate along `K_inner` | `(0 + P // 2) % 2` | `(2//2) % 2 = 1` |
| coordinate along `M_inner` | `(0 + P // 1) % 2` | `2 % 2 = 0` |
| register slot | `(0 + P//2 % 2) % 2` | `1` |
| shared source slot | `(iter + P // 4) % 2` | `(0 + 0) % 2 = 0` |

So this instruction reads `A[K_inner1, M_inner0]` out of shared buffer 0 into register buffer 1 —
and that is exactly what the unrolled view prints:

```
      ds_read A[K_inner1,M_inner0] -> register[buf1]<-lds[buf0] 8reg   # read  advance=2
```

Three checks fall out of that arithmetic, and they are the ones to run when a read-ahead is
suspected:

1. **The advance is consistent.** `advance=2` is `look-ahead depth (1) × stride of the reduction
   axis over the reload axes (2)`. The strides come from renumbering the operand's *reload* axes
   only (presence minus free siblings) — `K_inner` outer, `M_inner` inner, so strides 2 and 1. The
   same `+2` appears inside every sub-expression above. If `advance=` and the `+N` inside the
   formulas disagree, they were computed by two different code paths, which is the recurring defect
   shape in this package.
2. **The compute consumes the previous fill.** The compute line reads `A=reg[buf(K_inner)%2]`, i.e.
   `buf0` at `K_inner = 0`, while the read on the same line writes `buf1`. Correct for a depth-2
   ring with a one-step look-ahead. Equality there would mean the read is clobbering the value the
   compute is about to use.
3. **The shared rollover is at the right radix.** The source slot's floor-divide is by 4 — the
   product of the extents of `A`'s reload axes (`2 × 2`) — so `P = 2` does not roll over and the
   read stays in this chunk's buffer, while a substep at `P ≥ 4` would advance to `iter + 1`. That
   is the look-ahead crossing into the next chunk, and it is what creates a chunk-crossing true
   dependency on a copy issued in the same trip.

##### 15.13.6 Step 6 — the drain, and the two step kinds

```
    # --- DRAIN (peel 2 of iter, Lemma 1) ---
    iter = T-2:
      ... reads with advance=2, unguarded ...
    iter = T-1:
      for K_inner in range(2):
        M_inner = 0:
          if M_inner+K_inner*2+2 < 4:  # read-ahead suppress: drop the substep that would read the out-of-bounds next chunk
            ... the A read ...
          for N_inner in range(2):
            if N_inner+K_inner*2+2 < 4:  # read-ahead suppress ...
              ... the B read ...
            ... the compute, unguarded ...
```

The two drain steps are different in kind. Step `T-2` still prefetches — it is feeding step `T-1` —
so its reads are unguarded. Step `T-1` is the last, so any read whose advanced position runs past the
end of this chunk must be dropped, and it is dropped **declaratively**: `Cond(P < 4)`, where the
predicate is the advance's own bound (the flat position plus the shift, against the reload extent
product). The compute is never guarded — every compute in the drain has a real value.

The width of the suppressing window is the **derived chunk reach** — how many whole chunks the
advance the emitter *actually issues* crosses into — not the requested depth. Those differ whenever
a group is clamped or vetoed, and reading the request there widened the suppression window and
silently dropped eight reads on a deeper-prefetch configuration.

In the unrolled view the same drain reads look like this:

```
    # iter = T-2
    ds_read A[K_inner1,M_inner0] -> register[buf1]<-lds[buf(iter+(M_inner+K_inner*2+2)//4)%2] 8reg   # read  advance=2
```

Note the mixed frame — the register slot is a concrete `buf1`, the shared source slot is still
symbolic in `iter`. That is the deliberate per-expression pinning of 15.9.2: the drain leaves `iter`
unbound because the runtime trip count is not a compile-time number, so a concrete shared buffer
index there would be a fabrication, while the register slot genuinely is resolvable. A dump that
shows `<-lds[buf0]` under an `# iter = T-1` header is the pre-fix rendering and must not be trusted.

##### 15.13.7 Step 7 — the degenerate arm

```
  else:  # short-loop (T < peel-depth: prologue meets drain)
    iter = 0:
      tdm     A                -> shared[buf0]     4096B   # copy
      tdm     B                -> shared[buf0]     4096B   # copy
      for K_inner in range(2):
        M_inner = 0:
          ds_read A[K_inner,M_inner] -> register[buf(K_inner)%2]<-lds[buf(iter+(M_inner+K_inner*2)//4)%2] 8reg   # read
          ...
    if T > 1:  # short-loop step validity: this peeled step has a real chunk only if T > t
      iter = 1:
        tdm     A                -> shared[buf1]     4096B   # copy
        ...
```

Compare the read line here with the steady one. **No `advance=`, no `+2` inside the formulas, and
the coordinate is the bare loop variable.** This arm is the *unpipelined* emission of the same
schedule point: every producer precedes its consumer within the arm, the retime-carried displacement
is zeroed, the copies lead rather than trail, and the issue-order refinement is deliberately not
applied (both of its deferrals order for a successor trip, and this arm has none). Three separate
defects were fixed by making the arm reset all three of those displacements; the dump shows all
three at once, and `advance=` is the quickest tell — if you see it in the `else` arm, the arm has
inherited a read-ahead it cannot warm up.

Step 0 is unguarded (`T > 0` is trivially true); step `t ≥ 1` is guarded by `T > t`.

#### 15.14 What is still not surfaced

Stated plainly, because the value of a debugging chapter is knowing where the instrument stops.
Everything below is a field or derived quantity that exists in the model, affects behaviour, and
does **not** appear in any curated view. The raw dump reaches the first group (they are dataclass
fields); nothing reaches the second.

**Node fields no curated view prints.**

| Field | Consequence of its absence |
|---|---|
| `Inst.agent` | Every line renders as though one agent issued it. On a multi-agent schedule the dump cannot show work partitioning at all. The model only ever sets a single role today, so this is currently a placeholder rather than a loss — but it will become a real gap the moment agent specialization is implemented. |
| `Placement.reg_off` / `byte_off` | `Placement.render` appends `@r<n>` / `@b<n>` only when non-zero, so these *do* reach the load line when set; the emitter leaves them zero on every shipping path, so they are never seen. Do not conclude from their absence that they are unprinted. |
| `Loop.body_ranges` | Visible in the raw view as `body i [lo,hi):` and *implied* in the rolled view by the sub-body header, but a wider-than-singleton sub-range prints as `for m in range(1, 4)` with no marker distinguishing it from an ordinary loop. |
| `Load.part` / `n_parts` | `n_parts` prints as ` /N` on a shared-destination line only; `part` (which of the N transfers this is) never prints, on either branch. |
| `Await.count` | Printed when set, never set. Harmless today. |

**Derived quantities the geometry table does not carry.**

* **`load_regs`** — registers moved by one per-lane instruction. Without it, the `ds_reads` column
  cannot be reconciled with the stream view's fragment count (15.11.4); you have to compute
  `frag_regs ÷ load_regs` from the hop's vector width, which is also not printed. Adding
  `load_regs` as a column would make that reconciliation a subtraction instead of a derivation, and
  it is the single highest-value addition to this table.
* **`readahead_reach`** — the derived chunk reach that sizes the drain suppression window. The table
  prints the per-group depth (`readmode`) and the peel prints its own depth, but the reach that
  connects them is invisible, and the request-versus-derived confusion it guards against has caused
  three separate defects.
* **the per-hop presence sets** — the table's `presence` column is the operand's; neither hop's own
  presence is shown (15.11.4).
* **the quantum axes** — which axes a quantum absorbed. `_shape_str` prints the two expressions, but
  not the derived set of axes they span, which is what was subtracted from presence.
* **the fusion partition** — which op-classes merge into one cooperative instruction. It is *visible*
  indirectly, as a `A+B` token on a load line, but there is no line saying what the groups are, so
  an operand that was expected to fuse and did not is invisible.
* **which of the two look-ahead vetoes fired** — stated in the legend as an explicit limitation
  (15.11.6).
* **the notes attached to the schedule point** — `theta.notes` is printed by
  `bridge.kernel_to_ir_text` *after* both renderers, not by `render_geometry`. If you call
  `render_geometry` directly from a shell, you lose them. They record, among other things, when a
  requested region split was **not applied** to a copy hop.

**A structural limitation of the geometry table**: it is derived from the schedule point and the
depth map, never from the emitted IR. It therefore cannot detect an emitter that deviates from
either. The stream views are derived from the IR and cannot detect a schedule point that is wrong.
Neither dump alone is a check; the pair, read against each other, is.

#### 15.15 Complexity, cost, and where to put effort

**Complexity.** Every walker is a single pre-order traversal, so the stream views are linear in the
node count of the tree they walk. For the rolled view that is `O(#op-classes × #levels)` — on
shipping shapes, 5 operands × 6 levels, i.e. a few dozen nodes, and dumps of 100–150 lines. For the
unrolled view it is linear in the *expanded* node count, `O(#op-classes × Π extents)` per pipeline
stage, with the outer runtime level contributing exactly one representative iteration. The reference
fixture expands to 261 lines; the widest scaled-format fixture is a few thousand. String building is
`"\n".join` over a list, so there is no quadratic concatenation anywhere.

`render_geometry` is `O(#operands × #groups)` plus whatever the derivations cost —
`operand_footprint_regs` and `plan_transfers` are arithmetic, `group_readahead_depth` walks the
inner axes once per group. All negligible.

**Compile-time cost.** Zero on the default path: `OutputLoopIR` is off, and nothing in the codegen
path imports `render`. With the flag on, the cost per kernel is one extra `build_S`, one extra
`emit_mainloop` (`kernel_to_ir_text` decodes independently rather than reusing the writer's cached
schedule point — see below), and the rendering itself, which is negligible beside the decode. On a
large library build with the flag on, the dominant cost is the file write, not the render.

**The one real inefficiency, and whether to fix it.** `bridge.kernel_to_ir_text` calls
`kernel_to_params` → `params_to_theta` → `emit_mainloop` from scratch, while the codegen path has
already built and cached a schedule point and depth map for the same kernel. So with the flag on,
every kernel is decoded twice. That is deliberate: the dump must not be able to perturb the cached
state the emitter is using, and it must work for kernels that the codegen path never decodes at all.
Do not "optimize" it by reading the cache unless you also prove the dump cannot mutate it — the
whole design of this file is that it is a pure function of its input.

**Concrete advice for extending it.**

1. **Add columns, not views.** The geometry table is the right place for anything derived. The
   marginal cost of a column is one format specifier and one legend line; the marginal cost of a
   fifth view is a fifth walker that will drift from the other four. Start with `load_regs` and
   `readahead_reach` (15.14).
2. **Route every leaf through `_one_line`.** The two stream views produce byte-identical instruction
   lines because they share it. If you add a third view, share it too, or the next audit will find
   the two spellings and one of them will be the wrong one.
3. **When a fact becomes load-bearing, print it in the same change.** Both dump audits found the
   same pattern: a field is added to make a schedule correct, and the dump that people use to reason
   about schedules does not show it, so the next investigation reasons from its absence. The
   discipline that catches this is a diff of the dataclass fields against the renderer, and it is
   cheap to re-run.
4. **Prefer a legend over a smarter column.** Three columns in this table are misleading and all
   three were fixed by *labelling* them, not by changing what they compute — because the numbers
   themselves are the ones the model uses, and making the display "friendlier" would have decoupled
   the dump from the model.
5. **If you make the renderer faster, you have almost certainly made it wrong.** There is no
   performance problem here. Memoizing a slot evaluation or caching a rendered `Expr` would buy
   nothing and would introduce the possibility of a stale render, which is the one failure mode a
   debug view must not have.
6. **The one structural improvement worth doing** is a *diffable* mode: a rendering that suppresses
   the long symbolic formulas and prints only `(verb, tokens, coordinate, destination slot,
   advance)` per line, so two schedule points can be diffed without the noise. Today, comparing two
   configurations means diffing 90-character formula strings that differ in one digit. That is a
   sixth view, which contradicts advice 2 — so implement it as a *flag on the existing walkers* that
   `_load_line` and `_mma_line` read, not as a new traversal.

#### 15.16 The unit tests as a contract

`render.py` was historically the least-tested module in the package — for the obvious reason that a
renderer has no behaviour to assert. Four tests exercise it today; three were written specifically
by the dump audit and each encodes both a contract and a historical defect. They live in
`Tensile/Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py` unless noted, and all of them run under a plain `pytest` with
no GPU and no compiled extension.

**`test_geometry_shows_the_region_agent_asymmetry_and_await_kind`.** Renders the geometry table for
a four-agent scaled-format schedule point and asserts four things: the word `ASYMMETRIC` appears;
every operand whose hops genuinely disagree is named; `free_split=` appears; `agents = ` appears. It
then renders the IR and asserts that **every** await line carries one of the closed set of hazard
kinds in angle brackets. Two guards make it non-vacuous: it computes the asymmetric set from the
schedule point *first* and asserts it is non-empty, so the test cannot pass on a symmetric fixture;
and it asserts that an operand whose hops **agree** is *not* labelled asymmetric, so it cannot pass
on a renderer that prints the word unconditionally.

**`test_the_unrolled_drain_does_not_invent_a_buffer_index_for_unbound_iter`.** The most instructive
test in the file. It asserts, on the drain of a real schedule point, that at least one shared-source
slot stays symbolic in the outer induction; that on those *same lines* the register slot is
concrete; that `Placement.at({}, keep_unresolved=True)` hands an unresolvable expression back
**by identity** while still pinning a resolvable one; that the plain `at({})` default is unchanged
(with the comment recording that making it unconditional broke 409 tests and both codegen paths);
and — the non-vacuity guard — that some *steady* read does render a concrete shared slot, so the
drain assertion is not satisfied by a renderer that simply never pins anything. Four assertions for
one behaviour, in both directions, plus a direct test of the mechanism underneath. Copy this shape.

**`test_a_load_line_shows_its_quantum_and_advance_and_a_wmma_names_its_real_operands`.** Builds a
`Load` with a hand-constructed quantum and `advance=3` and asserts both appear; builds a plain
`Load` and asserts **neither** string appears, so the first assertion cannot be satisfied by
boilerplate; builds an `Mma` with deliberately non-standard operand names (`LHS`, `RHS`, `ACC`) and
asserts the line names *those*, not the letters A/B/C. Then, on two real kernels, it counts
`advance=` occurrences and asserts the count is positive with local prefetch on and exactly zero
with it off. The quantum branch is exercised through a hand-built node rather than a kernel because
no shipping fixture produces a non-identity quantum — and the test's own docstring states the
principle: an unexercised branch that prints the wrong thing is still wrong.

**`test_region_split_copy_is_ROLLED_at_its_region_level`** (a test of the emitter, in `test_loopmodel.py`)
uses `render_ir` as its *observation instrument*: after asserting the copy-node count structurally,
it asserts that the dump contains a `for <region axis> in range` header over the copies. This is the
only test that pins the rolled view's loop-header rendering, and it does so as a side effect of
testing something else — worth knowing, because a change to `_loop_header` or `_subbody_header` will
surface there rather than in a render test.

**Two tests in `test_gir.py` use `render_stream` as a string oracle for issue order**
(`test_a_refilling_copy_re_establishes_the_boundary` and its fused sibling). They split the dump on
the literal steady-loop header `"for iter while"` and then search for `"await   A+B@global"` and
`"ds_read"` by index, asserting the boundary precedes any read in the steady body. That is a real
contract on the *text*: **`_loop_header`'s outer form and `_await_line`'s `dep` spelling are load-bearing
strings**, and changing either — including the three-space gap after `await` produced by the
