`{'await':8s}` field width — breaks tests in a different file with an error message that will not
mention the renderer. If you reformat these lines, grep both test files for the literals first.

##### 15.16.1 What the tests do not cover

* `render_ir_raw` has no direct test at all. Its `Branch` and `Cond`-with-label arms are unreachable
  from any emitter output and unexercised.
* The `Branch` arms of both stream walkers are likewise untested and unreachable.
* `_subbody_header`'s wide-range form (`for m in range(1, 4)`) is not asserted anywhere; only the
  singleton-binding form occurs in the fixtures.
* `_await_line`'s `!UNKNOWN-KIND` path and its `(<= N)` count path are untested.
* `_VERB`'s fallback and the whole of `_SPACE` are unreachable (15.2.1).
* `_coord_str` is dead (15.2.3).
* Nothing asserts that `render_geometry`'s legend agrees with the `vgpr` column it describes — which
  is exactly the defect of 15.11.5. A test that recomputes the footprint from the printed factors
  and compares it against the printed total would have caught it, and is the most valuable test this
  module still lacks. It is straightforward: parse the `vgpr` column, recompute
  `region_count × Σ(W × |part|) × frag_reg` from the schedule point, and assert equality across the
  scaled-format matrix.

#### 15.17 Summary for a maintainer in a hurry

* Turn the dump on with `--output-loop-ir`; read `ir/<kernel>.txt` beside `<kernel>.s` and
  `<kernel>.gir`.
* Check the four peel numbers agree (`if T > M`, `peel M of iter`, `iter < T-M`, `X:copy@iter=M`).
* Check `mma grid`'s product against the compute-line count in one unrolled steady trip.
* Check the `vgpr` column against the printed footprint legend, remembering that `region_count` is a
  separate factor from `free_tiles`.
* Check `readmode` against `advance=`: `prefetch(d≥1)` must coincide with a non-empty prologue and a
  non-zero advance on every steady read of that group; `inplace(0)` must coincide with an empty
  prologue and no `advance=` anywhere. A mixture is the named defect.
* Check the refill copies are last in the steady trip and carry an anti-dependency await with the
  `[issue AFTER those readers]` tag.
* In the drain, expect a symbolic shared-source slot and a concrete register slot on the same line;
  a concrete shared slot there is a stale renderer.
* In the `else` arm, expect **no** `advance=` at all.
* When something in a stream view is inexplicable, drop to `render_stream(ir, raw=True)` before
  suspecting the emitter — the pretty-printer is the cheaper hypothesis to eliminate.


---

### 16. `translate.py` — parameters to schedule point

#### 16.1 What this module is, and why it is allowed to break the rule

No module in the core may *read* a TensileLite parameter (section 0.2 states the rule exactly, and
0.2.1 catalogues the four inert exceptions that do exist). `translate.py` is one of the two modules
that are exempt, and it is the one that matters: it is, together with `bridge.py`, the only place
where a name like `MIWaveTile`, `PrefetchGlobalRead`, `DepthU` or `TDMSplit` appears in a form the
code actually *reads*. Its single public job is

```
params_to_theta(p: dict) -> Theta
```

— take a flat dictionary keyed by TensileLite parameter names and return a fully-formed schedule
point (section 1.1): a list of `Mode`s, a list of `Operand`s each with its hop trajectory and
register fragment, the retime matrix `off_map`, the fusion partition, the agent count, and a list
of human-readable notes explaining what was decided.

The exemption is deliberate and load-bearing for three reasons.

**First, it makes the core testable without a GEMM generator.** Because no core module imports
`translate`, the entire decoder — presence, read-ahead, peel depths, the ledger, the emitter, the
structural gate — can be exercised by hand-constructing a `Theta`. The unit suite does exactly
that in places, and every core test runs under plain `pytest` with no `rocisa` and no GPU.

**Second, it makes the vocabulary boundary auditable — but by a narrower grep than the obvious
one.** `grep -l MIWaveTile LoopModel/*.py` returns `bridge.py geometry.py placement.py translate.py`
today, and that is **not** a layering violation: the two core hits are `MEASURED` provenance
comments naming the kernel configuration a defect was observed on. A bare identifier grep cannot
tell a provenance note from a violation, so it is not the enforcement mechanism, and an earlier
revision of this report claiming it was is retracted in 0.2.1.

The grep that does mean something looks for a `Solution` **subscript**:

```
grep -nE '\["(MIWaveTile|DepthU|PrefetchLocalRead|PrefetchGlobalRead|TDMSplit[AB]?|MXBlock[AB]?|ScheduleIterAlg|LoopOrder|VgprPartition)"\]' LoopModel/*.py
```

Anything it returns outside `translate.py` and `bridge.py` is a violation. There is still no import
guard, no linter rule and no test asserting the property; the discipline is social, and it survives
only because the exempt set is small enough to remember and the addon layer is not imported by the
core (which the import graph does enforce — see 17.2.3).

**Third, and most practically, it concentrates *fidelity risk* in one file.** The core is exact
with respect to whatever `Theta` says. If `Theta` says A's read hop moves 8 elements per lane and
the emitted kernel moves 4, every downstream derivation — the register footprint, the movement
quantum, the presence set — is wrong, and it is wrong *silently*, because nothing in the core can
tell. The module docstring states this in as many words: getting the generic fields exact for
every datatype and matrix-instruction shape is *this layer's* responsibility, and refinements
belong here rather than in the core. That is why the file is 896 lines for what is nominally a
dictionary translation: most of its bulk is the recorded derivation of each mapping, including
the mappings that were wrong once.

#### 16.2 The interface: who calls it, and with what

There are exactly two producers of the parameter dict and four consumers of the resulting `Theta`.

| Producer of `p` | Site |
|---|---|
| A real TensileLite `Solution` dict, mapped key-by-key | `bridge.py:kernel_to_params` (section 13) |
| A hand-written literal, in tests and fixtures | `Tests/unit/test_loopmodel.py`, `Tests/unit/gir_fixtures.py`, `Tests/unit/loopmodel_scenarios.py` |

| Consumer of the returned `Theta` | Site |
|---|---|
| Codegen: build θ once per kernel and cache it | `KernelWriter.py:_loopModelTheta` |
| The GIR lowering, in tests | `Lowering/loopir_to_gir.py` |
| The observability dump | `bridge.py:kernel_to_ir_text` |
| Every unit test in `test_loopmodel.py` and `test_gir.py` | via the local `_theta(params)` helper |

The hand-written-dict path is not a testing convenience bolted on afterwards; it is a design
constraint that shapes the module. Several parameters (`ReadVectorElems`, `ReadQuantum`,
`TDMSplitWaveRegions`) are **target facts** that no `Solution` key carries — they are
resolved on the writer or by a separate geometry module and handed in through `bridge`. Because a
hand-built dict has no writer to ask, every one of them must have a default that is *safe rather
than accurate*: absent `ReadQuantum` means one tile per instruction (the narrowest and always-legal
merge), absent `ReadVectorElems` for a data operand falls back to `LocalReadVectorWidth`, absent
`TDMSplitWaveRegions` means the wave spans every region (the pre-existing behaviour). Each of
those falls in the direction that under-claims rather than over-claims, and each is discussed at
its own point below.

`params_to_theta` is **pure** — it reads nothing but its argument, allocates nothing global, and
touches no filesystem. It is called once per kernel on the codegen path, and a few thousand times
across the unit suite. Its cost is negligible relative to everything downstream (section 17).

#### 16.3 The parameter surface: `DEFAULTS`, `PARAM_HELP`, and what is actually read

Two module-level dictionaries describe the accepted parameters.

`translate.py:DEFAULTS` is the merge base. The first line of `params_to_theta` is
`k = dict(DEFAULTS); k.update(p)`, so **every** key the body reads has a value, and a caller may
supply as few or as many as it likes. The defaults describe a bf16 16×16×64 kernel with
`DepthU=128`, `MIWaveTile=[1,2]`, `PrefetchGlobalRead=2`, `PrefetchLocalRead=1`, no region split,
no microscaling and no fusion.

There is a sharp edge in that default worth naming, and the source names it too: the default
`MatrixInstruction` of `[16,16,64,1]` is **not a real gfx1250 opcode** for fp16 — the catalog
instruction is 16×16×32 with 8 VGPRs per fragment. The 64-deep shape is kept because it makes
`DepthU/MI_K = 128/64 = 2` substeps, which is the two-rate register shape the model was originally
validated against. A configuration intended to describe real hardware must set
`MatrixInstruction` explicitly. The fragment-element derivation (`_frag_elems`, below) uses the
grounded per-lane formula regardless of which shape is supplied, so only the substep count is
affected.

`translate.py:PARAM_HELP` is a parallel dictionary mapping the same names to one-to-several-line
prose explaining what each parameter means and where it lands in θ. It is **documentation only**:
no code in the tree reads it, and it is not printed by any renderer. It is nevertheless the single
best index of the module — if you are adding a parameter, adding its `PARAM_HELP` entry is how the
next reader will find out what you did. Its entries carry the `[NEW]` marker for the knobs invented
for the schedule search (as opposed to the ones that already existed in TensileLite), and one entry
(`PerRegionCompletion`) is explicitly marked `[INTERNAL, not a Solution param]`.

The table below is the complete list of what `params_to_theta` **reads**, and where each value ends
up. Anything in `DEFAULTS` or `PARAM_HELP` that is not in this table is inert; those are listed
separately afterwards, because an inert parameter that *looks* live is a trap.

| Parameter | Read at | Lands in |
|---|---|---|
| `MatrixInstruction` | `_k_tiles`, `_frag_elems`, `_mx_frag_elems` | substep count (extent of `K_inner`); `Operand.frag_elems` for A, B, C |
| `DepthU` | `_k_tiles` | substep count |
| `InnerUnroll` | `_k_tiles` | substep count (multiplier) |
| `MIWaveTile` | `params_to_theta` (`fanM`, `fanN`) | extents of `M_inner` / `N_inner` after the wave-region division |
| `ElemBytes` | `params_to_theta` | `Operand.elem_bytes` for A and B |
| `PrefetchGlobalRead` (+ `…A`/`…B`/per-operand) | `off_map` loop | `off(copy, <outer level>)` |
| `PrefetchLocalRead` (+ per-operand) | `off_map` loop | `off(read, <substep level>)` |
| `TDMSplit` | region derivation | `M_split`/`N_split`/`K_split`/`K_splitA`/`K_splitB` extents; `Hop.split`; `Operand.free_split` |
| `TDMSplitWaveRegions` | region derivation | the inner-fan divisor; `Hop.region_agent_relative` |
| `LoopOrder` | `_loop_order_word` → `_canonical_ord` | the order of `Theta.ord` |
| `GlobalReadVectorWidthA` / `…B` | `hops` | `Hop.vector_elems` on the copy hop (and on a DTV read hop) |
| `LocalReadVectorWidth` | `_read_hop` fallback, `_coalesce` | `Hop.vector_elems` on a data operand's read hop |
| `VectorWidthA` | `_coalesce` | a note string only (see below) |
| `ReadVectorElems` | `_read_hop` | `Hop.vector_elems` on a named operand's read hop |
| `ReadQuantum` | `_read_hop` | `Hop.quantum` |
| `DirectToVgprA` / `…B` | `hops`, LDS depth | one-hop trajectory; `lds_buffers = 0` |
| `NumLdsBlk` | LDS depth | `Operand.lds_buffers` preset |
| `LDSBufferA`/`B`/`MXSA`/`MXSB` | LDS depth | `Operand.lds_buffers` override |
| `VgprPartitionA` / `…B` | `reg_fragment` | `Fragment.parts`, `Fragment.labels` |
| `VgprReuseStrategyA` / `…B` | `_register_policy` | `Fragment.group_policy` |
| `MXBlockA` / `MXBlockB` | scale-operand block | whether `MXSA`/`MXSB` exist; their `frag_elems` |
| `TDMFuse` | fusion block | `Theta.fuse`, `Theta.fuse_groups` |
| `NumWaves` | tail | `Theta.agents` |
| `LdsPadA` / `LdsPadB` / `LdsBlockSizePerPad` | padding block | `Theta.lds` |
| `TDMIterateMode` | padding block | a warning note only |
| `PerRegionCompletion` | tail | `Theta.per_region_completion` |

##### 16.3.1 The inert parameters, named honestly

Four entries appear in `DEFAULTS` and `PARAM_HELP` but are never read by any branch:

* **`HalfPLR`** — described as a two-bit A/B mask selecting a mixed read-ahead depth. The
  per-operand `PrefetchLocalReadA`/`PrefetchLocalReadB` knobs express the same thing more
  generally and *are* read, so `HalfPLR` is superseded. It is still in `DEFAULTS`, so a caller
  setting it gets silence rather than an error.
* **`TDMInst`** — a two-bit mask enabling the bulk cooperative mover per operand. `translate`
  unconditionally builds a `kind="tdm"` copy hop for any non-`DirectToVgpr` operand, so the mask
  has no effect. This is defensible today because the shipping gfx1250 path always enables the
  bulk mover for both operands, but it means a hypothetical `TDMInst=1` (A only) would be modelled
  as though B also used the bulk path, which would give B's copy hop the wrong presence set (bulk
  hops are broadcast over every inner axis; a per-lane copy is not).
* **`1LDSBuffer`** — the single-shared-buffer switch. The *effect* of that switch reaches θ
  through `NumLdsBlk`, which `Solution.py` already derives from it, so reading `1LDSBuffer` here
  would be a second derivation of one fact — exactly the failure shape section 1 warns about. It
  survives in `DEFAULTS` only because the error message for an over-deep LDS ring mentions it as
  a remedy.
* **`WaveSeparateGlobalReadA` / `…B`** — read by nothing, and **deliberately so**. A long comment
  in the ρ block records that this parameter was mapped onto ρ (the agent assignment) twice by
  mistake, because the name invites it. What it actually does is rewrite the load-tile
  decomposition constants that decide which slice of the macro-tile each thread reads; every wave
  still loads part of A and part of B, so the *carrier set* is unchanged and no agent assignment
  is expressed. A faithful mapping would have to target the copy hop's thread decomposition, which
  the decoder does not model at all.

`VectorWidthB` is in `DEFAULTS` but only `VectorWidthA` is read (by `_coalesce`), so an asymmetric
`VectorWidth` pair is silently modelled as though B matched A.

Two *outputs* are likewise inert, and this is worth stating because they look like live fields on
the returned object:

* **`Theta.lds`** — the `{operand: {"pad", "block"}}` padding map built from `LdsPadA`/`LdsPadB`.
  A tree-wide grep finds **no reader**. Padding affects addresses, and the core is address-opaque,
  so there is nothing for it to do; it exists so the dump can show that padding was requested.
* **`Theta.fuse`** — the raw integer `TDMFuse` value. Also unread; consumers use
  `Theta.fuse_groups`, the resolved partition. Keeping the integer means the dump can name the
  policy that produced the groups.

Neither should be deleted casually — they are the only record in θ of a decision that was made —
but neither should be relied on to change behaviour.

#### 16.4 The arithmetic helpers

Five small functions carry every piece of numeric mapping that is not structural. Each is pure,
takes the merged parameter dict `k`, and returns an integer.

##### 16.4.1 `translate.py:_per_operand(k, base, operand, preset)`

The override-resolution rule shared by every per-operand knob. It looks up the key
`"<base><operand>"` — e.g. `base="LDSBuffer"`, `operand="A"` → `"LDSBufferA"` — and returns the
`preset` when that key is absent or negative, otherwise `int(value)`.

```
_per_operand(k, base, op, preset):
    v = k.get(base + op)
    return preset if (v is None or v < 0) else int(v)
```

Three properties make this the right shape:

* **`-1` is the "not overridden" sentinel**, not `None`. The parameter dicts that reach here come
  from YAML and from `Solution` state, where a key either exists with a value or does not exist at
  all; a tri-state needs an in-band sentinel, and a negative depth/offset is meaningless anyway.
* **The default is the whole-kernel preset**, so a caller that sets nothing sees exactly the
  historical single-value behaviour. `test_per_operand_override_defaults_to_the_preset` pins this
  for all three bases (`LDSBuffer`, `PrefetchGlobalRead`, `PrefetchLocalRead`) by asserting that
  explicitly passing `-1` reproduces the reference θ's shared depths and its entire `off_map`.
* **An op-class with no matching key simply takes the preset.** That is why the MX scale operands
  and the accumulator need no entries in `DEFAULTS` for the prefetch bases: the `off_map` loop
  applies `_per_operand` to *every* operand by name, so `PrefetchGlobalReadMXSA` works if someone
  sets it and presets to the kernel's `PrefetchGlobalRead` if not.

This function is the mechanism behind the model's claim that the retime `off` is a matrix over
(op-class × level) and the buffer depth `S` is a per-placement map (section 1.6, section 1.8) —
before it existed, both were single scalars, which was the implementation's restriction and not
the model's.

##### 16.4.2 `translate.py:_k_tiles(k)`

The number of reduction substeps in one chunk:

```
_k_tiles(k) = max(1, DepthU // MatrixInstruction[2]) * InnerUnroll
```

`MatrixInstruction[2]` is the instruction's K depth. At the shipping bf16 point
(`DepthU=64`, `MI_K=32`) this is 2. The result becomes the extent of the whole K inner traversal
before the region split divides it (see `_canonical_ord`). `InnerUnroll` multiplies rather than
divides, because it subdivides the K axis further into more, smaller compute steps.

Naming note: the function is called `_k_tiles` and `geometry.py` also exports a `k_tiles`. They
compute the same quantity by different routes — `geometry.k_tiles(theta)` is the product of the
extents of the *reduction modes actually present in `ord`*, whereas `translate._k_tiles(k)` is the
parameter-level number *before* the region factorization splits it across `K_split`, `K_splitA`,
`K_splitB` and `K_inner`. They agree by construction (the four extents multiply back to `ksub`),
but they are not interchangeable and the translate one is not exported.

##### 16.4.3 `translate.py:_frag_elems(k, free_mi)`

How many elements one lane holds for one matrix-instruction tile fragment:

```
_frag_elems(k, free_mi) = max(1, free_mi * MI_K * MI_B // 32)
```

where `free_mi` is `MI_M` for A and `MI_N` for B, `MI_K` is the instruction's K depth, `MI_B` its
block count (defaulting to 1 if the `MatrixInstruction` list is shorter than four entries), and 32
is the gfx1250 wave width (`translate.py:WAVE32`). This is the wave-total element count of one
fragment divided by the number of lanes, which is exactly how the generator's own
per-thread-input derivation computes it. The docstring records that the RDNA-style override
(per-thread input = `MI_K`) applies to earlier ISA generations, not to gfx1250, which uses this
MFMA-style formula.

Worked examples from the docstring, both verified against the generator's tables: a 16×16×32 fp16
instruction gives `16·32·1/32 = 16` elements → 8 registers at 2 bytes each; a 16×16×128 fp8 A
fragment gives `16·128·1/32 = 64` elements → 16 registers at 1 byte each. The elements-to-registers
recast is *not* done here — it is `geometry.frag_regs` (section 2.2.6), which divides by the
elements-per-register scale. `translate` only supplies `Operand.frag_elems`.

##### 16.4.4 `translate.py:_mx_frag_elems(k, free_mi, mxblock)`

The same quantity for a microscaling scale tensor:

```
dup = max(1, 32 // MI_M)                       # duplicate factor: 2 at MI_M = 16
_mx_frag_elems = max(1, _frag_elems(k, free_mi) // max(1, mxblock) * dup)
```

One scale value covers `mxblock` data elements, so the scale fragment is the data fragment divided
by the block size — then multiplied by a **duplicate factor** `32 // MI_M`. That factor exists
because the matrix instruction's M extent is smaller than the wave, so the same scale value is
replicated across the lane groups that share an M row. At `MXBlock=32` with a 16×16×128 fp8
instruction: `64 // 32 · 2 = 4` elements, which packs into a single register.

Both `_frag_elems` and `_mx_frag_elems` clamp to at least 1. That clamp hides a degenerate
configuration (a scale block larger than the whole fragment) rather than reporting it; if you ever
need to distinguish "one element" from "less than one element", this is where it is lost.

##### 16.4.5 `translate.py:_coalesce(k)` — computed, and used only for a note

```
_coalesce(k) = max(1, LocalReadVectorWidth // max(1, VectorWidthA))
```

The intent, per the docstring, is the number of consecutive reduction substeps that share one
loaded register group — the generator's own read-coalescing count. At the default two-rate kernel
(`LRVW=4`, `VW=2`) it is 2.

**It reaches nothing.** The single call site assigns it to a local and interpolates it into the
first entry of `notes`; no `Operand`, `Fragment`, `Hop` or `Theta` field is derived from it. This
is worth stating plainly because the module docstring lists `coalesce` among the generic geometry
fields this layer is responsible for setting, which is no longer true — the reuse rate it was meant
to express is now derived inside the core from mode extents and broadcast sets
(`theta.group_rate`, section 4.4). `_coalesce` is therefore vestigial: an observability string
and nothing more. It is cheap and harmless, but a maintainer chasing "where does coalescing enter
the model" should stop here rather than looking further.

#### 16.5 The canonical mode vocabulary

This is the structural heart of the module: the fixed set of traversal axes it may create, and the
rule that turns a `LoopOrder` string into a permutation of them.

##### 16.5.1 The eight canonical names

`translate.py:CANON_NAMES` is the ordered list

```
["K_split", "K_splitA", "K_splitB", "K_inner",
 "M_split", "M_inner", "N_split", "N_inner"]
```

The vocabulary rests on one idea: **each of the three GEMM axes K, M, N contributes a
(storage-region axis, tile axis) pair**, and these are different things that only *coincide* when
the fan happens to equal the split.

* `X_split` — the **storage-region** axis. Its values enumerate the storage-disjoint pieces the
  bulk cooperative mover cuts the tile into (section 1.10). One value = one copy instruction.
* `X_inner` — the **tile** axis. Its values enumerate the compute tiles inside one region. One
  value = one matrix-instruction fragment.

K gets three region modes rather than one — `K_split`, `K_splitA`, `K_splitB` — for reasons given
in full in section 16.6. M and N get one each because those axes are per-operand already (A is cut
on M, B on N), so there is no sharing to factor.

The canonical order `0..7` above is the *index* order, not the emission order; emission order comes
from the `LoopOrder` word. The comment above the list records the structural claim that makes the
default order safe: every axis is (split outer, inner inner), so a region's whole tile fan
completes before the region index advances, and no two regions' staging buffers are live at once.
That holds for the K region chain too — a DU-split kernel finishes K-region 0 before K-region 1.

##### 16.5.2 `LoopOrder` as a word — `_loop_order_word`, `_word_to_modes`, `canonical_loop_order`

`LoopOrder` is a string over the letters `{K, M, N}` and there are two accepted spellings.

* A **3-letter shortcut** (`"KMN"`, `"NMK"`, …) means "keep each axis's (split, inner) pair
  contiguous, in this axis order". There are 6 of these, one per whole-axis permutation.
* A **6-letter word** (`"KMKNMN"`, …) in which each letter appears exactly twice: the **first**
  occurrence of a letter places that axis's `_split` mode, the **second** places its `_inner`
  mode. This lets regions interleave — a split's tile fan need not complete before another axis
  advances. There are 90 distinct 6-letter permutations of `KKMMNN`.

`translate.py:_loop_order_word(order)` normalizes to the 6-letter form: it upper-cases, expands a
valid 3-letter shortcut by doubling each letter (`"KMN"` → `"KKMMNN"`), and then rejects anything
whose sorted letters are not exactly `K,K,M,M,N,N` with a `ValueError` naming both accepted forms.

The encoding has a structural consequence the docstring calls out: because the first occurrence is
*always* the split, **inner→split orders are inexpressible**. A word can never place `M_inner`
outside `M_split`, i.e. it can never index a region from inside its own tile fan. That is the rare
and unwanted tail of the permutation space, excluded by the notation rather than by a validity
check.

`translate.py:_word_to_modes(word)` turns the 6-letter word into the ordered list of canonical role
names, outer→inner:

```
_word_to_modes(word):
    seen = {}
    for c in word:
        emit (c + "_split") if c not in seen else (c + "_inner")
        seen.add(c)
```

So `"KMKNMN"` → `[K_split, M_split, K_inner, N_split, M_inner, N_inner]`. It contains a one-entry
identity map `AXIS = {"K": "K", "M": "M", "N": "N"}`, which is a no-op left over from a version
that renamed axes; it can be deleted.

##### 16.5.3 `translate.py:canonical_loop_order(order)` — the one exported non-θ function

This is the module's second public entry point, and the only one called from outside the LoopModel
package by non-test code. **The caller is `SolutionStructs/Solution.py`, during parameter
validation** — before any kernel is written, on every solution that carries a `LoopOrder` key, on
and off the LoopModel path alike. It is invoked inside a `try` whose `except ValueError` *rejects*
the solution with the exception's message, and on success the validator **overwrites**
`state["LoopOrder"]` with the returned spelling. So this function is the only place in the package
that can veto a solution, and the only one whose result is written back into its caller's state;
section 17.10 places it in the end-to-end picture as Path C, and 17.10.1 gives the two
`LoopOrder`-related rejections that run immediately after it.

The call also has to run **before** those two rejections, and the ordering is deliberate: the
`== "KMN"` test must see a doubled word such as `KKMMNN` collapsed to `KMN` (it *is* `KMN`, and a
non-LoopModel kernel spelling it that way must not be rejected), and the six-letter gate must see
only genuinely interleaved words, which is exactly what survives canonicalisation.

It returns the **canonical spelling** of a `LoopOrder` value:

```
canonical_loop_order(order):
    w = _loop_order_word(order)                 # normalize / validate; raises ValueError
    if w[0]==w[1] and w[2]==w[3] and w[4]==w[5]:
        return w[0] + w[2] + w[4]               # doubled word -> its 3-letter shortcut
    return w                                    # interleaved: no shortcut exists
```

**Why it exists.** `_loop_order_word` expands `"KMN"` to `"KKMMNN"`, so those two strings name *one*
traversal. `LoopOrder` is a kernel-**name** parameter: it is part of the string that identifies a
generated kernel. Leaving both spellings valid therefore produces two kernel names — `LOKMN` and
`LOKKMMNN` — for a byte-identical kernel. The benchmark harness reports them as two independent
data points and the deduplication cannot merge them, because the names genuinely differ.

The alternative would have been to *narrow* the accepted parameter set to 90 words, rejecting
`"KKMMNN"`. That was rejected because the decoder parses it happily; refusing a legal input to keep
the name space clean makes the accepted set and the decodable set disagree in the other direction.
Collapsing instead keeps "everything the decoder parses" accepted and "one name per traversal"
emitted.

An **interleaved** word (one where some axis's split and inner are not adjacent) has no 3-letter
equivalent and is returned unchanged. It is also the only form that produces a non-contiguous
traversal, i.e. the shape that reaches the multi-sub-body loop emission (sections 3.12.2 and 12.3).

It raises the same `ValueError` as `_loop_order_word` for an illegal word, so parameter validation
has exactly one authority.

**Call site.** `SolutionStructs/Solution.py` calls it while deriving the Solution, *before* the two
`LoopOrder` gates that follow it, and rejects the Solution with the `ValueError` text if it raises.
Running it first is deliberate: the gate "non-KMN requires the LoopModel path" must see `"KKMMNN"`
as `"KMN"` (because it *is* KMN), and the gate "a 6-letter word needs a live split axis" must see
only genuinely interleaved words, which is precisely what survives canonicalization.

**The accepted-versus-emitted arithmetic**, pinned by
`test_gir.test_EVERY_SPELLING_is_accepted_and_canonicalizes_to_90_traversals`:

* accepted = 6 shortcuts + all 90 permutations of `KKMMNN` = **96** strings, which is exactly what
  `Common/ValidParameters.py` lists for `LoopOrder`;
* canonical = **90** distinct traversals;
* the 6 that collapse are exactly the doubled spellings `KKMMNN, KKNNMM, MMKKNN, MMNNKK, NNKKMM,
  NNMMKK`.

A companion test, `test_every_one_of_the_90_orders_DECODES_and_gets_a_DISTINCT_name`, decodes all
90 through `params_to_theta` + `emit_mainloop` and asserts both that each produces an empty ledger
and that the 90 kernel-name fragments are pairwise distinct. Both halves matter: a word that does
not decode is a kernel that fails to generate, and two words sharing a name fragment means one of
them silently never runs.

##### 16.5.4 `translate.py:INNER_TO_SPLIT`

A three-entry map `{"K_inner": "K_split", "M_inner": "M_split", "N_inner": "N_split"}` naming each
tile axis's paired region axis. Read only by `_canonical_ord._keep`, immediately below, where it
answers "is my split partner live?".

#### 16.6 `_canonical_ord` — building `ord`

`translate.py:_canonical_ord(substeps, kSplit, kResA, kResB, mSplit, mInner, nSplit, nInner, order)`
is the function that turns eight integers and a word into the traversal.

**Signature and return.** It returns a triple `(ord_modes, names, extents)`:

* `ord_modes` — the `list[Mode]` that becomes `Theta.ord`, outermost first, with the outer
  reduction level prepended;
* `names` — `{role_name: Mode}` for *all eight* canonical roles plus `"iter"`, whether or not the
  mode survived into `ord`. Operand construction binds free / region / grouping modes by role
  through this map, and naming a dropped mode is harmless because the core intersects every mode
  set with the inner modes actually present;
* `extents` — `{role_name: int}`, the raw extents before the drop filter. `params_to_theta` reads
  this to decide which region axes to list per operand.

**Algorithm.**

```
kRegions = kSplit * kResA * kResB                    # total distinct K region values
kInner   = max(1, substeps // kRegions)              # the leftover inner K traversal
extents  = { K_inner: kInner,  K_split: kSplit,  K_splitA: kResA,  K_splitB: kResB,
             M_split: mSplit,  M_inner: mInner,
             N_split: nSplit,  N_inner: nInner }     # each clamped to >= 1
modes    = { role: Mode(role, extents[role]) for role in CANON_NAMES }

roles = _word_to_modes(_loop_order_word(order))      # 6 entries over the K/M/N word
roles = expand each "K_split" entry into (K_split, K_splitA, K_splitB)   # 8 entries

inner_ord = [ modes[r] for r in roles if _keep(r) ]
if inner_ord is empty:  inner_ord = [ modes["K_inner"] ]   # fully degenerate fallback

iter_mode = Mode("iter")                             # extent 0 => an OUTER level
return [iter_mode] + inner_ord, modes, extents
```

Three parts of that deserve their own explanation.

##### 16.6.1 The outer reduction level `iter`

`translate` **owns the name and the placement** of the outer reduction-chunk level. It creates
`Mode("iter")` with the default `extent=0`, which is the sentinel meaning "trip count not
statically known" (section 1.4), and puts it at position 0 of `ord`. Its runtime trip is a problem
dimension (`K // DepthU`) that emit supplies; nothing is stored on the `Mode`.

The core never writes the literal `"iter"`. It reaches this level through
`Theta.outer_modes()` and `Theta.reduction_chunk_mode()` / `reduction_chunk_name()`, which are the
single authority (section 4.2). That indirection is what lets a future coarser outer level — a
persistent, grid-stride tile loop — be added as another `extent=0` mode without touching a decoder
branch. Correspondingly, if you add such a level here, prepend it *outside* `iter`; the reduction
chunk is defined as the **innermost** outer level.

##### 16.6.2 The K region chain: why three modes and not one

The DU (K) axis is the one axis both operands cut, and they may cut it by different factors.
`params_to_theta` computes

```
kSplit = gcd(aDU, bDU)          # the SHARED link, both operands prefix it
kResA  = aDU // kSplit          # A's own residual
kResB  = bDU // kSplit          # B's own residual
```

so `kSplit · kResA · kResB = lcm(aDU, bDU)`, which is exactly the number of distinct
(A-region, B-region) pairs the traversal must visit. The question this factorization answers is not
*how many* values the axis has but **how they are named**, and that distinction is the whole point.

*The one-mode form and how it failed.* A single K region mode of extent `lcm` (or, in a still
earlier form, of extent `min(aDU, bDU)` with the deeper operand's leftover folded into
`Hop.split` as a nameless number) makes the **coarser** operand present on the axis *at a stride*:
its region index becomes `coord // (lcm / own)`, a division that no consumer performs. Every
consumer that *reasons* about a region reads the coordinate straight off the tile; only the
instruction count reads the number. The recorded consequences, in order of discovery:

* at `[A_MT,B_MT,A_DU,B_DU] = [1,1,4,2]`, A had **four** regions as instructions (the sizing layer
  issues `op.split` of them) and **two** as coordinates (the axis extent). Two of A's four loads
  were unaddressable, un-tokened, and unprovably disjoint;
* the region-coordinate reader returned partly `None` for the strided operand, the flattening
  helper then returned `None`, and the downstream region walk **silently dropped** that operand —
  both of its loads landing on region 0;
* the verifier meant to catch this skipped the operand on the same `flat is None` rule, so the
  defect was invisible to the check written for it.

*The two-mode chain and why it was also wrong.* An intermediate form used `gcd → lcm/gcd` with each
operand taking a **prefix** of the chain. That requires `aDU | bDU` — only then is the coarser
operand's count a prefix product — and a guard existed to reject coprime factors.

*The per-operand residual form, which ships.* With `K_split × K_splitA × K_splitB`, A's region is
the product `K_split × K_splitA` and B's is `K_split × K_splitB`. Both are plain mixed-radix
products of coordinates the operand **owns**, so neither operand is ever strided-present. An
operand is simply **absent** from the other's residual mode — ordinary presence, which the model
handles everywhere — and that absence *is* the first-touch guard the stride was trying to express,
now stated as mode membership rather than as an arithmetic condition no reader can see. The
divisibility guard is gone with it: `aDU=2, bDU=3` gives `K_splitA(2) × K_splitB(3)`, total 6, A
owning 2 and B owning 3.

**Where the expansion happens.** `_word_to_modes` speaks the three-letter K/M/N alphabet, so it
emits one `K_split` entry. `_canonical_ord` expands that single entry in place into the triple
`(K_split, K_splitA, K_splitB)` — **shared link outermost, then the two residuals** — so wherever
the word puts K's region axis, all three land there contiguously and each operand's own modes stay
adjacent in the traversal. That contiguity is what makes an operand's region index a plain
mixed-radix product of the digits it owns.

##### 16.6.3 `_canonical_ord._keep(r)` — the extent-1 drop rule

```
_keep(r):
    if extents[r] > 1:                    return True
    if r == "K_inner":                    return any(extents[n] > 1
                                                     for n in (K_split, K_splitA, K_splitB))
    return extents.get(INNER_TO_SPLIT.get(r, ""), 1) > 1
```

An extent-1 mode contributes a radix-1 digit and a trip-1 loop, so dropping it keeps `ord` small
and keeps every downstream mixed-radix index arithmetically identical. The rule drops such modes —
**except** an inner (tile) mode whose paired split (region) mode is live. `K_inner` gets a special
case because *any* link of the three-mode K chain counts as its live partner.

**Why the exception exists.** `X_inner` is the tile axis and `X_split` is the storage-region axis;
they are different roles that merely coincide in extent when the fan equals the split. Dropping the
degenerate one does not simplify the model — it **merges two roles onto one mode**. At
`MIWaveTile=2` with a 2-way split, `M_inner` has extent 1, and with it gone `M_split` is
simultaneously the region axis and the only free-tile axis. Every consumer that asks "which tile"
and every consumer that asks "which region" then reads the same coordinate, so a region-split tile
at that shape cannot state the two facts separately. That is precisely why `MIWaveTile [2,2]`
behaved differently from `[4,4]`, where `M_inner` survives at extent 2 and the two stay distinct.

`test_loopmodel.test_a_SPLIT_operands_degenerate_tile_axis_SURVIVES_and_an_unsplit_ones_does_not`
pins both halves: at wave tiles 1, 2 and 4 with a split, `ord` contains both `M_split` and
`M_inner` (and both N modes); unsplit, `ord` at wave tile 1 is exactly `["iter", "K_inner"]` and at
wave tile 2 exactly `["iter", "K_inner", "M_inner", "N_inner"]`.

**Why the exception is scoped to a live split, and what that scoping cost.** Keeping *every*
degenerate inner mode would be simpler to state, and the docstring records a measured argument
against it. Over a 96-configuration sweep (wave tile × loop order × global prefetch × local
prefetch × split) with `_keep` forced to keep every degenerate mode, comparing the fully-unrolled
act sequence with its concrete buffer slots:

```
84 / 96   byte-identical (op, operand, register slot, shared slot) sequence
12 / 96   differ, and in ALL TWELVE the multiset is the same — a pure REORDERING of acts
 0 / 96   any change to the per-(op, operand) slot multiset
```

So the slot **values** are invariant, exactly as the totality requirement predicts (section 4.4.4):
a trip-1 level emits its body once and contributes a radix-1 digit, so every flat index is
arithmetically unchanged. The shared-memory slot *expression* grows terms like `M_split*2`, but
each such mode is pinned at 0. What moves is the emission **order** — the interleave of the
operands' reads, and where the first-touch guards materialize, because a kept extent-1 mode becomes
a real enclosing level for the invariance test. With no live split there is no second role to merge
away, so keeping the mode buys nothing and is *not* free after all; those configurations pass
today, so the condition is "my split partner is live", not "I am an inner mode".

The docstring also carries a **retraction** worth preserving: an earlier version of it claimed that
register slots were rewritten by the change. They are not, and that claim had never been measured.
The residual 12-of-96 reordering gap between "does not affect the tree" and what was measured is an
open question, filed but unresolved.

**The fully-degenerate fallback.** If `_keep` rejects every role — a 1×1 wave tile with no split and
a single substep — `inner_ord` would be empty, and a `Theta` with no inner modes breaks every
presence derivation. `_canonical_ord` therefore forces `[modes["K_inner"]]` (extent 1) as the sole
inner level. This is the "all-1 degenerates to a one-loop nest" case; it is reachable from a
parameter dict and is exercised by the unsplit wave-tile-1 assertion above.

#### 16.7 Region splits, wave spans, and the inner-fan derivation

##### 16.7.1 Reading `TDMSplit`

`TDMSplit` arrives as a positional four-list `[A_MT, B_MT, A_DU, B_DU]`, right-padded with 1s, with
a legacy boolean form (`True` → `[2,2]`, `False` → `[1,1]`) still accepted:

```
ts = k["TDMSplit"]
if isinstance(ts, bool):  ts = [2,2] if ts else [1,1]
ts = list(ts) + [1]*(4 - len(ts))
aMT, bMT, aDU, bDU = (max(1, ts[i]) for i in 0..3)
mSplit, nSplit = aMT, bMT
```

The MT (macro-tile) axis is **per operand** — A is cut on M, B on N, each its own free axis — while
the DU axis is the **shared** K reduction, handled by the gcd/residual chain of section 16.6.2.
`Solution.py`'s own knobs are narrower (`TDMSplitA`/`TDMSplitB` name one axis per operand at factor
2); the widening to the general four-list happens in `bridge`, so `translate` keeps the general
form and the model can be exercised ahead of the code generator.

`test_gir.test_the_listed_region_axes_multiply_to_EXACTLY_the_operands_region_count` sweeps 17
split vectors — including factor 3 and 6, coprime DU pairs, gcd-2 pairs, and both axes live at once
— and asserts that A's region count is `A_MT · A_DU` and B's is `B_MT · B_DU`.

##### 16.7.2 The wave-region span, and the inner-fan derivation

```
_wr    = list(k.get("TDMSplitWaveRegions", []) or []) + [0, 0]
_waveA = max(1, min(aMT, int(_wr[0]) or aMT))
_waveB = max(1, min(bMT, int(_wr[1]) or bMT))
mInner = max(1, fanM // _waveA)
nInner = max(1, fanN // _waveB)
```

`TDMSplitWaveRegions` says **how many of the operand's regions one wave occupies**. It is a target
fact — it follows from the generator's wave-offset assignment, not from any authored parameter —
so `bridge` supplies it and a hand-built dict omits it. Absence (`0`, or a missing entry) resolves
to the split factor itself, i.e. "the wave spans every region", which is the pre-existing
behaviour exactly. `min(aMT, ...)` clamps a nonsensical over-large span.

**The inner-fan derivation is the load-bearing line.** `MIWaveTile` (`fanM`, `fanN`) is what **one
wave** holds. The tile axis extent must therefore be the wave's tiles divided by the regions *the
wave* spans — **not** by the tile's total region count. Dividing by the tile's region count empties
`M_inner` whenever a wave sits inside one region, and the wave's tiles then have nowhere to live
but `M_split`, which is the *copy's* axis. That is the conflation: at `MIWaveTile=2` with a 2-way
split it produced `M_split(2) × M_inner(1)`, so wave 0's second tile — physically inside region 0,
because the generator's tile assignment puts a whole wave inside one region — was coordinated as
**region 1** and carried region 1's memory token. At `wave_region_span == 1` the whole of
`MIWaveTile` now lands on `M_inner` and `M_split` is left to the copy. The expression is identical
to the old one whenever the wave spans every region, so the previously-covered matrix is unchanged.

##### 16.7.3 The agent-relative region — the single most re-learned idea in this codebase

This subsection is deliberately long, because the concept has been mis-stated in at least four
places (two source comments, one verifier message, and one debug renderer) and each mis-statement
cost real work.

**The setup.** A region-split operand's tile is cut into storage-disjoint pieces. A *coordinate*
names one of them: the tile at coordinate `M_split=1` lives in region 1. That is the natural
reading and it is what every consumer assumed.

**The problem.** With several waves cooperating on one tile, the generator's tile assignment fixes
each wave's free-axis offset at a fixed row stride. When that stride equals the region height —
which happens at a 2×2 wave group with a 2-way M split — wave 0's tiles land entirely inside
region 0 and wave 1's tiles, *executing the very same read instruction*, land entirely inside
region 1. One instruction, two regions, selected by **which agent runs it**.

**The distinction, stated once and precisely:**

> The region coordinate says which region **the coordinate names**. That is the region **the access
> touches** only when every agent running the instruction touches the same one.

So the region is:

* **a COORDINATE on the copy hop.** The bulk cooperative mover walks every region as part of its
  own traversal; region `j` is a value of the copy's own loop, and the coordinate is exact.
* **an AGENT fact on the read hop.** The per-lane read instruction is emitted once and lands in
  whichever region its executing wave sits in. The coordinate names one of them; the access reaches
  all of them.

**The same operand carries both.** This is the asymmetry, and it is why the flag lives on `Hop`
rather than on `Operand`:

```
_agent_rel = {"A": _waveA < aMT, "B": _waveB < bMT}
```

— the operand is agent-relative exactly when one wave spans **fewer** regions than the operand has
— and the flag is then set on the **read hop only**, inside `_read_hop`. The copy hop constructed
by `hops()` never sets it. A per-operand summary of this fact would re-introduce the very
conflation the field exists to remove.

**What the flag is for.** A memory token for a read that can reach any region must name **every**
region the instruction can reach, or the read is ordered against one producer and left un-ordered
against the other. The downstream token analysis widens an agent-relative read's token set
accordingly. Additionally, `Theta.agent_served_modes` (section 4.3) uses the flag to classify the
region axis as a *third* kind of inner axis — neither free nor reduction — which is subtracted at
exactly one place so that presence, register naming, the compute-grid projection and the register
footprint cannot disagree about it.

**Two retractions recorded in the source, both worth keeping.**

*First:* a long comment used to cite a measurement as proof that the agent-assignment field `rho`
was required to model this. Dropping `M_split` from the read's broadcast set produced verifier
output of the form "operand A has 2 storage regions [0, 1] but its reads name [0]", and that was
read as "one program reads one region while its copy writes two". Both steps were wrong. The
message came from a coverage check that asked a **coordinate** question about an **agent** fact:
wave `w` naming region `w` alone *is* the correct answer, and the union over agents does cover both
regions. The check now exempts under-coverage on an agent-relative operand and the same shape
reports clean. `rho` was never the missing piece, and it still has zero readers anywhere in the
tree.

*Second:* a debug renderer once printed "AGENT-relative: wave w reads region w, so ONE agent's
reads name ONE region" as a per-operand summary. That is false as stated — measured across eight
agent-relative operands, **all eight** have hops that disagree — and the renderer now prints the
per-hop split and defers to the geometry view. `test_geometry_shows_the_region_agent_asymmetry_and_
await_kind` pins this with a non-vacuity guard on both sides: it first asserts the fixture really
contains an operand whose hops disagree, then asserts the word `ASYMMETRIC` appears for it, then
asserts that an operand whose hops *agree* is **not** labelled asymmetric.

**What is still not fixed, and why one edit here cannot fix it.** Moving the region off the
coordinate entirely is right for the read and *wrong for the copy*: the copy must still walk both
regions, and a fused group tiled on different region axes then has no region coordinate to walk
with — the assembly emitter refuses that shape, and 16 fp8 kernels hit the refusal. `Hop.
region_agent_relative` is **per hop** while `ord` is **global**, which is exactly why no single
change in `translate` can express the asymmetry fully. The region therefore stays on the read
coordinate for now, and the wrong token is the lesser, visible defect.

##### 16.7.4 The per-operand region-axis tuples

```
aRegions = tuple(r for r in ("M_split", "K_split", "K_splitA") if cext[r] > 1)
bRegions = tuple(r for r in ("N_split", "K_split", "K_splitB") if cext[r] > 1)
```

Each operand lists **its own free axis, the shared K link, and its own K residual — never the
peer's**, and only those with extent > 1. The product of the listed extents is exactly that
operand's region count by construction, since `gcd · (own/gcd) == own`.

Both failure directions have been measured. *Over-listing* — naming an axis the operand does not
cut — made a 2-region operand's reads name regions 0..3, at `[A_MT,B_MT,A_DU,B_DU] = [1,1,2,4]`.
*Listing the shared axis for an operand that does not cut it at all* put a region displacement into
what should have been a contiguous image, which is the asymmetric-DU defect. The invariant test
named in section 16.7.1 exists to hold this line over arbitrary split vectors.

Note that an unsplit operand now lists **nothing**. That is what stops the shared reduction axis
from leaking into an operand that does not cut it, and it demotes the read-side region gate
downstream from load-bearing to belt-and-braces.

#### 16.8 Hop construction

Two nested closures inside `params_to_theta` build every trajectory.

##### 16.8.1 `params_to_theta._read_hop(name, default)`

```
_read_hop(name, default) =
    Hop(SHARED, REGISTER,
        vector_elems = int(read_elems.get(name, default) or default),
        quantum      = read_quantum.get(name),
        region_agent_relative = bool(_agent_rel.get(name, False)))
```

with `read_elems = dict(k["ReadVectorElems"])` and `read_quantum = dict(k["ReadQuantum"])`.

Three fields, three separate stories.

**`vector_elems` — the per-lane instruction payload, and why it is per operand.** A data operand's
shared→register instruction moves `LocalReadVectorWidth` elements per lane, which is the `default`
argument every call site passes. A **scale** tensor's does not: it moves its own width, which is
what makes one scale read cover several tiles. That number is the target's instruction selection,
not an authored parameter, so it arrives through `bridge.kernel_to_params(..., target=)` as
`ReadVectorElems` and is keyed by operand name. Falling back to `LocalReadVectorWidth` for a scale
left the scale read's true instruction width unstated — and that width is exactly the *domain* the
outside computation reads when it resolves the tile fold. The fallback is kept anyway, for two
reasons: it is the **safe** direction (a narrower quantum is always admissible, section 1.9), and a
hand-built parameter dict has no target to ask.

**`quantum` — supplied, never derived.** `Hop.quantum` is the movement quantum (section 1.9): two
expressions over the tile coordinate, `carrier(t)` and `slot(t)`. Which tile coordinates one
instruction covers follows from the address layout and the emitter's folding behaviour, neither of
which the core can see, so it is computed outside where the target facts live and handed over
already in GEMM terms. `translate` does not construct one; it only passes through whatever key the
caller supplied, and `None` (the default) is the identity merge — one tile per instruction, always
admissible. This has the same standing as the depth map `S`: a value from outside that the model
reasons over but does not choose.

**`region_agent_relative` — set here and only here**, from the `_agent_rel` map of section 16.7.3.
This is the asymmetry: read hop yes, copy hop no.

##### 16.8.2 `params_to_theta.hops(dtv, grvw, split=1, name=None)`

The trajectory builder for the data operands:

```
hops(dtv, grvw, split, name):
    if dtv:                       # DirectToVgpr: one per-lane global -> register hop
        return [ Hop(GLOBAL, REGISTER, vector_elems=grvw) ]
    return [ Hop(GLOBAL, SHARED, vector_elems=grvw, kind="tdm", split=max(1, split)),
             _read_hop(name, lrvw) ]
```

The two-hop form is the normal staging path: a **bulk** cooperative copy (`kind="tdm"`, meaning one
instruction moves a whole tile) carrying the region split, followed by a per-lane read. The
one-hop form is the direct-to-register path, where global memory is read straight into registers;
`theta.HOP_ROLE` classifies a global→register leg as a **read**, so that single hop's op-class role
is `read` and it has no copy op-class at all.

The retime `delta` is deliberately **not** on the hop. It is the first-class `Theta.off_map`, built
at the end of `params_to_theta` and read via `off_at(op, role, level)`. A hop is one op-class edge;
`off` is indexed by (op-class × level), so putting it on the hop would lose the level.

Note that `Hop.kind` is set explicitly to `"tdm"` on the copy leg even though `Hop.__post_init__`
would infer exactly that from `(GLOBAL, SHARED)`. The explicit spelling is harmless and documents
intent; a non-bulk global→shared leg (an asynchronous copy) would be expressed by passing
`kind="load"`, which `translate` never does today.

#### 16.9 Register groups

Three functions build the `Fragment` — the register-buffer structure of an operand's register
placement (section 1.8).

##### 16.9.1 `translate.py:_region_labels(n_parts)`

```
_region_labels(2) == ("lo", "hi")
_region_labels(n) == ("g0", "g1", ..., "g{n-1}")   for n != 2
```

Purely cosmetic group names. The depth map and the width-policy dict key on these labels, so they
must be unique within a fragment, but nothing interprets them. The `lo`/`hi` special case exists
because a two-way partition of an operand's tile fan into a lower and an upper half is the shape
the register model was originally validated against, and `[lo:4, hi:2]` reads better in a dump than
`[g0:4, g1:2]`.

##### 16.9.2 `translate.py:_register_policy(parts, strategy, group_labels)`

Turns the integer enum `VgprReuseStrategy` into the per-label width-policy dict the core consumes:

```
_register_policy(parts, strategy, labels):
    if strategy == 0:   return { g: "unroll" for g in labels }        # max scheduling
    return { labels[0]: "unroll" } | { g: "inplace" for g in labels[1:] }
```

* **0 = max scheduling** — every group gets `'unroll'`, i.e. width `W = R`, one buffer per distinct
  value. Most registers, most scheduling freedom.
* **1 = min VGPR** — the first group keeps the deep rotation, the rest fall to the in-place refill
  (`'inplace'`).
* **2 = auto-balanced** — a register-budget-driven choice, **deferred**; it is treated as 1 until a
  budget knob exists. This is a live sharp edge: setting `VgprReuseStrategy=2` today silently gets
  you strategy 1, with no note emitted.

The `parts` argument is accepted and **never read** — the function derives everything from
`strategy` and `group_labels`. It can be dropped.

Crucially, this layer picks the **intent**, not the number. The order-aware clamp into the legal
width band `[L, R]` happens in the core (`theta.group_width`, section 4.4): `'inplace'` resolves to
`W = 1` where the group is sequentially refillable and is otherwise **clamped up** to the live-peak
floor `L`. Putting the clamp here would duplicate a derivation the core already owns, and the two
would eventually disagree.

##### 16.9.3 `params_to_theta.reg_fragment(parts_req, strategy, bcast, grp_mode, fan_extent)`

The closure that assembles a `Fragment`:

```
reg_fragment(parts_req, strategy, bcast, grp_mode, fan_extent):
    n = max(1, int(parts_req))
    if n > 1 and fan_extent <= 1:
        note("VgprPartition=n but in-region fan grp_mode has extent 1 — clamped to 1")
        n = 1
    if n > 1 and fan_extent % n != 0:
        raise ValueError("VgprPartition=n does not divide the in-region fan (equal partition required)")
    labels = _region_labels(n)
    policy = _register_policy(n, strategy, labels) if n > 1 else {"*": "unroll"}
    gm     = grp_mode if fan_extent > 1 else None
    return Fragment(broadcast_axes=set(bcast), parts=n, labels=labels,
                    grouping_mode=gm, group_policy=policy)
```

Called twice:

```
fragA = reg_fragment(VgprPartitionA, VgprReuseStrategyA, N_BCAST, "M_inner", mInner)
fragB = reg_fragment(VgprPartitionB, VgprReuseStrategyB, M_BCAST, "N_inner", nInner)
```

with `N_BCAST = {"N_split","N_inner"}` and `M_BCAST = {"M_split","M_inner"}`. A is constant over
every N mode and B over every M mode — that single fact drives presence, reload rate and live range
throughout the core (section 1.3). Naming a mode that got dropped from `ord` is harmless: the core
intersects every such set with the inner modes actually present.

**The grouping mode is the important field.** `Fragment.grouping_mode` names the tile mode whose
**values** the register groups partition — a group is a subset of that mode's values (lower
matrix-instruction tiles versus upper), a genuine data partition rather than a register-file split.
A is bound to `M_inner`, B to `N_inner`: the *in-region* fan. Binding it is what folds the fan into
`|part| × region_count` in the footprint product rather than letting it inflate the rotation
**rate**, which is what prevents the fan from being counted twice for either operand (section 5.3).
When the in-region fan is absent (`fan_extent == 1`) there is nothing to partition and
`grouping_mode` is set to `None`, leaving the fan inside the rate.

**Three separate degeneracy behaviours, and they are not the same:**

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `parts_req > 1`, fan extent 1 | clamp `n` to 1 and **emit a note** — there is no fan to split |
| `parts_req > 1`, fan extent not divisible by `n` | **raise `ValueError`** — equal partition is required |
| `parts_req == 1` | one group, policy `{"*": "unroll"}` |

The uneven case raises rather than falling back, and that is consistent with the sizing layer
(section 5.3), which also refuses an uneven partition loudly rather than computing a wrong number.

**Why a single group is `'unroll'` and not `'floor'`.** The comment in the source is explicit, and
this is a case where the alternative was tried and lost. The register ring must hold every distinct
value the K-substep rate cycles — `R` generations — or two simultaneously-live substeps share one
register name, which is the width-band race (`W >= L`, section 4.4.3). `'floor'` picks
`W = L_prefetch`, which collapses to 1 when there is no read-ahead at all, giving a single-buffer
reuse that the emitter does not correctly lower for interleaved K substeps. `W = R` is inside the
band (since `L <= R`), matches the reference kernel, and is the safe default.

**A known gap.** A partition greater than 1 is currently a **silent no-op at emission**: the group
structure reaches `Theta` and the depth map, and it changes the reported register footprint, but the
emitter does not yet lower separate groups into GIR. So `VgprPartitionA=2` today changes the model's
accounting without changing the emitted kernel. This is recorded as open work; the parameter is
reachable, and a maintainer measuring its effect will find none.

#### 16.10 Operand construction

##### 16.10.1 A and B

```
splitA = mSplit * aDU        # regions THIS operand's copy moves = its own count on each axis
splitB = nSplit * bDU

A = Operand("A", "M_inner", hops(DirectToVgprA, grvwA, splitA, "A"), fragA,
            frag_elems=_frag_elems(k, MI_M), elem_bytes=elem_bytes,
            lds_buffers=ldsBufA, region_modes=aRegions, free_split=max(1, aMT))
B = Operand("B", "N_inner", hops(DirectToVgprB, grvwB, splitB, "B"), fragB,
            frag_elems=_frag_elems(k, MI_N), elem_bytes=elem_bytes,
            lds_buffers=ldsBufB, region_modes=bRegions, free_split=max(1, bMT))
```

Two of those arguments carry a distinction that is easy to lose.

**`split` on the copy hop is the operand's OWN region count** — `mSplit * aDU`, the product of its
own factors — not the shared K axis's extent. With the K axis factored at the finest split, the two
differ exactly when this operand is the coarser one, and that difference is its **stride** on the
axis rather than a nameless leftover factor.

**`free_split` is `aMT`/`bMT` only** — the **free-axis** region count, carried as a plain number.
It is deliberately *not* `splitA`/`splitB`, which fold the reduction axis in. Its purpose is to be
the ord-independent anchor for the read-ahead's free-sibling veto (section 6.6): `region_modes`
answers the same question today, but it answers it by *naming a mode*, so it is only as durable as
that mode's presence in `ord`. A region axis whose extent collapses to 1 is dropped by
`_canonical_ord._keep`, which empties `region_modes` and would silently release the veto — measured,
the read-ahead carry returns and a scale operand's fold pair gets cut across chunk boundaries. The
split is a fact about **storage**, not about which mode happens to carry the coordinate, so it is
recorded here as a number.

The **free axis only** scoping is likewise deliberate: a reduction-axis (DU) split is *not* a
sibling enumeration — its two regions are successive substeps of one tile held in one register
group — and folding it in here breaks the two-axis `K_split × K_inner` register rotation, measured
at 12 failures.

##### 16.10.2 C — the accumulator, and why it defines the reduction axes

```
C_BCAST = {"K_split", "K_splitA", "K_splitB", "K_inner"}
C = Operand("C", "M_inner", [], Fragment(broadcast_axes=set(C_BCAST)),
            frag_elems=_frag_elems(k, MI_M), elem_bytes=REG_BYTES, role="output")
```

The accumulator is an op-class with **no hops at all** in the main loop: it is register-resident,
zero-initialized, and its reverse register→(shared)→global path belongs to the epilogue, which is
not yet modelled. `role="output"` makes `trajectory_sense` call it reverse, and `elem_bytes` is
the register width (4) rather than the input element size, because an accumulator holds
compute-precision values.

**Its broadcast set is the definition of the reduction axes.** `Theta.reduction_modes()` is
computed as `inner_modes − presence(output) − agent_served_modes` (section 1.3), so whatever the
accumulator is broadcast over *becomes* the contraction. This is general — it works for batched and
general-contraction shapes with no name test — but it also means the set above is not a
description, it is a **declaration**, and omitting an axis from it does not make that axis "not a
region axis": it makes it a **free** axis.

That is not hypothetical. Measured: with `K_splitB` (the residual) missing from `C_BCAST`, an
asymmetric DU split at `gcd == 1` — where the only live K region mode *is* a residual — turned the
reduction into a free mode, and every matrix-multiply instruction read a register no read had
filled. Every K region mode must be listed here.

`frag_elems` for C is the per-lane output fragment. It is not load-bearing for presence; it is
sized so that footprint reporting includes the accumulator.

##### 16.10.3 The MX scale operands

When `MXBlockA > 0` (respectively `MXBlockB > 0`) the kernel carries a microscaling **scale
tensor**, and `translate` gives it its own op-class:

```
gmA = "M_inner" if mInner > 1 else None
MXSA = Operand("MXSA", "M_inner",
               [ Hop(GLOBAL, SHARED, vector_elems=grvwA), _read_hop("MXSA", lrvw) ],
               Fragment(broadcast_axes=set(N_BCAST), grouping_mode=gmA),
               frag_elems=_mx_frag_elems(k, MI_M, MXBlockA), elem_bytes=1,
               lds_buffers=ldsBufMXSA, region_modes=aRegions, free_split=max(1, aMT))
```

and symmetrically for `MXSB` with `N_BCAST`, `N_inner`, `bRegions`, `bMT`.

**A scale follows its parent.** Same grouping mode, same region modes, same free split, same
broadcast set, its own `lds_buffers` and its own retime offsets (each preset to the parent's
resolved value). `elem_bytes` is 1: scales are byte-sized. Note the copy hop is constructed with no
explicit `kind` and no `split` — it takes the inferred `"tdm"` and split 1.

Three of those choices were each arrived at by losing kernels the other way, and all three are
recorded in the source.

**(a) The width policy is the parent's `'unroll'`, not `'floor'`.** An earlier comment credited the
floor policy with folding the free-axis fan into the group; that is actually what `grouping_mode`
does, and `gmA`/`gmB` already do it. What the policy governs is the width of the rotation over the
**reduction substep**, and a scale is re-read per substep exactly as its parent is. Flooring it is a
different claim — that one register can serve every substep — and that claim is only true under an
ordering the emitter does not produce. `W=1` sits inside the derived band `[1, 2]` because the
post-write-after-read floor says the group is "sequentially refillable" (read k, use k, read k+1,
use k+1), but the steady body emits the multiply for substep `k` **before** the read that defines
its scale register, so every multiply consumed the previous trip's scale. Measured: **171 of 268**
cells at local prefetch 0 failed numerically, and 124 of 124 at the default loop order, against 6
of 264 at local prefetch 1 where the read-ahead depth forces `W=2` anyway. Nothing gates this — the
issue-order refinement position-checks shared-ring anti-dependencies only, not register rings — so
the safe policy is `'unroll'`, giving `W = R` (a distinct name per live generation) so the
definition/use order cannot invert. The in-place `W=1` group remains reachable through
`VgprReuseStrategy`, and making the emitter honour it is separate work.

**(b) The scale rings are their own, preset to the parent's resolved depth.** Leaving
`lds_buffers` unstated is not neutral: the core then falls back to `S = delta`, which its own
docstring calls a trap for anything that knows the real number. At global prefetch 2 the fallback
*coincides* with the double-buffered count and everything agrees; at global prefetch 1 the scales
get `S=1` against A/B's `S=2`. `S=1` is the in-place refill, so the scale copies are classified as
anti-dependency refills (which must be emitted **last**) in the same steady body where A and B's
chunk-crossing copies must be emitted **first** — one body, two incompatible issue orders, which
surfaces as a structural-gate failure rather than as a wrong number. Measured: microscaling with
global prefetch 1 and local prefetch 1 was the only failing cell of the four prefetch combinations,
and prefetch 2 passed for exactly that coincidence.

**(c) The scales keep the parent's `region_modes` even though their own region count is 1.** This
looks like a violation of the "listed extents multiply to the region count" invariant of
section 16.7.4, and it is — but it is **not safe to "correct"**. Both corrections were tried on
hardware and both lost kernels:

| Attempted correction | Measured consequence |
|---|---|
| `region_modes -> ()` | the scale's reload rate went `R=2 -> R=4`, because the free-axis region mode then entered the rate instead of being broadcast over it. That re-widths the rotation and moves every scale register's slot. |
| gate shared storage on the region **count** instead of the tuple | the scales dropped from 4 shared buffers to 2 (the region-1 pair stopped being named at all). The extra tokens are not dead weight; removing them lost ordering the kernel relies on. |

Both took the microscaled fp8 matrix from 6 failures to 32, including a configuration that had been
green. So the tuple is load-bearing in *both* maps — the rate needs the axis broadcast, and shared
storage needs the buffers it implies — and the product-equals-count invariant simply does not extend
to an operand that is *indexed* on an axis it does not itself *partition*. The invariant test in
section 16.7.1 therefore asserts it for A and B only, and says so. Leave this alone until the
two-map reading is modelled properly rather than trimmed at one consumer.

#### 16.11 Shared-ring depths and the allocation bound

```
numLdsBlk  = k.get("NumLdsBlk", 2)
ldsBufA    = 0 if DirectToVgprA else _per_operand(k, "LDSBuffer", "A", numLdsBlk)
ldsBufB    = 0 if DirectToVgprB else _per_operand(k, "LDSBuffer", "B", numLdsBlk)
ldsBufMXSA = _per_operand(k, "LDSBuffer", "MXSA", ldsBufA)      # preset = the PARENT's
ldsBufMXSB = _per_operand(k, "LDSBuffer", "MXSB", ldsBufB)
```

`Operand.lds_buffers` is the shared ring depth `S_shared` (section 1.8): how many staging buffers
this operand's copy rotates through. Three properties.

**It is a READ of a target fact, never a derivation.** `NumLdsBlk` is the real kernel-derived
buffer count (2 = double-buffered, 1 = single/in-place), computed by `Solution.py` and passed
through `bridge`. Deriving the depth from the retime `delta` instead is what broke the global
prefetch 1 configuration: the kernel still has 2 shared blocks while `delta` is 1, a depth-1 ring
has no rotation, and the decoder emitted **no swap** while the kernel's addressing kept alternating.
`test_shared_depth_is_the_buffer_count_not_the_prefetch_depth` pins both sides of the coincidence
by asserting the depth is 2 at both prefetch 1 and prefetch 2, and
`test_pgr1_emits_the_lds_swaps` pins the regression itself at the level that actually broke, by
asserting the lowered program contains at least one swap marker.

**A direct-to-register operand carries 0, meaning "not applicable" — not 1.** Writing 1 would
assert that it rotates a single shared buffer, which is a different and false claim; the field is
meaningless without a shared hop. The core's `_shared_depth` **raises** for such an operand rather
than returning a number nobody should use. `test_dtv_operand_has_no_shared_ring_depth` asserts all
three halves: `lds_buffers == 0`, that asking for the shared depth raises with "no shared
placement", and that the depth map has no shared row for it while its partner still does.

**The scale rings preset to the PARENT's resolved depth, not to `NumLdsBlk`.** The scale block
lives inside the parent's shared allocation and rotates with the same buffer index — one swap moves
A, B and their scales together — so `LDSBufferA=1` against `NumLdsBlk=2` must carry its scales with
it. They remain independently overridable so the depths can be searched apart.

##### 16.11.1 The allocation bound, and why it is asymmetric with the register side

```
for name, v in (("A", ldsBufA), ("B", ldsBufB), ("MXSA", ldsBufMXSA), ("MXSB", ldsBufMXSB)):
    if v and v > numLdsBlk:
        raise ValueError("LDSBuffer<name>=<v> exceeds the kernel's allocated NumLdsBlk=<n> ...")
```

This is the module's second hard rejection. Register buffers can be *grown* to match θ — the
allocator sizes the register file from the depth map. Shared memory cannot: `Solution.py` sizes the
shared block from `NumLdsBlk` and checks it against the hardware maximum, so a ring **deeper** than
it reserved is an out-of-bounds shared-memory write, not merely a tighter schedule. A **shallower**
ring is merely wasteful (a reserved block goes unused) and is allowed, which is exactly what makes
per-operand search useful here at all.

The error message names the remedy (raise the single-buffer switch or the chunk depth so the
allocation grows, or lower the request). `test_lds_buffers_above_the_allocation_is_rejected` pins
the raise and matches on the message text.

`test_per_operand_lds_buffers_and_off_are_independent` pins the useful direction end to end: with
`LDSBufferA=1`, θ reports depth 1 for A and 2 for B, and the lowered program's swap markers contain
none for A while still containing some — A is a depth-1 ring and contributes no swap. The same test
checks the offset side, asserting `off(A, copy, chunk) == 1` beside `off(B, copy, chunk) == 2`
under `PrefetchGlobalReadA=1`.

#### 16.12 Fusion — `FUSE_GROUPS`, `FUSE_NAME`, and the resolution block

##### 16.12.1 The table

`translate.py:FUSE_GROUPS` maps the integer `TDMFuse` enum onto **load-domain** groups; each inner
list is the set of operands whose movements merge into one cooperative instruction (section 1.10).
`translate.py:FUSE_NAME` is the parallel display-name map.

| value | name | groups |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `none` | — |
| 1 | `AB+MX` | `[A, B]`, `[MXSA, MXSB]` |
| 2 | `A_MX` | `[A, MXSA, MXSB]` |
| 3 | `B_MX` | `[B, MXSA, MXSB]` |
| 4 | `MX_AB` | `[MXSA, MXSB]`, `[A, B]` |
| 5 | `paired` | `[MXSA, A]`, `[MXSB, B]` |

These are load-domain only: they say which *instruction* carries which movement, and are
independent of how operands pair at the multiply.

**Value 1 carries the MX pair too, and that is the shipping behaviour rather than an extension of
it.** A wave-separated cooperative mover aliases one descriptor per pair, and the generator sets up
*two* of them — one for A/B and again for the two scale tensors when both scale blocks are set. So
on a microscaled kernel, "the mover is wave-separated" means **both** pairs are fused. Naming only
`[["A","B"]]` modelled the scales as independent movements against descriptors the generator had
already aliased, which reached the emitter as an assertion that an unfused advance had been
requested while A and B shared one aliased descriptor. Because groups are filtered to the operands
that exist, a kernel without scales sees exactly `[["A","B"]]` and nothing changes for bf16 or plain
fp8.

The comment above the table marks this as **temporary and deliberate**: it makes the shipping
pairing reachable from the binary knob the `Solution` actually has, so the existing behaviour can be
tested. Value 4 remains the explicit spelling of the same grouping, and if the two pairs ever need
to be fused independently, this is the line that splits.

##### 16.12.2 The resolution block

```
fuse         = k["TDMFuse"]
tdm_split_on = (splitA > 1 or splitB > 1)
present      = { op.name for op in operands }

if fuse in (2,3,4,5) and not (hasMXA or hasMXB):
    note("WARNING: TDMFuse=<f>(<name>) needs MX scales but none present -> falling back to ...")
    fuse = 1 if tdm_split_on else 0

groups = [ [t for t in g if t in present] for g in FUSE_GROUPS.get(fuse, []) ]
groups = [ g for g in groups if len(g) > 1 ]
```

Two filters, in order. The **fallback** handles a scale-requiring enum on a kernel with no scales:
it degrades to the A/B pairing when a region split is live and to no fusion otherwise, and emits a
`WARNING:` note rather than raising. The **presence filter** then drops any member that does not
exist as an operand, and drops any group left with fewer than two members — a "fused group" of one
is not a fusion.

`Theta.fuse_groups` is set to the survivors, and `Theta.fuse` to the (possibly rewritten) integer.

##### 16.12.3 The mixed-split note

```
_split_of = { op.name: max(1, op.split) for op in operands }
for g in groups:
    counts = { n: _split_of.get(n, 1) for n in g }
    if len(set(counts.values())) > 1:
        note("NOTE: fused group <g> has mixed region splits <counts> — region-index pairing is "
             "undefined, so the group moves WHOLE and the requested split is not applied to its "
             "copy hop (the reads stay split)")
```

A fused group pairs its members **by region index** — region `j` of A moves with region `j` of B —
and the two operands may be cut on *different* axes; the pairing is by index, not by a shared mode.
That is only well defined when every member has the same region count: a group mixing a 1-region
scale with a 2-region data operand has no region-1 instance of the scale to pair with. Such a group
therefore moves as one whole movement and the members' region split is **not** applied on the copy
hop. The reads stay split.

That is a legal schedule — a coarse copy feeding a split read is explicitly allowed — but it
silently ignores a requested parameter, so the code **says so** in the notes rather than letting the
request vanish. This is the module's characteristic failure-reporting style: raise only when the
result would be unsafe, otherwise emit a note that survives into the dump.

A related gap is open and worth flagging: a fused group whose members disagree about whether their
copy must be emitted **first** or **last** is currently resolved by an existential rather than
rejected.

#### 16.13 Padding, `rho`, and `pi`

##### 16.13.1 Shared-memory padding

```
lds = {}
for opn, padk in (("A","LdsPadA"), ("B","LdsPadB")):
    pad = k[padk]
    if pad not in (-1, 0):
        lds[opn] = {"pad": pad, "block": k["LdsBlockSizePerPad"]}
if lds:
    note("LDS padding -> <lds>")
    if k["TDMIterateMode"] not in (-1, 0):
        note("WARNING: TDMIterateMode + LdsPad both encode padding — mutually exclusive")
```

`-1` and `0` both mean "no padding" (`-1` is the generator's "auto" sentinel, `0` an explicit zero).
The result lands in `Theta.lds`, which as established in section 16.3.1 **has no readers**: padding
is an address fact and the core is address-opaque. The block exists so the dump records that
padding was requested, and so the mutual-exclusion warning gets emitted — the hardware iterate mode
and explicit padding both encode the same descriptor field, so setting both is a configuration
error the model can see and the generator cannot.

##### 16.13.2 `rho` — now the agent map (was: always empty)

> **SUPERSEDED BY #303 (2026-08-25) — the text below describes the PRE-ρ state and is kept for the
> history.** `ρ` is now the agent MAP the paper specifies (`ρ.resort`: a set of
> `(mode, agent-level, extent)`, §2.8 move 2 / §2.9 / §3.3), and the SINGLE authority for agent
> facts: `Hop.rho_span`, `Hop.region_agent_relative` and `agent_served_modes()` are projections of
> it. The old typing — an equality-only `{op-class → opaque selector}` — is *why* the field sat
> empty and unread: it could answer only a question `theta.agents > 1` already answered, while its
> real content reappeared as three unnamed per-hop scalars recovered from *address-shaped* facts.
> Paper §2.8 L215 names the trap: opacity governs a placement's *content*, not the mode→level map.
> See `RHO_DESIGN.md`. What remains genuinely empty is `ρ.roles` (the `specialize` producer/consumer
> split) — no shipping configuration needs it (#165).

```
rho = {}
```

`rho` would say **which agent carries which op-class** — the finer claim "this movement is confined
to *these* agents". No TensileLite parameter expresses that today, so it stays empty and no consumer
reads it. The tempting mapping (`WaveSeparateGlobalRead`) is not it, for the reasons in
section 16.3.1: it rewrites the load-tile decomposition, not the carrier set.

The one agent fact anything currently needs is the **count**, `Theta.agents`, taken from `NumWaves`
at the tail of the function (`agents=max(1, int(k["NumWaves"]))`). That is deliberately not `rho`:
the count is what decides whether a shared buffer's hazards are cross-agent (a byte written by one
agent and read by another has no program-order edge between them), and in a GEMM every agent reads
the whole staged tile, so any shared buffer touched by two or more agents is cross-agent. Fusion is
explicitly *not* part of that test — a lone operand cooperatively loaded by four waves is
cross-agent with no fusion anywhere.

Report readers should not describe `rho` as implemented. A later investigation refuted the premise
that it was required for the agent-relative region problem outright (section 16.7.3), and it still
has zero readers.

##### 16.13.3 `pi` — region completion granularity

```
per_region = bool(k["PerRegionCompletion"])
if per_region and not any(op.split > 1 for op in operands):
    note("PerRegionCompletion=True but no operand is region-split — the setting has no effect")
```

`pi` is the completion-class granularity of a region-split movement (section 4.3). `False` (the
default, and what the backend implements today) means every region instance of an op-class shares
**one** completion token, so a read must await every region and none can remain in flight. `True`
means one token per region, so a read of region `j` leaves the others in flight; realizing it
end-to-end needs per-region completion tokens on the backend side.

It is marked `[INTERNAL, not a Solution param]` in `PARAM_HELP`: it is reachable only from a
